Now Piedmont Choirs, and Troubadours are the only options for Piedmont teens interested in singing. Alumni of the high school’s music program may be shocked to hear of its demise after enjoying school musicals with well over 100 singers every year. What happened? After the school brought in Sid Quinsaat to handle vocal music and AP Music Theory, Quinsaat suddenly disappeared in January of 2020 without notice to the school, students or parents. Quinsaat was eventuSee Vocal Music on page 21 Teachers rally at City Hall for improved salaries, benefits By Clea Villaluz On Wednesday, September 13, Piedmont teachers gathered outside City Hall, rallying for raises and cost of living adjustments (COLA). The sea of red-shirted teachers and supporters entered City Hall chanting for “COLA” as the school board meeting commenced. The crowd bearing signs remarking “R is for RAISE,” “Fair PAY=Teachers Stay,” “Every Year Without COLA Is a PAY CUT,” received support from motorists who honked as they drove by. High school drivers blared their horns, and elementary-school passengers rolled down their windows to holler for their teachers. This year’s COLA calls for an 8.2% raise, roughly a 1% increase from last year’s COLA. Teachers are asking to keep pace with an inflation rate of 4.9%. According to Teachers Union president Dr. Elise Marks, Kaiser Permanente will be raising premiums by an average of 17.2% in January. For the highest level of coverage (Family, High), employees’ monthly premium contributions have ballooned from $422 to $792. Fifty-seven teachers in the district have this level of health coverage. articles.text: Safety Committee and the Police Department to reduce crime, especially violent crime. “We have 350 community members in Piedmont that are concerned about having a safe and liberal city,” said Chris Moore, founder of Piedmont Neighbors Together. “We don’t see City Council having enough focus. We know it’s important to them, but we need to see them focusing on this every week.” Anja Hart learned about the rally from a Facebook group. “I was looking to understand what was actually going on with the crime rates…and where the issues are according to Chief Bowers,” said Hart. At the beginning of the meeting, Moore voiced his concern to City Council that Chief Bowers’ presentation on crime information was scheduled last on the council’s agenda for the evening. “We’d like to see a lot of attention placed on public safety in the community…When it comes to city council meetings, we believe it’s appropriate to have [public safety] items scheduled early and not have everyone wait until the end of the evening,” she said. In Chief Bowers’ presentation of crime statistics, he detailed police efforts to fight rising crime in Piedmont, but he asked for the community’s patience when it comes to requests for increased staffing. “It takes about a year and a half to grow a cop, so saying ‘we need more cops’ is not going to do anything for us,” said Bowers. PPD’s crime response plan currently includes adding an additional dispatcher position, reclassifying two animal control officers to community service officers, and staffing crime suppression cars with officers on overtime. “I wouldn’t want someone to come into Piedmont and not feel welcome.” said Danielle Hilton, one of the leaders of Piedmont Neighbors Together. As a former prosecutor with the District Attorney’s office and a person of color, Hilton wants to respect public concerns that police target people of color. “We have the ability because we are such a small community… to make specific and pinpointed strategies to combat and prevent crime without trampling on others’ civil liberties,” she said. Resident Ryan Horn said that he left the City Council meeting with a feeling of optimism. “It’s a very positive vibe, very encouraging... It appears everyone is on the same team, which I think will be very useful to solve this problem.” Danielle Hilton, a leader with Piedmont Neighbors Together, stands with a sign outside Piedmont City Hall. “Are you suits still satisfied that it cost nothing to have lunch with our attorneys?”

articles.text: The 22nd Annual Piedmont Jazz Festival returns this year on Sunday, September 24, on the main stage in Piedmont Park starting at 11 a.m. This weekend, jazz enthusiasts will be able to relax in the park and soak in the sounds of music with their friends. “The purpose of the festival is to highlight local Piedmont musicians and to expose the Piedmont community to the artists and jazz music,” said Greg Slatoff, Piedmont Jazz Festival organizer. “In a broader sense, jazz centers upon the ability to improvise or modify a specific melody so that it spontaneously reflects the artist’s mood at the moment of playing. In this regard, the Jazz Festival has included not only traditional jazz performers but also blues, country, and rock performers,” he added. This year’s musicians reflect a mix of genres, some jazz and some not. The Albany Jazz Band returns 12:00 noon - 1:00 p.m. 1:00 p.m. - 2:00 p.m. Savage Bond is a self-described “AmeriCali” band that blends genres like Old-Time, Bluegrass, and Folk into a fresh, unique sound. as the main draw for their sixth year at the festival. The band has performed at concerts and dances in the San Francisco Bay Area since 1996. Its repertoire includes instrumentals and vocals that span classic and contemporary big band music, Latin, and pop. Savage Bond is this year’s wildcard, an American roots ensemble featuring original Americana songs with Old-Time, Bluegrass, Folk, and a little Country in the mix. Fronted by musicians Hope Savage and Alan Bond, the band is always working up fresh material and exploring new frontiers for American music. They will be performing songs from their newly released CD, Americali Alley. Rick Schiller will play solo guitar to open the festival. He played guitar professionally for many years but took a long hiatus. His style of playing appears somewhere between improvisational jazz and the stylings of Chet Atkins. The Jazz Festival is a time-honored community tradition in Piedmont. Many festival alumni have gone on to become successful professional musicians including Ari Berl from the indie rock project Pink Skies, as well as Cole Becker, Max Becker, and Joey Armstrong from the neopunk band SWMRS. “The Piedmont Jazz Fest has probably launched more professional musicians than there are high schools that launched national pro-athletes,” said Slatoff. articles.text: This Saturday, September 23, Magnolia Avenue between the high school and the Exedra will shut down for the Piedmont Police Department’s 5th annual Cops, Coffee and Car Show. As of press time, owners of 82 classic and exotic cars had signed up with Officer Tyler Petit confirming they will be in this year’s show. The popular event is free and will take place from 9 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. on Magnolia Avenue between Piedmont Park and Piedmont High School. In years past, the show has included as many as 100 classic cars from Piedmont locals and car collectors in the greater Bay Area. “Developing the one-onone relationships are incredibly important to not only establish positive connections, but creating a strong and unbreakable bond of trust between our citizen and police department,” said Petit. The police department will provide free coffee, and breakfast burritos will be available for purchase. Cars from coveted Piedmont collections will be in full display. In years past cars have included a 1929 Ford Model A, a 1963 Studebaker Avanti, a 1987 Ferrari Testarossa, and Formula Ford race cars. The event was started by retired Police Sgt. Steve DeWarns in 2018. “Since the start of the Coffee, Cars & Cops events, my connections in the community have increased significantly. This is important for our community. This car show opens doors for people to talk to officers and get to know us one on one outside of calls for service,” said Petit. Piedmont residents interested in participating in the city’s version of the unofficial Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit by Friday at coffeecarscops@piedmont.ca.gov. Include your name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of your car. Some of the exotic cars in the car show include Ferraris and Lamborghinis. Classic cars will be waxed and ready for spectators to view this Saturday.
articles.title: 5th Annual Piedmont Car Show on Saturday

articles.text: Piedmont teachers participated in the second 90-minute session of negotiations with the school district over salary and benefits on September 13. Teachers have been firm in their requests this time even before the first discussions with new School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. They have been rallying curbside in front of several schools, wearing red shirts, and marching to City Hall for a school board meeting. They even joined a coalition of 20 The Association of Piedmont Teachers’ negotiation team includes Elise Marks, Craig Best, Ben Spencer, Mercedes Foster, and Katie Terhar. The regional CTA representative is Gray Harris. The teachers are asking for more health care coverage and raises to match the Cost of Living Adjustment, The school district is represented by Superintendent Hawn, Stephanie Griffin, Sukanya Goswami, Karyn Shipp, Anne Dolid, and CFO Ruth AlaHawn, along with new Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich, have inherited negotiations with a poised teachers union consortium that has already mentioned the term “impasse” prior to negotiations. Hawn has been praised by constituents publicly but faces frustrations dating to the tenure of former Superintendent Randy Booker. Booker left at a time when parents were forming groups, conducting independent surveys and starting the hashtag #RecallRandy. Under Booker, the district’s difficulty in communicating was evidenced by the creSimilarly, the comments about an “impasse” also felt premature to Hawn. When groups cannot reach an agreement, one or both groups can declare impasse, a process also called “fact finding.” “It would take a great deal of time to engage in such a process,” said Hawn. Teachers, however are standing with their negotiation tactics. In comments to the Post, Marks has said, “It’s rough out here,” “We can’t go on like this,” and “We’re in a really bad place right now.” The first factor in negotiations deals with salary. As APT asks for a 8.22% raise, the school district has offered a 1.5% raise. Further trouble comes from Kaiser Permanente’s decision to increase the cost of health insurance premiums for all its members. Though health care providers plan to increase their rates, the school district appears to have capped its contribution to health care. “Our school district gets its own specific increase based on things like how expensive it is to actually provide us with healthcare. Because so many of our staff are on the older side and we’re more likely to need more expensive medical interventions, we tend to have higher costs overall than a younger, healthier crew.” “We negotiate with Kaiser alone,” Marks explained. Raises in health care costs to teachers vary according to the health care plan chosen, but almost 300 teachers are currently on Piedmont School District’s health plan with Kaiser. Rates for the top three most popular plans are shown in the chart at bottom left. Piedmont teachers are asking for 100% health care coverage. “The district’s counter offer is zero increase to our health insurance. In fact, they are also proposing eliminating even partial health insurance of any kind (medical, dental, or vision) for part-time employees who work less than 80% [of a full time schedule],” said Marks. “Anyone under 80% full time employment (FTE) who depends on health insurance provided through work will probably have to quit,” noted Marks. Hawn is doing her due diligence in analyzing the district’s budget. In her Week 7 “Piedmont Pulse” update Smore.com/637cta she noted the following increases in the budget: $120,000 – Increased cost of power last year $1,531,979 – Increased cost of special education from 2021-22 to 2022-23, a 15.5% increase $733,970 – Increased cost of retirement benefits for staff $211,137 – Increased contribution to health benefits last year $104,000 – State “clawback” of arts funding that was originally offered and then taken back Negotiations will continue in the following weeks, a process that will require bending and patience by both sides. “All of that said, it’s a great group, and I look forward to working through the issues,” said Hawn. – Dr, Elise Marks, President, Piedmont Teachers Union ation of an upper-level management position “Communications Director” with a big salary but without clearly defined roles. “Rallying for higher pay during student drop-off before we had even started the negotiations process was a surprise. It’s one thing to rally when things are not going well, but to rally before the process even started was perplexing,” said Hawn. PUSD Newsletter saying that she is working to grasp what is affordable for this year’s budget. It shows “a little over $422,300 that is currently unallocated.” Hawn said that even a one percent raise for staff would require approximately $340,000. Wildwood teacher Kelly Ellis, who has been with the school district for 19 years, voiced her frustration for a policy granting a 1.5 percent incentive raise to positions that remain unfilled and new teachers. “[It] completely ignores the teachers who have been serving for many, many years,” Ellis said. Marks encouraged the crowd outside City Hall to move their rally into the School Board’s open session. Following her lead, they chanted the word “COLA” as they entered. The cheering crowd packed into the small wood-floored hall, the floors squeaking beneath their feet. Three red-shirted teachers, Tiffany Cothran, Janine Mortan, and Lianne Morrison, came forward holding signs. “The single most important factor that determines student achievement is the presence of quality educators,” said Cothran. “Our district must prioritize retaining excellent teachers for our students.” During their allotted time to speak Marks spoke in tandem with Classified school staff union President Christine Petersen. After making their presence felt in City Hall’s chambers, teachers exited the hall chanting, “Healthcare.” Clea Villaluz is a junior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: A public meeting concerning the Witter Field renovation project will be held Tuesday, September 26, in the Wildwood School auditorium at 6:00 p.m. The meeting will give residents an opportunity to ask questions and discuss the progress on the project. District officials will give an updated Witter Field irrigation and drainage plan. Director of Facilities Pete Palmer will lead the discussion. Also participating in the meeting will be Piedmont Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, Devin Conway of Verde Design Civil Engineers, and School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Since construction began in June, neighbors have raised questions about possible flooding in neighborhoods below the field. They have challenged the accuracy of drainage calculations and have criticized the district for the lack of transparency. The school district has reduced the peak flow rate for the Witter Field area by approximately 20% at the request of the City. “PUSD reduced the storm water flow into the City storm drain system by reducing the size of the inlet pipe diameter [to slow the flow rate],” explained Palmer. At this time Bothman Construction is still planning on completing all work and reopening the field no later than December 1 despite a delay by EBMUD. Parking restrictions on Palm Drive will also be a topic of discussion at the meeting. Updates on the construction project are posted at https://www. piedmont.k12.ca.us/ref/facilities/ witter-field-renovation For more information, contact Pete Palmer at ppalmer@piedmont.k12ca.us or call 594-2877. Residents have a chance to ask questions about the construction project at Witter Field next Tuesday at a public meeting.

articles.text: As the sun sets, the night sky lights up as stars begin to shine. Stars range in size and color, but have you ever looked at a star and wondered how it formed? Nebulas Star formation begins inside nebulas, which are large clouds of gas and dust. With the help of gravity, the clouds collect and begin to collapse. This collapse creates the core that will become a star. The core is called a protostar and while spinning rapidly, heat and pressure rises within. The rising temperature and pressure cause a reaction, which takes us to the next stage of star formation. The Main Sequence The main sequence is the second stage of a star’s lifecycle. During this stage gravity and heat within the star has balanced, which stops any shrinking or growing. The star will begin to shine, but what makes the star shine? A reaction takes place within the star’s core, which gives the star the energy to shine and to prevent it from breaking down. The bigger the star, the faster it consumes energy. After depleting all energy, the star will move onto the next stage of its lifecycle, which is dependent on its size. We will first read about the journey of an average sized star and then we will look at the journey of a massive star. Average Stars When an average sized star runs out of energy it enters the phase called a red giant. During this phase, the star gets bigger and changes in color because of the temperature change. After this stage, the star goes through an explosion called a planetary nebula. As time passes, the outer layers from this explosion will fade away. What is left behind are remains known as white dwarfs. The lifecycle of most average sized stars will end as white dwarfs. Massive Stars When a massive star runs out of energy it will first become a super red giant. The size and color changes are more extreme because of the magnitude of the star. In time, the super red giant will break down and cause a gigantic explosion known as a supernova. This explosion will lead the star to become either a neutron star or a black hole. We will first read about a regular massive star and then we will learn about a super massive star. A regular massive star will end as a neutron star. A neutron star is the core of the star that was left from the explosion. A super massive star will end as a black hole. A black hole is a space that holds a lot of strong gravity and consumes other objects. Each star has their own journey, but they all shine above us at some point in time. Stars are different, but in many ways they are alike. As we continue to explore space, we will learn even more interesting facts about star formation! Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement, located at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in the Oakland hills. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: The lifecycle of a star

articles.text: 11th Annual Home Brewing Competition includes German dinner on lawn The 11th Annual Artisanal Brewing Competition will bring homebrewers from around the Bay Area to 801 Magnolia Avenue on Friday, October 6. The event which runs from 5:30-7:30 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) will feature tastings from more than 12 craft brewers, and an authentic Oktoberfest dinner outside on the lawn provided by Piedmont Grocery. Admission to the beer tasting includes a custom PCA beer glass for unlimited tastings of the brewers’ creations. Patrons can also enjoy the traditional Oktoberfest fare of freshly grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage. Guests are encouraged to bring a picnic blanket to fully enjoy the fall weather and the lovely view of the sunset. This year’s talented brewers include Piedmont natives Zachary Jones, Carter Dunlap and Case Gardner vying for the bragging rights of Best Pale Ale, Lager, IPA and Best in Show. Talented brewers from the Bay Area Mashers Homebrew Club will be on hand looking to steal the show from the hometown favorites. Late entry and defending champion in the Lager and Porter Categories, Bob Davis of Happy Girl Brewing Co., will return this year with four new concoctions. Davis is excited to share a “Tastes Like Summer” Kolsch, a “Dead Piedmont’s annual Artisanal Beer Festival was jam-packed last year at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Man’s Hand” Black Double IPA, “Reflected Glory” a Trappist Tripel, and “Siren’s Song” a Black Pepper Saison. While the event is a celebration of brewers’ craftmanship, competition for the best beer in each class is steep. articles.text: In advance of the annual Piedmont Artisanal Beer Festival on Friday, October 6, at the Center for the Arts, several beermakers were asked about their involvement and why the event on the first Friday of October is so popular. The festival replicates a German beer festival, including a German dinner cooked and served on the lawn in front of the Center. Question: How long have you been interested in beer making? Zachary Jones: (English Pale Ale) My dad has been making Trevor Fleshman Aaron Bagnell Alan Bernales Brian Black Matt Gerhardt Zachary Jones beer for as long as I remember, and I would assist with the bottling part of the process. Eventually I wanted to experience the entire process and asked for a homebrew kit for Christmas. Brian Black: (Shelterwood Ale, Monastic Whisper) My wife bought me a one-gallon beer kit from Uncommon Goods as a quirky Christmas gift 12 years ago. I brewed from the kit on New Years Day 2012 so as not to let her Christmas gift to me go unused. I was hooked, and the rest is history. Alan Bernales: (Coco Kolsh, Unnamed Amber) I got into brewing with my cousin. Coming from Brazil where the main beer was a light Pilsner, we were tired of simple light beers with no flavors. We want to create a beer with body and character. Aaron Bagnell: (Colonial Kölsch) Got started in grad school brewing with roommates in our small apartment. Started with kits and recipes from the American Homebrewers website. Trevor Fleshman: (Beer Name TBA) The boys in my family had the pleasure of sharing a Father’s Day brewing experience when I was a senior in high school. I learned you don’t need to be 21 to purchase brewing ingredients. Kevin & Jessica Cross: (Tribute Steam Beer) I’ve enjoyed beer for a long time but was only inspired to brew my own after attending last year’s Piedmont Beer Festival! Matt Gerhardt: (Stub-YourToe-In-The Dark Ale, Slam Dunkel) I made my first batch of beer at age 22 with my then-roommate and it was undrinkable. We had brewed it in our other roommate’s terrarium and apparently hadn’t sanitized it sufficiently. Over 20 years later, after tasting friends’ homebrews, I tried it again, and yesterday I bottled my 37th batch. Question: How do you make your beers? Zachary Jones: I started with off the shelf kits to get an understanding of the basic recipe and what made various types of beer unique. Recently I have been tweaking the kits or buying ingredients individually. Brian Black: I generally design and/or refine my own recipes and source ingredients from local or online vendors, depending on availability. Oak Barrel Winecraft is my local shop of choice. Alan Bernales: We follow recipes and add our own twist. Aaron Bagnell: At this point I do my own recipes, but it’s pretty common for a brewer new to a style to research multiple published recipes for a beer style to see what ingredients they have in common, splitting the difference between them or using the most popular. Trevor Fleshman: I’ve run the gamut of kits to clones to my own recipes. I keep it classic. One of my favorite beers married my love for gardening with brewing when I grew my own cascade hops in our Oakland backyard. Kevin & Jessica Cross: The brew I’m bringing to the festival is a variation on a clone recipe I found in an old copy of a brewing magazine. I get my ingredients individually from local suppliers. Matt Gerhardt: I find recipes in books or online and modify them. I don’t use kits.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team is walking into its Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division schedule beaming with confidence after defeating upper Mission Division foe Encinal with a lopsided 41-3 win on Friday, September 15. It improves the Highlanders’ record to 2-2. In the past two games they have outscored opponents 87-10 after dominating Mt. Eden 46-7 the previous week. “It’s a big win for the program and a step in the right direction,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We’re trying to get this program back to where it has been, but we can’t get a false sense of security. It was a win we felt like we could achieve. There will always be things we can fix.” Despite having a roster onehalf the size of the Jets, Piedmont kept high energy through all four quarters and never took their foot off of the gas. It was a testament to their conditioning in offseason and in practice. “I’d hate to jinx us but we’re approaching Week 4 and we haven’t suffered a serious injury yet, just a couple of minor dings. It’s a tribute to our conditioning in the offseason and how we push them in practice. We have a solid regimen throughout the week. They are starting to see why we have them running on weekends – to get the lactic acid out.” “I put my Masters in kinesiology to use sometimes,” added Seiden with a laugh. It was a terrific game for receiver, defensive back, and return specialist Sam Shelby, who recorded five receptions for 139 yards and two touchdowns, to go along with 48 rushing yards on two carries, and an interception. One of the junior receiver’s touchdowns was a 77-yard catch and run down the left side after breaking a tackle. Shelby could be nicknamed after the Shelby GT500, using his speed to sprint away from the Jets’ defensive backs. He credits his breakaway speed to what he learned under track coach Pouyan Assadi, Staff Photos Receiver Sam Shelby had 187 all-purpose yards with two touchdowns plus an interception. Emmett Maxwell celebrates after a 28-yard touchdown against Encinal. Quarterback Markos Lagios threw for three touchdowns and rushed for one. where he helped the 4x400 relay team qualify for the CIF State Championship. “It’s all thanks to track. I think it’s completely changed my path in football. It’s been such a big influence on my mentality towards the game and gives me that edge to help me break loose,” said Shelby. Senior running back Emmett Maxwell also had a big day, running for 97 yards on 13 carries, including a 28-yard touchdown after breaking two tackles. He also recorded a huge run against Mt. Eden where he carried multiple defenders to convert a first down. “I just took a big breath before the snap and thought, ‘this is it, I’m gonna do it right here.’ I broke the first tackle and I saw the end zone. I couldn’t believe what was happening… I just don’t like to go down. I want to run the ball as far as I can possibly take it,” said Maxwell. PHS looks ahead to Arroyo in San Lorenzo this Saturday, September 23 for the start of their league schedule, with momentum on their side. The Dons are currently 1-3 with their only win against Encinal, 58-22.. Game Recap Piedmont opened the game strongly with a 14-0 lead within five minutes. PHS recorded an onside kick attempt by Encinal and scored on a four-play series capped by a short touchdown run by quarterback Markos Lagios. Shelby picked off Encinal’s opening pass, which eventually led to a touchdown reception by Cash Elmquist. The Highlanders then went up 21-0 with 2:35 left in the first quarter on a 20 yard carry by Tommy Ashton, who bulldozed a defensive back over the goal line. In the second quarter, Encinal drove to Piedmont’s 20, but Jordan Alemania forced a fumble on a 3rd down and Ashton recovered. On the ensuing series, Shelby scored on his mercurial 77-yard touchdown reception on a screen pass, breaking a tackle and speeding his way to the end zone,
articles.title: 2nd consecutive blowout win for PHS in 41-3 drubbing of Encinal

articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis team finished a strong week with a pair of dominant wins over North Coast Section Division 2 opponents. They swept St. Mary’s 7-0 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center in the Highlanders’ home opener on Thursday, September 14, and defeated Head-Royce 5-2 in Oakland the following day. “St. Mary’s lost their toptwo players from last year and was a weaker team this year. We split the singles against HeadRoyce but played great tennis all around,” said PHS coach Jim Landes. Making strong appearances in this year’s singles lineup are sophomores Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum, who paired together as freshmen in 2022. “I’ll always miss playing doubles with Arianna. We were the icon freshman duo last year and had a lot of fun together. But I really enjoy playing singles and hope to grow as a player,” said Jumper. “It’s definitely different than playing with someone having your back out there. But neither of us have any regrets. We both are really enjoying playing singles,” added Kortum. Jumper won 6-1, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot against St. Mary’s but lost 6-4, 6-2 at No. 2 versus HeadRoyce. “It’s definitely different than playing doubles. You don’t have a teammate to keep you disciplined on the court, so it becomes your job. It takes a lot of inner growth to switch from a doubles player to a singles player in a short amount of time,” said Jumper. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, September 20, 2023 Sports 2nd consecutive blowout win for PHS in 41-3 drubbing of Encinal By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s football team is walking into its Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division schedule beaming with confidence after defeating upper Mission Division foe Encinal with a lopsided 41-3 win on Friday, September 15. It improves the Highlanders’ record to 2-2. In the past two games they have outscored opponents 87-10 after dominating Mt. Eden 46-7 the previous week. “It’s a big win for the program and a step in the right direction,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We’re trying to get this program back to where it has been, but we can’t get a false sense of security. It was a win we felt like we could achieve. There will always be things we can fix.” Despite having a roster onehalf the size of the Jets, Piedmont kept high energy through all four quarters and never took their foot off of the gas. It was a testament to their conditioning in offseason and in practice. “I’d hate to jinx us but we’re approaching Week 4 and we haven’t suffered a serious injury yet, just a couple of minor dings. It’s a tribute to our conditioning in the offseason and how we push them in practice. We have a solid regimen throughout the week. They are starting to see why we have them running on weekends – to get the lactic acid out.” “I put my Masters in kinesiology to use sometimes,” added Seiden with a laugh. It was a terrific game for receiver, defensive back, and return specialist Sam Shelby, who recorded five receptions for 139 yards and two touchdowns, to go along with 48 rushing yards on two carries, and an interception. One of the junior receiver’s touchdowns was a 77-yard catch and run down the left side after breaking a tackle. Shelby could be nicknamed after the Shelby GT500, using his speed to sprint away from the Jets’ defensive backs. He credits his breakaway speed to what he learned under track coach Pouyan Assadi, Staff Photos Receiver Sam Shelby had 187 all-purpose yards with two touchdowns plus an interception. articles.text: Kat Melian scored nine against Lick-Wilmerding, the highest scoring output by a PHS player since Annika Disney in 2017. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team narrowly lost a 15-14 thriller to Lick-Wilmerding in San Francisco on Thursday, September 14. It was a huge performance by Kat Melian, scoring nine goals for the largest scoring output by a Highlander since Annika Disney in 2017. Piedmont trailed 5-4 to end the first quarter and 9-8 to enter halftime. The two teams went into the fourth quarter in a 12-12 deadlock until Lick-Wilmerding scored the game-winner in overtime and held on for the victory. In the first quarter, Sydney Olson scored the game’s first goal to put Piedmont up 1-0 after 30 seconds, but Lick tied on its next possession. Melian put PHS ahead 2-1 with her first goal with 6:02 to play but Lick quickly tied and eventually went ahead 5-2 with 1:35 on the clock. Melian scored twice at 1:13 and with 15 seconds left to make it the deficit 5-4. Lick scored the first three goals of the second quarter to lead 8-4 with 4:32 to play, but PHS went on a four-goal scoring run to tie with 1:56 left in the half thanks to three straight goals by Melian. However, Lick-Wilmerding on their final heave with 2 seconds on the clock, regaining the 9-8 lead. In the third quarter, Esme Krumins tied the match at 9-9 in a player-advantage situation 40 seconds into the quarter with 6:20 to go. Lick scored on its next possession, 10-9, but Melian tied with 5:35 on the clock. PHS briefly held the lead when Abigail Jacoby scored with 3:44 remaining in the quarter, but Lick tied with 2:04 to go and got back to the front 12-11 with 42 seconds in the third. But Melian tied it up at 12-12, once again, launching in a goal after just seven seconds. articles.text: Scots getting closer to breaking into win column Layth Haddawy Piedmont’s JV football team played a tight neck-and-neck game at Skyline High in Oakland on Friday, September 15. In spite of the loss, the score represented a marked improvement. Quarterback Cash Panico had a big day, helping lead the offense to an early touchdown on a quarterback sneak. During the Titans’ ensuing drive, Skyline’s center airmailed his snap over the quarterback allowing Piedmont to recover. However, the Highlanders didn’t make the most of the turnover, and allowed Skyline to bounce back with a touchdown and two-point conversion go ahead 8-6. Both teams traded possessions in the remainder of the first half, and at halftime the score remained 8-6. Piedmont opened the second half and looked like it was about to break the game open when freshman running back Rehan Mumtaz made an impressive 61-yard run for a touchdown. It was nullified due to a holding penalty, but despite the call, Panico helped get PHS back on the board with multiple scrambles and a pivotal pass to Marius Arno before tossing a 25-yard touchdown pass to running back Ryan Riddel, for a 12-8 lead. In the fourth quarter, Piedmont’s offense stalled and was forced to punt, and that’s when disaster struck. On the punt attempt, PHS snapped the ball too high, allowing the Titans to block Riddel’s kick and giving Skyline excellent field position. With nine seconds left, Skyline ran down the middle for a touchdown and a 14-12 lead. On Skyline’s two-point conversion, Panico at linebacker and Jason Shum at free safety met the Titans’ quarterback near the goal line, but Skyline was awarded 2-point conversion. articles.text: Dahlia Osman leaps to grab one of her two interceptions against Alameda. Thursday, September 14 marked a historic day for Piedmont High girls’ sports with the flag football team playing its inaugural season-opening game. Although the Highlanders lost 13-0 to the Alameda Hornets at Thompson Field on the island, Piedmont walked out with heads held high knowing they just made school history as the first official flag football team to wear the Purple and White. “It’s an historic day. There were a lot of women and former Piedmont students who were in those stands thinking, ‘I never got the chance to play.’ These girls got to experience that today, and that’s bigger than a win or a loss right now,” said coach Beth Black. “But now we want to win,” she added. It was back-and-forth action for both teams until Alameda broke the deadlock midway through the second half with 10:06 left in the game. Piedmont’s offense came close to scoring on a couple of series, and its defense was solid until conceding two second half scores. “It had the first-game feeling. We noticed in the WACC Jamboree that we got really hyped and then had to adjust. Today we came out similarly but adjusted quicker. I cannot say enough about our defense. There are things to correct, but they played a great game,” said Black. Defensive back Dahlia Osman had a big day, making two interceptions and being among the leading tacklers. One of her interceptions was a takeaway in Piedmont’s end zone to prevent a Hornets’ touchdown. “When the quarterback throws long, it tends to give me time to adjust and get in front of who I’m defending, and I just caught it. The second one was similar. I had time to see where it was going, so I jumped off of my original player to get it,” said Osman. Offensively, Miya Fujimoto made her presence felt with her speed out of the receiver position, often out running defenders to the wings. She’s a two-sport athlete with softball in the spring and was named the Post’s’ Freshman of the Year last year. “Miya is a weapon. It was nice to see her have some big runs. She’s running hard and putting it all out there,” said Black. The Highlanders are scheduled to play Mt. Eden in Hayward tomorrow, Thursday, September 21 for another Western Alameda County Conference match. Game Recap After forcing Alameda to turnover on downs in the game’s first possession, PHS retained at its own 25-yard line on the 80-yard field, but tossed an interception on their second play to put the Hornets at Piedmont’s 10 yard line. On first down, Alameda attempted a pass to the end zone, but Osman nabbed an interception. Piedmont drove to the AHS 35-yard line, but the Hornets picked off another pass. Alameda then drove down to PHS’ oneyard line, but failed on 4th-and-1 with an incomplete pass with 1:29 left in the first half. articles.text: Performers recreate The Lone Ranger before live audience “Hi-Yo, Silver!” booms the voice of the Lone Ranger. Our masked hero is about to embark on a journey fraught with bandits, bank robbers, and well-meaning but easily deceived doctors. But at this performance, there were no masks, no costumes, and not a single prop gun in sight. Only nine performers, three microphones, and a very dedicated audio engineer. On Sunday, September 17, Piedmont Center for the Arts hosted a show by the Radio Broadcast Legends, a performing group made up of retired radio and television professionals from the Bay Area. For the last 30 years, the Radio Broadcast Legends have recreated live episodes of classic radio programs in an attempt to keep the spirit of oldtime radio alive. Su nd ay’s p e r fo r m a n c e included a complete reading of “The Telltale Bullet,” an episode of The Lone Ranger radio program from 1953. “We do the whole show with sound effects and music cues,” explained Peter Cleaveland, President of the Radio Broadcast Legends. “The copy of the script we’re using comes from that actual broadcast.” One of their members, Dave Parker, used to work at the WXYZ radio station where the Lone Ranger originally aired. Staff photos Carolyn Compton and Peter Cleaveland re-enact an old Cheerios commercial as part of their Lone Ranger radio episode. Which is how they got the script. “What people forget is that for most of that time [in radio], everything was live,” Cleaveland said. Protection of radio actors by their union prevented mass recordings and distribution of broadcasts. This ensured their job security. “As a result, everything was done twice – once for the East Coast and Central Time Zone. and once for the Pacific,” Cleaveland added. Their performance was a compilation of old radio show openings, kids programs, soap operas, serials, commercials and real-life bloopers, all faithfully recreated by the performers verbatim. “This is CBS—the Columbia Broad System Casting” declares an announcer in one such blooper. The audience roars with laughter. Cleaveland views his role part performer, part historian. “The number of people who lived during the era of radio when radio is what television is now – well, there are fewer and fewer of us around. A lot of people just want to see what it was like.” Radio Broadcast Legends’ next show will be on Saturday, October 14 at the Bay Area Radio Hall of Fame, located at 2152 Central Avenue in Alameda. Tickets are available online at https://broadcastlegends.org/ events/barhof-2023-event. Community members gathered last Sunday at the Piedmont Center for the Arts to see Radio Broadcast Legends perform a classic episode of The Lone Ranger. Pictured are Zachary Wilson (left), Peter Cleaveland, Carolyn Compton, Matt Elmore, Bruce W. articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company’s production of Born with Teeth will be performed through October 1. The two-man play by Liz Duffy Adams stars Dean Linnard as poet and English spy Kit Marlowe and Brady Morales-Woolery as Will Shakespeare, an upstart looking to make his name in the world of art. The play is set in the back room of a tavern in a polarized and paranoid England where civilian death sentences abound. The two writers, Kit and Brady, take on a risky collaboration and their artistic partnership becomes a dangerous dance of inspiration, artistry, seduction, and betrayal. Born With Teeth had its world premiere at the Alley Theater in Houston in 2022 and is the recipient of a 2021 Edgerton Foundation New Play Award and Best Play and Production. A post-show discussion with playwright Adams and the creative team will be held on Thursday evening, September 28. Visit https://www.aurorathea t r e.o r g /i n d ex .ph p /s how s - events/20232024-season/bornwith-teeth to purchase tickets. articles.text: San Francisco-based Smuin Ballet will perform its ‘Dance Series One’ at the Cowell Theater at San Francisco’s Fort Mason, and at Mountain View Center for the Performing Arts now through October 7. The ballet company kicked off its 30th season at Lesher Center for the Performing Arts in Walnut Creek last week with two audience favorites as well as a world premiere. The program includes The Man in Black by James Kudelka, Tutto Eccetto il Lavandino (Everything But the Kitchen Sink) by Val Caniparoli, and the world premiere of Salsa ’til Dawn by Darrell Grand Moultrie. The performance opens with longtime Smuin collaborator Caniparoli’ and his Tutto Eccetto il Lavandino. Tutto is a playful, more energetic piece that premiered in 2014 and has been an audience favorite since. Kudelka’s The Man in Black is a ballad-style piece with choreography set to the music of country singer Johnny Cash whose music often contained themes of sorrow, moral tribulation and redemption. The dance celebrates working class grit, and examples of several popular American country dance styles – line dancing, square, swing and step. The Man in Black ballet premiered in 2010. Upcoming performances feature the world premiere of Moultrie’s Salsa ’til Dawn, with music by Charles Fox. Composer Fox collaborated with company founder Michael Smuin on two ballets, A Song for Dead Warriors, commissioned for the San Francisco Ballet, and Zorro! for Smuin Ballet. His entire output of music is soon to be recognized at the Library of Congress. “Music is always the complete inspiration for me,” said Moultrie. “It’s been such an honor to work with an artistic giant like Charles and bring his music to life by marrying it with the physicality of dance.” Performances at Cowell Theater at Fort Mason are Friday, September 29 through Saturday, October 7. Performances in Mountain View are Thursday, September 21 through Sunday, September 24. For tickets, see https://www. smuinballet.org/events/dance-series-one-30/. The Man in Black performed by Smuin Ballet

articles.text: SF Jazz will host the world-renowned, New York City-based Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra with Wynton Marsalis for two performances on Sunday, October 1 in Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz. New Orleans Jazz musician Marsalis is a multi-Grammy award winning trumpeter, composer, and teacher whose work was the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Marsalis, the artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center, comes from a lineage of jazz greats, His brothers Branford, Jason and Delfeayo are all well-known professional musicians. Marsalis returns with the Orchestra for his first SF JAZZ performance since receiving the Lifetime Achievement Award presented at the SF Jazz Gala last year. The Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra is led by Marsalis. Tickets are available for 3 p.m. and 7 p.m. performances. The evening performance is almost sold out. articles.text: This weekend is the last chance to see The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England art exhibit at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco. The Tudors is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It will include works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. The exhibition features many paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world that bring the Tudor dynasty to life. Pieces range from 1485 to 1603. The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England is on view through this Sunday, September 24. Visit the museum the day before for free. Every Saturday, the Legion of Honor offers free general admission to all residents of the nine Bay Area counties, including Alameda County. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. For more information, visit https://www.famsf.org. Nicholas Hilliard (English, 1547–1619), Queen Elizabeth I

articles.text: If time is a thin reed, or experienced as a Mobius strip allowing a traveler to leap forward and backward, think of the possibilities. Actually, Hollywood and literature have gone to this well often, and sometimes with compelling results. Back to the Future comes to mind. The Time Traveler’s Wife takes all the inherent problems of time travel and embeds them in a tender and fragile love story and, all things considered, succeeds nicely. Based on Audrey Niffenegger’s bestseller, the film tells the story of Henry (Eric Bana) who, since boyhood, has, against his will, traveled in time, both into the past and into the future. All that he leaves behind is his clothing, arriving at his unknown destination naked. Time travel is one of the most difficult and interesting tropes in film or literature. From the outset the audience must suspend its disbelief and all but lend a hand filling in any illogical holes. The Time Traveler’s Wife manages quite well to deal with the multiple time traveling surprises without falling into the trap of being nonsensical. Close, but not quite. Henry’s (not Eric) unexpected traveling is never presented as a stunning achievement; rather, it is viewed as something that is deeply problematical for Henry and his new wife, Clare (Rachel McAdams). They are deeply in love (Clare has loved Henry since she was very young) and at the most inopportune moments, some scary to be sure, Henry, without warning, vanishes like so much smoke just moments before they are to be married, Henry disappears only to return as an older version of his younger self (you see the problem). But these moments are intriguing and never off-putting. Every romantic story – Titanic, Ghost Story, Love Story, Romeo and Juliet – has embedded in it the possibility of a tragic outcome. Hence the filmmakers must search for the sweet spot, that elusive geography where the couple fashions a bond so strong that the audience invests in their relationship as well. Despite a few jar ring moments, The Time Traveler’s Wife achieves that emotional connection. Of course, as a film it’s not a perfect. The Niffenegger book would be all but impossible to fully adapt. But director Robert Schwentke makes a fine effort and, with excellent performances of Bana and McAdams, manages to find the sweet spot. Time Traveler’s Wife . Directed by Robert Schwentke. Starring Eric Bana, Rachel McAdams, Ron Livingson and Arliss Howard. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Eric Bana and Rachel McAdams star in The Time Traveler’s Wife
articles.title: The Time Traveler’s Wife finds the sweet spot

articles.text: Hollywood learned long ago that formula films work. Find a template and use it until it’s frayed and even then return, promising something familiar but with a twist. Take the road trip recipe. It can be a wonderful if sometimes predictable concept involving multiple characters, settings and encounters. As a genre, it’s as comfortable as an old sneaker, and easily slipped on. The film Everybody’s Fine is such a sneaker. In the set up, Frank (Robert DeNiro), a recently widowed, retired factory worker is shown readying the house and backyard for a visit from his four children who live in various parts of the country. He shops and vacuums and waters the plants and then sadly gets four phone calls conveying four excuses as to why they can’t come. Soon, they each promise. Soon they’ll visit. Frank is not content with soon, and against his doctor’s advice (he has health issues), he decides to visit them instead. He wants it to be a surprise. So, with suitcase in hand, his medication in his pocket, he hits the road: first, New York City to see his son David, an artist, who, as it turns out, is not home; then onto Chicago to visit Amy (Kate Beckinsdale), who’s in advertising, married, and has a teenage son; next is Robert (Sam Rockwell) in Denver, a percussionist with a symphony orchestra; his last visit is to Rosie (Drew Barrymore), a dancer, who lives in Las Vegas. Each is surprised and happy to see him, but not enthusiastically happy. There’s family baggage to be sorted out. Everyone is not fine. And here is where the film could have become an interesting and edgy drama. It would not have been a stretch for any of the actors in this film. Instead the screenwriter and director choose to avoid any issues of substance, allowing the film to quickly devolve into a familiar Hollywood happy meal. Things in need of a resolution: Frank is still grieving and deeply lonely. When his children were young, he pushed them relentlessly, expecting perfection, and they responded by lying to him about the content of their lives. How Frank’s rigid insistence that his children turn out as he expects is never dealt with. Even when his oldest son, David, who has left New York, dies from a drug overdose in Mexico, this crisis fails to become the catalyst for a family epiphany. Instead, Frank has a health crisis and the film concludes with everyone sitting around the Christmas table, having, well, that happy meal. Drama-lite, to be sure. But it’s still a sweet movie. Everybody’s Fine. Directed by Kirk Jones. Starring Robert DeNiro, Drew Barrymore, Kate Beckinsdale and Sam Rockwell. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Everybody’s Fine – a DeNiro delight

And here is where the film could have become an interesting and edgy drama. It would not have been a stretch for any of the actors in this film. Instead the screenwriter and director choose to avoid any issues of substance, allowing the film to quickly devolve into a familiar Hollywood happy meal. Things in need of a resolution: Frank is still grieving and deeply lonely. When his children were young, he pushed them relentlessly, expecting perfection, and they responded by lying to him about the content of their lives. How Frank’s rigid insistence that his children turn out as he expects is never dealt with. Even when his oldest son, David, who has left New York, dies from a drug overdose in Mexico, this crisis fails to become the catalyst for a family epiphany. Instead, Frank has a health crisis and the film concludes with everyone sitting around the Christmas table, having, well, that happy meal. Drama-lite, to be sure. But it’s still a sweet movie. The Time Traveler’s Wife finds the sweet spot By Chris Honore’ If time is a thin reed, or experienced as a Mobius strip allowing a traveler to leap forward and backward, think of the possibilities. Actually, Hollywood and literature have gone to this well often, and sometimes with compelling results. Back to the Future comes to mind. The Time Traveler’s Wife takes all the inherent problems of time travel and embeds them in a tender and fragile love story and, all things considered, succeeds nicely. Based on Audrey Niffenegger’s bestseller, the film tells the story of Henry (Eric Bana) who, since boyhood, has, against his will, traveled in time, both into the past and into the future. All that he leaves behind is his clothing, arriving at his unknown destination naked. Time travel is one of the most difficult and interesting tropes in film or literature. From the outset the audience must suspend its disbelief and all but lend a hand filling in any illogical holes. The Time Traveler’s Wife manages quite well to deal with the multiple time traveling surprises without falling into the trap of being nonsensical. Close, but not quite. Henry’s (not Eric) unexpected traveling is never presented as a stunning achievement; rather, it is viewed as something that is deeply problematical for Henry and his new wife, Clare (Rachel McAdams). They are deeply in love (Clare has loved Henry since she was very young) and at the most inopportune moments, some scary to be sure, Henry, without warning, vanishes like so much smoke just moments before they are to be married, Henry disappears only to return as an older version of his younger self (you see the problem). But these moments are intriguing and never off-putting. Every romantic story – Titanic, Ghost Story, Love Story, Romeo and Juliet – has embedded in it the possibility of a tragic outcome. Hence the filmmakers must search for the sweet spot, that elusive geography where the couple fashions a bond so strong that the audience invests in their relationship as well. Despite a few jar ring moments, The Time Traveler’s Wife achieves that emotional connection. Of course, as a film it’s not a perfect. The Niffenegger book would be all but impossible to fully adapt. But director Robert Schwentke makes a fine effort and, with excellent performances of Bana and McAdams, manages to find the sweet spot. Time Traveler’s Wife . Directed by Robert Schwentke. Starring Eric Bana, Rachel McAdams, Ron Livingson and Arliss Howard. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. articles.text: An American Tail, directed by Don Bluth, was the second feature by the Bluth studio, following The Secret of Nimh. Like NIMH, it’s a wonderfully animated adventure film, layered with award-wining songs and focused on a 7-year-old mouse named Fievel Mousekewitz. The year is 1885, and Fievel’s journey begins in Russia where his family – Papa Mouskevitz (Nehemiah Persoff), Mama Mousekevitz (Patricia Vohn), and Tanya Mousekevitz (Amy Green) – is attacked by Cossacks and cats; their home is burned down. Fleeing Russia, they manage to board a tramp steamer on its way to America, where they believe there are no cats. During a thunderstorm, Fievel is separated from his family and washed overboard. His family is distraught, believing that Fievel is lost forever. But remarkably he is safely ensconced in a bottle, and washes up in the harbor of New York City where his quest to find his parents begins. Little Fievel is a stranger in a strange land, feeling very alone in a teeming city of tenements, yet determined to find his mother and father and sister. Safely on the dock, he first meets a French pigeon, Henri (Christopher Plummer), who takes him under his wing, so to speak. But he is only the first in what will be a rich cast of characters from a variety of countries. What he quickly learns is that there are indeed cats in America and one is named Tiger (Dom DeLuise) who befriends him. But there are also conniving rats, one called Warren T. (John Finnegan) who takes Fievel to a sweat shop where he is forced to work. He manages to escape with the help of an Italian mouse, Tony Toponi (Pat Musik). And so the quest continues. Fievel runs into the Mott Street Maulers, a take no prisoners gang of cats. In conflict with them is Gussie Mouseheimer (Madeline Kahn),a rich and domineering mouse. Meanwhile, Fievel’s parents grieve for their small son, convinced he couldn’t possibly have survived, however Tanya insists that her brother is alive, telling her parents that she can feel it. The plot is a bit convoluted as Fievel makes his way from one close call to the next, with cat chases galore, always pushing forward, ever convinced that he will soon be reunited with his family. An American Tail is a compelling, at times a softly harrowing adventure, one that will capture the attention of a young audience who will be captured by the escapades of a small Russian mouse. An American Tail. Animation. Directed by Don Bluth. With the voices of Philip Glasser, Dom DeLuise and Amy Green. 1 hr., 20 min. Rated G. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Monsters, Inc. has a wonderful premise that will resonate with kids of all ages. I mean, what youngster hasn’t woken up in the dark night, the house asleep, and peeked over the covers at the closed closet door and imagined what might be behind it. “Was that a sound? Did I hear a creak from across the room?” Pixar, masters of computer animation and wonderful storytelling, offers a boisterous, imaginative answer to those questions. In fact, that door is a magical portal to a rust-belt factory called Monsters, Inc., home to an assembly line of bedroom doors through which “scarers,” aka the boogey man, will pass, monsters such as James P. Sullivan (John Goodman), aka Sulley, a huge purple and green furry guy, and his sidekick buddy, Mike Warkowski (Billy Crystal), who is a one-eyed, lime-green dude with a huge mouth. Their mission is to scare those children hiding under the covers, bottle their scream, and then return through the designated door where they use the harvested energy from the frightened scream to run the town of Monsteropolis. The only problem is that kids are not as easily frightened as they use to be, hence there’s less energy to run the factory. And so begins the story. A small, pugnacious toddler somehow slips through her closet door and finds herself in the Monster, Inc. factory where she is discovered by Sulley. Her presence triggers the CDA (Child Detection Agency) alarm, triggering a search by CDA agents. Luckily, she is rescued by Sulley, who calls her “Boo,” and manages to smuggle her out of the factory in a bag. He and Mike make it their mission to return Boo back to her home. But first the two have to find Boo’s magical closet door, which is somewhere down on the factory floor. Meanwhile, Boo is in danger of being subjected to the Scream Extractor. And thus begins the Sulley and Mike adventure as they deal with their nemesis Randal Boggs (Steve Buscemi), a monster who competes with the duo for the most scares, and behind scenes conspires with Henry I. Waternoose III, C.E.O. of the factory, their purpose being to undermine Sulley and Mike. Monsters, Inc. has lots of twists and turns – at one point, the dynamic duo end up in the Himalayas and are taken in by an abdominal snowman, but soon make their way back to the factory. And they still have to get Boo home. It’s all good fun, and kids will more than enjoy the gags and antics of Mike and Sulley, who are never scary, just outrageously enjoyable to hang out with. Plus the story has a satisfying ending wherein Sulley takes over Waternoose’s job as C.E.O. and retools the factory to use children’s laughter, not screams, to provide energy for Monster, Inc. and the Monsteropolis. Monsters, Inc. Pixar Animation, Directed by Pete Docter, Voiced by John Goodman, Billy Crystal, Jennifer Tilly. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated G. Released 2001. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Disney+/Apple tv.

articles.text: There are times when the past, present, and future get all jumbled up. If so, James Joyce would have loved events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday and Sunday. On Saturday, guitarist, Arthur Dente, and percussionist Steve Robertson transformed the PCA into an intimate musical drawing room. James Joyce didn’t play the guitar, but if he did, he would have sounded like Arthur Dente. The duo… possibly inspired by James Joyce… applied colors to a musical canvas that transported the small audience to visions of rapture. It didn’t really matter what they played. Each of us in the audience was able to draw our own conclusions. The mental pictures were vivid. There was a vague suggestion that some of the music would be “fado”, a style of music unique to Portugal by way of Brazil. Fado has an emotional similarity to the Spanish “canto hondo”. The chief difference is that fado is much more improvised, while the Spanish version retains a very strong rhythmic center. As the evening progressed, the audience was drawn into the proceedings more and more. I marveled at the intricate fingerings of Dente on the guitar. It was almost as if he were a contortionist. The same could be said for Steve Robertson on percussion. Their musical communication was telepathic. I have stated this before. I am not a fan of amplification at any time. But Dente and Robertson made it work to best advantage. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, September 20, 2023 The Musical Gourmet Stream of consciousness By Joseph Gold There are times when the past, present, and future get all jumbled up. If so, James Joyce would have loved events at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday and Sunday. On Saturday, guitarist, Arthur Dente, and percussionist Steve Robertson transformed the PCA into an intimate musical drawing room. James Joyce didn’t play the guitar, but if he did, he would have sounded like Arthur Dente. The duo… possibly inspired by James Joyce… applied colors to a musical canvas that transported the small audience to visions of rapture. It didn’t really matter what they played. Each of us in the audience was able to draw our own conclusions. The mental pictures were vivid. There was a vague suggestion that some of the music would be “fado”, a style of music unique to Portugal by way of Brazil. Fado has an emotional similarity to the Spanish “canto hondo”. The chief difference is that fado is much more improvised, while the Spanish version retains a very strong rhythmic center. As the evening progressed, the audience was drawn into the proceedings more and more. I marveled at the intricate fingerings of Dente on the guitar. It was almost as if he were a contortionist. The same could be said for Steve Robertson on percussion. Their musical communication was telepathic. I have stated this before. I am not a fan of amplification at any time. But Dente and Robertson made it work to best advantage. Sunday with the Radio Legends The very next day we were returned “to those thrilling days of yesteryear.” A group of actors who perform as Broadcast Legends (Old Time Radio Players) showed us why old-time radio The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet was so marvelous. They seated themselves on the stage of the Piedmont Center for the Arts and re-enacted the world as we knew it through radio broadcasts, well before the era of television. First, they explained the many aspects of radio. They told us why soap operas were called soap operas. They explained why certain programs were in the morning, some in the afternoon, and others in the evening. Everything made perfect sense. Radio was “live” and mistakes occasionally were made. The actors of Broadcast Legends gave us some examples of extraordinary “bloopers”. Perhaps the most famous blooper was when the radio announcer introduced President Herbert Hoover as president Hoobert Heaver. What came next was the featured attraction. This was a complete reenactment of an episode of the weekly Lone Ranger series. It was exciting to see how radio programs were produced. What is often lost in the nostalgia is how important music was. Music directors selected the music with great care. Most of the programs made spectacular use of music. The theme song for the Green Hornet was Flight of the Bumblebee – how perfectly appropriate. But the Lone Ranger was most famous for its opening music, the William Tell Overture, Rossini’s last opera, written in 1829. We need to remember that all of the accompanying music on radio shows was equally appropriate. Listeners were limited only by their imagination. Radio was also the great musical educator. School teachers brought radios into the classroom and the kids listened to excellent music education programs. I daresay, things like this were standard in classrooms throughout the United States. Many of us lament the decline of music education in public schools. Perhaps a return to those “thrilling days of yesteryear” would be appropriate. Staff photo Bruce W. articles.text: Sept. 30 event features wine tasting, live music, silent auction George Mark Children’s House, a pediatric hospice, will host the Hummingbird Hill Garden Gala on Saturday, September 30, starting at 5 p.m. The program includes: 5 p.m. – House and garden tours, music and wine tasting 6 p.m. – Dinner and program 7:30 p.m. – Live auction and musical entertainment Guest speakers include Cristina Rendon, KTVU weekend anchor, as MC, Kathy Hull, George Mark Children’s House founder, Shekinah Eliassen, George Mark Children’s House CEO, and Michelle Gherlone of the Molly Smiles Foundation. The gala will be held at George Mark House, 2121 George Mark Lane in San Leandro. articles.text: Famous movie lines, like “Here’s looking at you, kid” from Casablanca, usually have some memorable quality, but not the best-known line from 1979’s Being There. It’s, “I like to watch TV,” and as uttered by the bumbling naif, Chance, played by Peter Sellers, it’s both funny and sad. And who is Chance, anyway? Is he a dim-witted loser? Or is he a saint? Audiences at Piedmont’s Second Thursday Film Fest got to decide for themselves last week when the movie was shown at the group’s September gathering. The middle-aged Chance has spent his whole life on the estate of a wealthy man who has just died. He’s never learned to read or write, so all he knows of life is what he’s seen on TV, and the TV clips that the movie offers us are mostly mindless drivel. Dressed a bit like the bowler-hatted man in Rene Magritte paintings, Chance is forced to head out, clueless, into modern America. And then he runs into Shirley MacLaine. Or, rather, MacLaine’s movie character, Elizabeth Rand, whose chauffeur drives into him. It starts their relationship when she mistakes his name as Chauncey Gardiner. Chance is barely scratched, but she invites him to her wealthy hubby’s Versailles-like mansion to be treated by the family doctor. There, his bland pronouncements about gardening are mistaken for wisdom and before you know it, he’s met the U.S. president, lands on national TV and becomes a household name. Smoothly directed by Hal Ashby, the movie is about the hollowness of American life and the gullibility of its citizens – the U.S.A. as TV sitcom. Its script is by Polish-born Jerzy Kosinski, based on his novel of the same name. Playing the wealthy Ben Rand, Melvyn Douglas (remember him opposite Greta Garbo in Peter Sellers stars in the 1979 movie Being There. Ninotchka?) won an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. In the post-movie discussion, a thumbs up versus thumbs down response, viewers who liked it thought it was hilarious and enjoyed the actors’ performances, especially that of Peter Sellers. The group also enjoyed looking back a few decades in time to the clothing and television shows of the past. And they liked how the movie explored how we can fool ourselves. Some viewers thought the pacing was slow, and a few found the sex scene uncomfortable. Still, no one asked for his/her money back. The Film Fest’s next offering on October 12 is the American classic A Place in the Sun starring Elizabeth Taylor, Montgomery Clift and Shelley Winters. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the Film Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m. with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is requested at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. You’re welcome to bring snacks or lunch. ®

articles.text: Walking through town it is impossible not to notice the aesthetic impact of different ancillary structures that are an integral part of the design of many homes. Falling somewhere between architecture and landscape architecture, fences, walls, and their associated gates are chief among these. They can enhance (or unfortunately sometimes compromise) the building, landscape and/or site design. So…what constitutes nice retaining walls, appealing fences or beautiful gates? Like all of the discussions in this column, I point out different ideas or considerations that hopefully help to answer this ongoing question. But there are usually many good answers as well as exceptions to every general rule. What is ultimately important is just what looks and feels right – what appeals to us. That being said, here are some thoughts. The first thing that comes to mind is that these secondary structures need as much study and consideration as the main building(s) or landscape treatment of which they are a part. It is unfortunately obvious when they are designed simply as an afterthought. Fences, walls and gates certainly must be in the same architectural “family” as the home, though this doesn’t mean they have to be exactly the same form, color or even the same material. They do need to relate most appropriately. They are indeed an opportunity to aesthetically deviate to some degree and add interest to both the building(s) and property. Fences or walls can be used to provide privacy, add security, or merely to demarcate the edge of private or semi-private spaces between adjacent properties, or between a property and the street. After adherence to the architectural style of the buildings, the intended use or function of the barrier will be the primary consideration in determining its type, shape and character, i.e., solid (wall) vs, airy (spaced boards), height, extent, and access or gate placements. Gates are, of course, a prominent part of fences and walls, almost automatically seen as a punctuation point because they usually break the horizontal character of the enclosure to which they are attached. Gates are the first thing people use and passthrough in the “entry experience” as we mentioned in a previous column. Both smaller swinging pedestrian gates and larger-scaled auto-access gates should be designed together within the same aesthetic considerations discussed above. The design of retaining walls is important because their appearance sides often function exactly like fences, forming boundaries for yards, patios, and terraces on their downhill and/or uphill sides. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. articles.text: The First Monday Reading Group met on September 11 outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park for their monthly discussion. A turnout of 18 readers showed up to discuss A Visit from the Goon Squad by American author Jennifer Egan. The book was the 2011 Pulitzer Prize-winning work of fiction and also won the National Book Critics Circle Award for fiction in 2010. A Visit from the Goon Squad is a set of 13 interrelated stories with a large set of characters, all connected to Bennie Salazar, a record company executive, and his assistant, Sasha. It deals with often self-destructive characters at different ages as they grow older and go off in unusual directions. The stories bounce back and forth in time from the 1970s to the present. Many of the locations are in New York City, but some are in San Francisco, Italy, and Kenya. Because of its unusual structure, some critics have characterized the book as a novel and others as a collection of short stories. Many of the book’s chapters were initially published as short stories, and Egan brought them together as this book. “Goon squads” were originally groups of violent thugs sent to assault workers who tried to form labor unions. Later, “goon” was used to describe any violent thug. One character in the book says, “Time’s a goon, right?” He is referring to the way time and fate rob most of the book’s characters of their youth, innocence, and success. A Visit from the Goon Squad was a great book for the group – some readers loved it while others hated it, making it perfect for a good discussion. Those who liked it enjoyed the book’s major themes of chaos, the craziness in people’s lives, and the impact of age on people. Some readers said they usually don’t like short story collections. One said she feels this type of fiction doesn’t give her enough character development or life events to feel satisfied. Readers could relate to how people are visited each day by the “goon squad of time” and how they can be knocked around by it. Readers said they could also relate to how crazy, young people can grow and change over time. They enjoyed how the characters’ lives came together at the book’s end. Most readers found the first chapter that introduces Sasha and her problem as a kleptomaniac to be intriguing, but some were disappointed that Sasha and her problem disappear in the next chapters and don’t return until the book’s end. Some readers found the often unrelated chapters, characters, and timing of events confusing. It was noted that this bouncJorell Chavez was hired as the new vocal music teacher. Dance Instructor Amy Moorhead taught the lone choir course, with around a dozen students, for the 2022-23 school year. “The school was committed to trying to keep the program going,” said Moorhead. “With budget cuts, they can no longer run classes that small.” Hiring a vocal music teacher is made more difficult because there is only one section of the course remaining. Some readers prefer a more linear chronology and focused character development in their books. The group had previously selected The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid by Bill Bryson for October, The Trees by Percival Everett for November, and The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman for December. The group’s next discussion will be on Monday, October 2 at 1:30 p.m. at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. Pressure to take AP and honors courses is another factor contributing to the demise of the program, as vocal music is not a weighted course. The things to consider to bring it back are student enrollment, the effect on other electives, a teacher to teach it, and finances,” she stated.

articles.text: A strong turnout of 49 walkers and two K-9 best friends participated in last week’s walk that went from Bellevue to the top of the city, Bell Avenue. Before leaving the Exedra, Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit told them about the police department-sponsored Classic Car Show coming up on September 23 from 9 a.m. to 12 noon. This is an annual, community engagement event in the center of town. It was also announced that next week’s walk would be led by Piedmont architect, urban designer, planner, and Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams. The group tries to walk every safe street in Piedmont each year but there are still some streets they haven’t walked, including Bellevue Avenue. The “roads not taken” theme prompted a request that Dave DeRoche, with his deep baritone voice, read to the group Robert Frost’s poem, “The Road Not Taken.” This poem ends, “Two roads diverged in a wood, and I - I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.” The walkers began on the little traveled Sierra Avenue, noticing two Julia Morgan designed homes that Will Adams had pointed out on an earlier Wednesday. Then it was on to Caperton Avenue and the little-traveled Richardson Way, and Lakeview Avenue, eventually to the little-known Poplar Way. It serves as an alley for garages of homes on Lakeview and Mountain, however it is lovely with redwoods and other trees – but no poplars. As the group emerged on Mountain Avenue, they noted the large redwood tree in the middle of the intersection of Bellevue and Mountain. The story is that this tree was planted long ago by a Chinese cook who worked at a nearby home. The walkers came to the front gate of a beautiful, large home with a long driveway. From the street and front yard there is a majestic view of San Francisco Bay. Will Adams pointed out the house was placed on the lot specifically so that the driveway entrance would provide this view. The group continued on to the steep Pacific and Hagar Avenues, enjoying fabulous views of San Francisco along the way. On Bell Avenue, at the top of Piedmont, there were more great views. They descended on Scenic Avenue to Alta Avenue, and then back to Scenic via a 163-foot set of steep stairs to the lower portion of Scenic. From there it was an easy return to town center via Blair, Scenic, Pacific, Mountain, and Highland Avenues. The walkers noted that Blair breaks up Scenic, and Scenic disappears for a block before it returns. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Participants in last week’s Walking on Wednesday included Sherry Jacobs, Brenda Ferrero, David Haecker, Albert Chen, Kay Kewley, Greg Keller, Ian Morgan, Mimi Engle, Adrienne Hamlin, Helene Farber, Ann Quinby, Pat Keller, Sharon Anderson, Nancy Henn, Phil Witte, Melba Yee, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Eric Behrens, Karen Palmer, Carol Lyons, Lois Price, Bob Wong, Jim Kuo, Dottie Hutch, Lois Price, Peggy Shultz, Mike Henn, Judy Love, Jennifer Peltzer, Will Adams, Helen Long, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Christine Calliste, Ken Hubbert, Nancy Olsen, Larry Olsen, Nancy DeRoche, Dave DeRoche, Martin Levy, Priscilla Wanerus, Stella Houston, Tina Shum, Quincy Dong, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Dina Aburous, Yvette Kirby, Mel Johnston with her K-9 best friend Molly, and Piedmont Recreation Commissioner Lisa Gardner with her K-9 best friend Bo.
