articles.text: Many families today are faced with the reality of caring for their aging loved ones. In a time where compassionate care and tools for promoting quality of life for seniors are in demand, two companies have stepped in to bridge the gap. Homewatch CareGivers of Oakland and The Hummingbird Project have forged a partnership that focuses on engaging older adults and helping them feel connected to the world around them. Leah Bloom, Director of Community Outreach and Co-Owner of Homewatch CareGivers of Oakland, shares her thoughts on the best parts of working in the senior care industry and how her company’s partnership with The Hummingbird Project can transform lives. When did you join the senior care industry? My husband and I have owned a home care company for seven and a half years. Prior to that, I worked with families recovering from domestic violence. I’m an ardent supporter of peace and social justice and I enjoy bringing those principles to my work with the senior community. What is your favorite part about serving home care clients? Do you have a favorite memory of a special client you were able to help? Serving clients is my absolute favorite thing. I love helping to create an environment where we can talk safely about uncomfortable and scary things. I find it exciting to help people work through stigmas and fears surrounding aging, illness and family disharmony. I have a lot of favorite memories of working with clients but one in particular comes to mind. One of our clients had brain cancer and her daughter reached out to us for help. When we showed up, the whole house was decorated with fun, bright crafts and homemade art. It turns out that the client’s sister and brother-in-law were very talented, famous clowns. They introduced me to the idea of play being a part of healing. It made me realize that we can think creatively about disease and about how people live with disease. This concept ties in very closely with the philosophy of Homewatch CareGivers, because we focus on the power of creative problem-solving in the care that we provide. You recently partnered with The Hummingbird Project to provide unique activity boxes to your clients. Can you share some details about these boxes and how your clients can receive them? The activity boxes are called Joy Boxes. The Joy Boxes start with the belief that people living with illness still have so much to contribute and they are a tool to help bring out that contribution. They provide step-by-step instructions and activity ideas to help clients and caregivers try new things, rediscover old interests, and create joyful moments together. They are self-guided tools for both family and professional caregivers. I think they are brilliant, because the activities help the client create a bond with the caregiver whether they know them already or not. Anyone who signs up for 20 hours or more of service with us over the next few months will receive a complimentary joy box. Are there different themes for the Joy Boxes? Yes, there are three themes for the Joy Boxes centered on the following ideas: Creativity, Living Legends and Comfort. The Creativity Box is designed to stimulate creativity and ignite artistic expression within seniors. The Legends & Legacies Box is all about telling your story. It comes with a book called “The Book of Myself – A Do-It-Yourself Autobiography In 201 Questions.” Additionally, it comes with a special pen designed in a way that is easy for elderly or arthritic hands to use. The Comfort Box focuses on bringing comfort to adults who are in more advanced stages of aging. It includes items such as a cozy blanket, tea, and a book of affirmations. All the contents of the Joy Boxes are high-quality, well-curated, durable and thoughtful. What made you decide to join forces with The Hummingbird Project? I wanted to partner with The Hummingbird Project because their whole mission is about being creative and unafraid of bringing joy to a situation. On a more personal note, for readers who would like to get to know you, what do you enjoy doing outside of work? I love being with my family and gardening. I also deeply enjoy breaking bread with people. Every Friday, we open up our home to family and friends and I think sharing a meal together is a really transformative medium. For more information about how Homewatch CareGivers of Oakland can help you or your loved one, please call (510) 953- 5112 or visit www.homewatchcaregivers.com/oakland today.

READ IT IN THE POST Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I see that the iPhone 15 has been released. I have an iPhone 12. Do you think I should upgrade? –Doris G., Oakland Dear Doris: I have been getting this question for several weeks now. Your phone just came out three years ago and may still work just fine. Let’s look at the similarities and differences to help you make your decision. You can still put the newest operating system on your 12 and it is compatible with the upcoming iOS 17 to be released in the fall. It should be able to take further updates for 2-3 years more. Audio quality is likely the same; I did not hear any information about big upgrades to the audio in the new model. And disappointing to many of us, like the 12, there is no separate audio jack for headphones. You must use an adapter or Bluetooth earphones. The new model still uses Face ID like the iPhone 12. It is also slightly heavier (iPhone 12 is 164 g and the 15 is 171 g). The charging speed is the same on each model, but of course your battery life is likely shortened on the 12 if you have been using it steadily during the time you have had it. Speaking of battery life, the iPhone 12 was known to disappoint consumers with a poor battery life. This was corrected in the iPhone 13 and Apple claims the battery life in the iPhone 15 is greatly improved. If the iPhone 14 is any mark for that, I look forward to an impressive battery life. One of the biggest changes in charging is the death of the lighting connection (the end that plugs into the charging port on your phone). Apple, late to the game, has finally incorporated USB-C into the iPhone 15. That means your old charging cables will not work with the iPhone 15. But it also means that you can charge your phone with the same cable that the 2020 MacBook Air, and the 12.9 inch iPad Pro use, as well as many other devices. Of course, the processor on the new iPhone is faster. The 12 uses the A14 Processor, while the 15 uses the A16, which is also more power efficient. The 15 also has 6 GB RAM while the iPhone 12 has 4 GB RAM. So the new phone is faster. Also, while you could get the iPhone 12 at 64GB storage, the base storage for the iPhone 15 is 128GB. Also, the iPhone 15 uses an eSIM while the iPhone 12 uses a physical SIM card but also has the capability to use eSIM technology. One noticeable difference is the brightness of the screen. The iPhone 12 has a peak brightness of 1200 nits, while the iPhone 15 is brighter at 2000 nits peak brightness. Also, the notch at the top of your screen on the iPhone 12 is replaced by a “dynamic island.” Debuted on the iPhone 14 last year, front-facing sensors and cameras will be integrated into a small cutout at the top of the screen, which will change information depending on what app you are using. If you travel a lot and like to take pictures, the camera on the iPhone 15 is much more advanced. The main camera on the iPhone 12 is 12 megapixels while on the iPhone 15, the main camera is 48 megapixels. That’s a huge difference. Apple went to 48 mp on the iPhone 14 Pro and I can tell you that the camera is amazing. You may or may not know, but I am a passionate wildlife photographer and while I don’t use my phone for wildlife, I do often use it for landscape or portrait photography. I may have my wildlife equipment on my tripod waiting for a bird to take flight and see a beautiful landscape scene. Instead of changing lenses on my Nikon, I whip out my iPhone and often get a better shot than I would with my dedicated camera! I would not hesitate to upgrade to an iPhone 15 in your case for the battery life and camera alone. The iPhone 15 is rated IP68 for water resistance. This means that it should be able to survive an accidental drop in the sink. I don’t have mine yet (MacMama upgrades every year), but I will at the end of next week. There are many more changes under the hood that leads Apple to promise that the iPhone 15 the best one yet and I am anxious to get my hands on one to see if this is true. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional who provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: Brown Gables, the Alexander home at Sea View and Hampton, was named for its prominent gables, painted brown. Their grand three-story mansion was completed in 1909, which they named “Brown Gables” for its massive gabled dormers with bargeboards, painted brown. The first floor was faced in brick and half timbering covered the upper stories. Two large porte cocheres were also trimmed in brown gables. Diamond-paned, leaded glass windows graced the entry and large bay windows offered expansive views from every room in this most elegant early home in Piedmont. City records indicate that the Alexander house had three living rooms, five bedrooms and five bathrooms. Koa wood and other exotic woods enhanced the interior. It was an exceptional house in 1909 with 3240 square feet and was the site of many festive balls. The gardens of the Alexander home also hosted many garden parties that benefited local charities. Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Ladies Relief Society, the Matilda Brown Home and the Women’s Guild of the Piedmont Church. She also organized the Bay Area chapter of the Red Cross at the onset of World War I and led it for over 30 years. Their beautiful gardens extended over nine of today’s lots on Sea View and King Avenues. A low brick wall with a subtle detail surrounded the property. The wall is visible in the photo of the house and portions still stand today on Hampton. The Alexander carriage house, which still exists at 84 King, had servants’ quarters and an indoor swimming pool. Helen Wills Moody, the Wimbledon tennis star in the 1920s and 1930s, practiced on the tennis court there. The Alexander family formed a small community near Sea View and Hampton. In 1911, Wallace’s mother built her own home across the street at 92 Sea View — designed by Charles W. Dickey — and Mary’s mother built her home down the street at 236 Sea View. Wallace Alexander was president of the Alexander and Baldwin sugar firm, Vice President of the Matson Navigation Company, director of several other Hawaiian companies and a trustee of Stanford University. Although he was active in many businesses, he found time for many civic and charitable organizations in Piedmont. In addition to constructing the stores and saving Piedmont Park, Alexander was also the driving force behind the construction of the Piedmont Interdenominational Church (now Piedmont Community Church), arranging for the purchase of the land and again hiring Albert Farr to design the church. Wallace Alexander also established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council. He arranged for the scouts to meet in the basement of the church, as they still do today. In 1929, he leased land from the Forest Service near Keddie in Plumas County and established Camp Wallace Alexander, a Piedmont scouting tradition fondly remembered by generations of Piedmont Boy Scouts. The land lease expired in 1982 and Camp Wallace Alexander was dismantled. In 1939, Wallace Alexander suffered a fatal stroke at his second home in Honolulu. He was eulogized as “Piedmont’s leading private citizen.” Wallace left a large bequest to the Piedmont Community Church and to the Piedmont Boy Scouts. His philosophy was that he “was but a trustee of the money that came to him.” Upon his death, Mary Alexander followed her husband’s wishes that the property be subdivided into 13 lots. The entire estate would not be sold to a single builder. She stated that the lots would be purchased by individuals who intended to build their own homes. The Alexanders wanted more families to live in Piedmont. Footnote on the Stores My previous column on Piedmont’s “stores” brought out a few comments by readers. One fondly remembers the steps leading up to the stores. They were a favorite place for students to hang out. “Kids with cars would ‘cruise by’ checking out the scene. pages.text: Wednesday, September 20, 2023 25 The History of Piedmont Wallace M. Alexander – Piedmont’s philanthropist Wallace Alexander was Piedmont’s premier philanthropic citizen and a leader in establishing many of Piedmont’s institutions. By Gail G. Lombardi In previous columns I have mentioned Wallace Alexander. He was instrumental in the 1913 construction of the Piedmont Commercial Center, Piedmont’s first stores, and in the 1921 purchase of the upper Piedmont Park land, saving it from development. Wallace Alexander, a profile Wallace McKinney Alexander was born on the island of Maui in 1869. His father, Samuel Alexander, was related to the Baldwin and Cooke families and was a pioneer in sugar planting and refining. When it was time for Wallace and his sisters, Juliette and Annie, to attend high school, the family moved to Oakland where Wallace attended Oakland High School. He later attended Andover and graduated from Yale University. He married his Oakland classmate Mary Barker in 1904. In her memoir, Queen of the Hills, Evelyn Craig Pattiani tells the story of the Alexanders choosing their homesite at the prominent corner of Sea View and Hampton (then called Union Street). The Piedmont Historical Society invites you to become a member You will receive our annual newsletter Piedmont’s History And an invitation to attend our Annual Meeting with speakers on history Membership Dues ❏ $25.00: Individual ❏ $40.00: Couple ❏ $75.00: Friend ❏ $125.00: Sponsor ❏ $250.00: Patron ❏ $500.00: Benefactor ❏ New Membership Amount Enclosed: $_____________ Name _______________________________________________ Address _____________________________________________ Please complete this form and mail with a check payable to the Piedmont Historical Society to 358 Hillside Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Your Membership is Tax Deductible Brown Gables, the Alexander home at Sea View and Hampton, was named for its prominent gables, painted brown. Their grand three-story mansion was completed in 1909, which they named “Brown Gables” for its massive gabled dormers with bargeboards, painted brown. The first floor was faced in brick and half timbering covered the upper stories. Two large porte cocheres were also trimmed in brown gables. Diamond-paned, leaded glass windows graced the entry and large bay windows offered expansive views from every room in this most elegant early home in Piedmont. City records indicate that the Alexander house had three living rooms, five bedrooms and five bathrooms. Koa wood and other exotic woods enhanced the interior. It was an exceptional house in 1909 with 3240 square feet and was the site of many festive balls. The gardens of the Alexander home also hosted many garden parties that benefited local charities. Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Ladies Relief Society, the Matilda Brown Home and the Women’s Guild of the Piedmont Church. She also organized the Bay Area chapter of the Red Cross at the onset of World War I and led it for over 30 years. Their beautiful gardens extended over nine of today’s lots on Sea View and King Avenues. A low brick wall with a subtle detail surrounded the property. The wall is visible in the photo of the house and portions still stand today on Hampton. The Alexander carriage house, which still exists at 84 King, had servants’ quarters and an indoor swimming pool. Helen Wills Moody, the Wimbledon tennis star in the 1920s and 1930s, practiced on the tennis court there. The Alexander family formed a small community near Sea View and Hampton. In 1911, Wallace’s mother built her own home across the street at 92 Sea View — designed by Charles W. Dickey — and Mary’s mother built her home down the street at 236 Sea View. Wallace Alexander was president of the Alexander and Baldwin sugar firm, Vice President of the Matson Navigation Company, director of several other Hawaiian companies and a trustee of Stanford University. Although he was active in many businesses, he found time for many civic and charitable organizations in Piedmont. In addition to constructing the stores and saving Piedmont Park, Alexander was also the driving force behind the construction of the Piedmont Interdenominational Church (now Piedmont Community Church), arranging for the purchase of the land and again hiring Albert Farr to design the church. Wallace Alexander also established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council. He arranged for the scouts to meet in the basement of the church, as they still do today. In 1929, he leased land from the Forest Service near Keddie in Plumas County and established Camp Wallace Alexander, a Piedmont scouting tradition fondly remembered by generations of Piedmont Boy Scouts. The land lease expired in 1982 and Camp Wallace Alexander was dismantled. In 1939, Wallace Alexander suffered a fatal stroke at his second home in Honolulu. He was eulogized as “Piedmont’s leading private citizen.” Wallace left a large bequest to the Piedmont Community Church and to the Piedmont Boy Scouts. His philosophy was that he “was but a trustee of the money that came to him.” Upon his death, Mary Alexander followed her husband’s wishes that the property be subdivided into 13 lots. The entire estate would not be sold to a single builder. She stated that the lots would be purchased by individuals who intended to build their own homes. The Alexanders wanted more families to live in Piedmont. Footnote on the Stores My previous column on Piedmont’s “stores” brought out a few comments by readers. One fondly remembers the steps leading up to the stores. They were a favorite place for students to hang out. “Kids with cars would ‘cruise by’ checking out the scene. Many an afternoon was spent watching our Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Red Cross and established the Bay Area chapter at the onset of World War I. small world go by.” The flip side of kids hanging out on the steps is that the Piedmont women on their way to shop hated to have to make their way through all those students on the steps. If you enjoy reading these history columns, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving the annual newsletter. More information on Piedmont’s history and membership is on the website, Piedmonthistorical.org, or contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@pacbell.net. articles.text: Visitors at the city’s Harvest Festival on September 24 are in for a special treat. Highlights of Piedmont Garden Club’s successful flower show earlier this year will be on view inside the Community Hall for the entire community to enjoy. The presentation emphasizes the importance of the essential oak tree. “We celebrate our majestic Oaks, keystone species in our native habitat, considered sacred by indigenous peoples,” said Patty Reed. “An ecosystem powerhouse of leaves, bark, and acorns feed and shelter many native insects, invertebrates, birds and mammals. Oaks sequester carbon and their roots retain water and sustain microorganisms that nourish our soil.” This grand oak display will inform Piedmonters of all ages. Birds will be flying in the oak tree, butterflies flitting everywhere and small animals hiding in the limbs of the trees. There will be a special display of the many insects which live in the oaks and the native plants which grow around them. Julia Burke, currently Treasurer of Piedmont Beautification Foundation, led the team which created the exhibit. PBF Trustee Christiana Macfarlane was on the team in addition to Reed, former Mayor Valerie Matzger, and Cathy Glazier. Completing the group of creators were members of the Piedmont Garden Club Conservation Committee Chris Heins, Elise Lorenzo, Annis Kukulan, Barbara Guiffre, and Kerri Lublin. Piedmont Garden Club is now celebrating its 100th birthday. PBF, which is sponsoring the display at the Harvest Festival, was created by Piedmont Garden Club jointly with the Piedmont City Council in 1964 and serves as one of the best examples of public-private partnership to promote the common good in Piedmont. The Oak Tree Exhibit received a national award from the Garden Club of America in New York City. You need to travel no further than the Harvest Festival in Piedmont to see this spectacular presentation.
articles.title: Oak tree exhibit added to Harvest Festival

articles.text: A Piedmont mother was carjacked on Sunday morning, September 10, at approximately 9 a.m. as she was buckling her young child into the car. The incident occurred in the 1200 block of Grand Avenue. She was approached by two men in their early 20’s who demanded her purse, keys, cell phone and her vehicle, a black 2018 BMW. The suspects told her to get her baby out of the car, then to wait on the curb. The woman removed her child, under two years old, from the vehicle. One suspect fled the scene in a 4-door green BMW and the other left with the stolen car. Neither the woman nor the child were injured, and no weapons were displayed. Piedmont Police immediately began tracking the vehicle Sunday. With the help of Oakland Police and California Highway Patrol, the car was recovered and one suspect arrested the same day. “Throughout the day we were getting various updates and checking different locations,” explained Piedmont Police Capt. Chris Monahan. “The Highway Patrol had a helicopter in the air. At 4:12 p.m. the CHP helicopter found the suspect’s vehicle, and Oakland PD moved in to make the arrest.” The suspect, Quran Moban, 19, from Rodeo, CA was driving the stolen vehicle with four women in the car when Oakland police pulled him over. Moban was arrested and has been positively identified by the victim. He was sent to Santa Rita Jail and is currently charged with carjacking and possession of the stolen vehicle. The other suspect described as a Black male in his early 20’s is still at large. The victim’s car, phone, and wallet have been returned to her by the police. articles.text: Piedmont’s teachers union has begun negotiations over salaries and benefits with new School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. Before sitting at the bargaining table on September 7, teachers rallied for support from the community at their respective schools. Teachers plan to continue to make their pocketbooks a topic visible to parents and students with rallies in front of schools during student drop off on September 21 and 28 as well. Teachers also plan to rally today, September 13, at 5:45 p.m. at City Hall prior to the School Board meeting. They plan to speak at the meeting which starts at 7:00 p.m. The union, the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT), has joined the East Bay Coalition for Student Success, a group of 19 teachers unions including Pleasanton, Dublin, San Ramon, Pittsburg and Orinda. “I’d say it’s a pretty conservative estimate to say we’d need something like a 14.5% salary increase just to get us back to the spending power we had this time last year. For those lower on our salary schedule, it would actually take more than that,” said union president Elise Marks. The PUSD budget has $422,300 currently unallocated. The cost to give all staff members a 1% raise would be $340,000. In Superintendent Hawn’s most recent “Piedmont Pulse” weekly update, she mentioned some challenges, including a “claw-back” of funds by the state, a comparatively low reserve, and additional red-tape caused by PUSD submitting a “qualified budget” which did not meet financial obligations. Hawn’s update can be seen at Smore.com/k34hd. Tonight’s meeting can be streamed at zoom. us/j/82377699467.
articles.title: Piedmont teachers begin salary negotiations

articles.text: Five public safety cameras for police surveillance will be installed on September 19, according to the City of Piedmont. The cameras will be placed at strategic intersections to help police maximize their response to crimes. “It’s exciting to be at this point,” said Lisa Douglas, Support Services Commander for the Police Department. “After several delays related to both logistics and the installation of power and fiber, we are ready for install.” The cameras to be installed will be live-feed cameras, taking video at 30 frames per second. The cameras have a range of 150-200 feet and are intended to strengthen the existing network of Automatic License Plate Readers (ALPR) which are already installed at various entry ways in the city. ALPR use their cameras to identify vehicle license plates and quickly alert police when a stolen vehicle or plate enters the city. The new surveillance cameras will provide the police with additional context, including the flow of traffic, and the ability to acquire images of suspects. articles.text: It was great to read the article in the September 6, 2023 Piedmont Post, titled ‘Piedmont now the largest community youth robotics league in U.S.” Piedmont youth receive considerable benefit from embracing the FIRST organization’s robotics programs, FLL, FTC and FRC. With this success comes a responsibility to support the FIRST organization. When our sons Charlie and Henry showed interest in FTC, my wife Helen Potter and I not only supported two FTC teams in Piedmont, we also supported FIRST by working at the FTC regional tournaments. These tournaments are the competitions that teams attend to test their creations and compete with other FTC teams. While teams learn from designing and building a robot to accomplish specific tasks, they really complete the learning process in the competitions. After volunteering at several FTC tournaments in Northern California, we got to know other team mentors and organizers as well as the leadership of the FIRST organization. These relationships developed and helped tremendously in starting the Highlanders 8033 FRC team in Piedmont. These relationships also led FIRST to ask if Piedmont would support an FTC tournament. With the growth in FLL and FTC, there are not enough tournament slots for all the FTC teams to compete in Northern California. While Piedmont is hosting an FLL tournament on November 5, there are no plans for continuing to host an FTC tournament. Having staffed several FTC tournaments, we were apprehensive to take on such an event, but we jumped in feet first and rallied the Piedmont School District, Piedmont Makers as well as many great volunteers from Piedmont. PUSD and Piedmont Makers blocked out the Morrison Gym and provided support moving tables and chairs, setting up wireless microphones and managing the WiFi environment per FIRST requirements One side of the Morrison Gym was used to support the pits for 16 teams to prepare robots to pass inspections and be ready for competition. The other side of the gym supported the competition field and competition management systems, referees, and field technical support as well as the audience. Yes, this was a lot of work and typically covered a two-day period for set up and tear down. FIRST depends on communities like Piedmont to step up and support FTC competitions, especially a community that has the largest youth robotics league in the U.S. It seems a bit disingenuous for six Piedmont FTC teams to take up tournament slots in Northern California without contributing tournament slots for other FTC teams. Piedmont has supported three FTC tournaments, most recently following the COVID shut down in 2022. We urge the Piedmont robotics community to continue to host FTC tournaments for as long as FTC teams exist here. There is an established knowledge base; lessons have been learned, tournament operations have been documented for the Morrison gym. Hosting an FTC tournament is a large effort, but should be a standard annual event for the community woth tth the largest youth robotics league in the United States. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS
articles.title: Need for FTC Robotics Tournaments to continue in Piedmont

articles.text: One of my favorite biblical scenes comes at the end of the Book of Genesis. Here, the Joseph saga draws to its dramatic finish. In Egypt where Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers, has risen to become second in command to the King of Egypt; where Joseph has used his vast power to save his family, and apparently much of ancient Middle East, from famine by storing great quantities of grain during seven years of abundant harvest; where Joseph has revealed his identity to his brothers who did not initially recognize him; the patriarch Jacob, the father of Joseph and his eleven brothers dies. The brothers tremble in fear believing that with the death of their father Joseph will now turn on them in vengeful wrath. In the face of their trembling Joseph speaks, “You meant to do me evil. God used your evil for good, saving many human lives from starvation in the process.” The theology behind Joseph’s words is profound. While God does not cause evil, pain and suffering, God can use these, indeed, transform these in order to bring about good. Chaos, terror and grave inhumanity litter the landscape of human history. It is the work of God to see all the brokenness, to gently gather it up and, out of the rubble, fashion faith, hope and love. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, September 13, 2023 Opinion Need for FTC Robotics Tournaments to continue in Piedmont By John Lambert It was great to read the article in the September 6, 2023 Piedmont Post, titled ‘Piedmont now the largest community youth robotics league in U.S.” Piedmont youth receive considerable benefit from embracing the FIRST organization’s robotics programs, FLL, FTC and FRC. With this success comes a responsibility to support the FIRST organization. When our sons Charlie and Henry showed interest in FTC, my wife Helen Potter and I not only supported two FTC teams in Piedmont, we also supported FIRST by working at the FTC regional tournaments. These tournaments are the competitions that teams attend to test their creations and compete with other FTC teams. While teams learn from designing and building a robot to accomplish specific tasks, they really complete the learning process in the competitions. After volunteering at several FTC tournaments in Northern California, we got to know other team mentors and organizers as well as the leadership of the FIRST organization. These relationships developed and helped tremendously in starting the Highlanders 8033 FRC team in Piedmont. These relationships also led FIRST to ask if Piedmont would support an FTC tournament. With the growth in FLL and FTC, there are not enough tournament slots for all the FTC teams to compete in Northern California. While Piedmont is hosting an FLL tournament on November 5, there are no plans for continuing to host an FTC tournament. Having staffed several FTC tournaments, we were apprehensive to take on such an event, but we jumped in feet first and rallied the Piedmont School District, Piedmont Makers as well as many great volunteers from Piedmont. PUSD and Piedmont Makers blocked out the Morrison Gym and provided support moving tables and chairs, setting up wireless microphones and managing the WiFi environment per FIRST requirements One side of the Morrison Gym was used to support the pits for 16 teams to prepare robots to pass inspections and be ready for competition. The other side of the gym supported the competition field and competition management systems, referees, and field technical support as well as the audience. Yes, this was a lot of work and typically covered a two-day period for set up and tear down. FIRST depends on communities like Piedmont to step up and support FTC competitions, especially a community that has the largest youth robotics league in the U.S. It seems a bit disingenuous for six Piedmont FTC teams to take up tournament slots in Northern California without contributing tournament slots for other FTC teams. Piedmont has supported three FTC tournaments, most recently following the COVID shut down in 2022. We urge the Piedmont robotics community to continue to host FTC tournaments for as long as FTC teams exist here. There is an established knowledge base; lessons have been learned, tournament operations have been documented for the Morrison gym. Hosting an FTC tournament is a large effort, but should be a standard annual event for the community woth tth the largest youth robotics league in the United States. God using others’ evil for good By Pastor Jim Hopkins One of my favorite biblical scenes comes at the end of the Book of Genesis. Here, the Joseph saga draws to its dramatic finish. In Egypt where Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers, has risen to become second in command to the King of Egypt; where Joseph has used his vast power to save his family, and apparently much of ancient Middle East, from famine by storing great quantities of grain during seven years of abundant harvest; where Joseph has revealed his identity to his brothers who did not initially recognize him; the patriarch Jacob, the father of Joseph and his eleven brothers dies. The brothers tremble in fear believing that with the death of their father Joseph will now turn on them in vengeful wrath. In the face of their trembling Joseph speaks, “You meant to do me evil. God used your evil for good, saving many human lives from starvation in the process.” The theology behind Joseph’s words is profound. While God does not cause evil, pain and suffering, God can use these, indeed, transform these in order to bring about good. Chaos, terror and grave inhumanity litter the landscape of human history. It is the work of God to see all the brokenness, to gently gather it up and, out of the rubble, fashion faith, hope and love. It is the ongoing story of creation, out of the chaos God creates. It is the ongoing story of liberation, out of our well-documented history of enslaving, God sets the captives free. It is the ongoing story of resurrection. out of the crosses on which humanity has suffered and the tombs designed to hold us in, God brings new life, new hope, new spirit. I cannot, in good conscience, say that God protects us from evil or shields us from calamity. I can however, point us to the story of Joseph and his words “You meant it for evil, out of that evil God brought good.” God does not protect. Yet, in all things, God creates. In many of our lives there are great regrets – words said and words left unsaid, deeds done and deeds left undone, failures to love, surprising capacities to hate, losses public and losses private. articles.text: Meetings to be held at both City Hall and Community Hall The City of Piedmont and the Police Department have organized three upcoming meetings for community members to voice their concerns surrounding crime and public safety in the city. Monday, September 18, 6 pm City Council meeting Quarterly Crime Report to City Council Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers will present the quarterly crime report to City Council with a description of crime statistics through June 30. Bowers will discuss recent crime trends and the strategies the Police Department is currently pursuing. Bowers will also inform the Council on five new placed surveillance cameras. Community members will be given the opportunity to comment on the presentation and ask questions. Residents may attend the meeting in person or on Zoom via the City of Piedmont’s website at piedmont.ca.gov. Wednesday, September 27, 5:30 p.m. Town Hall meeting on Public Safety Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue The City has scheduled a Town Hall meeting on public safety on September 27 with the Police Department and City officials. Police Chief Bowers will begin the meeting with a brief presentation of recent crime data and police efforts to combat crime. A question-and-answer session will follow the presentation. This meeting is intended to be less formal and will provide community members the opportunity to voice their concerns, share their experiences in a discussion about public safety in the city. Thursday, October 5, 5:30 p.m. Public Safety Committee Meeting City Hall The City’s Public Safety Committee will have a regularly scheduled public meeting on October 5. At the meeting, Police Chief Bowers will provide another presentation on crime data and police strategies as well as share his insight from the September 27th town hall meeting. Following public comments, the Public Safety Committee will hold a discussion of the presentation. Community members are encouraged to attend one or all of the upcoming meetings.

articles.text: The Piedmont Unified School District has confirmed that a public meeting regarding the Witter Field project will be held on Tuesday, September 26, in the Wildwood School auditorium at 6 p.m. The meeting will give residents the chance to discuss the progress on the project and receive an updated Witter Field irrigation and drainage plan. Director of Facilities Pete Palmer will lead the discussion. Also attending the meeting will be Devin Conway of Verde Design Civil Engineers, Daniel Gonzales the City of Piedmont Public Works Director, and School Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. For a number of months neighbors have raised questions about possible flooding in neighborhoods below the field, and drainage calculations have been questioned. The school district has reduced the peak flow rate for the Witter Field area by approximately 20% at the request of the City. “PUSD reduced the storm water flow into the City storm drain system by reducing the size of the inlet pipe diameter [to slow the flow rate],” explained Palmer. At this time Bothman Construction is still planning on completing all work and reopening the field no later than December 1 despite a delay by EBMUD. Parking restrictions on Palm Drive will also be a topic of discussion at the meeting. Updates on the construction project are posted at Piedmont. k12.ca.us/ref/facilities/witter-field-renovation For more information, contact Pete Palmer at ppalmer@piedmont.k12ca.us or call 594-2877. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will host its 5th annual Cops, Coffee and Car Show on Saturday, September 23. For Officer Tyler Petit this will be his third year in charge of the event, which he sees as crucial to the fabric of the community. “Watching people get together who share a common interest is a great experience. You see a community grow before your eyes. Conversations thrive, contact numbers are exchanged, and new friendships develop, creating a better and stronger community,” said Petit. The car show will run from 9 a.m. to noon on Magnolia Avenue between Piedmont Park and Piedmont High School. In years past the show has included over 100 classic cars from Piedmont locals and car collectors in the Bay Area. Free coffee will be provided and breakfast burritos will be available to purchase. Last year’s show included a Bentley Mulsanne, a 1955 Split window Chevy Camaro, a 1915 Ford Model-T Roadster, and three Formula Ford Indy cars. “The crowd pleasers have always been the Lamborghinis, Ferraris, Ford Gt, and the Jaguar KX120,” said Petit. “This year, some of the owners of the vehiMichael Malone of Oakland with his 1979 Formula Ford Can Diemen RF79. Officer Tyler Petit is the car show lead organizer for the third year. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers (left), with David Friedkin, owner of a 1967 Jaguar XKE, and Officer Hayley Shedd. cles have purchased new cars, or traded for different ones.” Under Petit’s guidance the event has served as a conversation starter between police and residents. With crime a hot topic, outreach programs like the car show are of greater importance. “Police Departments are more successful when the community can trust in them; developing one-on-one relationships is incredibly important,” said Petit. To register your classic or exotic car in the show, email Petit at: coffeecarscops@piedmont. ca.gov. An estimated 600 people attended the Car Show last year.

articles.text: Friends and neighbors are invited to attend the 4th Annual Piedmont Art Walk, scheduled for Sunday, October 1, from 12 noon to 5 p.m. If you’re an art enthusiast, you’ll be inspired by modern and contemporary painting, ceramics, sculpture, photography, mixed media, and textile arts. More than 40 local artists will show their work at their home studios throughout Piedmont and at art pavilions at Havens School and Piedmont High School. Notably, this year’s Art Walk will include a 4-day art show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. On Saturday and Sunday the weekends of September 23-24 and September 30 - October 1. An artists’ reception will take place at the Center on Friday evening, September 29, from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m. Art purchases at the Piedmont Art Walk are a show of support for the arts in Piedmont schools. Twenty percent of all proceeds help fund Piedmont’s art programs in all grades. Grants from the Piedmont Arts Fund help support art education by providing art supplies for middle school and high school classes, and new computers for animation classes at the middle school.

articles.text: Meeting for new parents scheduled for September 19 The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn will co-chair this year’s Giving Campaign. Hunter is the parent of kids at Piedmont Middle and Piedmont High Schools, and Osborn, who grew up in Piedmont, has two at Havens. “I was in Chicago and came back to the Bay Area to be close to my family. We chose Piedmont so our kids could get the same foundational education that helped me,” she said. Hunter has a specific memory. “We were living in Oakland and drove through Piedmont one day and saw all these enchanting scarecrows. I thought this was an incredibly creative place. We moved here when my boys were still toddlers, and we were thrilled to find a community that truly embraced us.” Both Hunter and Osborn joined the Giving Campaign this year because they know “it’s for the schools. There’s no question that our kids are getting a good education and that they’re enjoying learning,” said Osborn. “They understand the reciprocal relationship between the schools and the city.: “The schools are the heart of the community, and the community supports the schools,” added Hunter. PEF and the Giving Campaign committee invite the community to celebrate the launch of this year’s campaign with a popsicle party at Piedmont Park on Tuesday, September 19, from 3-4 p.m. at Beach School. Popsicles will be donated by Mulberry’s Market. Parents new to Piedmont schools are invited to a reception that evening at 7 p.m. at the Community Hall to learn more. Watch your mailboxes for this year’s Giving Campaign letter with information on how to support our schools. Photo by Julie Reichle Catie Osborn (left) and Kim Hunter will be co-chairs of this year’s Giving Campaign for Piedmont schools.
articles.title: Ed. Foundation announces Giving Campaign Co-Chairs

articles.text: Parenting requires a creative mindset. Every day is a new opportunity to solve a problem, learn something new about yourself or your kids and develop a new way of doing things in your routines. All of these things are creative acts. Sometimes creativity is critical for just getting through the stresses in life – like when it’s time to get to the airport and your kids are having meltdowns and you have to figure out how to get everyone out the door. Other times the creative path can help you make the most of the experience of just every day small routines. There are so many benefits to you and your family by following the Creative Path. Here are four that you can focus on: Presence, Process, Potential and Enjoyment. Presence: Be here, in the right now. Not in the future, not in the past. The Creative Path asks you to be completely present. And when it comes to kids, there is nothing more important than being with them in whatever state of mind they are experiencing. It’s so easy when someone is having a tantrum or telling you a detail about their favorite game that you truly don’t care about, to distract ourselves with our phones or work emails. But the Creative Path says, what is here for me to notice and learn if I am fully present? Process: Allow the journey itself to be the destination. It’s not about an end goal. In parenting, we can think every day about what college will my kid attend or what they will do for a career, but, in the end, we have no control over those outcomes. What we do have control over is the process of getting there. Every day are we seeing what our children are passionate about. Are we engaging with our children on what they are learning and loving in life? The Creative Path is about the path, not the destination. Enjoy it. Potential: Live in the excitement of “what if” because if you can dream it, you can create it. On the Creative Path, we can truly become our own wizards and magicians. We can dream and vision and work to create, knowing that it might not end up exactly as we think it might, but also realizing that every moment and every situation has the potential to be exciting and interesting. What is the opportunity to welcome more music into your life? How can we become the best bread baker in the neighborhood? Is there a new dance move that we all want to learn together? All of these can become amazing “what ifs” if you welcome them. Enjoyment: It’s fun! And we all need fun in our lives. Creativity is fun. It allows for laughter and joy. The slog of life can be super hard. Don’t we deserve some light-hearted enjoyment? The Creative Path can give you that fun because it can be about what feels good. Remember, there is no outcome, it’s all a process. A totally legitimate creative question that can open all sorts of doors for your family is, “How do we solve for fun today?” Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Speaker, Consultant and Coach. https://gocreate.zone/
articles.title: Family benefits of following the creative path

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 13, 2023 11 By Matt Simons The 21st annual Chalk Art Festival at Beach School last Sunday morning, September 10, transformed the school’s blackChalk Art Festival brings out kids’ artistic side top playground into a patchwork of color for as far as the eye could see. “The thing I love about the Chalk Art Festival is that you see everyone doing art,” said Jon Schleuning, in charge of the Festival for the second year. “You see little kids doing their favorite cartoons. You see people drawing about the pancakes. You see adults working with their kids. Two children blend blue and purple chalk together with paintbrushes at the Piedmont Chalk Art Festival. (Photo by Sophie Hess) The black top at Beach Elementary School was crowded with children and their families last Sunday during the Chalk Art Festival. (Photo by Sophie Hess) Katherine Ackerman (Grade 4) and Imogen Weber (Grade 4) draw a picture of flowers together. (Staff Photo) An untitled chalk art piece by “Aya + Toby.” (Staff Photo) A simple, but moving rainbow chalked by two young artists at the Chalk Art Festival. (Staff Photo) “Milky Way” by Salma Bendix, Ellery McCarthy, and Ellora Medhekar (2023) (Staff Photo) Two artists were clearly inspired by their love for sports in this volleyball-themed piece. (Staff Photo) Two young artists work together to create a colorful piece of art at the annual Chalk Art Festival. (Staff Photo) You see groups of people who come back year-after-year. But the most exciting part is seeing people actually making art. They’re doing it individually. Then you step back and you see this beautiful community quilt we’ve created.” The playground was divided into nearly 100 chalk squares. For twenty dollars, families could purchase a square for their art along with a box of brightly colored professional pastel chalks donated by Flax Art & Design art store in downtown Oakland. One-hundred percent of the proceeds support art programs in Piedmont schools as part of the Piedmont Arts Fund. Drawings ranged from murals of picturesque landscapes with beautifully blended rainbows, to detailed portraits of zombies rising from the grave to play soccer. Halloween is just around the corner and there were more than a few spooky homages to the upcoming holiday season. Witches’ hats, brooms, and black cats were common themes. Techniques were diverse among the artists. Where some kids filled in the backgrounds with solid colors to emphasize their creations, other avant-garde renegades left theirs blank. Other artists also blended different chalk colors into a gradient with dry paintbrushes or added some water to create a smear effect. Fourth grade classmates Katherine Ackerman and Imogen Weber worked together to create a painting they described as “a bunch of flowers.” When asked See Chalk Art Festival on page 32

articles.text: The Highlanders accomplished their first varsity football win since 2021 in dominant fashion, knocking off Mt. Eden at the Monarchs’ home field in Hayward 46-7 on Friday, September 8. Their win comes against a Western Alameda County Conference school, that competes in the Mission Division, one step above Piedmont’s Shoreline Division. The game offered a gauge of where the team is in its return to conference play after having to play last without a league in which it could compete. Saturday’s victory marked the first varsity win since beating Kennedy 12-6 in October 2021. “There was a weight on us that we haven’t won a varsity game in two years. It’s a big monkey off of our back,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “I feel like we really saw what we can do. We saw it last year, too, when our JV guys got rolling,”. It was a big day for quarterback Markos Lagios, who had four touchdowns, two by air and two by land. Receiver Sam Shelby consistently burned the defense, recording three touchdowns. The biggest play was a 92-yard connection between Lagios and Shelby on a bomb down the right sideline. “We put three receivers on the opposite side and had Sam isolated on one defender. I just read the safety and drew him over by looking to the left. The safety moved over, I went back to the right, and…touchdown,” reflected Lagios on the play. “I can trust Markos to put it on me,” said Shelby. “ I got a little bit of separation and it was a great ball right there for me. I almost got tripped up, but I was able to take it to the crib” It was a sweet victory for Lagios, who made his varsity debit as a freshman when Piedmont was shut out 35-0 to Mt. Eden in 2021. “My freshman year we came here and got blown out. This game was circled when the schedule came out. I’m just happy to get it done and we were all locked in from the jump,” said Lagios. The win also marked a successful day for offensive coordinator Paul Perenon, who came to Piedmont as Seiden’s assistant after spending the last 13 yards as Mt. Eden’s head coach. After the game he was surrounded by former Monarchs players who came to see their previous coach. Piedmont looks ahead to one more Mission Division opponent, Encinal, this Friday. Their team is now coached by former Highlander offensive and defensive line coach, Derrick Lyons. Game Recap Both teams traded possessions throughout the first quarter until the Highlanders regained possession at 1:54 with an extremely short field. After forcing the Monarchs into a 4th-and-35 situation, the punt from deep inside their own end zone sailed to around the 30-yard line to Shelby, who Markos Lagios runs the ball into the end zone as Piedmont’s sideline celebrates. Lagios had two passing and two rushing touchdowns. Tommy Ashton dives for the pylon, scoring his second touchdown of the night. returned the ball to the 10-yard line. On 2nd-and-10, Shelby scored a touchdown carry on an end-around from the receiver spot. With 1:09 on the clock. In the second quarter, Piedmont scored on a nine-play, five-minute drive that capped off with a 23-yard fade from Lagios Sam Shelby reels in one of his two touchdown receptions. He also had a rushing touchdown.

articles.text: P ie d m o n t ’s vol le y b a l l home opener was spoiled by Lick-Wilmerding on Wednesday, September 6, in. a 3-0 loss to the Tigers by scores of 25-14, 25-17, 25-18. They also lost 3-0 on the road to San Rafael on Tuesday, September 5. “It’s an unforced error type of game. I feel like we’re doing what we need to do in the back row, but we’re just not executing offensively,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. The loss to Lick showed some of the same characteristics to Piedmont’s recent 3-0 loss at Skyline, where the Highlanders showed moments of offensive power and defensive stability, but with inconsistent execution. “We’re trying to figure out who fits where. We’re changing things in a lot of sets because we’re trying to figure out what works best. I’m not trying to exhaust my options, we’re just trying to find that click,” said Cardeñas. Both matches were against Division 4 North Coast Section opponents. 3-0 loss to Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont came out of the gates firing and led 8-4 in the first set thanks to a pair of aces by Kim. However, Lick-Wilmerding powered back to a 9-8 lead. PHS then lead 11-10 after two kills by Sadie Town, but Lick then won 10 of the next 11 points to lead 20-12. The Tigers closed out the set 25-14, winning four of their points due to Piedmont errors. In the second set, PHS kept things close until midway through the set when Lick-Wilmerding took control. Piedmont battled from a 9-4 deficit to tie at 11-11 and 12-12—a stretch that included kills by Maddy Mullin, Izzy Grimmer, Bauer Peterson, A Hattan-Kutter, and a block by Peterson. But with Lick holding a 15-14 lead, they went on 10-3 scoring run on their way to the finish. Piedmont similarly kept the match close until midway through the third set, With Lick leading 7-5, PHS scored six straight points on a kill by Town and five straight serving aces by Grimmer. Another Town kill made it 12-8 Piedmont. But from there, Lick went on a 12 point scoring run before Piedmont’s next point, making it 20-13. PHS battled to make the deficit 22-17, but Lick scored three of the next four points to win it 25-18. They also lost 3-0 on the road to San Rafael on Tuesday, September 5. “It’s an unforced error type of game. articles.text: Girls team finishes 3rd; Schulte-Sasse 9th of 124 Piedmont’s cross country team traveled to Hidden Valley Park in Martinez for the Ed Sias Invitational last for the start of the season. The Highlanders’ girls’ team ran to a third-place finish out of 16 schools in the small-school category, while the boys’ were eighth of 18. “We have a very young team this year, and it was exciting to see so many of our new runners off to a great start. It was a two-mile course in distance and included two fairly challenging hill climbs – one at the beginning of the race and another right at the end,” said first year head coach Steve Zirkelbach. Leading the girls’ team was sophomore Skylar Best, placing 19th of 119 runners with a time of 13:34.9, while close behind in 23rd was freshman Cora Brozowski Schrader, clocking 13:57. “Cora was really impressive in her high school debut. Skylar Best was the third fastest sophomore in her race and Cora was the fifth fastest freshman,” said Zirkelbach. Rounding out Piedmont’s top five were senior Jamie Schwarz in 26th with a time of 14:02.2, sophomore Cora Chun in 36th in 14:27.6, and sophomore Quincy Antaya 44th in 14:40.1. “To come in third as a team in a field featuring some very strong NCS contenders like Maria Carrillo, Campolindo, and Carondalet, is very exciting,” Piedmont girls’ team finished 3rd of 16 schools. Pictured are Jamie Schwarz (left), Cora Chun, Gladwin Horlsey, Caroline Taylor, Skylar Best, and Quincy Antaya. said Zirkelbach. “With five out of seven varsity runners being underclassmen, the coaches can’t wait to see what will come as they continue to improve throughout this season.” Boys Team Results It was a strong day for senior captain and four-year starter Xander Schulte-Sasse, who finished ninth of 124 runners with a time of 10:46.6 on the two-mile course. “Xander went out hard right at the back of the lead pack. He was just four seconds off the lead runner from Bishop O’Dowd (Lyle Phillips) and 31 seconds off the winner from St. Ignatius College Prep (Trey Wright),” said Zirkelbach. Behind Schulte-Sasse was senior Julien Lee in 15th, clocking a time of 11:03.9. Freshman Sebastian Swain had an impressive varsity debut, placing 25th in 11:12.1. Rounding out Piedmont’s to five were junior Oliver Horlsey and his brother Henry in 65th and 68th in 12:34. “Sebastien Swain blazed out to a 25th place overall in his high school debut race, ranking as the fastest freshman boy in his race. Overall, the team performed very well for this early in the season,” said Zirkelbach. NEXT UP Piedmont looks ahead to its first Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season next Wednesday September 20 at Hayward High at 3:30 p.m. Freshman Sebastian Swain was 25th of 124 in 11:12.1.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team opened its season on Friday and Saturday, September 8-9 in a tournament at Newark Memorial High School. The Highlanders lost 12-6 to James Logan on the opening day and lost 6-5 in an overtime barnburner to Granada of Livermore the following day. They closed the tournament with a 14-2 loss to league rival Bishop O’Dowd. It was a productive tournament for Kat Melian, who scored six goals in the three matches including four of PHS’ five goals in its 6-5 loss to Granada. 12-6 loss to James Logan Piedmont trailed 4-2 at the end of the first quarter with goals by Anne Reardon and Abigail Jacoby. But James Logan blew the game open in the second quarter with seven unanswered goals to lead 9-2 by halftime. In the third, PHS conceded two goals by added scored by Melian and Sydney Olson. Vivian Burke scored both of Piedmont’s last goals. Final stats: Burke scored twice, while Melian, Olson, Jacoby, and Reardon had individual goals. Goalie Sophie Nicoll had five saves and one steal. 6-5 overtime loss to Granada The first quarter was scoreless until the final seconds of the first quarter, It was a defensive second quarter with Piedmont equalizing the game with a goal by Jacoby with 44 seconds left before halftime, but Granada reclaimed the lead with 15 seconds left. In the third, Melian tied the match shortly after Piedmont drew a penalty against Granada with 3:54 to go, but Granada got the lead again with 2:24 on the clock. articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s production of Il Trovatore is playing onstage now through October 1. The opera in four acts by Giuseppe Verdi is set to an Italian libretto written by Salvadore Cammarano and based on the play El trovador by Antonio García Gutiérrez. The play opens with a mother being burned at the stake for suspected witchcraft. She is avenged by her daughter who throws the child of the executioner into the fire. The daughter’s father seeks vengeance for the act and forces his surviving son to devote his life to avenging his brother’s death. Soprano Angel Blue sings the lead role of Leonora, who finds herself in the middle of this cross-generational family feud. The Verdi classic is a story of witchcraft, murder, vengeance and family relationships. Performance dates are September 12, 17, 20, 23, 29 and Soprano Angel Blue sings the role of Leonora in Verdi’s Il Trovatore at San Francisco Opera through October 1. October 1. The opera is conducted by Artistic Director Eun Sun Kim and produced by Sir David McVicar. Other cast members include Arturo Chacón-Cruz and George Petean. articles.text: Pianist Tom Borrow will perform a concert at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall, hosted by Cal Performances, on Sunday afternoon, October 1. The 23-year old is a protégé of Murray Perahia, a world renowned pianist and the first North American pianist to win the Leeds International Piano Competition in 1972. Borrow has won every national piano competition in Israel, his native country, where he was part of the Jerusalem Music Centre’s Outstanding Young Musicians program. Bor row’s program will include Debussy’s Images, Book 1, Chopin’s Etudes Nos. 1, 6, 10-12 from Op. 25, Rachmaninoff’s Preludes No. 2, 4 and 5 from Op. 23 and Prelude No. 10. The highlight of his UC Berkeley debut recital is Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No. 6 in A major, Op. 82, the first of the composer’s “War Sonatas.” “I’m thrilled and excited to come to Cal Performances, an institution with an incredible international reputation,” Borrows said. “I wanted to offer a program worthy of the occasion. It’s challenging for the pianist but also a real and profound journey for me and for the audience.” To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://calperformances.org/events/2023-24/ recital/tom-borrow-piano. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Photo by Tal Givony Pianist Tom Borrow will appear at Hertz Hall on October 1 in a concert sponsored by Cal Performances.

Soprano Angel Blue sings the lead role of Leonora, who finds herself in the middle of this cross-generational family feud. The Verdi classic is a story of witchcraft, murder, vengeance and family relationships. Pianist Tom Borrow at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall Oct. 1 By Allyson Aleksey Pianist Tom Borrow will perform a concert at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall, hosted by Cal Performances, on Sunday afternoon, October 1. The 23-year old is a protégé of Murray Perahia, a world renowned pianist and the first North American pianist to win the Leeds International Piano Competition in 1972. Borrow has won every national piano competition in Israel, his native country, where he was part of the Jerusalem Music Centre’s Outstanding Young Musicians program. Bor row’s program will include Debussy’s Images, Book 1, Chopin’s Etudes Nos. 1, 6, 10-12 from Op. 25, Rachmaninoff’s Preludes No. 2, 4 and 5 from Op. 23 and Prelude No. 10. The highlight of his UC Berkeley debut recital is Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No. 6 in A major, Op. 82, the first of the composer’s “War Sonatas.” “I’m thrilled and excited to come to Cal Performances, an institution with an incredible international reputation,” Borrows said. “I wanted to offer a program worthy of the occasion. It’s challenging for the pianist but also a real and profound journey for me and for the audience.” To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://calperformances.org/events/2023-24/ recital/tom-borrow-piano. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production of POTUS: Or, Behind Every Great Dumbass are Seven Women Trying to Keep Him Alive, premieres this Saturday, September 16. The comedic take on White House events is a feminist-focused satire, premiering just in time for presidential primaries. Playwright Selina Fillinger’s newest play, POTUS, premieres on Saturday, September 16, at Berkeley Repertory Theater. When the president unknowingly spins a public relations nightmare into a global crisis, seven brilliant but beleaguered women must risk it all to keep the commander-in-chief out of trouble. The play features Harriet Deirdre Lovejoy as chief of staff, Kim Blanck as press secretary, Susan Lynskey as secretary, Stephanie Pope Lofgren as the first lady, Dominique Toney as a journalist, Stephanie Styles as the president’s dalliance and Allison Guinn as his sister. POTUS is written by Selina Fillinger and directed by Annie Tippe. Post-show discussions are held on September 29, October 5 and October 10, guided by members of Berkeley Rep’s artistic team. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/potus/.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s POTUS premieres this Saturday

articles.text: BroadwaySF welcomes conservationist icon Jane Goodall in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist, conservationist and activist Jane Goodall will be on stage to discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960 and her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. Goodall is an iconic activist in conservation. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. As a U.N. Messenger of Peace since 2002, she continues to help the United Nations focus attention on environmental issues, primarily world wildlife and their habitat. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of her talk. Tickets are available online at: https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s production of A Chorus Line ends this Saturday. Directed by the Playhouse’s Bill English and based on the book by James Kirkwood Jr. and Nicholas Dante, the musical follows 17 Broadway dancers who are auditioning for eight spots in a chorus line. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company’s (MTC) adaptation of Homer’s ancient poem Odyssey is playing onstage now through September 24. Writer and director Lisa Peterson’s adaptation of Odyssey is based on Emily Wilson’s 2018 translation of the ancient poem, the first English translation published by a woman. The world premiere of the play opens MTC’s new season. The play features Layla Khoshnoudi, Zamo Mlengana, Anya Whelan-Smith and Sophie Zmorrod, and is set in a present-day relocation center for refugees on the Isle of Lesbos. The four young women are fleeing war and conflict in their home countries and await the next step of their journey on the Isle. They take turns reading and reenacting the ancient epic The Odyssey, finding that it intertwines with their own personal journeys. Layla Khoshnoudi, Zamo Mlengana, Anya Whelan-Smith and Sophie Zmorrod in Marin Theatre Company’s current production of Odyssey Tunsian refugee Anoud, played by Khoshnoudi, is the ‘ringleader’ of the four; Rwandan refugee Zee is played by Mlegngana; Whelan-Smith is Hana from Albania; and Zmorrod plays Syrian refugee Béa. The music and lyrics are by Masi Asare. To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://www.marintheatre.org/productions/odyssey. Show times are 7:30 p.m. on Wednesdays through Saturdays; and 2 p.m. on weekends. Marin Theatre Company, 397 Miller Avenue, Mill Valley, Phone: (415) 388-5200
articles.title: Marin Theatre presents Odyssey through Sept. 24

Opera is often called the most sophisticated of all the arts. It combines vocal and instrumental music, drama, graphic and visual art, and often elaborate dancing. Did I leave anything out? As in all education, it’s good to introduce kids to opera at an early age. That is the thrust of an excellent opera company in Walnut Creek, which is devoted to bringing opera to kids… and bringing kids to opera. Did you ever hear of Solo Opera? They recently presented an opera specially for kids of all ages. The Three Feathers is a classic story of international and intercultural significance. If you investigate the story, you will see what I mean. The performance on Friday night was a delight in many ways. Composer Lori Laitman and librettist Dana Gioia endeavored to present this story in a new light. I did some of my own research and discovered that there are many versions of the story… Including the one that was represented on Friday. Every version of the story makes certain social observations. It all concerns a king and three of his kids. Whether they are all boys or all girls or a mixture, many points can be made. The version that was presented on Friday was a king and his three daughters. In many ways, the story is a bit like Cinderella combined with the Magic Flute. Composer Laitman wrote a lively musical score, and librettist Joya provided good lyrics. The entire cast was excellent. The opera began with a vigorous overture, conducted by Alexander Katsman, featuring some of the finest professional musicians in the Bay Area who are not members of the San Francisco Symphony. Second childhood and all that jazz Saturday night at the PCA Back home in Piedmont on Saturday night, we were treated to a concert at the Center for the Arts with a jazz ensemble with singer Jamie Davis and a quintet of superb jazz musicians. Even though I am not a jazz musician, I appreciate the many aspects of this musical art. My high school music teacher, Samuel R, Browne, was one of the most important jazz pianists of his era. I always like to arrive at the Piedmont Center for the Arts early when the performers are often engaged in a warm- up. Pianist Glenn Pearson seated himself at the piano and began to play. I said to myself: “Pearson sounds a lot like Count Basie.” When Pearson finished his warm-up, all of the musicians began to converse. Wouldn’t you know it… Pearson was directly inspired by Count Basie. All the other musicians are stars in their own right: John Wiitala played bass, Leon Royce Jr. was the very elegant drummer, and Michael O’Neill played saxophone. The featured singer was mellow-voiced Jamie Davis. I think that he brought everyone together. For me, the show was a beautiful look into the past. The first thing I noticed was that every one of the musicians was elegantly dressed, and their demeanor was distinctly professional. Everything seemed to be improvised, but that is the nature of jazz. But these musicians play so well together, you might think that they rehearse on a regular basis. This type of artistry is inspiring. As Davis took the microphone, he introduced each song. He knows exactly how much to talk and exactly what to say. (Oh, how I wish other people would learn this.) Needless to say, the audience loved it all. I have one suggestion only. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has very “live” acoustics. Artificial amplification is never needed. articles.text: It was Jules Feiffer who wrote, “Maturity is a phase. Adolescence is forever.” Indeed. What is there about being an adolescent that leaves such a profound imprint that the memories seem to last a lifetime? Is it that life is lived so intensely, involving a degree of engagement unlike anything that comes before or after? For some, it is only reluctantly left behind, the struggles never completely resolved, and even distorted by time, never forgotten. The film Eighth Grade, written and directed by Bo Burnham, captures perfectly that moment when newbie teen, 13-year-old Kayla (Elsie Fisher), in her last week of middle school, finds herself coping with riptides of emotions, her teen life awash with contradictions that can push her to the edge of panic and desperation while she grasps for control. All the while she creates a façade behind which she can hide what she is actually feeling. This is a remarkable film. But know that it’s not a documentary. It is regrettable that it included material that, while honest, earned it an R rating. Eighth Grade is a fictional narrative that is so steeped in truth it’s painful to watch. It possesses an honesty so stark as to be discomforting. That is how good it is. To be 13 is to live with an abiding sense of anxiety and uncertainty, feelings colliding with the need for affirmation, for acceptance, all of which, in the aggregate, are achingly elusive. As Kayla demonstrates in scene after scene (the film is a series of vignettes of her days in class and at home), to be a tweenteen is to experience change, both physically and emotionally. So direct and yet nuanced is this film, so authentic and even quietly harrowing, that the emotions Kayla experiences permeate every frame and are transferred to the audience. Her interactions can seem both conflicted and comical. In one scene, Kayla’s dad, Mark (Josh Hamilton), is driving her to the mall to meet some kids. Nose in her phone, pauses and glances over at her dad and rolls her eyes, saying to him, “Do you have to stare straight ahead like that?” Mark, ever resilient, but a bit of a helicopter parent, wanting above all to make contact with his daughter, patiently answers, “I’m just staring at the road ahead.” Kayla responds, saying, “Well, can you do it another way?” Supremely contraindicated, Kayla posts installments on YouTube wherein she takes on the persona of a life coach, giving advice to anyone out there in the social media ether who might be listening. In one post, looking directly into the computer’s camera, she says, “A big part of confidence is being brave, and you can’t be brave without being scared.” In truth, she understands in spades the scared part (she’s voted the quietest girl in her class, her default setting). What is aspirational for Kayla is the brave part, as she conducts her youthful quest for that geography known as “cool” and “popular.” The contradiction is that her desire to be “fun” is in conflict with her wish to be, at times, anonymous – to just disappear, such as when she’s invited to a popular girl’s house for a pool-birthday party. Her mantra is “Be brave,” yet while standing behind a glass sliding door, dressed in a swimsuit, looking out at a patio-pool filled with kids, she wishes she were anywhere else. What is at the center of Eighth Grade is Kayla’s abiding self-consciousness. She so much wants a social life, a best friend, a boyfriend; yet, feeling the absence of even one kindred spirit she retreats to social media, her only refuge. In the words of coach Kayla, “Life is putting yourself out there – but where is ‘there’?” What she doesn’t realize is that her peers are also clueless about the whereabouts of “there,” no matter how confident they may appear. Eighth Grade. Directed by Bo Burnham. Starring Elsie Fisher, Daniel Zolghadin, Imani Lewis. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/MAX/Apple tv.
