articles.text: Film review By Chris Honoré Before discussing writer/ director Sam Mendes’ film 1917, I would be remiss not to mention Peter Jackson’s extraordinary movie, They Will Not Grow Old. He was given access to hundreds of archival World War I news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum – scratched, grainy, and hand cranked film that using state-of-the-art restorative technology, he not only colorized but brought back to life. It’s as if he opened a portal in time. We see young Brits gathered on a battlefield, waiting, some staring into the camera, smiling, their youthful faces filled with an optimistic eagerness that would soon be devastatingly transformed. World War I, which began in July 1914 and lasted until November 1918, was one of the deadliest wars in history. Nine million combatants and seven million civilians were killed as a direct result. Indirectly, 50 to 100 million deaths occurred worldwide, attributed to what was referred to as the “Spanish Flu,” the pandemic thought to have begun in the damp, muddy, disease-ridden trenches on the battlefields, conditions that were almost as lethal as the withering machine gun fire, shelling and chlorine gas faced by the troops. WWI was an extraordinary display of nationalistic hubris, bordering on a collective insanity in which millions of men, on all sides, were sacrificed for mere yards of soil. It was a nightmare of the awful, a killing field of stasis that continued beyond all reason. This is the context for Mendes’ most remarkable film, 1917, set in northern France, at the height of the war. The story is deceptively simple: two young soldiers – Lance Corporal Schofield (George McKay) and Lance Corporal Blake (Dean Charles Chapman) – are ordered by their general to deliver a letter to a command post some eight miles away, instructing the commanding officer for his troops of two battalions, numbering 1,600 to stand down. They are told that all lines of communication have been cut. The intelligence in the letter explains that the Germans have fashioned a trap and should the dawn assault take place, casualties will be grave. The caveat is that to arrive at the command post, the distance to be crossed is a No Man’s Land, comprised of German troops thought to have retreated, desiccated terrain and trenches. The general adds that among the battalions waiting is Corporal Blake’s brother. And so, the two climb up a ladder onto the lip of a deep trench, urging one another on, Schofield expressing his reluctance, yet both feeling the urgency of their mission. What they leave behind are green fields and wildflowers; it’s a beautiful spring afternoon in April. But what they find as they move ever deeper into enemy territory is a landscape of utter destruction – deep craters filled with water and bodies, dead horses, stretching barbed wire, and a horror of mud, death and unrecognizable carrion covered with flies and feeding birds. It is a visit to Hell. Their sense of urgency is palpable; to fail would be catastrophic; they must survive in order to deliver the letter carried inside Corporal Blake’s tunic. Any hint of exposition – backstory, shared memories of origin or tales of home – is inconsequential. What we hear are the sounds of their breathing, the rasp and clank of their gear as Blake and Schofield crouch forward, rifles with bayonets ever at the ready. This is the narrative arc. However, what writer/director Mendes and legendary cinematographer Roger Deakins do is create the illusion that the camera is the third person on the journey and the entire film is shot in one long take, never cutting away. That is not the case, but the impact of this most effective photographic technique is not a conceit and is striking. In other words, 1917 is a truly visual film. It is the camera that propels it forward, Blake and Schofield moving constantly, the story revealed as they grimly survey all that is before them. The question posed is can Mendes and Deakins capture and then sustain the attention of the audience as the fraught images escalate, the faces of the two made grimly fearful by what they witness, leaving them to wonder what, among all this carnage, awaits them. I would suggest that 1917 is an engaging, photographic marvel and an extraordinary achievement. In addition, the film possesses a wonderful score by Thomas Newman and truly fine performances by both MacKay and Chapman. 1917. Directed by Sam Mendes. Starring Dean-Charles Chapman, George MacKay, Daniel Mays, Colin Firth. I hr., 59 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Nominated for Academy Award as Best Feature movie.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 13, 2023 21 Features Walking on Wednesday Tennis, anyone? Walkers visit Davie Tennis Stadium, still locked By Dick Carter The weather was sunny and mild for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays walk on September 6. A good turnout of 37 walkers and two K-9 best friends showed up to enjoy it. The walkers hadn’t been to Piedmont’s south side for a few weeks, and it had been over a year since they visited the Davie Tennis Stadium. They held off going to the stadium because it was “temporarily closed” in February by the City of Oakland after winter storms knocked down a eucalyptus tree near the entrance to the courts. It was reported the City of Oakland didn’t remove the tree because it was a low priority as it didn’t affect anyone’s health and safety. No reopening has been announced, but it was time for the walkers to go south. The chosen route was via Requa Road. They went past the Community Hall, made their way up the short hill to Guilford Road, and took an almost hidden path down to Hazel Lane and Requa Road, with beautiful views of San Francisco. The group emerged on Wildwood Avenue, walked over to a bench that overlooks Witter Field, and viewed its resurfacing project. The walkers couldn’t decide if it looked more like Death Valley or the Gobi Desert, but there seems to be lots more work to be done. The walkers took the lower portion of Wildwood to a path at the end of the street leading to down to Ranleigh Way and Annerley Road. On Annerley they stopped in front of the house where former Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara grew up. Robert McNamara, born in San Francisco in 1916, served as the eighth Secretary of Defense, from 1961 to 1968, under presidents Kennedy and Johnson. McNamara played a major role in promoting the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War. He graduated from Piedmont High School in 1933 and UC Berkeley in 1937, where he earned a varsity letter in crew. He and Clint Eastwood may be Piedmont’s most famous former residents. Martin Levy wanted the group to go down Portsmouth Walk to his Lakeshore Avenue home, which had a “Death’s Door” sign on the gate. and many surrounding cacti. Martin had a couple of bags of cuttings from his cacti collection. The walkers continued up Lakeshore to Park Lane and Oak Road to the entrance of Davie Tennis Stadium. Its gate was still locked, 6 months after the winter storms. The stadium’s history was shared with the group. Stone quarries were an important part of Oakland’s growth and development, and this led to more than a few quarries throughout the area. A quarry was opened here in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company. It reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892. The land was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by former Oakland mayor John L. Davie and his family. The facility was finally built in 1936- 1937 as a WPA project during the great Depression. The land is primarily in Piedmont, but Davie giving it to the City of Oakland may explain why the stadium is managed by the City of Oakland. It was time for the walkers to start their return, following Oak Road to Oakmont Avenue, to Prospect Road and then onto Wildwood Avenue. It was warming up, so they returned through Piedmont Park where it was cooler. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Last week’s Wednesday walkers included Joyce Ahern, Sharona Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Allison Isaacs, Sharon Anderson, Karen Palmer, Martin Levy, Joanne Larson, Pat Keller, Greg Keller, Jim Kellogg, Rick Eigenbrode, Rob Smith, Mike Henn, Eric Behrens with K-9 best friend Mocha, David Haecker, Matt Gerhardt, Will Adams, Adrienne Hamlin, Stella Houston, Bill Ahern, Alicia Rivera, Peggy Shultz, Sherry Jacobs, Judy Love, Lois Price, Tina Shum, Helen Dong, Chuck Oraftik, Priscilla Wanerus, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Brenda Ferrero, Nancy Henn, Bob Wong, Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, and Dick Carter. What to know about HSAs and FSAs Paying for health care can be challenging – but are you taking full advantage of all the resources available to you? You might have access to a Health Savings Account (HSA) or a Flexible Spending Account (FSA), so let’s look at both. Health Savings Account (HSA) An HSA is a personal savings account used to pay health care costs. If you’re enrolled in a high-deductible health plan, you also may be eligible to contribute to an HSA. You aren’t taxed on the money you put into this account or on the earnings generated from your contributions, as long as withdrawals are used for qualified health care costs such as deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. And there’s no “use it or lose it” provision with HSAs – the money stays in your account until you use it. In fact, you can carry your HSA with you all the way until retirement, when you can use the money to pay for qualified expenses that Medicare or Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) doesn’t cover. In 2023, you can contribute up to $3,850 to an HSA, or $4,850 if you’re 55 or older; for family coverage, you can put in up to $7,750. It’s important to keep in mind that your HSA’s tax benefits only apply when your withdrawals are used for qualified heath care costs. If you use the money for non-qualified expenses, it is considered taxable income, and you may also face a penalty of 20% on the amount withdrawn. However, once you turn 65, you can use your HSA funds for any purpose without a penalty, though the withdrawals will still count as taxable income. Flexible Spending Account (FSA) Now, let’s turn to the Flexible Savings Account. An FSA may be available to you if you get health insurance through your employer. And because you fund your FSA with pretax dollars, your contributions can reduce your taxable income. (In 2023, you can contribute up to $3,050 to an FSA.) Your employer may also choose to contribute to your FSA. Once your account is funded and active, you submit claims with proof of your medical expenses, along with a statement that these expenses aren’t covered by your plan, and you can be reimbursed for your costs. It’s helpful to have a good estimate of your yearly medical expenses for a Flexible Savings Account. That’s because an FSA generally needs to be spent before the end of the plan year – if you don’t use all the money, you can only carry over some of it and any remaining balance is forfeited. (You can carry over up to $610 from 2023 into 2024.) You can’t contribute to an HSA and a traditional FSA in the same year. But if you have an HSA, you might be able to use what’s known as a Limited Purpose Flexible Spending Account (LPFSA) for dental and vision expenses. You’ll need to check with your plan to see if this option is available. Managing your health care expenses should be a key part of your overall financial strategy – so consider putting an HSA or FSA to work for you. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. TJ Stevko is a Financial Advisor with the Piedmont office of Edward Jones, 370 Highland Ave., Suite 201. Tel. 510-547- 4589.

articles.text: As artists commonly practice, he honed his copying skills at the Louvre. In Paris, he called himself James, a first name he had used since his youth, dropping his birth-name of Jacques Joseph. He’d always tilted toward anything Anglicized which was all the rage in France at the time; and his upbringing close to the Atlantic channel spanned England and France by commercial trade. Some of his early paintings were earnest efforts but were panned as pastiche, showing village scenes and people with enigmatic interactions, arranged at a dockside crowded with large boats (reminiscent of his youth); but criticized for lacking a central story or theme. His drawing technique showed promise, but the background and settings were too bland and flat, unaided by any social context. He painted several classical scenes in church interiors, one of which was purchased at his first public showing. By the next year and through the 1860s, Tissot proved very entrepreneurial in Paris. James Tissot, an unfamiliar modernist, was a famous and financially successful society painter during an era when Impressionists were the darlings of art critics and continued to define late nineteenth-century art. Born in 1836 in Nantes, a port city of Atlantique-Loire, his father was a prosperous textile merchant in the drapery business, and his mother created millinery fashions. From childhood he retained a fascination with fashion and boats, and elements of ships and fashion would show frequently in his mature work. His parents sent him for schooling at the Jesuit Brugelette in Flanders, which borders northeast France; and he grew in admiration for the Belgian painter Henri Leys and Dutch masters of the past century painting captivating scenes of village life. When he showed a talent for sketching, his father tried to steer him to architecture; but determinedly, he moved to Paris at age twenty to become an artist and attend Ecole des Beaux-Arts. In Paris, he called himself James, a first name he had used since his youth, dropping his birth-name of Jacques Joseph. He’d always tilted toward anything Anglicized which was all the rage in France at the time; and his upbringing close to the Atlantic channel spanned England and France by commercial trade. Some of his early paintings were earnest efforts but were panned as pastiche, showing village scenes and people with enigmatic interactions, arranged at a dockside crowded with large boats (reminiscent of his youth); but criticized for lacking a central story or theme. articles.text: Tom Lister, a longtime resident of Piedmont with a laugh that drew everyone closer, passed away on July 1, 2023. Born on November 7, 1934, his family moved to Grosse Pointe, Michigan when Tom’s father was transferred to Detroit by the Santa Fe Railroad. He grew up swimming in Lake St. Clair, playing the bass fiddle, playing football and baseball, and running track. Favorite early memories included trips to Pasadena for the Rose Bowl when his father arranged transportation there for the Michigan football teams. In 1951 Tom returned to California with a group of high school classmates led by a teacher, visiting Mount Rushmore, Banff and Lake Louise, the Calgary Stampede and Glacier, Grand Teton and Yellowstone National Parks and other spots, eventually arriving in San Francisco, never knowing he would one day live in California. Tom received his first driver’s license at age 14, allowing him to drive his mother and grandmother to ladies’ luncheons and other social events. His father refused Tom’s request to use his lawn mowing earnings for the purchase of a Ford pickup truck, urging him instead to focus on his studies. He did, and was one of the speakers at his high school graduation. His dream of owning a truck was finally realized in the 1990’s with the purchase of a black Chevrolet pickup. Always interested in helping others, Tom became known as Sherpa Tom, and his truck became the Urban Yak. Tom spent vacation time in Michigan “turning nuts and bolts” on new cars at the Chrysler plant and working as a “lumper” on a beer delivery truck. At the time, he was not of legal drinking age, so the truck’s driver was only too happy to collect Tom’s share of the daily allotment of “suds.” Following high school graduation, Tom attended Princeton University, where he studied history and economics. His senior thesis focused on the Moravian community in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. Another part of his Princeton experience was working with other classmates to help his Classics professor repair a storm-damaged summer home in Maine -- many aches and pains from rebuilding a stone wall, and the consumption of a lot of boiled lobster, too. Tom returned to Chrysler following his Princeton graduation, planning to become a labor relations lawyer, until he observed union employees dancing on a mahogany conference room table Tom Lister died on July 1 at age 88. in their hobnailed boots. Working in Chrysler’s Guided Missile Division, he obtained military draft deferments for many of their engineers, when the draft board informed him that he was next on their list. He opted to join the Navy and went to Officer Candidate School in Newport, Rhode Island. Service in the Navy brought Tom once again to California, where he was assigned as a young lieutenant to the Pacific fleet, operating out of San Diego. He recalled time spent on “Formosa Patrol,” monitoring aircraft carrier movements, and launching rockets off Waikiki Beach in celebration of the statehood of Hawaii. Tom married Jeanie Hoyne, a Vassar graduate from Illinois, in 1957. Following their divorce, he married Ann Brockhoff Lewis, who he met while going to watch Fourth of July fireworks from the roof of the apartment building where they both resided. Subsequent to his Naval service Tom enrolled in the Graduate School of Business at Stanford University, where he earned a Master’s degree in Business Administration. This led to a lengthy career with Chevron, including work in the marketing and accounting functions and many years as Chevron’s Risk and Insurance Manager with worldwide responsibilities. He traveled extensively, including many trips to Europe, the Middle East, Asia and the Caribbean. He represented Chevron as a board member of Oil Insurance Limited in Bermuda, was active in the financing of Kentucky Agricultural Energy Company, and in the merger of Chevron and Gulf Oil, where he later served as an Assistant Treasurer. Tom led a very active life following his retirement from Chevron in 1990. He was a strong believer in being of service to his family, friends, church and community, always with a wonderful smile. He served as President of the San Francisco Chapter of the Chevron Retirees and of the Stanford Business School Alumni of the East Bay and on several Alumni Consulting Team projects. He was a board member of the Camron-Stanford House and the Bellevue Club Foundation, both in Oakland. He was a jovial Santa Claus for the children of friends and those of city employees and others in the community. For the City of Piedmont, he served on the Municipal Tax Review Committee, the Park Commission, and as a Retired Senior Volunteer for the Police Department for nearly 30 years. At Piedmont Community Church Tom was a Deacon, leading to the formation of the Loaves and Fishes cooking guild, which has provided food for hundreds of church meals and receptions for over three decades. He worked tirelessly on the church’s Habitat for Humanity project and later on other church projects. He also taught Sunday school for a time and was proud to be a participant in the Men’s Bible Study group. Tom and Ann enjoyed frequent travels, with at least annual visits to Carmel and Palm Desert. They took cruises on the Mediterranean, on the Mississippi, and to Alaska and by way of the Panama Canal. There were also wonderful trips with former classmates to Charleston, South Carolina, Santa Fe, New Mexico, and St. Petersburg, Russia. Tom is survived by his loving and beloved wife, Ann Lister; son Thomas Lister and wife Amanda of New York, grandchildren Davis Lister and Anna Lister of New York; daughter Karen van Zee and husband Pieter van Zee of Corvallis, Oregon. He is also survived by grandchildren Erynne van Zee of Seattle, Washington, and Maarten van Zee of Eugene, Oregon; step-daughter Susan Lewis Swift and husband Joel Swift of Auburn, California, and grandchildren Zachary and Dylan Swift. He is additionally survived by his sister Cynthia Lister Krause of Hilliard, Ohio; nephew Bentley Andrew Krause and wife Joann of Athens, Ohio; niece Emily Krause Corzine and husband Jeffrey Corzine of Dublin, Ohio, and great-niece Camryn Corzine. A memorial service for Tom will be held on Saturday, September 23, at 2:00 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations be made to Piedmont Community Church, the Salvation Army, or George Mark Children’s House.

Place the clean, dry quarter-sheet baking pan (9” x 13”) on the rack to preheat it as well. Rinse the vegetables then pat dry. Cut the potatoes into quarters, or into about 1-inch chunks. Slice the squash into 1-inch pieces. Cut the red bell pepper into about 1-inch pieces. In a large mixing bowl, toss the potatoes and vegetables with the extra-virgin olive oil making sure they are evenly coated. When the oven and baking sheet reach the desired temperature, carefully remove the sheet pan and place only the potatoes on it. It’s slightly tedious to sort through the mixed vegetables, which is why using a large bowl helps. Spread the potatoes out evenly and bake for 10 minutes. Meanwhile add the rosemary, salt, and pepper to the remaining vegetables in the bowl and stir to disperse evenly. After 10 minutes, remove the potatoes from the oven and use a spatula to turn them onto a different side in contact with the sheet pan. Add the remaining vegetables to the sheet pan, again spreading them into an even layer. Return to the oven and bake an additional 10–15 minutes until the potatoes and squash are tender. The vegetables should all get a deep golden toast to them. We like this served hot, but it can also be served at room temperature. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/. pages.text: Wednesday, September 13, 2023 25 Easy Sheet Pan Summer Vegetables By Deborah Quok Sheet pan cooking is popular for good reasons – it’s easy and is a way to get plenty of tasty food cooked fast. This is my go-to method for roasting vegetables, this time with purple potatoes that have recently been available at my farmers’ market. In about 30 minutes you’ll have fragrant sides for dinner. I preheat a clean, dry baking sheet whilst the oven is also preheating. This helps the potatoes form crispy edges and shortens overall baking time. The potatoes need longer to bake, so they go into the oven on their own before the vegetables. While this uses a 9 x 13-inch, quarter sheet pan, you could adjust to a larger sheet pan and include chunks of chicken, fish or sausages for a complete meal. Be sure to pick a protein that can be fully cooked in the same amount of time as the vegetables. Similarly, this is the perfect method for mix and matching vegetables you enjoy: eggplant, wedges of fennel bulbs or onions, cherry tomatoes, etc. Scale this according to the quantity you need. When I’m cooking for two, my go-to is a convection toaster oven that makes this dish a breeze. Easy Sheet Pan Summer Vegetables INGREDIENTS • 10-ish ounces summer squash such as zucchini, crookneck, pattypan (I used 3 smallish zucchini) • 10-ish ounces new potatoes such as purple, red, Yukon Gold or fingerlings (I used 4 small-medium) • 1 small red bell pepper • 6 whole garlic cloves, peeled • 2 tablespoons olive oil, a robust extra-virgin • • 2 teaspoons fresh rosemary, minced Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste, about 1/2 teaspoon each INSTRUCTIONS Place an oven rack to the lower third position of the oven and preheat the oven to 400°F on the convection setting, or 425°F if convection is not available. Place the clean, dry quarter-sheet baking pan (9” x 13”) on the rack to preheat it as well. Rinse the vegetables then pat dry. Cut the potatoes into quarters, or into about 1-inch chunks. Slice the squash into 1-inch pieces. Cut the red bell pepper into about 1-inch pieces. In a large mixing bowl, toss the potatoes and vegetables with the extra-virgin olive oil making sure they are evenly coated. When the oven and baking sheet reach the desired temperature, carefully remove the sheet pan and place only the potatoes on it. It’s slightly tedious to sort through the mixed vegetables, which is why using a large bowl helps. Spread the potatoes out evenly and bake for 10 minutes. Meanwhile add the rosemary, salt, and pepper to the remaining vegetables in the bowl and stir to disperse evenly. After 10 minutes, remove the potatoes from the oven and use a spatula to turn them onto a different side in contact with the sheet pan. Add the remaining vegetables to the sheet pan, again spreading them into an even layer. Return to the oven and bake an additional 10–15 minutes until the potatoes and squash are tender. The vegetables should all get a deep golden toast to them. We like this served hot, but it can also be served at room temperature. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/. Or herself.” —Alexandria Hammett, Serendipity Books, Chelsea, MI The Book of More Delights: Essays By Ross Gay, Algonquin Books, Essays “Oh, to have delights again! No one writes about the dearness of our human frailty with the generosity and good humor of Ross Gay. I can’t wait to wear these delights out to the same degree as the first, and become more present in doing so.” —Abbey Paxton, Storyhouse Bookpub, Windsor Heights, IA My Roommate Is a Vampire By Jenna Levine, Berkley, Romance “Clever, charming, steamy – all a reader could want from a paranormal romantic comedy. Part Kate & Leopold; part What We Do in the Shadows; and witty, warm prose that makes it feel refreshing. It sunk its teeth into me and I was a willing victim!” —Sarah Jackson, The Book & Cover, Chattanooga, TN He Who Drowned the World By Shelley Parker-Chan, Tor Books, Fantasy “The perfect follow up to She Who Became the Sun. Parker-Chan’s latest continues to expertly explore themes of power, desire, and gender queerness. An absolutely riveting and intricate sequel. This book will make you feel all the things!” —Julia DeVarti, Books Are Magic, Brooklyn, NY Every Drop is a Man’s Nightmare By Megan Kamalei Kakimoto, Bloomsbury Publishing, Short Stories “Overflowing with female sexuality and Hawaiian mythology, Every Drop is a Man’s Nightmare punches out one fearless story after the next. The awesomeness of space exploration, the Challenger tragedy, the unreasonable press questions – experience it all with this accomplished group.” —Rosemary Pugliese, Malaprop’s Bookstore/Café, Asheville, NC The Secret Hours By Mick Herron, Soho Crime, Thriller “As the Monochrome is disbanded, two members are slipped info about a mission in Cold War Berlin with serious consequences. Filled with hairpin plot twists, cutting dialogue, and dark humor, this spy novel is my favorite book of 2023 so far.” —Timothy Benz, Joseph-Beth Booksellers, Cincinnati, OH The September House By Carissa Orlando, Berkley, Horror “This was a ride! With a seemingly unreliable narrator and a house full of either real or imagined horrors, The September House is a story of mental illness, domestic abuse, and the resilience of women. This was an incredibly layered novel.” —Lauren Nopenz Fairley, Curious Iguana, Frederick, MD The Breakaway By Jennifer Weiner, Atria Books, Fiction “A scenic bike tour, tricky love triangle, emotionally honest family drama, and fascinating food for thought about body image all come together in this breezy summer read with something to say about the joys of early-middle age.” —Jesse Post, Postmark Books, Rosendale, NY Mother-Daughter Murder Night By Nina Simon, William Morrow, Mystery “I adored this twisty thriller set in the beauty of the marshlands of California. Highly recommend!” —Elizabeth Barnhill, Fabled Bookshop & Café, Waco, TX Creep: Accusations and Confessions By Myriam Gurba, Avid Reader Press/Simon & Schuster, Essays “Through a historical and literary lens, Creep exposes racist dog whistles you may not be aware of, biases you don’t even realize, and shines a light on oppression marginalized people face. It is full of heart, humor, and hard truths.” —Alana Haley, Schuler Books, Grand Rapids, MI The Square of Sevens By Laura Shepherd-Robinson, Atria Books, Historical Fiction “Come for the orphaned, Dickensian fortune teller in 18th-century Cornwall and stay for a sweeping epic of Georgian high society, mystery, and divination. Deeply researched and intricate, this is outstanding historical fiction.” —Debra Ginsberg, Diesel, A Bookstore, Santa Monica, CA Terrace Story By Hilary Leichter, Ecco, Fiction “This novel blew me away. Each successive story opens up Everything/Nothing/Someone: A Memoir By Alice Carrière, Spiegel & Grau, Memoir “Everything/Nothing/Someone depicts the non-linear trajectory of mental health, relationships, and memory. Carrière intimately unravels the personal to convey the journey of getting better, even when it doesn’t feel like an option.” —Jesse Bartel, BookHampton, East Hampton, NY The Heart of It All By Christian Kiefer, Melville House, Fiction “The Heart of It All’s beauty is its subtlety. articles.text: Construction workers at a residence on Estates Drive were robbed at gunpoint on Tuesday, September 5, shortly before noon. A newer model Lexus sedan pulled into a driveway, two men got out, and aimed handguns at the workers, demanding their tools. A ridged camera snake system to look in drainage systems, valued at $12,000 was stolen (see photo). The burglars wheeled the tool to the getaway vehicle and left. No one was injured. The burglars were wearing hoodies and masks, along with reflective worker vests. The Lexus had a getaway driver who did not leave the vehicle. The license plate on the suspects’ vehicle had been switched so it did not trigger the city’s surveillance camera as a stolen vehicle. Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan said the crime appears to be linked to other crimes in Oakland. “We are coordinating with OPD. The search goes on,” he said. Monahan urged residents to be aware of unusual activity and to call the police immediately upon seeing an activity that seems suspicious. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact Detective John Lagios at 420-3015. Surveillance video shows a suspect pointing a handgun at a construction worker on Estates Drive after getting out of a white Lexus sedan. Two suspect load a stolen $12,000 tool, a ridged camera snake system, into the getaway vehicle.

articles.text: became the love of his life. He was inspired to paint her loveliness onto every canvas, creating some of his most beautiful and emotional works. Sadly, Kate became ill with tuberculosis and suffered for two years before overdosing and taking her own life in 1882, at just age 28. His grief was enormous, and within a week of her death, Tissot abandoned his home, paints, brushes, and unfinished canvases, and left London to return to Paris. A retrospective of Tissot’s work was first exhibited recently at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor, and then to Paris’s D’Orsay Musée. Due to coronavirus, the Paris opening was delayed to late June and closes next week. One distinction between the two exhibitions is how they were themed. The San Francisco retrospective was titled “Fashion and Faith.” The Fashion is evident by the telling of his youth and how Tissot elegantly clothes his subjects. Faith is another matter. Significantly, he was raised by his mother to be a pious Catholic and regained his faith late in life when he suffered a tragedy that dramatically shifted his work. 60-works exhibition is themed “L’Ambigu Moderne” meaning “An Ambiguous Figure of Modernity” or possibly “Ambiguously Modern.” The French acknowledge the artist’s shift from temporal subjects to ecclesiastic. After London, Tissot’s return to the art world of Paris was unforeseeably difficult. He assembled a hundred of his paintings for a big show that stunningly was met with disinterest by the public and the critics. “A Parisian of London now becomes a Londoner of Paris…” doned his oils and had some success. He enterprisingly spent two years creating 15 over-sized oil canvases for a series La Femme à Paris, showing lively scenes of Parisian women across social The Princess de Broglie, pastels, 1895: Pauline, the wife of Prime Minister of France. articles.text: The wait for the big breakfast event is almost over. The Beach Dads Club gears up for their annual fundraising event this Sunday morning, September 10. More than 40 dads signed up this year to help flip the flapjacks and sizzle the bacon from 9 a.m. to 12 noon on the Beach school playground. The 18th annual event will be the hottest, and tastiest spot in town Sunday as the Dads get ready to cook thousands of pancakes in a couple of hours to a hungry crowd. 700 sausage links, and 100 pounds of bacon have been ordered as well. The dads have received big donations by the three local markets: Piedmont Grocery, Mulberry’s Market, and Village Market. “We don’t use a mix,” said Dad’s Club president Michael Gross, “The pancake batter is all made from raw ingredients.” Scouts from Troop 4 will be on hand to help the operation run smoothly. “We have a lot of really good energy this year, lots of new and returning dads,” said Gross. “Our volunteer signup sheet filled up two weeks ago, which is unprecedented. articles.text: In last night’s meeting of Piedmont City Council, two proposals were presented that are designed to make it easier to create new housing in Piedmont. The proposals are separate, but both have been discussed and considered extensively by residents and council members. They include pre-approved design plans for affordable Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) primarily for apartments. As city ordinances, they both must come before council and be voted on twice. Tuesday’s 5-0 vote in favor set the stage for the MOD and ADU proposals to become law at the next vote. The proposed amendments would declare Piedmont Municipal Code and the revisions to the City’s Design Guidelines are exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Both proposals were discussed by the Planning Commission in meetings in June, July, and August this year. The Commission unanimously voted to recommend both proposals to the City Council on August 14. The Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) and new affordable Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) incentives, are the result of several years of public engagement, including workshops, in-person events, visual preference surveys, and polls. New incentive for affordable ADUs To encourage the creation of affordable ADUs, the City has developed a series of permit-ready designs appropriate to Piedmont’s built and natural environment. These designs could be submitted as-is, along with existing and proposed site plans and other materials, to receive a Planning permit, giving applicants a head start on the permitting and development process. Detailed construction and engineering plans unique to the site’s slope and soil conditions would still need to be developed for each ADU before a building permit is issued. ADUs that use the City’s pre-approved designs would be rent-restricted for 10 years. During this period, if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet “very low income” affordability thresholds for the Alameda County area set by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. Very low income is defined as 50% or less of the area median income (AMI). In Alameda County that amount is $49,600 for two people and the maximum rent would be $1,364 per month (roughly 1/3 of the income). Designs include: • A detached studio ADU, 500 sq. ft., shown in Tudor, Craftsman, and Spanish styles. • A detached one-bedroom ADU, 800 sq. ft., shown in Tudor, Craftsman, and Spanish styles. • A garage conversion, 484 sq. ft. The maximum height of the preapproved ADUs is 16 feet. Multifamily Objective Design Standards Under this proposal, eligible multi-family and mixed-use commercial/residential development

articles.text: Editor: It took FIFA four days to open a disciplinary investigation into Spanish FA President Luis Rubiales and another two days to suspend him for the unwanted kiss he placed on Jennifer Hermoso’s lips following Spain’s World Cup victory last weekend. Given FIFA’s long-broken moral compass, this came as no surprise to me. But the appalling messaging from FIFA’s pathetically slow and anemic response has actually been reinforced in the press, with the vast majority of news coverage referring to it as a “kiss.” Jenni Hermoso herself called it an “assault.” Read familiar? Recall when Taylor Swift was groped while taking a picture? Well, she also described it as an assault, not a grope. Jenni, and Taylor, had it right. FIFA’s response is particularly shocking as there was no ambiguity on what transpired between the two. In contrast, this occurred with cameras rolling and literally the entire world watching on the single biggest stage in international soccer competition. And while I imagine most readers at this point are nodding in agreement with disgust at what happened to this woman only minutes after the pinnacle of a lifetime accomplishment, I doubt we’ll all agree on the path forward. It is understandable and predictable for institutions such as schools and sports clubs to defer addressing these types of news events to private discussions in the home. And I can appreciate why – discussing these things in a classroom or on the pitch after practice could trigger a traumatic reaction and/or backlash from parents if messaging was unintentionally off-target. But misogyny, like racism, is structural - it’s not just a few bad apples, but instead a systemic disease that will remain unchanged absent a systemic remedy. Further, current events very much are, and should be, part of our children’s education. It made me quite sad as I discussed the week past with my 12-year old daughter, a soccer player herself, and realized she knew more about India landing on the moon than she did about what happened to Jenni Hermoso. If not now, then when will it be time to discuss these things with our children within institutions such as schools and sports clubs, and not just in private around a dinner table? It seems to me that time has long passed. –Anant Ahuja Piedmont father of four 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com REVIEWERS
articles.title: Why the Jenni Hermoso incident is so important

articles.text: BroadwaySF welcomes conservationist icon Jane Goodall in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist, conservationist and activist Jane Goodall will be on stage to discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960 and her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. Goodall is an iconic activist in conservation. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. As a U.N. Messenger of Peace since 2002, she continues to help the United Nations focus attention on environmental issues, primarily world wildlife and their habitat. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of her talk. Tickets are available online at: https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/. Anthropologist and conservationist Jane Goodall will speak in San Francisco on September 15. articles.text: No public vote required, per City Attorney The City of Piedmont’s revised 6th Cycle Housing Element is now open to a seven-day public comment period which ends this Friday, September 8, at 5:00 p.m. Changes are visible in the document and additions are highlighted in blue at Piedmontishome.org. Of importance is the topic of whether or not a vote must be conducted as the city of Piedmont makes plans to allow up to 587 new residences. Whether the changes amount to a change in zoning has been an ongoing question. In the 2022 city election, some candidates indicated their interpretation of the city’s charter as requiring a city-wide vote to change zoning. The City Attorney has interpreted the city charter to state that the charter does not prevent the city from adding new housing and no vote must be made. Changes are visible in the Housing Element on page 68 under the heading “4.G Clarifying the City Charter.” Pie d mont Com mu n ications Manager Echa Schneider explained that the city will conduct public education and outreach regarding what the city charter requires and what the zoning laws require. Any revisions would not alter the core of the City’s plan for accommodating 587 new homes by 2031. The Housing Element will set forth the City’s fair housing goals, policies, and programs to address the need for all housing and household types. The City intends to submit a revised Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review this Friday, September 8, for a 60-day review period. Comments on the revised housing element may be made by emailing PiedmontIsHome@ piedmont.ca.gov. • Size, placement, and materials for windows and outdoor spaces like balconies and decks • Location and visibility of parking areas The standards would apply only to developments in existing multifamily and mixed-use zones and do not change any existing regulations about density, height, minimum setbacks, or parking. They are intended to streamline the review process for multi-family and mixed-use housing developments that are already allowed by Piedmont’s zoning code.
articles.title: Revised Housing Element available for comment until Friday

Staff photo The Piedmont Police Department will host its fourth annual classic car show Saturday, September 23, from 9 a.m. to noon in the middle of town between Piedmont Park and Piedmont High School. The show is one of several public events organized by the department under the rubric Coffee, Cars and Cops, a take-off on a national trend among police departments known as Coffee with a Cop. Locally it is overseen by Officer Tyler Petit. The event features a wide range of distinctive, beautiful and rare vehicles. It began in 2018 by now-retired Sergeant Steve DeWarns and is widely viewed as a strong community tradition. Last year, 2022, it featured some 120 vehicles, and to date more than 65 cars have been signed up for this year’s show. The show was not held in 2020 September 23, 2023 9 AM - 12 PM 800 MAGNOLIA AVE. articles.text: The Piedmont Arts Fund is hosting its annual Chalk Art Festival this Sunday, September 10, from 9 a.m. to 12 noon at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. Join in as the school’s blacktop turns into a radiant quilt filled with chalk masterpieces. To fuel your creative spirits, start the morning with made-from-scratch pancakes served hot and fresh at the Beach Dads Club Pancake Breakfast, the same location as the Chalk Art exhibit. “I always love watching the playground come alive with color,” said Jon Schleuning, former Beach Dads Club President and an active member of Piedmont Arts Fund. “I love how everyone expresses their inner artist. from bright-eyed kindergarteners to established artists. We have families and friends come back year after year to do a chalk square together,” he added. Squares are $20 each and come with a box of premium chalk generously donated by FLAX Art in downtown Oakland. You just need to fill it with your imagination. One-hundred percent of proceeds support art programs for kindergarten through high school students in Piedmont schools. Scenes from last year’s Chalk Art Festival at Beach School Staff photos

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) approved the immediate distribution of up to $90,000 from its reserve fund to Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) last week. These funds are intended to enable the addition of up to three new sections in the 10th grade at Piedmont High School, bringing impacted class sizes in line with the District’s stated goals. According to PUSD, an additional section of each English 3-4 and Modern World History has been created, with the possibility of adding a section to AP Art History. The goal was to move approximately 20 students into the new sections, which will reduce the number of students in each existing section. “It brings us great pleasure to share that Dr. Hawn’s response to the news of the grant was one of elation,” said PEF Board Chair, Tonya Antonucci. “We are truly impressed by her swift implementation of these additional resources, which will undoubtedly make a positive impact on our students and their learning environment.” In a letter to PHS parents, Principal Sukanya Goswami expressed her gratitude to PEF and explained the next steps in the process, assuring students and parents that changes to the schedule will be minimal. Any schedule changes will go into effect this week. “Additional sections allow us to reduce class sizes across multiple sections, meaning there is an improved teacher to student ratio with more opportunity for individual focus,” said Goswami. “More sections mean more learning opportunities.”
articles.title: Ed. Foundation grant helps reduce class sizes at PHS

articles.text: The Piedmont Unified School District’s budget has been a limiting factor this year, leading to a school board directive to maximize enrollment in as many classes as possible. Budget measures to contain salary expenses have impacted the learning experiences in classes including physics, chemistry, world history, art history, math, and literature. Piedmont Teacher Union president and PHS English teacher Elise Marks teaches the same number of AP Literature classes as she did last year, but this year she has twenty-three more students. At PHS a full-time teacher has five class sections; when a new section is opened, the teacher must be paid an additional 20 percent of their salary. Marks described new obstacles her 32-student classroom faces. “It’s harder for people to join in discussion and it’s easier for shy students to hang back. There’s a difference in how well teachers get to know their students individually,” said Marks, “It’s hard to see people’s faces.” The benefit of small classes has been researched and proven. In a study conducted by Frederick Mosteller Ph.D. 6,500 students were placed in class populations of either 13-17 or 22-25, and the research showed that students in smaller classes advanced 2-5 months ahead of their peers. In later years they advanced one full academic year. Marks spoke of a former California state law mandating that freshman English classes were not to exceed 20 students. The law was aimed to optimize the classroom environment for freshman students learning the essential skill of writing. Marks recalls smaller classes at the beginning of her career at PHS. “When I started, Piedmont English classes averaged 24. We [now] want below 28,” she said. The start of the current school year saw an alarmingly high attendance numbers in many AP classes. The district has since hired science teachers at PHS to teach three sections of chemistry and anatomy. A $90,000 grant by the Piedmont Education Foundation [PEF] has helped reduce class sizes. The funds from PEF have gone to paying for additional sections of sophomore English and modern world history which were especially impacted by large class sizes. With salary negotiations coming up for teachers, large class sizes will certainly be among the hot topics of debate. Clea Villaluz is a junior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: Why AP classes at PHS are crowded

articles.text: The Great Chili Cook-off, held on Wednesday, August 20, in the Student Center at Piedmont High, had a repeat winner. Girls on Fire, the team of seniors Ruby Guzdar, Sara Broach and Jane Hempeck, repeated as two-time winners after capturing the top prize last year. A crowd of students, parents, and faculty members tasted each of the five chili entries. As the tasting crowd filed in, the reigning champions were hopeful, with their trophy from last year’s victory proudly displayed on a plaid-clothed table beside plates of cornbread. Guests at the cookoff were both taste-testers and voting judges. Everyone was given three tickets at the door to vote for their favorite chili makers. The Girls on Fire possessed a winning recipe, which includes a variety of beans and a secret chili powder. ”Most importantly,” said Guzdar, “it’s made with love.” The competitors consisted of a range of PHS community members–parents, freshmen, seniors, and faculty, with judging by their peers. Lively chatter filled the Student Center as mingling tasters gathered before Back-ToSchool night later that evening. “It’s a very fun, sort of homegrown kind of thing to do,” said PHS librarian Kathryn Levenson. Excited competitors brought their best chilis, including parents Eric Oldrin and Jason Venner’s state-award-winning chili recipe Photo by Erin Igoe The “Girls on Fire” team, Jane Hempeck (left), Sara Broach and Ruby Guzdar, won the Chili Cookoff for the second consecutive year. from Oldrin’s father. “He wrote the recipe down on his timecard,” said Oldrin, “So, it’s very nondescript. Hopefully we did it justice.” The team of freshmen under the name WDC began their cooking venture just an hour before the event, sourcing their ingredients from Mulberry’s. The firstyear students highlighted the recipe’s inclusion of sweet potatoes, the secret ingredient. As the tickets were tallied, excitement erupted from the Girls on Fire table, and the room turned to applaud the victors, the twotime champions. PHS counselor Chris Hartford’s chili, “Marik’s Minions,” won silver for second place in the evening’s fearsome battle. “I think it is [exciting] to bring the community together,” said PHS principal Sukanya Goswami, as photographers gathered for photos of the winning team. Photo by Clea Villaluz The Third Annual Great Chili Cook-Off took place in the Student Center at Piedmont High School on August 30.
articles.title: Girls on Fire team wins Chili Cook-off for 2nd year

articles.text: A First Lego League Explore team kicks off their Masterpiece season. Piedmont now boasts the largest community youth robotics league in the United States, with over 530 students and 76 teams participating across grades K through 12. Organized by Piedmont Makers, the teams span all four divisions of FIRST Robotics: 44 FIRST LEGO League Explore teams (K-3rd grade), 25 FIRST LEGO League Challenge teams (4th-7th grade), 6 FIRST Tech Challenge teams (7th-12th grade), and our world championship qualifying FIRST Robotics Competition team (9th - 12th grade). The theme for this year’s season is FIRST in Show, with each challenge shining a spotlight on the role STEM plays in the arts and empowering young people to design and build a world of endless possibilities. FIRST is a global nonprofit that designs accessible, innovative programs and pursue opportunities in STEM while building self-confidence, knowledge, and life skills. Elementary School With the new school year beginning, our youngest teams in the FIRST LEGO League Explore division have been kicking off their seasons in homes and living rooms all across town. FIRST LEGO League debuted the MASTERPIECE challenge on August 1 and these teams are hard at work imagining and innovating new ways to create and communicate art across the globe. “The number of participants grew by over 60% this year, and over the last five years we’ve increased female participation from 6% to almost 40%” said Pat Holder, parent co-coordinator of FLL Explore with Scott Miller. “We have a great group of 90 committed parent volunteers that are coaching the 40+ FLL Explore teams, and most attended our Sunday morning coaches training in August.” The FLL Explore teams will conclude their season with an endof-season festival in December. FIRST LEGO League Challenge teams also have surrendered their living rooms or garages to all things LEGO. Teams build a LEGO SPIKE Prime robot and program it to solve missions on a competition table with just Technic attachments and Scratch or Python programs. In addition to the robot game, students are challenged to complete an innovation project to identify a problem and design a solution to present to adult judges. All 24 teams will first compete in a Piedmont league scrimmage on October 15 at PMS Morrison Gym. Local qualifying tournaments in November include the Piedmont Qualifier tournament on Sunday, November 5. Select teams will advance to the regional championship in January with top teams from across Northern California. “We are blown away by the enthusiasm for youth robotics across every grade. Walk onto any Piedmont school campus and you’ll see just as many kids in their robotics team t-shirts as those in sports jerseys” said parent Benjamin Stein, co-commissioner of FLL Challenge. “Because we’re a volunteer-run organization, we could never pull this off without the tremendous support of so many amazing parent coaches.” added Paul Morrison, the other co-commissioner. Middle School For our middle school and high school robotics teams, the FIRST Tech Challenge Centerstage season kicks off Saturday, September 9. Teams will raise the curtain on the power of design, creativity, and precision to create all new experiences. Piedmont teams will participate in a league scrimmage on Sunday, October 22 at the PHS Student Center. Qualifying tournaments run from November through February, with top teams advancing A rookie FLL Challenge team assembles their Mission Models on their competition table. to the regional championship in spring. Maker of the Year Ayyana Chakravartula returns for her third year coaching her son’s team: “Our team is excited ... so we can get to work on hardware design and building new features into our code.” High School Our high school FIRST Robotics Competition team, Highlander Robotics, also kicked off their season in August at the Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For the first time the team is building an offseason robot from scratch, and it’s already off to a great start. This gives new team members the hands-on opportunity to practice a build season before the official kickoff in January. New members will get to CAD, manufacture, build, and program a brand new robot for a local off season competition. We hope to see you at the Harvest Festival on September 24th from 11-3! Come by the Highlander Robotics booth for free stickers and a fun game. The following weekend, September 31stOctober 1st, we will be in San Jose at Chezy Champs, a prestigious invitational-only offseason competition, for the third year in a row. For more information, contact Dave Ragones at dragones@ gmail.com. Members of first-year FTC team Circuit Breakers assemble their goBILDA chassis. Members of Highlander Robotics go through safety training on the Cannon Engineering Patio at Piedmont High.

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is known for taking on major projects where its more motivated members can take on planning and organizational responsibilities to undertake significant challenges that provide significant and tangible service to people in need. This fall, PCSC hopes to fund and build a tiny house for the new Richmond Tiny House Village, Farm and Garden which will serve homeless teens so they will be able to help themselves via the farm and garden. The construction of the new tiny house will provide PCSC teens and parents a way to not only learn construction skills, but gain general confidence in their ability to plan and achieve goals. The work is guided by local adults who provide oversight and teach skills, ideally to youth members that practice managing their peers. Shown here is the crew moving the floor structure to the trailer bed. Pictured are Matt Lewis (right), Rob Kelly, Ryan Parkhurst, Nate Seevak, Devon O’Shaugnessey, Frankie Broening, Claire Lichty, and Patrick Lerchi. PCSC’s first tiny house build was done in 2019 thanks to Rob Kelly who hosted the project and served as our technical lead. The tiny house now underway will be built on top of a trailer bed so that the house can be relocated as needed. The typical first step is to construct a wall frame on the ground, and then lift it into place. Pictured are Dan Phillips (back), Quelam Tran-Perez (left), Nick Ormond, and Toshi Troyer. In just a few work days the structure was completely framed out. Many more days were needed to insulate, apply exterior siding, windows & doors, electrical wiring, interior finish walls, and trim. The new house is expected to take roughly 15 days. Members of the work team: (front) Ken Li (left), Dan Cavenaugh, Kaia Kim, Kaeli Huh, Becky Isaac, Katherine Stormer, Roberto Castro;(first row on trailer): Nic Lukehart, Shelby Cavenaugh, Elena Blanco, Clara Stormer, Tom Ramsey; (top row on trailer): Nick Ormond, Rob Kelly, Jack Gross-Whitaker.

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, September 6, 2023 How to support Community Service Crew Tiny House Build project The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is known for taking on major projects where its more motivated members can take on planning and organizational responsibilities to undertake significant challenges that provide significant and tangible service to people in need. This fall, PCSC hopes to fund and build a tiny house for the new Richmond Tiny House Village, Farm and Garden which will serve homeless teens so they will be able to help themselves via the farm and garden. The construction of the new tiny house will provide PCSC teens and parents a way to not only learn construction skills, but gain general confidence in their ability to plan and achieve goals. The work is guided by local adults who provide oversight and teach skills, ideally to youth members that practice managing their peers. Shown here is the crew moving the floor structure to the trailer bed. Pictured are Matt Lewis (right), Rob Kelly, Ryan Parkhurst, Nate Seevak, Devon O’Shaugnessey, Frankie Broening, Claire Lichty, and Patrick Lerchi. PCSC’s first tiny house build was done in 2019 thanks to Rob Kelly who hosted the project and served as our technical lead. The tiny house now underway will be built on top of a trailer bed so that the house can be relocated as needed. The typical first step is to construct a wall frame on the ground, and then lift it into place. Pictured are Dan Phillips (back), Quelam Tran-Perez (left), Nick Ormond, and Toshi Troyer. The crew is asking for help from the community, It needs to raise roughly $15,000 to purchase the building materials in the next few weeks, and find adults who will help guide the youth on the building process. For funding support, please pledge a donation before September 15 using the response form at https://forms.gle/w2RKy5VeSxvCpsEC9. We will follow up with details later this month. For project support by local adults, contact crew advisor Ken Li (Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net) and indicate times available. A companion group, Piedmont Service Club, is for middle school aged youth and their parents. We emphasize youth leadership, and typically plan two activities per week. For more information and to join, contact advisor Ken Li (Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net) and visit the website www.pcservicecrew.org. In just a few work days the structure was completely framed out. articles.text: 5 ways to support your toddler’s language development One of the greatest joys of parenthood is watching your child experience all of life’s “firsts”- first laugh, first food, first steps, first words… After taking time to rejoice in these “firsts” and celebrate your little one’s big accomplishments, you may be left wondering “how do we keep this momentum going?” Here are five tips to help your toddler grow from “first words” to chatterbox. 1. Model, model, model At this stage, your toddler is always watching and always learning. They are a little walking sponge, soaking up everything they can gather (for better or for worse). Every interaction is an opportunity for them to hear new vocabulary, learn pragmatic skills, and make sense of the world and the words around them. You can infuse language into your child’s surroundings by labeling objects in their environment, describing the new sights, smells, tastes and experiences around them, and by narrating events/routines and giving them a “play by play.” 2. Expand on whatever your child says When your child produces a one-word utterance or short phrase, you can demonstrate how to expand their thoughts/ideas and language. For example, if your child says “doggy,” you can respond with “That’s a big dogHelp your toddler expand their vocabulary. gie” or “Yes! Doggy is barking.” It is helpful to vary the type of word you use to introduce a variety of verbs, nouns, adjectives and adverbs into your child’s lexicon. 3. Get on their level Get down on the floor, use a highchair- whatever it takes to be face-to-face with your child. When you are at eye level, it helps your child meet your gaze, watch your facial expressions and see your mouth movements. 4. Honor all attempts at communication In those early years, caregivers become excellent detectives, deciphering their child’s needs and learning their child’s own unique language. When caregivers respond to their child’s attempts at communication (words, gestures, signs), the child will feel heard and motivated to communicate more. 5. Follow your child’s lead As humans, we are motivated to engage in conversation about things that are of interest to us. It is so important to take a step back and see what your child naturally gravitates towards. Children are more likely to engage in play and communication when they are interested and the interaction is more enjoyable for all involved. Remember, children learn from exposure. The more you speak to your child and around them, the more expressive vocabulary they will learn and use. Paige Bailey is a pediatric speech language pathologist and feeding therapist. She is the owner of Speech By The Bay. https://www.speechbythebay.org. The discussions about salary Negotiations are scheduled for tomorrow, September 21 and 28. articles.text: The Piedmont cross-country team opens its 2023 season with a new head coach, Steve Zirkelbach, who takes over after 10 years under coach Jeanine Holmlund. Zirkelbach stepped into the role of distance running coach on the track team last spring under new coach Pouyan Assadi. Zirkelbach will take the boys’ and girls’ cross-country teams to the Ed Sias Invitational at Hidden Valley Park in Martinez this Saturday, September 9, the first meet of the season. Zirkelbach competed for Concord High School before being part of the University of California cross country program and graduating in 1994. “I’ve been a runner and I love Skylar Best who led the crosscountry team last year as a freshman, returns for her second year Staff Photos Steve Zirkelbach (left) has been named the new Piedmont High cross country coach. We want to make sure our runners are peaking at the right time,” said Zirkelbach. Returning to the team is sophomore Skylar Best, who led last year’s girls’ team and was the only team member to qualify for the CIF State Championship. Joining her will be senior Jamie Schwarz and junior Caroline Taylor. They will be surrounded by a young cast, including sophomores Quincy Antaya, Cora Chun, and Amina Greene. “Skylar has been very dominant. Jamie and Caroline are two of our captains. Quincy Antaya and Cora Chun are two runners who were impressive as freshmen last season,” said Zirkelbach. He said he has also been impressed by freshmen Gladwin Horsley and Cora Brozowski Schrader. “Two freshmen who have been running really strong are Gladwin and Cora. Cora came out of nowhere and Gladwin has been a terrific member of our team since our very first summer conditioning back in early July,” said Zirkelbach. The boys’ team will have a difficult time replacing former stars like Parker Long and Christian Taylor. But seniors Xander Schulte-Sasse and Julien Lee are back as leaders, and Miles Antaya, Evan Byun, Henry and Oliver Horsley have been emerging as talented runners. Freshman Sebastian Swain, meanwhile, was the team’s third-fastest runner in a timetrial hosted by the team at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park in Oakland. “The roster is comprised of two top seniors in Julien and Xander, along with Miles as another senior. Evan Byun ran really well as a sophomore last year. And Sebastian Swain showed up to our time trial and clocked the third-fastest time,” said Zirkelbach. Although the high school Is without a track for a half year while the football field is being replaced, the team has been working out on the small confines of the softball field and running through the hills of Piedmont.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ water polo season got started at the Labor Day Bash tournament last weekend hosted by Irvington High in Fremont on Friday and Saturday, September 1-2. The Highlanders opened Friday with two narrow one-goal wins over Newark Memorial 10-9 and Liberty 12-11. On Saturday, Piedmont lost 14-6 to Terra Linda but defeated Mission San Jose 10-2 to finish the tournament second-place overall. It was an impressive tournament for George Stein, who scored 12 goals in the four matches. Daniel Banin also had an impressive hat trick in Piedmont’s 12-11 win over Liberty. 10-9 over Newark Memorial Piedmont ended the first quarter in a 1-1 deadlock, but Newark stormed ahead 5-2 in the second quarter. In the third quarter, George Stein scored 30 seconds into the second half, but Newark responded 15 seconds later at 5:16 after drawing a penalty in front of goal—6-3. Piedmont scored on a man-advantage of its own with 4:43 to go, but conceded right away, once again, just 12 seconds later. At that point, PHS turned things around. From there, Declan Linnane scored back-toback goals at 1:55 and following a turnover at 1:28, making it 7-6 to end the third. In the fourth, Finn Burke tied it at 7-7 just 24 seconds into the quarter. Stein then put the Highlanders ahead 8-7 with 3:18 left in the game, but Newark tied it 16 seconds later. Stein regained the lead for Piedmont at 2:41, but Newark was able to score on its next possession for a 9-9. With 1:23 left in the game, Piedmont drew a penalty but was unable to score. Then, with 31 seconds left, the Highlanders drew another exclusion penalty on Newark. With 14 seconds left I on the clock, the ball was worked to Burke, who launched in the game-winner. Final stats: Stein had four goals, two assists, and one steal. Linnane had three goals, two assists, one steal. Krumins had a goal and assist. Burke scored twice. Goalie Luke McAuliffe recorded two saves, while goalie Gus Von Metszch had one save. 12-11 over Liberty In another intense one-goal win, Piedmont ended the first quarter in a 2-2 deadlock, and trailing 4-3 at halftime. But an explosive third-quarter helped a slow comeback with back-andforth scoring. Piedmont battled to tie the match at 6-6, but Liberty scored twice to go up 8-6. Daniel Banin was able to score with just three seconds remaining with a man-advantage. Liberty scored to lead 9-7 after 45 seconds in the fourth, but PHS rallied with goals from Banin and Krumins to give the Highlanders their first lead at 10-9 with 2:54 left in the game. Liberty scored on its next possession, but PHS went up 12-10 with goals from William Krieckhaus with 1:34 left. With just 14 seconds left in the game, Banin gave PHS its insurance goal for a 12-11 victory. Final stats: Banin had three goals. Krumins and Wright scored twice. Linnane had two goals and a steal. Krieckhaus had one goal, two assists. Stein Photos by Lynne Wright George Stein scored 12 goals in the Labor Day Bash water polo tournament. Daniel Banin scored three goals in Piedmont’s 12-11 win over Liberty.
articles.title: Highlanders finish 2nd in Labor Day water polo tourney

Quincy Antaya and Cora Chun are two runners who were impressive as freshmen last season,” said Zirkelbach. He said he has also been impressed by freshmen Gladwin Horsley and Cora Brozowski Schrader. “Two freshmen who have been running really strong are Gladwin and Cora. Cora came out of nowhere and Gladwin has been a terrific member of our team since our very first summer conditioning back in early July,” said Zirkelbach. The boys’ team will have a difficult time replacing former stars like Parker Long and Christian Taylor. But seniors Xander Schulte-Sasse and Julien Lee are back as leaders, and Miles Antaya, Evan Byun, Henry and Oliver Horsley have been emerging as talented runners. Freshman Sebastian Swain, meanwhile, was the team’s third-fastest runner in a timetrial hosted by the team at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park in Oakland. “The roster is comprised of two top seniors in Julien and Xander, along with Miles as another senior. Evan Byun ran really well as a sophomore last year. And Sebastian Swain showed up to our time trial and clocked the third-fastest time,” said Zirkelbach. Although the high school Is without a track for a half year while the football field is being replaced, the team has been working out on the small confines of the softball field and running through the hills of Piedmont. articles.text: Bauer Peterson recorded five aces against the Titans. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team suffered a rough 3-0 loss to Skyline in Oakland on Thursday, August 31 by scores of 25-21, 25-13, 25-17. Skyline is the defending Oakland Athletic League champion, and reached the 2022 CIF State Division 5 regional semifinals as the No. 1 seed. “It was a very unique environment at Skyline with how hot their gym is, how low the ceiling is, and having to face a really good team with some strong hitters,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. Piedmont looked its best in the first set, when they briefly held leads at 11-10 and 21-19. However, the Highlanders struggled with consistency throughout the night, committing several errors in all three sets. “We can’t win if we can’t be consistent,” said Cardeñas. “If we commit more errors than we have successful moments, we’re not going to be a winning team. It’s really just the unforced errors. We had 16 errors in the third set. We need to be more proactive instead of reactive.” In the first set, the two sides traded points throughout the opening. With Skyline holding a 10-8 lead, PHS put up three straight points with help of two straight aces by Bauer Peterson. However, Skyline scored five straight points to regain the lead. The Highlanders then took an 18-17 lead following a spike by Molly Wagener and an ace by Annika Hattan-Kutter. Wagener had another spike to make it 20-19, while Peterson had a big block at make it 21-19 for Piedmont. But then the Titans roared back by winning six straight points to win the first set 25-21. Piedmont committed four errors to allow Skyline to win the game. Skyline controlled the second set, getting out to a quick 13-5 lead and extended their advantage on their way to a 25-13 win. 15 of Skyline’s points came off of Piedmont errors. Sadie Town goes up for a spike against Skyline.

articles.text: Photos by Anne Murphy Piedmont’s JV football team took a tough 40-18 loss to Miramonte. and Layth Haddawy Piedmont’s junior varsity football team survived a 40-18 loss to Miramonte on Friday, September 1 in Orinda. The JV team, much like varsity, is working its way through difficult non-league opponents ahead of its league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference. It was rough from the get-go, with the Matadors ending the first half with a 20-0 lead. Miramonte played exceptional defense to thwart the Highlander offense through much of the first half. Piedmont’s defense, however, had a strong performance with an interception by sophomores Marius Arno and Ryan Ridell forcing a fumble. The Scots turned up their intensity in the second half. Toward the end of the third quarter, sophomore receiver Marius Arno took a short slant route for a 46-yard touchdown, the team’s first of the season. That moment seemed to build Piedmont’s confidence. Sophomore defensive back George Bishop made a spectacular interception. After conceding a touchdown, freshman Diego Hurwitz received the ball at the 20-yard line and follow his blockers, finding the gaps through Miramonte’s kickoff coverage for an 80-yard touchdown return. On Miramonte’s next possession, freshman defensive back Colby Hong made a highlight-reel one-handed interception grab to get the ball back for Piedmont. With four minutes left in the game, freshman backup quarterback Rehan Mumtaz entered the game after starting quarterback Cash Panico suffered a leg injury. Mumtaz didn’t show any nerves and made an instant impact, scoring on a 20-yard rushing touchdown while evading several Miramonte tacklers, NEXT UP Piedmont (0-2) head to Mt. Eden in Hayward on Friday, September for a game at 5:00 p.m. Diego Hurwitz celebrates after scoring on an 80-yard kickoff return. Quarterback Cash Panico throws a screen pass against Miramonte.
articles.title: JV football falls to Miramonte Matadors

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team is under new leadership with head coach Georgia Lewis, who was promoted from leading the junior varsity for the last two years. The varsity squad went 8-11 last season with a fifth-place finish in the Western Alameda County Conference tournament. “I’m really excited, it comes with a lot of responsibility. It feels like I have 20 children who are my own and that feels amazing and very stressful at the same time,” said Lewis. “For me, coaching and having this role is about finding the balance between love, support, and improving their water polo skills.” Lewis recently completed her senior year as a member of Santa Clara University’s water polo team after spending the first two years of her collegiate career at Bucknell University. Her time at Santa Clara was concurrent with her two seasons coaching Piedmont’s JV team, giving her an interesting perspective as a teacher and current player. “I was at Bucknell and transferred to Santa Clara. It gave me a unique opportunity to have two very different types of coaching styles at the Division 1 level. Because that was so recent, I think I was really able to choose the things I liked or didn’t like and apply that to coaching,” said Lewis. Staff Photo Kat Melian returns as a senior leader on Piedmont’s water polo team. Georgia Lewis takes over as head coach of Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team. She recently finished her senior year on Santa Clara University’s water polo team and was the junior varsity head coach at Piedmont the previous two years. Walking into the head coaching role, she wants to observe players and determine where they fit best on the team. “We have a lot of talent. I’m not going to force anyone to play a position they don’t want to play and I want everyone to get a chance to play new positions. We have work to do to make it all fit together and be cohesive, but I know we have the talent and are working on the skills. The more
