articles.text: Without winning a tournament he gains national media attention Former Piedmont tennis player Mackie McDonald made national news at the U.S. Open in New York last week , upsetting the world’s No. 15 ranked Felix Auger-Aliassime of Canada in four sets, 7-6 (7-5), 4-6, 6-1, 6-4 on Monday, August 28. Two days later, he lost in three sets to Borna Gojo of Croatia in the second round, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4, Such is the roller coaster life of a professional tennis player and its accompanying perils. Mackie’s world ranking is now No. 40 The media frenzy following McDonald’s win put the Piedmont-pro in the national spotlight. Following his second-round loss, the New York Times featured Mackie, highlighting his run-up to the match with Auger-Aliassime as a 28-year-old professional on the world tour. McDonald explained the repetitive nature of the professional tennis tour, going from one tournament to another. “Things can get monotonous week after week, locker room after locker room, hotel after hotel,” McDonald said. “It’s good to have those small goals or little things that drive you that make you believe that you can get better… They definitely show the glamour of the sport on TV. It is all the behind the scenes, it is the day to day and the around-theyear tournaments that we play that Photo courtesy of U.S. Open Mackie McDonald made national news after defeating No. 15 Felix Auger-Aliassime in the U.S. Open. Photo courtesy of Vanity Fair McDonald recently did a feature in Vanity Fair magazine in August. Photo courtesy of U.S. Open Mackie McDonald beat Felix Auger-Aliassime in four sets, 7-6 (7-5), 4-6, 6-1, 6-4. really get us to these moments.” Earlier last month on August 15, Vanity Fair magazine also did a feature piece on McDonald in an article about tennis stars in fashion. Against Auger-Aliassime, McDonald’s matched lasted three-and-a-half hours, including a grueling first set that went 7-6 (7-5) in Mackie’s favor. McDonald has previously described playing on hard courts – such as at the U.S. Open at Forest Hills, New York, as his strongest skill set. McDonald dropped the second set but returned with a dominant 6-1 win in the third set. In the fourth set, the two traded games until the set was tied at 3-3. Then McDonald took control by winning the fourth game as the returner and winning the fifth game on serve. McDonald is still searching for his first win above the ATP Challenger tour. He last won an ATP Challenger in Khazakstan in 2021 and reached the Citi Open Final in 2021, where he lost to Jannik Sinner. “I want to win a title so bad,” said McDonald. “I always find that each week, your opportunity each week, can be that week that can shift things, and I think that dream is what we’re all chasing.” McDonald also competed in the U.S. Open’s Men’s Doubles ladder with Andreas Mies of Germany. They won 7-6 (7-4), 6-1 in the first round on August 30, followed with a 6-4, 6-3 win over Nikola Mektic and Robin Haase on September 2, but lost 6-3, 3-6, 6-2 against third-ranked Rajeev Ram and Joe Salisbury.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald upsets Auger-Aliassime to reach second round of U.S. Open

articles.text: Staff Photos The “Mission Peeker” summit pole atop Mission Peak Regional Preserve marks the completion of the trail at 2,520 feet in elevation. The Mission Peak Summit is among the most popular trails of East Bay Regional Park District and considered the most frequented attraction in the City of Fremont. On any weekend, the location can become a highway of foot traffic, bikers, families, and dog walkers making their way to the Mission Peeker Summit Pole for their photo opportunity. Reports from this week indicate the iconic Mission Peeker pole was vandalized over the weekend, and was cut down by vandals using a metal saw. The “Mission Peeker” was created up in 1990 and quickly became the most photographed spot in Fremont. The peak is commemorated in the City of Fremont’s crest. The pole was created by park ranger and artist Leonard Page. Tubes noticeably stuck through the pole, were included to allow hikers to view their surroundings. An East Bay Regional Parks District spokesperson issued a statement regarding the vandalism. “We are saddened to learn about this incident in our park. Any vandalism from destruction to graffiti affects what should be a positive, happy experience for community members to enjoy open space and the many trails in our regional parks,” read the statement. The 3.1 mile hike to the 2,520- foot summit often brings in droves of patrons looking for a tough workout. At the top, you have sweeping views of the Bay Area; looking down on Fremont, Union City, Hayward, and the San Mateo Bridge. You can see San Francisco off in the distance and the hills surrounding the Peninsula. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up to the 3.25 mile, 2,500’ peak. The view from the top of Mission Peak. The Mission Peak Regional Preserve provides some beautiful rock formations
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON Mission Peek summit pole vandalized, removed

The “Mission Peeker” was created up in 1990 and quickly became the most photographed spot in Fremont. The peak is commemorated in the City of Fremont’s crest. The pole was created by park ranger and artist Leonard Page. Tubes noticeably stuck through the pole, were included to allow hikers to view their surroundings. An East Bay Regional Parks District spokesperson issued a statement regarding the vandalism. “We are saddened to learn about this incident in our park. Any vandalism from destruction to graffiti affects what should be a positive, happy experience for community members to enjoy open space and the many trails in our regional parks,” read the statement. The 3.1 mile hike to the 2,520- foot summit often brings in droves of patrons looking for a tough workout. At the top, you have sweeping views of the Bay Area; looking down on Fremont, Union City, Hayward, and the San Mateo Bridge. You can see San Francisco off in the distance and the hills surrounding the Peninsula. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up to the 3.25 mile, 2,500’ peak. The view from the top of Mission Peak. The Mission Peak Regional Preserve provides some beautiful rock formations

articles.text: B. Noel Thomas plays Lola in Kinky Boots at Berkeley Playhouse. Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2023-24 season with the Tonyaward winning musical Kinky Boots, beginning September 8. Kinky Boots protagonist Charlie Price inherits his father’s beleaguered and nearly bankrupt shoe factory. He finds inspiration in customer Lola, a provocative entertainer, who wants to purchase a pair of sturdy stilettos. An unlikely pair, Charlie and Lola find they have more in common than they initially thought. The uplifting play features music and lyrics by Cyndi Lauper and is based on the 2005 British film of the same name. It was written by Geoff Deane and Tim Firth and is inspired mostly by true events. “It’s just a heartfelt, heartwarming show about community and that’s exactly what Berkeley Playhouse is about. It’s perfect,” Director William Thomas Hodgson said. “The vision is a celebration of queerness, a community in queerness. As representative as this show has been on Broadway, on the West End, and around the world, I feel like we have our own special sauce in Berkeley. The commodity of this show, the event of this show, is radical acceptance and this love through community, this love of one’s self, and of one’s own desires even.” The cast includes B, Noel Thomas as Lola and Simon, Seth Hanson as Charlie Price, Grace Margaret Craig as Nicola, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Lauren, Danny Cozart as Don, and Maia Campbell as Pat. The musical will be performed through October 15. Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, beginning September 8. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Kinky Boots premieres Friday at Berkeley Playhouse

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company premiered Born With Teeth on September 1. The two-person play by Liz Duffy Adams stars Dean Linnard as poet and English spy Kit Marlowe and Brady Morales-Woolery as Will Shakespeare, an upstart crow looking to make his name in the world of art. The play is set in the back room of a tavern in a polarized and paranoid England where civilian death sentences abound. The two writers, Kit and Brady, take on a risky collaboration and their artistic partnership becomes a dangerous dance of inspiration, Playwright Liz Duffy Adams artistry, seduction, and betrayal. Born With Teeth had its world premiere at the Alley Theater in Houston in 2022 and is the recipient of a 2021 Edgerton Foundation New Play Award and Best Play and Production. A post-show discussion with playwright Adams and the creative team will be held on September 8, 12, 20 and 28. The play will run through October 1. Visit https://www.aurorathea t r e.o r g /i n d ex .ph p /s how s - events/20232024-season/bornwith-teeth to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Aurora Theatre’s Born With Teeth premieres Friday

articles.text: San Francisco Opera begins its 101st season with a free concert in Golden Gate Park this Sunday. September 10. Music Director Eun Sun Kim will lead the San Francisco Opera Orchestra in an al fresco afternoon of arias and duets performed by leading stars from the upcoming fall season. The cast includes sopranos Aleksandra Kurzak, Olivia Smith and Julie Adams; mezzo-sopranos Daniela Mack and Hyona Kim; tenors Moises Salazar, Robert Alagna and Arturo ChconCruz; Baritone Brian Mulligan and bass-baritone Jongwon Han. The concert begins at 1:30 p.m. in the Robin Williams Meadow. For more information, visit https://www.sfopera.com/operainthepark/. The free event is a beloved San Francisco tradition.
articles.title: Opera in the Park at Golden Gate Park this Sunday

articles.text: An exhibition featuring over 20 pieces by local artist Bernice “Bingo” Bing (1936 - 1998) is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. Born in San Francisco’s Chinatown in 1936, Bing was a young artist among the city’s Beat Era art scene, creating works from the 1950’s on. Although she grew up in an orphanage and bounced between foster homes as a child, she was able to earn her B.F.A. and M.F.A. at the California School of Fine Arts, now the San Francisco Art Institute, where she studied alongside painter Elmer Bischoff and other greats. Her paintings and illustrations explore abstract expressionism and figuration as well as Zen calligraphy and Western abstraction. Bing only recently became recognized for her artworks, but was a fixture in the San Francisco arts scene until her death in 1998. Into View: Bernice Bing is the first in an ongoing series of collection exhibitions at Asian Art Museum that highlight the work of under-recognized modern artists. It will be on view through June 26. For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/into-view-bernicebing/. A visitor to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco views A Lady and a Road Map, 1962, by Bernice Bing (American, 1936–1998). Oil on canvas.
articles.title: Bernice Bing exhibition now on view at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Unique event takes place Sept. 8-12 in Golden Gate Park The San Francisco Botanical Garden will host its annual Flower Piano Lounge beginning this Friday, September 8, in Golden Gate Park. This unique event merges botanical beauty and classical music against the backdrop of San Francisco’s most famous park. Flower Piano Lounge transforms San Francisco Botanical Garden into an alfresco concert hall where everyone and anyone is invited to play and listen. Sunset Piano, which hosts the event in partnership with the garden, places grand pianos and baby grands throughout the gardens where musicians and artists will play an eclectic range of genres, from Jazz to classical to AfroCuban. The event has enjoyed seven successful years of turn-outs. The program series kicks off with a Flower Piano Opening Night Special Event in the Botanical Garden’s Celebration Garden from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. Performances by Pablo Estigarribia, a Latin Grammy winning pianist, arranger, and composer, begins at 6 p.m. with the Sumi Lee Quartet opening. Performances follow each day and all day Friday through Tuesday. All concerts take place at 1199 9th Avenue in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. For more information, contact Golden Gate Park management by email info@ gggp.org or call (415) 661-1316. For a full list of programming, visit https://www.sfbg.org/flowerpiano.
articles.title: SF Botanical Garden’s Flower Piano Lounge begins this Friday

San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) opened a new, permanent collection exhibition entitled Sea Change on Saturday, September 2. The exhibition is presented as a suite of thematic and monographic galleries all focused on waterways and oceans. The works of photography are by more than 50 artists from around the world. articles.text: Visitors to Bancroft Gardens swap succulents and buds with their neighbors. The Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek is hosting a plantswap this Sunday, September 10. Bring up to 25 plants that you would like to donate and swap them for other plants brought by your neighbors and fellow gardeners. Donors may bring cuttings or surplus plants to swap with other plant lovers and leave with new plants to add to your collection. Light refreshments will be offered on-site. All plants must be disease and pest free and identified to the best of your ability. Do not bring more than five of the same plants or more than 25 plants total. Houseplants, succulents and cacti are all welcome, except for Agave americana and Mother of Millions. Donors will get an opportunity to “bid” on plants. You can place up to three stickers per plant to increase your odds of winning it, and if there are multiple bidders, organizers will pull a name at random and announce the winner. Tickets, which cost $15, are required to attend. Visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ event/plant-swap/ to learn more and to purchase tickets. Ruth Bancroft Gardens is located at 1552 Bancroft Road in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: Bancroft Gardens “plant-swap” this Sunday

articles.text: Benny Safdie (left) as Edward Teller and Cillian Murphy as J. Robert Oppenheimer in Chirstopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer Review by Chris Honoré Oppenheimer, written and directed by the prolific Christopher Nolan (The Dark Knight, Inception, Interstellar, Dunkirk), is based on the 2005 Pulitzer Prize-winning biography, American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. Since the film’s recent release it has garnered consistent praise and has filled theaters. Hence, with much anticipation, I stood in a long line, waiting to buy a ticket. But almost from the get-go I began to wonder why Nolan had picked Oppenheimer as the focus of this lengthy, restrained drama that, in truth, would have been better suited for the History Channel. While often referred to as a biopic, I would judge it as a character study of a complicated and brilliant man, portrayed by Cillian Murphy. It opens in 1926 when we are introduced to Oppenheimer as a young Ph.D. student who is fascinated with quantum mechanics. He seems dark, unmoored, and strangely depressive. This is illustrated in an early scene when he is shown injecting an apple with poison and leaving it on the desk of his professor, his motivation unclear. His affect is enigmatic, flat and detached, and it becomes increasingly difficult to care about him, no matter his extraordinary polymath genius and intellectual curiosity. After completing his doctorate in Europe, with an emphasis in theoretical physics, he returns to America, and is soon chosen by General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) to be the director of what will be known as the Manhattan Project, which is a race by a cohort of scientists to build the atomic bomb before the Nazis, who have a similar program underway. He also meets and marries Kitty Puening (Emily Blunt). Theirs is not a love story, and their relationship seems distant, even brittle throughout. And as hard as it is to imagine, Oppenheimer was known to be reckless and a womanizer and we see him carrying on an affair with a much younger woman, Jean Tatlock (Florence Pugh), as demonstrated in two jarring scenes, both devoid of any real passion. It is at the beginning of act three that the narrative shifts. Germany surrenders, ending World War II in Europe; however the war with Japan continues. Japan refuses to yield and the Americans realize that they have two stark choices: invade Japan at great cost, or use the atomic bomb which is still under development and being tested. Washington chooses the latter and ultimately drops this apocalyptic weapon on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The horrific destruction that follows transforms for Oppenheimer what was an abstract scientific problem into a reality of death and carnage, something that haunts him for the rest of his life. Because of his resulting vocal resistance to creating the hydrogen bomb (Russia has now become America’s adversary in a nuclear arms race), Oppenheimer finds himself swept up in the 1954 McCarthy anti-communist black-listing hysteria wherein his loyalty is questioned, and his top-secret clearance withdrawn. His fall from grace (he was on the cover of Time Magazine) is tragic. But though confronted with unproven accusations, his outrage seems leached from the story as he choses to cooperate with what amounts to a kangaroo court. Instead of fighting for his reputation, despite Kitty’s insistence that he not give in to their denigrating charges, he meekly testifies or remains withdrawn. But that seems consistent with his persona throughout this disappointing film. Oppenheimer. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Matt Damon. 3 hrs. Rated R. Released in theaters only 2023.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Oppenheimer ultimately disappoints

articles.text: Free Solo is a National Geographic documentary film, directed by award-winning filmmaker Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and shot by world-renowned photographer and mountaineer Jimmy Chin. It is a stunning and unflinching portrait of professional mountain climber Alex Honnold and focuses in the main on his obsessive preparation to fulfill a lifelong dream: climbing the face of the world-famous rock, the 3,200ft El Capitan in Yosemite National Park – without safety gear of any kind, meaning that singular line that is attached from either above or below to someone on belay and to the climber. What “free” means is that such a climb surpasses all definitions of extreme sports, existing in a realm that defies all description and enters the mystical, a silent meditation on life and of course death. To climb El Capitan solo is one of the greatest athletic feats of any kind. There is nothing else in sports that compares. The actual filming of such an attempt is also breathtaking in its beauty and sustained sense of risk and, of course, vertigo. It’s beautiful. There is also a sense of controlled and disciplined panic on the part not only of Honnold but of Chin and the film crew that is quietly, grippingly conveyed with each harrowing pitch. The ultimate barrier to be reached and sustained is perfection in its purest form. The outcome is grimly bifurcated: a successful attempt or what can only be chillingly imagined as a seconds-long drop to certain death. How could Free Solo be anything less than exhausting not only for Honnold, but equally for the photographers and director, who, as the film shows, are deeply conflicted by recording and enabling what could so easily be a wrenching tragedy. The film attempts to explore the “why?” and pushes Honnold, not the most emotive of persons, for explanations that he is either unable or unwilling to share. He says simply that he is doing what he loves to do and is fortunate to be able to support his passion. Inherent in his choice, he admits, is the impact it has on those who care about him, especially his partner Sanni McCandless. It is her tears at the end of the film that are parenthetical to a reality she can’t bear to contemplate. It is an emotion that haunts this compelling, most amazing film. Free Solo. Documentary. Directed by Elizabeth Chi Vasarhelyi. Photographed by Jimmy Chin. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/hulu/Disney+/ Apple tv. Free Solo is a documentary on Alex Honnold’s climb of El Capitan.
articles.title: Free Solo – where El Capitan is the star

How could Free Solo be anything less than exhausting not only for Honnold, but equally for the photographers and director, who, as the film shows, are deeply conflicted by recording and enabling what could so easily be a wrenching tragedy. The film attempts to explore the “why?” and pushes Honnold, not the most emotive of persons, for explanations that he is either unable or unwilling to share. He says simply that he is doing what he loves to do and is fortunate to be able to support his passion. Inherent in his choice, he admits, is the impact it has on those who care about him, especially his partner Sanni McCandless. It is her tears at the end of the film that are parenthetical to a reality she can’t bear to contemplate. It is an emotion that haunts this compelling, most amazing film. Free Solo. Documentary. Benny Safdie (left) as Edward Teller and Cillian Murphy as J. Robert Oppenheimer in Chirstopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer Review by Chris Honoré Oppenheimer, written and directed by the prolific Christopher Nolan (The Dark Knight, Inception, Interstellar, Dunkirk), is based on the 2005 Pulitzer Prize-winning biography, American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer, written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin. Since the film’s recent release it has garnered consistent praise and has filled theaters. Hence, with much anticipation, I stood in a long line, waiting to buy a ticket. But almost from the get-go I began to wonder why Nolan had picked Oppenheimer as the focus of this lengthy, restrained drama that, in truth, would have been better suited for the History Channel. While often referred to as a biopic, I would judge it as a character study of a complicated and brilliant man, portrayed by Cillian Murphy. It opens in 1926 when we are introduced to Oppenheimer as a young Ph.D. student who is fascinated with quantum mechanics. He seems dark, unmoored, and strangely depressive. This is illustrated in an early scene when he is shown injecting an apple with poison and leaving it on the desk of his professor, his motivation unclear. His affect is enigmatic, flat and detached, and it becomes increasingly difficult to care about him, no matter his extraordinary polymath genius and intellectual curiosity. After completing his doctorate in Europe, with an emphasis in theoretical physics, he returns to America, and is soon chosen by General Leslie Groves (Matt Damon) to be the director of what will be known as the Manhattan Project, which is a race by a cohort of scientists to build the atomic bomb before the Nazis, who have a similar program underway. He also meets and marries Kitty Puening (Emily Blunt). Theirs is not a love story, and their relationship seems distant, even brittle throughout. And as hard as it is to imagine, Oppenheimer was known to be reckless and a womanizer and we see him carrying on an affair with a much younger woman, Jean Tatlock (Florence Pugh), as demonstrated in two jarring scenes, both devoid of any real passion. It is at the beginning of act three that the narrative shifts. Germany surrenders, ending World War II in Europe; however the war with Japan continues. Japan refuses to yield and the Americans realize that they have two stark choices: invade Japan at great cost, or use the atomic bomb which is still under development and being tested. Washington chooses the latter and ultimately drops this apocalyptic weapon on the cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The horrific destruction that follows transforms for Oppenheimer what was an abstract scientific problem into a reality of death and carnage, something that haunts him for the rest of his life. Because of his resulting vocal resistance to creating the hydrogen bomb (Russia has now become America’s adversary in a nuclear arms race), Oppenheimer finds himself swept up in the 1954 McCarthy anti-communist black-listing hysteria wherein his loyalty is questioned, and his top-secret clearance withdrawn. His fall from grace (he was on the cover of Time Magazine) is tragic. But though confronted with unproven accusations, his outrage seems leached from the story as he choses to cooperate with what amounts to a kangaroo court. Instead of fighting for his reputation, despite Kitty’s insistence that he not give in to their denigrating charges, he meekly testifies or remains withdrawn. But that seems consistent with his persona throughout this disappointing film. Oppenheimer. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Cillian Murphy, Emily Blunt, Matt Damon. 3 hrs. Rated R. Released in theaters only 2023. Free Solo is a documentary on Alex Honnold’s climb of El Capitan.

articles.text: Rachel McAdams in a scene from Morning Glory Morning Glory is sweet and funny while relying on the very recognizable template of a young working girl climbing up the corporate ladder. In this case it’s Becky Fuller (Rachel McAdams), morning television producer who is filled with energy, a dimpled smile, lots of roll up your sleeves grit, and an impossible new job at IBC’s morning show, which currently is in the cellar in ratings. She convinces her skeptical boss, Jerry Barns (Jeff Goldblum), that she can pull the show out of the doldrums and nail the ratings race. All she needs is a solid anchor to join Colleen Peck (Diane Keaton), who has been doing morning “chat ‘em up” stories with aplomb and good grace. Becky discovers that an old warhorse reporter, Mike Pomeroy (Harrison Ford), is hanging around collecting a huge paycheck but doing little else. She just needs to convince him to get on board. Ah, there’s the rub. Pomeroy is angry and petulant for most of the film, saying with regularity, “no, I don’t do that.” He actually refuses to say the word, “fluffy” on air, driving Becky to terminal distraction. So, while Becky is all positive energy, a cheerleader for the show, Pomeroy is cantankerous, insisting that a news guy of his international credentials, a journalist who has been in the trenches, definitely doesn’t do cooking. Apron? Right, he doesn’t do that. The tension between Becky and Mike, as well the inherent tension between hard news and news as entertainment, could have resulted in some great moments. There is a terrific movie inside this happy meal that is trying to get out. They could have had some wonderful arguments about what has happened to news over the last two decades and how it has devolved into stories that are nonsensical, interviews that are the definition of prurient and banal, absent any real investigative edge. Banal is what Becky is after, however, if it will elevate the ratings and save her job and the show. There is no discussion of creating a robust hybrid with Pomeroy taking the lead. It’s all about kissing a frog (which is exactly what Colleen does, twice) if that’s what it takes to get people watching. So. Morning Glory skirts some contemporaneous issues and settles for a predictable romantic comedy instead: working girl makes it in the big apple and finds love along the way in the person of Adam Bennett (Patrick Wilson). The movie is light-hearted and entertaining. It could have done some heavy lifting as well. The filmmakers chose not to. Morning Glory. Directed by Roger Michell. Starring Rachel McAdams, Harrison Ford, Diane Keaton, Jeff Goldblum and Patrick Wilson. 1 hr., 59 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Morning Glory – sweet and funny

articles.text: Film version of a comic book without the panels Spider-Man: Into the Spider-verse is a family friendly adventure-comedy, superbly animated, colorful, bold and captivating while moving at a breakneck pace. It is best-suited for kids age 10 and older. Spider-verse features a newbie teen (8th grade), Mike Morales (Shameik Moore), who is a mixed-race, Puerto Rican-African American kid from Brooklyn. He is struggling to fit into his new school, make friends, while naturally missing his old buds that he had to leave behind when his family moved. Kids will love its richly created, free-for-all wackiness. At the outset, Mike is bitten by a radioactive spider that transforms him into the classic Stan Lee comic book, TV series Spider-Man. The villain of the story is an evil-doer named Kingpin (Liev Schrieber) who has invented a monster laser that he unleashes, creating a tear in the universe and suddenly we have multiple universes, each with its own version of Spider-Man. To start with, there’s Mike; an animé Spidey, Penni Parker (Kimiko Glenn); plus Spidey noir (Nicholas Cage). There is, of course, the original Peter Parker (Jake Johnson); and not to forget Spidey Ham (John Mulvaney), and Spider-Woman Gwen (Hailee Steinfeld). The cohort decides it is up to them to join together to save the world and defeat Kingpin. And it’s at this point that things get really exciting. There are explosions, chases, and lots of stuff that ricochets with danger as situations change, as do the settings. The action transcends live action, which was the staple of the first Spider-Man features. This animated version is kinetic, with an unrelenting sense of humor. With victory over Kingpin, followed by the repair in the dimensional tear in the universe, the various Spider-men and woman can finally return to their places of origin, much to the satisfaction of Mike, who has finally mastered his superpower abilities. Spider-man: Into the Spider-Verse. Directed by Bob Persichetti. Voiced by Shameik Moore, Jake Johnson, Rooney Rothman. Animated adventure-comedy. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated PG. Released 2018. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv The many versions of Spider-Man

articles.text: French-American duo to perform Saturday night concert Guitarist & composer Arthur Dente A guitar-percussion duo concert by Arthur Dente and Steve Robertson will take place at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, September 16, at 7 p.m. Advance tickets at $20 are available at https://bpt. me/6124713, or $25 at the door - cash or checks only. Arthur Dente is a French guitarist, composer and performer, trained in both classical and improvised music. Of Portuguese origin, his compositions develop an interaction between the Iberian Peninsula, Europe and, by extension, world cultures. A gold medalist in classical guitar at the Montauban Conservatory, he studied composition and music history at the Toulouse Conservatory, then at the École Normale de Musique de Paris.. He holds a degree in musicology from the University of Aix-en-Provence, where he was a lecturer for several years. He obtained the CAPES, a State diploma that enabled him to teach music education and put his compositions into practice with students in music specialization. • Nominated for the CEMF (French music publishers’ union) competition, for writing a contemporary work, on May 28, 2023. • Participation as solo guitarist in the show « LA PÉPINIÈRE DES COMPOSITEURS », in Aix-en- Provence on June 5 and 6, 2023.Solo concert in Paris on June 17, 2023. • Duo concert: Guitar & Cello, given in Balogna, South Corsica, on July 11, 2023. • Participation in the « LES SUPERPHONIQUES » 2023 contemporary music competition, writing a piece for choir, guitar and flute. • Participation in the CEMF 2024 competition in the Repertoire category for the writing of a piece for orchestra accompanied by its musicological analysis. Percussionist Steve Robertson has been active performing, recording, producing and teaching in the Bay Area for more than 25 years. A graduate of San Percussionist Steve Robertson Jose State University with a BA in Music Performance and Education. He has performed and recorded in a variety of musical styles with artists including Bobby Hutcherson, Airto and Flora Purim, Laurindo Almeida, Claudia Villela, Othello Molineaux, Giovanni Hidalgo, Omar Sosa, John Calloway, Arthur Dente and many others. His musical focus is primarily in Jazz and World Music styles including Brazilian, Afro-Cuban and North Indian Classical music (on tabla). He studied orchestral percussion with Anthony Cirone at SJSU and is a tabla student of Ustad Zakir Hussain. He has also performed on percussion with the Monterey and Santa Cruz County Symphonies.

articles.text: The Broadcast Legends “OldTime Radio Players” will bring Golden Memories of Radio to Piedmont on Sunday afternoon, September 17, at 4:00 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. “The Old Time Radio Players” and technical crew will re-create examples of radio newscasts, kids’ shows, daytime Soap Operas, bloopers, commercials, jingles, plus the main event, a complete episode of “The Lone Ranger.” It’s a nostalgic presentation that will take audience members back to a time when “radio was king” and the “theatre of the mind” captured our imaginations. The cast includes Michael Bennett, Peter Cleaveland, Carolyn Compton, Matt Elmore, Bruce Jenett, Jason Nunan, Hoyt Smith, and Zachary Wilson. The Technical Director is Bob Brown.

Arthur Dente is a French guitarist, composer and performer, trained in both classical and improvised music. Of Portuguese origin, his compositions develop an interaction between the Iberian Peninsula, Europe and, by extension, world cultures. A gold medalist in classical guitar at the Montauban Conservatory, he studied composition and music history at the Toulouse Conservatory, then at the École Normale de Musique de Paris.. He holds a degree in musicology from the University of Aix-en-Provence, where he was a lecturer for several years. He obtained the CAPES, a State diploma that enabled him to teach music education and put his compositions into practice with students in music specialization. • Nominated for the CEMF (French music publishers’ union) competition, for writing a contemporary work, on May 28, 2023. • Participation as solo guitarist in the show « LA PÉPINIÈRE DES COMPOSITEURS », in Aix-en- Provence on June 5 and 6, 2023.Solo concert in and the Paris on June 17, 2023. • Old Time Radio Players Old Time Radio Players Old Time Radio Players Old Time Radio Players Old Time Radio Players Duo concert: Guitar & Cello, given in Balogna, South CorPresent sica, on July 11, 2023. articles.text: The Liminal Perspectives art show, featuring the work of East Bay Asian American artists Michelle Yang and Paul Wang, is now open at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Gallery hours are on weekends from 11 a.m. to. 2 p.m. through September 17. Both artists probe the transitional spaces of emotional boundaries and thresholds. Michelle’s portraits explore this in human ways whereas Paul’s work looks into these ideas in nature’s patterns. Yang incorporates elements that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination. She explores her subject matter in surrealistic details with a touch of abstraction. Her color palette combines contrasting colors, transitioning between warm and cool tones, along with symbolic objects in her artwork that represent the transitional state. She experiments with visual representations of the shift between different emotional and psychological states of humans. Wang’s career in animation is led by a lifelong interest and career in anthropomorphism, which has gradually led him to the quiet spaces found in the intersections of math and art. Often this is discovered through patterns found in nature, both at infinitesimal and celestial scales. His curiosity has led him to computer generated art as well as physical expressions directly from nature. Paul Wang, artist Paul is an award-winning artist and filmmaker, with a career spanning over 30 years. Paul’s work began in animation, where he was a key contributor to animated films such as Antz, Shrek, TMNT (teenage mutant ninja turtles film) and Astro Boy. He explores the connection between nature, math, art, physics, biology, serendipity, and color which he expresses both in physical “natural” art and digital works in algorithmic and generative art. Sentience and anthropomorphism is a persistent thread in his work. Paul is interested in art in all its various forms including animation, sound and words. MICHELLE YANG, artist Michelle Yang is a contemporary portrait artist renowned for her ability to capture the essence and emotions of her subjects. With a keen eye for detail and an intuitive understanding of human emotions, she creates captivating and intimate portraits. As a child she spent hours sketching and painting, honing her skills through self-guided exploration. After high school, Michelle pursued formal art education with a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree from a prestigious art institute in Beijing, China. Her preferred medium is soft pastel, which allows her to infuse her portraits with a rich depth and vibrancy. She incorporates elements that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination. She experiments with visual representations of the emotional and psychological states of humans. articles.text: Part 68 in a biweekly series. City or town plazas are at the other end of the spectrum from the huge monumental civic squares found in large cities we reviewed last time. As mentioned previously, the small scale found in most intimate town or village plazas typically contains more interactive civic spaces composed of restaurants, shopping and some smaller government functions. Because well designed plazas directly contribute so much to the vitality and energy of smaller towns and villages, they are easy to recognize as the heart and soul of the place. It must be remembered that the quality and ultimate success of these public outdoor spaces is largely independent of the architectural styles used. Many of the fine examples we see are formed by a surrounding classical architecture treatment because they were designed long ago when these styles dominated. But the same important urban design concepts can be employed using different contemporary architectural design styles as shown in some of the adjacent examples. There exist important and even critical requirements for all Photos by Will Adams The university town of Guanajuato in central Mexico has one of the most wonderful small-town squares I have ever seen. It has everything: location, enclosure, greenery, density, focus, mixed-use activities and charm. It is formed by mostly three- story buildings and punctuated by a historic theater. As a result, it is always in use by both locals and visitors and is clearly the center of the community. It can be contrasted with the San Jose del Cabo main square also in Mexico. A small city of 130,000 population, the huge main square fronting on the church is completely out of scale, and clearly uninviting. Who wants to walk across the shade-free barren concrete expanse? The four- and five-story buildings that enclose this relatively small-town central plaza in Coimbra, Portugal provide a wonderful theater for the daily free music performances on the steps of the adjacent ornate church. Cars actually creep through these streets at designated times but the pedestrians always have priority. To the right is one of many smaller plazas in the larger city of Lisbon. Everything from paving, to monuments, to light fixtures and landscaping is important to the vitality of the place. Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 3820 Broadway, Oakland

articles.text: New writing classes offered at Adult School If you are a writer – experienced or aspiring – Piedmont Adult School has a class for you this fall. Now is the time to tell the story you have thought about for so long. Gain valuable insights from the talented instructors, while enjoying a supportive community of writers. University Project at San Quentin State Prison. Fiction and Creative Nonfiction The popular Fiction and Creative Nonfiction Writing class is designed for beginners and experienced writers alike and will focus on the components of effective writing and strategies to maintain a writing practice. There will be short readings, writing exercises, discussions, and the opportunity to workshop. Instructor Caitlin McCarthy holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in writing, She currently teaches Literature and Language Arts at Corpus Christi School in Oakland. She is also a private writing coach and teaches writing workshops for all ages. Instructor Denise Bostrom Writing Together: A Poetry Studio In this workshop, students will write and read together, experimenting with new forms and prompts. The class will explore the poetry of everyday life through attention, exploration, and collaboration. This is a chance to try new things in a supportive environment, with time for both community and one-on-one approaches to growth as a creative artist. All levels welcome. Instructor Linda Norton is the author of Wite Out: Love and Work, a memoir with poems. Its prequel, The Public Gardens: Poems and History, was a finalist for a Los Angeles Times Book Prize. She is a former columnist-in-residence at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and has taught writing at SF State, the Emeryville Senior Center, and at the Yeats Academy of the Atlantic Technological University in Ireland. Instructor Caitlin McCarthy Family Stories and Memoir Writing Family Stories and Memoir Writing offers beginning and seasoned writers the tools to discover, reflect on, and write family stories. Using the text “The Art of Memoir” by Mary Karr, the class will cover setting, character investigation, approaches in structuring the work, and a writer’s voice. Excerpts from different memoirs will be analyzed, as students develop, revise, and workshop their stories with a goal of exploring layers in one’s work and supporting publishing goals. Instructor Denise Bostrom, a former Piedmont resident, has written scripts for PBS, HBO, and the Lifetime Channel, and for independent films. She has taught screenwriting and nonfiction/memoir script writing at SF State, SF City College, and the Instructor Linda Norton To register for these and other classes, visit www.piedmontadultschool.org or call the Adult School office at (510) 594-2717. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over.

Like a great Beaujolais, it is lively and vibrant in the mouth and immensely satisfying. Drink slightly chilled with a plate of prosciutto and melon. • 2021 T. Berkeley Ophelia Cabernet Franc This is a beautiful rendition of Cabernet Franc, with dark, brooding blueberry and blackberry fruit, some forest floor and floral notes, a dense purple color and soft, silky tannins. Medium to full-bodied, this is a big juicy, complex wine with good richness and intensity. Should have many good years ahead of itself in the cellar. • 2018 Elaine Chardonnay Calypte Vineyard The 2018 Elaine Chardonnay offers lush aromas of peaches, saline, hazelnuts and notes of dried flowers. In the mouth, it has a medium weight, ultra-silky texture and expansive flavors, framed by delicious juiciness and a long, long finish. On August 13 the Family Winemakers of California held their second ever tasting in Oakland. It is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their nametags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Tempranillo or Alicante Bouchet? Come on in, they’re all here. I was never really able to find out exactly what constitutes a “family winemaker.” The vast majority of the wineries seemed to span the spectrum from small mom and pop operations to small/ medium size operations making under 10,000 cases per year. With the help of fellow wine and food writer Ittai Shui I meandered through the table-filled venue, focusing on small wineries with which I was unfamiliar. There were so many great wines at the tasting – literally hundreds. The following list catalogues the wines that stood out among a huge sea of also-rans. They are wines of great character and quality and are worth searching out. They show that some of the finest wines of the state are created in small, relatively little known, out of the way places by wineries fueled by family love and devotion. • 2013 Viluko Cabernet Sauvignon (BEST VALUE) Usually, Cabernet Sauvignon poured at wine tasting is often way too young and green to be appealing. So, I was delighted to come across this 10-year old bottling from the Mayacamas Mountain area. The nose opens with profound notions of blueberry preserves, tapenade and earth. Medium-bodied rich ripe and concentrated, it has solid structure and exquisite balance finishing long and perfumed. At $50 on their website, this is one of the best deals available in Napa & Sonoma Cabernet. • 2021 DePeche Scarpatta Aglianico What a delightful surprise to come across a California Aglianico. Grown along a dry escarp- • 2018 Intent Syrah Odyssey Vineyard This micro-cuvee (86 cases) from the Russian River Valley has a deep ruby-purple color and classic aromas of cassis, black pepper, blackberry, chocolate, tar and anise. Full-bodied and powerful with rounded tannins, it has good freshness but is still tightly coiled on the finish. Should improve for at least a decade in the cellar. • 2020 Starfield Cinsault Cinsault is a lesser-known blending grape used in the south of France and it’s nice to see it highlighted in this El Dorado County bottling. It has a charming floral nose that jumps from the glass with hints of blueberries and raspberries. In the mouth there is a gusher of round voluptuous fruit followed by fresh juicy acid, finishing clean and vibrant. Best of Family Winemakers of California ment in San Benito County, this rare wine is immediately charming. The nose is perfumed and floral and the wines’ body slight and refreshing. Like a great Beaujolais, it is lively and vibrant in the mouth and immensely satisfying. Drink slightly chilled with a plate of prosciutto and melon. • 2021 T. Berkeley Ophelia Cabernet Franc This is a beautiful rendition of Cabernet Franc, with dark, brooding blueberry and blackberry fruit, some forest floor and floral notes, a dense purple color and soft, silky tannins. Medium to full-bodied, this is a big juicy, complex wine with good richness and intensity. Should have many good years ahead of itself in the cellar. • 2018 Elaine Chardonnay Calypte Vineyard The 2018 Elaine Chardonnay offers lush aromas of peaches, saline, hazelnuts and notes of dried flowers. In the mouth, it has a medium weight, ultra-silky texture and expansive flavors, framed by delicious juiciness and a long, long finish. By Pierre DuMont On August 13 the Family Winemakers of California held their second ever tasting in Oakland. It is one of my favorite wine events of the year. Many of the people pouring the wine have the same name on their nametags as the name on the wine label. There is a warmth, and yes, love for the wines that you do not find at the more “corporate” wine events. The span of different grape varietals was intriguing. Like to taste a Semillon or a Barbera? How about Tempranillo or Alicante Bouchet? Come on in, they’re all here. I was never really able to find out exactly what constitutes a “family winemaker.” The vast majority of the wineries seemed to span the spectrum from small mom and pop operations to small/ medium size operations making under 10,000 cases per year. With the help of fellow wine and food writer Ittai Shui I meandered through the table-filled venue, focusing on small wineries with which I was unfamiliar. There were so many great wines at the tasting – literally hundreds. The following list catalogues the wines that stood out among a huge sea of also-rans. They are wines of great character and quality and are worth searching out. They show that some of the finest wines of the state are created in small, relatively little known, out of the way places by wineries fueled by family love and devotion. • 2013 Viluko Cabernet Sauvignon (BEST VALUE) Usually, Cabernet Sauvignon poured at wine tasting is often way too young and green to be appealing. So, I was delighted to come across this 10-year old bottling from the Mayacamas Mountain area. The nose opens with profound notions of blueberry preserves, tapenade and earth. Medium-bodied rich ripe and concentrated, it has solid structure and exquisite balance finishing long and perfumed. At $50 on their website, this is one of the best deals available in Napa & Sonoma Cabernet. • 2021 DePeche Scarpatta Aglianico What a delightful surprise to come across a California Aglianico. Grown along a dry escarpCalling all writers & poets New writing classes offered at Adult School If you are a writer – experienced or aspiring – Piedmont Adult School has a class for you this fall. Now is the time to tell the story you have thought about for so long. Gain valuable insights from the talented instructors, while enjoying a supportive community of writers. University Project at San Quentin State Prison. Fiction and Creative Nonfiction The popular Fiction and Creative Nonfiction Writing class is designed for beginners and experienced writers alike and will focus on the components of effective writing and strategies to maintain a writing practice. There will be short readings, writing exercises, discussions, and the opportunity to workshop. Instructor Caitlin McCarthy holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in writing, She currently teaches Literature and Language Arts at Corpus Christi School in Oakland. She is also a private writing coach and teaches writing workshops for all ages. Instructor Denise Bostrom Writing Together: A Poetry Studio In this workshop, students will write and read together, experimenting with new forms and prompts. The class will explore the poetry of everyday life through attention, exploration, and collaboration. This is a chance to try new things in a supportive environment, with time for both community and one-on-one approaches to growth as a creative artist. All levels welcome. Instructor Linda Norton is the author of Wite Out: Love and Work, a memoir with poems. Its prequel, The Public Gardens: Poems and History, was a finalist for a Los Angeles Times Book Prize. She is a former columnist-in-residence at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and has taught writing at SF State, the Emeryville Senior Center, and at the Yeats Academy of the Atlantic Technological University in Ireland. Instructor Caitlin McCarthy Family Stories and Memoir Writing Family Stories and Memoir Writing offers beginning and seasoned writers the tools to discover, reflect on, and write family stories. Using the text “The Art of Memoir” by Mary Karr, the class will cover setting, character investigation, approaches in structuring the work, and a writer’s voice. Excerpts from different memoirs will be analyzed, as students develop, revise, and workshop their stories with a goal of exploring layers in one’s work and supporting publishing goals. Instructor Denise Bostrom, a former Piedmont resident, has written scripts for PBS, HBO, and the Lifetime Channel, and for independent films. She has taught screenwriting and nonfiction/memoir script writing at SF State, SF City College, and the • 2018 Intent Syrah Odyssey Vineyard This micro-cuvee (86 cases) from the Russian River Valley has a deep ruby-purple color and classic aromas of cassis, black pepper, blackberry, chocolate, tar and anise. Full-bodied and powerful with rounded tannins, it has good freshness but is still tightly coiled on the finish. Should improve for at least a decade in the cellar. • 2020 Starfield Cinsault Cinsault is a lesser-known blending grape used in the south of France and it’s nice to see it highlighted in this El Dorado County bottling. It has a charming floral nose that jumps from the glass with hints of blueberries and raspberries. In the mouth there is a gusher of round voluptuous fruit followed by fresh juicy acid, finishing clean and vibrant. I would drink this delightful wine slightly chilled on a warm afternoon. • 2021 Gondak Grenache This Russian River Grenache pours a brilliant fuschia in the glass and leads aromatically with raspberries, earth, tobacco and a • 2022 Field Gewurztraminer “I’orange” I am a huge orange wine fan as well as a Gewurztraminer aficionado, so to see them combined was exciting. Fifteen days of skin contact during fermentation gives the wine a lovely golden/ orange hue. Lush and piquant on the palate, with great intensity and beautiful bitters reminiscent of bitter oranges on the finish, this is a rich, tensioned, and vital Gewurtz that is immensely satisfying. I would drink by itself on the porch or deck on a warm afternoon. • 2021 Sir Ras Syrah Bennett Valley Produced by the Box Wine Company of Sebastopol, this is brooding and dark with notes of blackberry, anise, tobacco and black pepper. In the mouth, the tannins create a framework within which the fruit is coiled, and it slowly unfurls through the long finish. Tannic and extraordinarily fresh, this finishes with a spicy elegance. • 2019 Nove Grenache This is not the first time this Lake County Grenache has landed in the top of the Family Winemakers group. It offers a cherry core, with a pleasing dusty mineral essence, hints of wild herbs, sage and red fruit that shines with purity and finesse. Medium-bodied, the generously-layered Grenache unwinds on the palate to reveal juicy red fruit tones, delicate mineral tension and a slightly spicy note on the finish. • 2021 Sojourn Pinot Noir Sangiacomo Vineyard This lovely wine hails from the Sonoma Coast AVA. It has a generous, broody perfume of strawberry jam, tobacco, forest floor and earth. The palate is concentrated, chalky and refreshing with a striking blend of ripe fruit and earthy character and a long, perfumed finish. Perfect with grilled salmon steaks. • 2019 Kendric Syrah Petaluma Gap Instantly impressive, the Kendric Syrah is rich, round and mineral-driven with aromas of black pepper, flowers and blackberries with a touch of plum preserves. Full-bodied and generously layered, the Syrah fills the mouth revealing impressive complexity within a frame of fine-grained tannins that elevate the long savory finish. Delicious juice. 175 cases produced. articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group survived high temperature on August 30, and looked forward to a short walk with some shade. Their first “one block wonder” destination was Carmel Avenue. The group went down Magnolia Avenue past the site of the new aquatics center, where progress on retaining walls was evident. Then it was up Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue at the stop light, down a block, and across Carmel. Towards the end of street architect, urban designer, and Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams told the group he had recently written a column on the “contagious” landscape along Carmel. He pointed out the front yard of a home with an “Inca quality” stonework wall and drought tolerant landscaping. Will said it had inspired the homeowners next door to do a different, softer architectural treatment of their front wall. Will confessed he is the owner of the third next house, and to ‘keep up with the neighbors,” he had done front yard landscaping of his own. It was on to Blair Avenue, named after Walter Blair, the first European settler in what was to become Piedmont, and down El Cerrito Avenue to a set of stairs that took the walkers into Dracena Park. This park land was once part of the 8,000 acres Walter Blair owned and was quarried for stone starting in 1852. The material was used to pave Oakland and Piedmont streets and railways. In 1873, Blair’s crew, consisting of Chinese workers, struck water from a subterranean creek which turned the bottom of the quarry into a lake some 60 feet deep. Attempts to pump out the water failed. Tragically, over the years there were at least 12 drownings in the lake. The quarry was finally fenced and locked for more than 40 years. The lake was called “Blair’s Pond” with ducks until at least 1977. In 1976 citizens voted to create a recreational grass field by draining the pond. Around the turn of the century, the tot lot was renovated, and funds were raised to provide swings, a climbing wall, and restrooms. This work was completed in 2006. The group then walked through the park’s redwood grove, which originally was a creek bed, and now is an offleash dog path. The walkers passed under and then over Storyteller Bridge, where a plaque told them this replacement of the original Storyteller Bridge was Cole Becker’s 2014 Eagle Scout project. The group also walked parts of the pathways that loop through the park and were repaired in August to correct damage caused by last winter’s storms and normal aging. The group emerged from the park on Park Way and made their way to Waldo Avenue, a second “one block wonder.” This street was once the back of Walter Blair’s house. Waldo is now one of the most popular Piedmont streets for Halloween treat seekers. The long line of walkers crossed Highland Avenue and continued up Blair to their third “one block wonder,” Hardwick Avenue. The temperature was starting to rise, so the group passed on walking the short Langdon Court cu-de-sac, and continued to Oakland, Highland, and Craig Avenues. However, there was one more interesting item on Craig Avenue – a “secret entrance” driveway to the back of the Piedmont Community Church. Jim Kellogg led the walkers through a passageway to the church’s courtyard, which had lots of red roses and a lovely fountain. It was a cool way to finish a walk filled with wonders on a warm Piedmont morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Thirty-seven walkers were ready for a short walk last week on August 30. On hand were: Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Will Adams, Allison Isaacs with K-9 best friends Lulu and Bode, Stacey Isaacs with K-9 best friend Pepe Le Pug, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Key Kewley, Karen Palmer, Woody Bailey, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, Jim Kuo, Nancy Henn, Christine Calliste, Lisa Euphrat, Quincy Dong, Mike Henn, Peggy Shultz, Nava Shaham, Martin Levy, Ken Hubbert, Judy Love, Nancy Olsen, Tina Shum, Phil Witte, Stella Houston, Alan Goldhammer, Larry Olsen, Jim Kellogg, Helen Dong, Sarah Johnson, Chuck Oraftik, Ken Young, Rob Smith, Alissa Quan, and Dick Carter. The walkers were pleased to welcome first time walker Barbara Romain, and Susan Callen from Louisville, Kentucky.

There are no pat examples that can be copied indiscriminately. Although there are no hard and fast rules, the concept of “enclosure” (forming “outdoor rooms”) that we have discussed before requires surrounding buildings, trees or landscape features of a certain height – three or four floors is generally necessary to make the concept work. Tis carries a mutual benefit: the plaza gains a strong sense of ”place” plus the security of “eyes on the plaza” from the windows of surrounding (and “enclosing”) upper building levels, while the upper floors themselves have the amenity of a nearby view of the lower plaza open space. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Some day this central area in the heart of Piedmont will be redeveloped as was the adjacent Havens School, the nearby high school, and now the pool. We should be thinking now of how we can enhance this vital area of the city. To capture some of the advantages and community values that can be seen in our plaza examples, I think it is important that we require intelligent, exciting urban design in our definition of what the real estate world calls, “highest and best use”.

The mostly volunteer event is sponsored by the City. Scarecrow Alley – a lineup of scarecrows in the middle of the park, will be followed by a silent auction for purchase of the scarecrows, and a carnival will take place in the Community Hall parking lot, with games and treats for kids of all ages. Edibles Contest The popular Edibles Contest was begun in the Festival’s first year, after the event was created by Susan Hill and Bill Drum. The contest is a showcase for a wide range of fruits and vegetables grown in Piedmont, with categories including: biggest pumpkin, best sweet bread, most unusual vegetable, best apple pie, best jam, best salsa, and even best compost pile. articles.text: A City Council public hearing on Monday, September 18, at 6 p.m. will include a proposal to convert Guilford Road to one-way car travel and remove all street parking (20 spaces) along one side on the short U-shaped street. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the proposed project “was started by a petition signed by all households along Guilford Road requesting that we look into the feasibility of reconfiguring the road. The main concern and reason had to do with emergency vehicle access - the fact that fire trucks, for example, can’t get through when cars are parked along both sides.” The construction impact would be very minor, said Gonzales, involving painting the curb and adding ‘no parking’ signs. articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Four Seasons Arts Four Seasons Arts, a classical music recital and chamber series in Berkeley, needs volunteer drivers to provide door-to-door transportation for subscribers in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Concerts are held on Saturday afternoons at 3 p.m., and subscribers who use the transportation service attend 5 concerts per season. Volunteer drivers are given a pair of complimentary concert tickets and complete directions to one or two convenient stops. Volunteers can drive once or to several concerts, depending on their availability. Drivers must use a reliable, safe, and insured vehicle, have a good DMV driving record and pass a basic background check. For more information, contact Mary Jo Hudgel by phone at 845-4444 or by email at mjhudgel@fsarts.org. Oakland Museum Volunteering at the Oakland Museum of California gives adults and teens the chance to get more involved with a local museum, and an opportunity to learn more about the state’s rich history. The museum is always recruiting volunteers to assist with school groups, events, office work, and more. Informational sessions are offered several times a year, where museum staff discuss the various types of opportunities available. Learn more about orientation dates and apply to volunteer by visiting shiftboard.com/museumca. Prisoners Literature Project The Berkeley-based Prisoners Literature Project is an all-volunteer grassroots nonprofit that has provided free books to prisoners for over 30 years. The organization is always looking for volunteers to answer letters, send out books, learn more about the prison system, and assist with fundraising or publicity efforts. Adult volunteers are encouraged to help, and youth volunteers aged 10 through 15 are welcome with a parent or guardian overseeing their work. Visit prisonlit.org/volunteer for more information. HandsOn Bay Area HandsOn connects community members with high-quality volunteer projects through an extensive network of local nonprofits and schools in need. articles.text: At its September 5 meeting, the City Council will discuss two proposals to make new housing easier to build in Piedmont with pre-approved design plans for affordable Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), and objective design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings. Accessory dwellings (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs, which are Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont, can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (Construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). The proposal would allow Piedmont property owners who submit these preapproved designs as-is to receive a planning permit, giving applicants a head start on the development process. ADUs that use the City’s pre-approved designs would be rent-restricted for 10 years. During this period, if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet “very low income” affordability thresholds for the Alameda County area set by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. However, the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing homeowners to submit ADUs larger than a standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Information on the permit-ready ADU styles, and larger ADUs is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Multifamily objective design standards (MODS) Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The MODS don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. generally urban infill areas, which comprise less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking – they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Community members may submit comments on the proposals ahead of the meeting by email to PiedmontIsHome@piedmont. ca.gov; by mail to the Piedmont Planning Commission, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611; or speak on the topic at the 5:30 p.m. August 14 meeting in-person or via Zoom. The agenda report for both items is available for download on PiedmontIsHome.org. Questions may be sent by email to: piedmontishome@piedmont.ca.gov. “Your speech to the analysts was great, Chief... but you need to be a little more obscure.”

articles.text: Staff photo The bollards at Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue are expected to be replaced by a permanent traffic island. A new traffic and safety design plan will lead to the removal of bollards currently at the intersection of Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue. The project will go out to bid in late September, with construction expected to start in January 2024 and finish that summer. The current painted-stripe “bollard island” at the intersection was approved by the City Council in April 2019, but has come under fire from neighbors. It will be replaced by a permanent, curb-defined traffic island with a pedestrian crosswalk through it. The island will provide direction to westbound drivers on Magnolia. The plan also includes an eastbound left turn pocket to allow sight distance for vehicles turning left from Magnolia onto Nova. The traffic island will be treated with mulch to allow for landscaping upgrades, and will be shaped to allow driveway access for all neighboring residents. A bulb-out will also be added to the 101 corner of Magnolia for traffic making the turn downhill and right onto Nova. The plan will not restrict or eliminate any currently available street parking. The Council approved the new traffic and safety design plan at its April 3, 2023, meeting. The total estimated construction cost is $100,000. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the project “goes back at least 10 years.” The current cluster of bollards met with protests from local residents who contended it was unsightly, confused drivers, and did little to protect pedestrians. In May 2022, one year ago, 120 residents signed a petition asking the city to make permanent improvements to the intersection. Gonzales said that, since then, Public Works held “many public meetings … and a number of follow up meetings with individuals who are impacted by the project, both one on one and then in small neighborhood working groups,” particularly in summer 2022. The meetings focused on traffic impact, pedestrian counts, maintaining access to driveways, and maintaining adequate sight distance for drivers turning left onto Nova from Magnolia. He said that this new plan for a permanent traffic island was made after the meetings and “generally … was very well received.” Questions and comments about the plan may be directed to Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov or phone at 420-3061. articles.text: The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is thrilled to announce that contributions to its fund to provide sustainable landscaping and to support the city’s effort to use green infrastructure for the community swimming pool have passed the $100,000 mark, thereby fully utilizing PBF’s $100,000 matching grant announced this spring. The funds will go toward completion of the new pool’s landscaping with elements and plantings that are both aesthetically appealing and ecologically sensitive. As of August 16, PBF has received contributions totaling $111,611. It is not too late for citizens to add to that total. PBF plans to publish the names of donors as of September 30; thus, there is plenty of time for everyone to become supporters of this landmark project. When informed of the success of the campaign to date, Eric Havian, a leader of the PRFO campaign to fill the original funding gap for the pool, had the following to say: “PBF’s extraordinary contributions have been most valuable because they send a message to the entire City that the value of the Community Pool is not limited to sports groups. The unprecedented support of civic organizations like PBF demonstrates to our residents that everyone will benefit from this jewel in the center of Piedmont. PRFO is profoundly grateful to PBF for stepping up in such a major way.” PBF has been a supporter of the pool from the beginning. It endorsed Measure UU, the bond measure providing the major funding for the pool. When bids came in higher than anticipated, the PBF Trustees voted to contribute $25,000 to help kick off PRFO’s campaign to fill the gap. Now, with the success of the matching grant campaign, Bob McBain, a former mayor and PBF member was delighted, saying, “I’m very grateful that PBF was an early and enthusiastic supporter of the pool project, and has now encouraged others to make contributions to make the pool an amazing facility.” With over $236,000 having now been contributed or pledged toward the pool, PBF hopes its total support may reach a quarter of a million dollars. The sustainable landscaping that PBF will fund will bring native plants and green infrastructure to the pool facility that will conserve water and reduce runoff and pollution. The plants will build the soil and provide habitat for birds and pollinators. This is clearly in line with PBF’s motto: “PBF in partnership with the City for a Safe, Sustainable and Beautiful Community.” Contributions to the pool landscaping campaign can still be sent to PBF at City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611- 4301. Or via the PBF website at www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 30, 2023 5 Beautification Foundation fundraising continues for landscaping at new pool By Cameron Wolfe The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is thrilled to announce that contributions to its fund to provide sustainable landscaping and to support the city’s effort to use green infrastructure for the community swimming pool have passed the $100,000 mark, thereby fully utilizing PBF’s $100,000 matching grant announced this spring. The funds will go toward completion of the new pool’s landscaping with elements and plantings that are both aesthetically appealing and ecologically sensitive. As of August 16, PBF has received contributions totaling $111,611. It is not too late for citizens to add to that total. PBF plans to publish the names of donors as of September 30; thus, there is plenty of time for everyone to become supporters of this landmark project. When informed of the success of the campaign to date, Eric Havian, a leader of the PRFO campaign to fill the original funding gap for the pool, had the following to say: “PBF’s extraordinary contributions have been most valuable because they send a message to the entire City that the value of the Community Pool is not limited to sports groups. The unprecedented support of civic organizations like PBF demonstrates to our residents that everyone will benefit from this jewel in the center of Piedmont. PRFO is profoundly grateful to PBF for stepping up in such a major way.” PBF has been a supporter of the pool from the beginning. It endorsed Measure UU, the bond measure providing the major funding for the pool. When bids came in higher than anticipated, the PBF Trustees voted to contribute $25,000 to help kick off PRFO’s campaign to fill the gap. Now, with the success of the matching grant campaign, Bob McBain, a former mayor and PBF member was delighted, saying, “I’m very grateful that PBF was an early and enthusiastic supporter of the pool project, and has now encouraged others to make contributions to make the pool an amazing facility.” With over $236,000 having now been contributed or pledged toward the pool, PBF hopes its total support may reach a quarter of a million dollars. The sustainable landscaping that PBF will fund will bring native plants and green infrastructure to the pool facility that will conserve water and reduce runoff and pollution. The plants will build the soil and provide habitat for birds and pollinators. This is clearly in line with PBF’s motto: “PBF in partnership with the City for a Safe, Sustainable and Beautiful Community.” Contributions to the pool landscaping campaign can still be sent to PBF at City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, CA 94611- 4301. Or via the PBF website at www.PiedmontBeautificationFoundation.org. articles.text: 6 student-teachers gaining credentials and Master’s degrees Some Piedmont students might find a second teacher in some of their classrooms this year, as the district now has six “Alder Resident” student-teachers. The Alder Graduate School of Education’s teacher residency program allows prospective individuals to earn their teaching credential and Master’s degree in one year while being mentored by a credentialed teacher. This year, four Alder Residents will be at Piedmont High and two are teaching at the elementary schools. The program is similar to Teach For America but at the state and local levels, not through a national program. Alder Residents are contracted through the Alameda County Office of Education (ACOE), which provides each with a $30,000 stipend. A wide range of grant, loan and scholarship options open up to student-teachers once they are accepted into the Alder Graduate School teacher resident program which costs $21,000 in tuition. Piedmont Alder Residents took one month of in-person classes at College of Alameda this summer. During their fall and spring semesters they concurrently take courses to earn a Master’s degree and teaching credential. By next year they will be certified. At PHS, Alder Resident Caleb Brown is paired with Dave Keller (Social Science), Norma Juarez (Spanish) teaches under Deysi Sahagon, Beth McNeill is in John Hayden’s math classroom and Lael Melchert is learning the ins and out of Biology lessons from Shelley Seto. Two more Alder residents are working with Piedmont elementary school special education teachers. Bunthoeun Hack works under Michelle Sage at Beach School, and Kwame Payne is learning on the job from Sally Samuth at Havens. Payne, Hack and McNeil worked in the district last year as classified staff or as substitute teachers. McNeil, also a mom of two Beach students, started to seriously explore a career in teaching at the start of 2023 by substitute teaching. She ended up finishing the school year as a long-term substitute for a Beach Kindergarten teacher on maternity leave for six weeks. McNeil told the Post there are plenty of options to get a credential but was drawn towards the Alder program because it gives her a Master’s degree and because it lets you work with a teacher in the classroom for a full year. She currently is the student-teacher in Hayden’s honors statistics and Math Analysis classes. “The program gives you a lot of freedom, and it can change every day. On Thursday I am doing a take-over of a couple classes,” she said. McNeil said other teachers in the math department have given her the green light to sit in on their lessons, too. PUSD’s Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich oversees the Alder Residents. He confirmed that the program gives the district a leg up on hiring new teachers, something critical during the current teacher shortage. “Superintendent Hawn and I both love the idea of the Alder Resident program; we need to grow that,” said Dolowich. A success story of the program is Piedmont native Russell Jeng (PHS 2014), who was mentored by 2nd grade teacher Nancy Roscelli last year, Roscelli’s final year of teaching before retirement. Jeng was hired as a certified 3rd grade teacher at Beach for the fall, where he teaches math, writing and science. “Teaching in Piedmont has been great, it’s wonderful to see how much these kids know and knowing that I was once in their footsteps a long time ago,” he said. “I would recommend this program. It’s intense and you’ll really need to be committed, but having a mentor and residency director will give you someone who you can always turn to for advice and help,” said Jeng. Current Alder Resident Beth McNeil is earning her teaching credential and Master’s degree while receiving in-class experience and mentorship at PHS.
