articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is ready to take on another great year of service. The Crew, a coed Venturing program through the Piedmont Scout Council, will host an Open House on September 10 to describe its many activities and projects taking place during the year. PCSC has been around for 19 years, providing a chance for generations of local youth (ages 10-20) to plan, participate in, and contribute to projects. It is a fun and easy way to get service hours while establishing bonds with fellow Crew members. While we do not impose any participation minimums, to keep it a low-stress organization, our members provide their own ideas on how to make community service beneficial to all. We confidently say that everything that we do as a crew is amazing. We plan and create our unique projects that interest us, often funding the costs as well. Many of our most popular events were originated and conceived by past members,” said Elena O’Connell, Vice President of Communications. A small sampling includes: sorting produce at the Alameda County Community Food Bank, cooking meals for the food insecure, painting murals, building Tiny Houses for homeless teens, improving and cleaning the local environment, and tutoring children, The Community Service Crew has roughly 150 members and organize multiple events each week. It provide leadership opportunities for its members, and a platform to share their own ideas, building self confidence in the process. Every spring the most involved members are encouraged to run for elected positions. The elected crew officers are mentored weekly by adult volunteers to take on responsibilities that are often associated only with adults. The VPs each lead their own team of assistants and are responsible for different aspects of running an organization. Cooking for the food insecure — Members enjoy the teamwork involved in cooking together, and one member takes on the planning of the menu and shopping for the food. We do this more than once per month. The crew’s fundraising team provides funding. Tutoring underserved elementary school kids — PCSC piloted a new weekly program with an East Oakland elementary school to help children from Spanish speaking families. Crew members sign up for each Wednesday that they are available; parents are needed to drive. Tiny House project — PCSC has funded and built several tiny houses for homeless teens over the past few years and is excited to start on a new project this September. We hope to raise $10,000 via donations in the next few weeks, then build the house on a trailer in Piedmont and deliver it to a new Tiny House village in Richmond. Crew members will be encouraged to work on weekends. Annual House Renovation project — Each spring, a select team of members form a project team working with Rebuilding Together Oakland to select a low income, elderly or disabled Oakland homeowner whose home will be renovated. The crew typically spends 3 months on the project and over a thousand hours. PCSC is one of very few volunteer groups that manages its project independently, and the only teen group doing that. Fundraising in the community — Our Fundraising VPs organize several fundraising events that give the crew visibility in our community. PCSC is a proud sponsor of the annual Piedmont July 4th pancake breakfast, a major fundraiser for future projects.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Service Crew to host Open House Sept. 10

articles.text: Piedmont football head coach Jordan Seiden called this year’s coaching staff the best in his 30 years of coaching. There’s a wealth of experience in Seiden’s second year at the school, bringing together a veteran staff that includes former longtime Bishop O’Dowd and Mt. Eden coach Paul Perenon as offensive coordinator. It also includes former Fremont of Oakland line coaches Isaac and Pauhila Tauaho. Former coordinator Mike Dixon remains an offensive assistant, while defensive coordinator Kerry Griffin and running backs coach DeMario Glenn enter their second year. Local football aficionados will know Perenon. He spent 25-years as Bishop O’Dowd’s coach from 1985-2009, then coached at Mt. Eden from 2010-2022. Seiden was an assistant and junior varsity coach at O’Dowd under Perenon. “Jordan coached our JV football team back in 2001 or 2002. I’ve just followed his career and we have kept in touch over the years. He was going to be on our staff in Mt. Eden in the fall of 2019 but some family issues precluded him being able to become our defensive coordinator. And then he got the job at Piedmont,” said Perenon. After spending 13 years as Mt. Eden’s head coach, Perenon made the decision to step down from the job due to a lack of necessary support from the Hayward school in aiding his student-athletes academically. He remains a PE teacher at Mt. Eden. “I had already set up the schedule at Mt. Eden and had full intention of continuing there, but circumstances changed,” Perenon said. “I talked with Jordan in June and he asked me how retirement was going. I told him I’m not retired, I’m just not coaching at Mt. Eden and I’d take the right situation if it came up. Jordan then invited me to their summer workouts,” said Perenon. Seiden told him that his coaching staff, including former coordinator and current offensive assistant Mike Dixon, wanted Perenon to run the offense. Perenon attended one of Piedmont’s 7-on-7 practices in June and decided to join the Highlanders soon after. Perenon enters a similar situation in Piedmont to when he joined Mt. Eden in 2010 and Bishop O’Dowd in 1985, both programs that were rebuilding. He took O’Dowd to three NCS titles in 1997, 1998 and 2004. He can take credit for helping send countless players to play in college, including Langston Walker, Burl Toler, Kirk Morrisson, and Piedmont-native Eric Bjornson, all of whom went toto play in the NFL. When starting at Mt. Eden, Perenon took a severely underfunded public school football team that went winless in the two previous years and turned them Staff Photo Former longtime Bishop O’Dowd coach Paul Perenon will be Piedmont football team’s new offensive coordinator. into structured and respected team. Coming to Piedmont, he is once again working with team that is rebuilding after two years effectively without a varsity program. “Rebuilding projects are in my DNA. I got the O’Dowd job back in 1985; the program was in the shadow of basketball. By the fifth-year, we went to 10-0 and an NCS playoff berth for the first-time in O’Dowd’s history. We had Eric Bjornson, who went to Piedmont Middle School and played in the flag program. There was a tough animosity when he decided to come to O’Dowd. We added a freshman team during my time there and started winning championships. I started teaching at Mt. Eden in 2011 and that program was on life support when we got there. It just wasn’t healthy. We put it back together and made it competitive,” said Perenon. Through his early-days with the Piedmont football team, Perenon has been mightily encouraged by seeing the “spark” switch on for players. For Piedmont to succeed in 2023, they’ll have to find ways to stay healthy with a modest roster of around 25 players “ My ex p e r ie nc e w it h low-number teams is you have to be in great shape, so you can’t compromise conditioning. The kids have to be ready for a 48-minute game; I tip my hat to Jordan for being able to condition them,” said Perenon. The Highlanders dropped their season-opener 33-21 to Pierce last weekend but look ahead to Miramonte in Orinda this Friday, September 1. The Highlanders then have a tantalizing matchup at Mt. Eden on September 8, when Perenon will get his first look at his former team.
articles.title: Football team hires Perenon as offensive coordinator

articles.text: Piedmont’s varsity football team traveled 100 miles to Pierce High School in Arbuckle (Colusa County) for its season-opener on Friday, August 25, losing 33-21. The Highlanders outgained Pierce 373 yards to 283 offensively, but committed three turnovers and failed to covert on three fourth-down situations. Piedmont opened the first drive with a touchdown on a long series that resulted in a oneyard burst across the goal line by running back Tommy Ashton for a 7-0 lead. However, the Highlanders wouldn’t get back on the scoreboard until early in the fourth quarter. “It felt like a classic example of letting one get away. We were up 7-0 and then had some turnovers and gave them a short-field. We were driving the ball well and they really couldn’t stop what we were doing offensively,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We just couldn’t finish drives and turned the ball over too often,”. The Bears tied the game on a 68-yard pass and run to end the first-quarter tied at 7-7, , Pierce Receiver Sam Shelby finished with seven receptions, 102 yards, and scored one touchdown. put up three more touchdowns to score 28 unanswered points, including touchdown runs of four-, one-, and 12-yards. Pierce stayed with its ground game and gained 191 rushing yards on 35 attempts, while only completing four passes, Seiden thinks defensive alignment played a factor in Piedmont’s miscues. Pierce has a roster of 50 players, about double the size of Piedmont’s team, allowing it to rotate players to take advantage of tired linemen. “I don’t think it was the talent of Pierce’s defensive line as much as it was their depth. They were able to come in waves,” said Seiden. “Depth is always going to be an issue for us – until it’s not an issue.” The Highlanders entered the fourth quarter trailing 27-7 but rallied to score 14 points in the final going. With 11 minutes left in the game, receiver Sam Shelby took a crossing route 52-yards to the house, starting at the right sideline and cutting it back across the field to score at the left end zone pylon. It was an impressive run by the junior wide out. “Sam played well. He probably could have had a couple more scores. He nearly scored on a kickoff return and just missed on a couple of fades to him,” said Seiden. Pierce scored on a six-yard carry to make it 33-13, but PHS scored the final touchdown of the game on a series capped off Quarterback Markos Lagios had 305 yards of total offense.
articles.title: Highlanders fall 33-21 in season-opener at Pierce

articles.text: Staff Photos Tanya Kononova enters her senior year after winning last year’s WACC singles title. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team is about to begin its season which starts with its annual non-league match at Miramonte in Orinda on September 6. Last year the Highlander compiled a record of 16-3 on their way to an undefeated Western Alameda County Conference title before reaching the North Coast Section semifinals. Coach Jim Landes and assistant coach Corey Reich are keeping watchful eyes to determine how this year’s singles and doubles lineups will resolve. Piedmont has a good cast of eight returning varsity players, but must replace five experienced layers dye to graduation, including No. 1 doubles team Michaela Bini and Mara LaForte, and No. 2 singles player Anne Jumper. “We lost a few girls who graduated and some starters, but I think overall we will be almost as strong if not as strong as last season,” said Landes. “We did very well last season; we almost won Sophomore Kate Jumper is Piedmont’s likely No. 2 singles starter. Sophomore Arianna Kortum has been impressive since joining the team last year. NCS and won the league.” Returning for her senior year and second year on the team is Tanya Kononova, the No. 1 singles player since her arrival a year ago as a refugee from Ukraine. She won last year’s Western Alameda County Conference singles tournament. She’s been competing in local tournaments, boosting her ranking as she gains more recognition from colleges. “We have Tanya back at No. 1,” confirmed Landes. “She’s better than she was last year, working hard and I’ve been helping her as much as I can, taking her to some tournaments. She’s been doing pretty well.” Kononova may have some serious competition this year from Bishop O’Dowd’s No. 1, Polina Marakhtanova, a native of Russia, who didn’t play last year. So far sophomore Kate Jumper, the younger sister of Anne, appears to be ready to claim the role of No. 2 singles. “Kate mostly did doubles last year but she’s really playing well. Right now, she’s the clear No. 2,” said Landes. Behind them, Landes is determining who looks best to round out their singles lineup and which players to pair together at doubles. Kate played doubles with classmate Arianna Kortum last year and performed well at the No. 3 spot. Senior Cecilia DeFazio and junior Emma Eisemon did well as a No. 2 doubles team, and have the possibility of playing singles this season. Returning players senior Ellie Broscow, junior Abigail Call, and junior Carolina Romanczuk. New varsity athletes who have impressed are sophomores Samantha Huynh, Inara Mehta, Madeline Tran, and juniors Sophie LaForte and Alina Shahid. “We’re not sure about 3-4 yet; we have about a lot of players who are really close in level,’ explained Landes. ”Some are better suited for singles and some for doubles. Carolina played No. 3 a lot last year. Ellie Broscow is a senior, and Arianna Kortum is a younger player who can play singles. Cecilia DeFazio is also a possibility at singles.” Following Piedmont’s season-opener at Miramonte in Orinda on September 6, they’ll participate in the Golden State Championships on September 8-9 a highly competitive tournament with 30 teams being hosted by Gunn and Palo Alto High School.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team survived a challenging game with Pierce High School in Arbuckle (Colusa County) on Friday, August 25, in their first game of the season. Despite some signs of hope, turnovers and the opposing team’s formidable running game proved to be decisive factors that contributed to a 50-0 victory for the home team. In contrast, Piedmont’s varsity played to a much more closely contested game with Pierce in a 28-21 loss. As the game kicked off, Pierce quickly took control with a running game, and scored quickly. Amidst the challenges Piedmont’s return specialists, George Bishop and Jason Shum, both made impressive returns of over 50 yards. However, Piedmont’s offense could do little to move the ball other than a 13-yard reception by Bishop and quarterback Cash Panico scrambling for 54 yards on the ground. The game unfolded under scorching conditions, with temperatures soaring to 95 degrees. This heat took a toll on Piedmont’s players, evident from fatigue shown whenever there was a break in the action. One bright spot was on Pierce’s lone passing attempt, when freshman Diego Hurwitz picked off the pass. After that Pierce never threw the ball again for the rest of the game. Defensive highlights included Cash Panico with 15 total tackles, Jason Shum eight tackles, and Nik Costello with a sack and seven tackles. In the second half, Pierce returned an interception for a touchdown and continued using its running game to exploit the Scots’ defense. pages.text: Wednesday, August 30, 2023 13 Piedmont’s defending WACC championship tennis team building towards season Staff Photos Tanya Kononova enters her senior year after winning last year’s WACC singles title. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team is about to begin its season which starts with its annual non-league match at Miramonte in Orinda on September 6. Last year the Highlander compiled a record of 16-3 on their way to an undefeated Western Alameda County Conference title before reaching the North Coast Section semifinals. Coach Jim Landes and assistant coach Corey Reich are keeping watchful eyes to determine how this year’s singles and doubles lineups will resolve. Piedmont has a good cast of eight returning varsity players, but must replace five experienced layers dye to graduation, including No. 1 doubles team Michaela Bini and Mara LaForte, and No. 2 singles player Anne Jumper. “We lost a few girls who graduated and some starters, but I think overall we will be almost as strong if not as strong as last season,” said Landes. “We did very well last season; we almost won Sophomore Kate Jumper is Piedmont’s likely No. 2 singles starter. Sophomore Arianna Kortum has been impressive since joining the team last year. NCS and won the league.” Returning for her senior year and second year on the team is Tanya Kononova, the No. 1 singles player since her arrival a year ago as a refugee from Ukraine. She won last year’s Western Alameda County Conference singles tournament. She’s been competing in local tournaments, boosting her ranking as she gains more recognition from colleges. “We have Tanya back at No. 1,” confirmed Landes. “She’s better than she was last year, working hard and I’ve been helping her as much as I can, taking her to some tournaments. She’s been doing pretty well.” Kononova may have some serious competition this year from Bishop O’Dowd’s No. 1, Polina Marakhtanova, a native of Russia, who didn’t play last year. So far sophomore Kate Jumper, the younger sister of Anne, appears to be ready to claim the role of No. 2 singles. “Kate mostly did doubles last year but she’s really playing well. Right now, she’s the clear No. 2,” said Landes. Behind them, Landes is determining who looks best to round out their singles lineup and which players to pair together at doubles. Kate played doubles with classmate Arianna Kortum last year and performed well at the No. 3 spot. Senior Cecilia DeFazio and junior Emma Eisemon did well as a No. 2 doubles team, and have the possibility of playing singles this season. Returning players senior Ellie Broscow, junior Abigail Call, and junior Carolina Romanczuk. New varsity athletes who have impressed are sophomores Samantha Huynh, Inara Mehta, Madeline Tran, and juniors Sophie LaForte and Alina Shahid. “We’re not sure about 3-4 yet; we have about a lot of players who are really close in level,’ explained Landes. ”Some are better suited for singles and some for doubles. Carolina played No. 3 a lot last year. Ellie Broscow is a senior, and Arianna Kortum is a younger player who can play singles. Cecilia DeFazio is also a possibility at singles.” Following Piedmont’s season-opener at Miramonte in Orinda on September 6, they’ll participate in the Golden State Championships on September 8-9 a highly competitive tournament with 30 teams being hosted by Gunn and Palo Alto High School. articles.text: Championship water polo team returns with eyes on NCS title Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team is back for 2023 and has been completely clear on their aspirations for this year, in spite of being in the second year without a hometown pool. After winning back-to-back Western Alameda County Conference titles and two-consecutive North Coast Section semifinals appearances, the Highlanders return with their target on capturing the school’s first NCS title. “We feel like this team is capable of winning NCS, that’s our goal,” said coach Rik Krumins, entering his second year at the helm. ”We have a lot of returning talent and think we can take that next step,” Piedmont won last year’s WACC Championship over Alameda with a resounding 13-4 victory and finished the season with a 20-7 overall record. They return several key players, including Peter Krumins, Declan Linnane, George Stein, Evan Dickason, Daniel Banin, Quincy Sherman and Finn Burke – all seniors. “I think we’ll be able to be versatile; everyone in the pool can play every position. In the past, not everyone could handle the ball, pass, and shoot. Now, I think all six people can handle that. I think we’ll all be threats,” said Linnane. Krumins recalled Piedmont’s 2021 WACC title win over Berkeley, 12-8, in which Piedmont had to rely on its starters for nearly every minute of the match. With a deeper team Piedmont will be able to attack with more players. “Now we can go to our starters, then make subs and be just fine,” said Krumins. Piedmont reached the 2021 North Coast Section semifinals, losing 7-4 to No. 2 Marin Academy. Last year the Highlanders lost to the same school, 6-5. The biggest change on this year’s team will be the absence of all-league goalie Dariush Kashani, who was voted the League Player of the Year. Junior Gus von Metszch and sophomore Luke McAuliffe will be competing for the position. “Those two are competing. Gus has a lot of length and Luke has a lot of experience with club. It’s fun to have those decisions,” said Rik Krumins. “Dariush made us comfortable in the water. We knew the day would come when he wouldn’t be Peter Krumins returns for his senior season. articles.text: On Saturday, August 26 at the Laney College pool, Piedmont High School’s boys’ water polo team hosted its annual Alumni Game. It brought together players going back to the very start of the program in the early 90s. The alumni won the game 19-15 with help of the school’s all-time leading scorer Patrick Conn and all-time leading assister Henry Saunders, classmates from 2019. “It’s great to bring the community together. It seems like every year it gets bigger. We’ve had some talented teams over the years and it’s great to put our team in the pool against players like Patrick and Henry. It’s really a testament to the Piedmont water polo community,” said PHS head coach Rik Krumins, who jumped in the pool with everyone else after the game. Conn and Saunders led Piedmont in the fall of 2018 to a 22-6 overall record, but narrowly lost in the WACC Finals to Bishop O’Dowd. The team lost in the NCS Semifinals to Cardinal Newman the following year. Conn continued his career at the University of Toronto and Saunders at USC. Piedmont’s Class of 2019 marked the final team to play in the Piedmont Pool. Since then, the Highlanders have been playing on the road. The pool is being replaced by a new $19 million aquatic facility, but not until the summer of 2024. The team captured the first two League (WACC) titles in school history in 2021 and 2022. Now, PHS is looking to get over its North Coast Section hump and capture a an NCS banner. “Events like today and community building activities really brings everyone together. These events help make the program what it is today,” said senior leader George Stein. “We’re a really driven team and we want to win, but at the end of the day it’s the community that gets people here.” “It helped us to see so many great players like Henry, Patrick, and Adam [Lowe] play at Piedmont. It really inspired us to push our game to play before high school,” mentioned fellow senior Declan Linnane. GAME RECAP In the first quarter, Piedmont High jumped ahead 3-0, however, the rallied to close the score to 3-2. PHS went ahead 4-2, but Conn scored to make it 4-3. PHS increased its lead to 5-3 until the Patrick Conn, Class of 2019, was a mainstay on the Alumni team. He is the school’s all-time leading scorer. Henry Saunders, Class of 2019, is Piedmont High’s all-time leader in assists. alumni tied it at 5-5 with goals from Saunders and Conn. In the second period, PHS surged ahead 7-5, but Saunders quickly responded for a 7-7 tie. After falling behind 8-6, Conn scored back-to-back goals to the game a 8-8. Just before halftime, the high school team scored again for a slender 9-8 edge, The teams traded goals until the Alumni took a 12-11 lead in the third quarter. At 12-12, the Alumni scored four goals to go up 16-12, the biggest margin in the game. But PHS was not done. They scored the opening three goals of the fourth period to make it a nail-biter at 16-15. Conn and Saunders re-entered the pool, and soon the scored soared to 19-15. At the end, everyone jumped in the pool for some mayhem, with more than 30 people having a great time.

articles.text: A 1.4 mile round trip hike in the Oakland Hills, the Bridgeview Trail provides whimsical thrills for kids, dog walkers, and those young at heart with its collection of hand-crafted rustic trolls hiding along the trail for visitors to find. The trend unofficially began in fall of 2020 and sparked in popularity during the pandemic when everyone was looking for a way to safely exercise. Located with trailheads on Bridgeview Drive or Monterey Boulevard near the Montclair Golf Course, the walk is great for all ages. More than 20 Trolls are tucked away along the trail. Several rope swings are there to take advantage of. You’ll pass by the Montclair Golf Course driving range about midway through the hike, as the trail leads down to four switchback turns heading to Sausal Staff Photos The Bridgeview Trail in Oakland has a collection of over 20 “Trolls”. Pictured here is one of the original trolls, “Bebe.” Creek. The walk has less than 200 feet of elevation gain, making it perfect for seniors and families with children. But the troll and swings combined make it a popular spot, meaning those annoyed by crowds should probably opt for an early weekday. Even on a Monday at 10 a.m., we saw 34 hikers. from our favorite trolls found on the Bridgeview Trail. Follow The Bridgeview Trolls updates on social media; Facebook: The Bridgeview Trolls. articles.text: Piedmont High’s volleyball team recently played a group of pre-season games as participants in Cougar Challenge hosted by Albany High School on Saturday, August 26. The Highlanders split their four matches, defeating Salesian 25-14, 25-12 and Alameda in three-sets, 25-12, 15-25, 15-12, They lost to Mission San Jose in three sets, 15-25, 27-25, 15-17, and were defeated by perennial powerhouse Albany, the host team, 20-25, 21-25. The Highlanders enter the 2023 season needing to replace some key players who graduated. They will return some experienced players from last year’s squad with Sadie Town, Izzy Grimmer, Maddy Mullin, Elena Stevens, sisters Bauer and Beck Peterson, and Molly Wagener. “We have a heavy roster of seniors. We’re just a bit undersized and trying to find a good rhythm. We’re working to see where the pieces need to go in order to be successful,” said coach Mariah Cardeñas. Last year marked a season of progress for the program After posting a 3-12 record in 2021, it finishing with a 10-14 overall record. Their goal this year is to qualify for their first North Coast Section appearance since 2018. “We’re aiming to make it into the playoffs. We haven’t seen a playoff berth during my time here. I want us to come in strong and solidify a spot. We want to be better every season – that’s the goal,” said Cardeñas. articles.text: August 18 San Francisco Choral Society concert Ukraine and Mozart, an unlikely coupling indeed, paired to light up Davies Hall recently in a gratifying choral-orchestral concert under Robert Geary. Geary’s S.F. Choral Society linked with Ukrainian composer Alexander Shchetynsky, 63, from afar unveiling his Requiem (1991- 2004), a serene lyrical outpouring with string orchestra. However somber a work, the composer establishes a mellifluous flow in his work with Latin text, closer to the spirit of Brahms’ Requiem. Among his original touches was the “Lacrimosa,” with choral sound segments seemingly coming from various directions. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s Hippest Trip - The Soul Train Musical is currently playing at the Toni Rembe Theater, 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Soul Train is based on the iconic TV show that originally aired on Chicago airwaves in the 1970’s. For over 30 years, it brought Black music, dance, and style into living rooms in America and was a celebration of black youth culture. The show’s self-proclaimed reputation was “the hippest trip in America,” hence the musical’s title. The creative team behind ACT’s reimagined Soul Train includes Tony Award–nominated playwright Dominique Morisseau known for The Detroit Project, Tony Award–nominated choreographer Camille A. Brown, and the Apollo Theater’s executive director Kamilah Forbes. Playwright Morisseau said she is looking forward to partnering with an all-female creative team to celebrate “the history and unsung heroes of our nation’s longest running televised music and dance series.” “I am so excited to help bring the narrative of one of our culture’s most influential and legend-making endeavors to the stage. Having grown up on this series and being immersed in the culture around it, I never knew what it took to make it the iconic staple that it is,” she said. The cast includes Angela Birchett as Delores, Quentin Earl Darrington as Don Cornelius, Amber Iman as Pam Brown, and Kayla Davion as Jody Watley. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/2023-24-season/soul-train/.

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) opens a new, permanent collection exhibition entitled Sea Change on Saturday, September 2, with photographer and Piedmonter Reagan Louie among the featured artists. Sea Change features works by Takashi Arai, Jonathan Calm, Tina Barney, Guanyu Xu, and Zoe Strauss, as well as solo presentations of work by Ilse Bing and Louie. Speaking on the show, Louie said “The exhibition’s title is an expression that denotes a dramatic change, a paradigm shift… I’m delighted to be in this timely show about the global transitional moment we are in. The monographic presentation of my work explores China during [the 1980s], arguably the most transformative period in its modern history.” While his father was born in a village in Guangdong, China, Louie is a fifth-generation Californian on his mother’s side and often cites this contrast and the challenges of assimilating between two developing, often competing societies as a major influence on his work. “The photographs reveal China’s emergence from the slumber of the Cultural Revolution to become a global superpower,” Louie added. Among the works to be featured in his solo presentation is “Birdman” from his Beijing, 1987 series, pictured above. Overall, the new collection at SFMOMA explores how modern photography bears witness to political and environmental shifts over time. The exhibition is presented as a suite of thematic and monographic galleries, mainly focused on waterways and oceans. The works of photography are by over 50 under-recognized artists from around the world. The exhibition will be on view through February 19, 2024. To learn more, visit sfmoma. org/exhibition/sea-change-photographs-from-the-collection. “Birdman,” from Piedmonter and photographer Reagan Louie’s Beijing 1987 series of photos. Louie is among 50 artists from around the world to be featured in Sea Change, a new, permanent collection exhibition at SFMOMA on view now through February 2024. articles.text: The Liminal Perspectives art show, featuring the work of East Bay Asian American artists, Michelle Yang and Paul Wang, opens this Saturday, September 2 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The show will be open on weekends from 11 a.m. to. 2 p.m. through September 17, with an opening reception on Saturday. September 2 from 2:00 to 5:00 p.m. Both artists probe the transitional spaces of emotional boundaries and thresholds. Michelle’s portraits explore this in human ways whereas Paul’s work looks into these ideas in nature’s patterns. Yang incorporates elements that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination. She explores her subject matter in surrealistic details with a touch of abstraction. Her color palette combines contrasting colors, transitioning between warm and cool tones, along with symbolic objects in her artwork that represent the transitional state. She experiments with visual representations of the shift between different emotional and psychological states of humans. Wang’s career in animation is led by a lifelong interest and career in anthropomorphism, which has gradually led him to the quiet spaces found in the intersections of math and art. Often this is discovered through patterns found in nature, both at infinitesimal and celestial scales. His curiosity has led him to computer generated art as well as physical expressions directly from nature. Paul Wang, artist Paul is an award-winning artist and filmmaker, with a career spanning over 30 years. Paul’s work began in animation, where he was a key contributor to animated films such as Antz, Shrek, TMNT (teenage mutant ninja turEmoji Lunar Bicycle 24” x 24” by Paul Wang tles film) and Astro Boy. He explores the connection between nature, math, art, physics, biology, serendipity, and color which he expresses both in physical “natural” art and digital works in algorithmic and generative art. Sentience and anthropomorphism is a persistent thread in his work. Paul is interested in art in all its various forms including animation, sound and words. cation with a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree from a prestigious art institute in Beijing, China. With a keen eye for detail and an intuitive understanding of human emotions, she creates captivating and intimate portraits. As a child she spent hours sketching and painting, honing her skills through self-guided exploration. articles.text: Music preview by Paul Hertelendy One of the newest and most versatile early-music singing groups locally is Tactus SF, now seven years old, affiliated with the San Francisco Early Music Society. Mention “early music” and you expect to hear polyphonic chorales from Europe. Not so, this time. This 20-member a cappella group put together an entire program of early New-World music, “Cantus Mexicanus,” digging out sacred renaissance choral music of “New Spain,” as it was then called, It is music we almost never get to hear, part of it sung in indigenous languages. One of the beauties of Bay Area residence is the chance to hear concerts with a broader repertoire, whether instrumental or vocal. The Tactus discovery trip transpired August 27 at St. Mark’s Episcopal Church in Berkeley, with the added asset of a period wind instruments trio, with some singers doubling as instrumentalists. Music Director Elizabeth Kimble has assembled a varied group, notable both for its versatility and its resounding lyric sopranos, to perform half-forgotten 16th- and 17th-century selections. The most accomplished of all these composers were two that started in Spain and emigrated to take on church posts in Mexico. Gutierréz de Padilla was a master polyphonist running the cathedral in Puebla. (Here, with two of his brief Latin excerpts, “Vidi turbam” and “Stabat mater.”) Even more remarkable was Hernando Franco, choirmaster in Mexico City less than a century after Columbus’ first New-World discovery journey. The implication is that he produced good works and performers for worship in record time. Besides the Latin, the polyglot ensemble Tactus also performed in local languages like Nahuatl and Peruvian Quechua, both ballasted by intimidating five-syllable words. Of special note was one of the Old-Testament Lamentations of Jeremiah portraying the suffering of the people, composed by the indigenous Juan de Lienas. Instrumental works by Bravo and Gaspar Fernandes featured Renaissance cornetto, sackbut and dulcian. Given the direction of repertory here, then certainly a future program of music from our California missions would be appropriate, particularly delving into the archives of Mission San Jose in Fremont, which developed some of the finest music programs of all the West Coast missions in the early 19th century under Fr. Narcisco Durán. Tactus SF, a Bay Area unaccompanied mixed chorus under Elizabeth Kimble, performing Aug. 26 and 27 on each side of the Bay, the latter at St. Mark’s Episcopal, 2300 Bancroft, Berkeley. Cortina Alta Chardonnay (Mendoza, Argentina, 2019) was the selected wine. Our third course was a spectacular warm duck salad served in three variations. This dish The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet featured a large portion of duck foie gras accompanied by shredded duck breast atop a wedge of toast with a side of roasted apples and grapes. Strangely enough, a Mount Carmel Pinot noir (Rita Hills, 2019) was the choice of wine here. But can you believe it – those were the preliminaries. Roasted Sea Bass with celery root and black truffle was the first main course. The selected wine was a unique Vin d’Ambre Sauvignon Blanc (Anderson, Valley, 2019. Then came the second main course, which was an herbcrusted rack of lamb with honey-stewed peppers, garlic butter, and a basil–citrus chutney. Once again, the side course of honey stewed peppers was a delightful surprise. And once again, the preparation for this colorful side dish is surprisingly easy. As dinner progressed, sommelier Erik Segelbaum explained his choices of wines and included some side comments about the food we were enjoying. The first dessert was Epoisses cheese with spice-roasted peach crostini. Sandeman, a 10-year old Tawney port from the Douro Valley in Portugal was the ideal dessert wine. A bowl of chocolate Mezcal truffle candies sent us into the beyond. Plating for the dinner was very simple with white dishes and simple wine glasses. While this dinner was spectacular beyond belief, you can have great success at home if you serve just one of the salads and one of the warm dishes as a main course. Your success is guaranteed! Chef Alessandro Stratta is a James Beard award winner. articles.text: The Broadcast Legends “OldTime Radio Players” will bring Golden Memories of Radio to Piedmont on Sunday afternoon, September 17, at 4:00 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. “The Old Time Radio Players” and technical crew will re-create examples of radio newscasts, kids’ shows, daytime Soap Operas, bloopers, commercials, jingles, plus the main event, a complete episode of “The Lone Ranger.” It’s a nostalgic presentation that will take audience members back to a time when “radio was king” and the “theatre of the mind” captured our imaginations. Broadcast Legends was founded over 30 years ago and boasts over 200 members – radio and television professionals who have worked in the broadcast industry for at least 20 years. “The Old Time Radio Players” serves as the Legends’ community outreach ar m, bringing the fun and excitement of live radio to appreciative audiences throughout the Bay Area. articles.text: French-American duo to perform a Friday night concert A guitar-percussion duo concert by Arthur Dente and Steve Robertson will take place at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, September 16 at 7 p.m. Advance tickets at $20 are available at https://bpt. me/6124713, or $25 at the door - cash or checks only. Arthur Dente is a French guitarist, composer and performer, trained in both classical and improvised music. Of Portuguese origin, his compositions develop an interaction between the Iberian Peninsula, Europe and, by extension, world cultures. A gold medalist in classical guitar at the Montauban Conservatory, he studied composition and music history at the Toulouse Conservatory, then at the École Normale de Musique de Paris.. He holds a degree in musicology from the University of Aix-en-Provence, where he was a lecturer for several years. He obtained the CAPES, a State diploma that enabled him to teach music education and put his compositions into practice with students in music specialization. • Nominated for the CEMF (French music publishers’ union) competition, for writing a contemporary work, on May 28, 2023. Guitarist & composer Arthur Dente • • • Participation as solo guitarist in the show « LA PÉPINIÈRE DES COMPOSITEURS », in Aix-en-Provence on June 5 and 6, 2023.Solo concert in Paris on June 17, 2023. Duo concert: Guitar & Cello, given in Balogna, South Corsica, on July 11, 2023. Participation in the « LES SUPERPHONIQUES » 2023 • Percussionist Steve Robertson contemporary music competition, writing a piece for choir, guitar and flute. Participation in the CEMF 2024 competition in the Repertoire category for the writing of a piece for orchestra accompanied by its musicological analysis. Percussionist Steve Robertson has been active performing, recording, producing and teaching in the Bay Area for more than 25 years. A graduate of San Jose State University with a BA in Music Performance and Education. He has performed and recorded in a variety of musical styles with artists including Bobby Hutcherson, Airto and Flora Purim, Laurindo Almeida, Claudia Villela, Othello Molineaux, Giovanni Hidalgo, Omar Sosa, John Calloway, Arthur Dente and many others. His musical focus is primarily in Jazz and World Music styles including Brazilian, Afro-Cuban and North Indian Classical music (on tabla). He studied orchestral percussion with Anthony Cirone at SJSU and is a tabla student of Ustad Zakir Hussain. He has also performed on percussion with the Monterey and Santa Cruz County Symphonies.

articles.text: Summer Hours is an award winning film from France. Summer Hours, written and directed by Oliver Assayas, is a film with an almost imperceptible narrative arc, a film absent moments of great tension, high drama, or irreparable confrontation. Instead, it is a film that mirrors life in all its subtlety and nuanced moments. And later, audiences may weigh the film’s richness and modulated pace, and acknowledge that perhaps French sensibilities are different from our own; or conclude, after some discussion, that perhaps they’re not. If there’s a dearth of such films made in America, perhaps it’s because Hollywood fears that movies like Summer Hours, will never find an audience. Filmgoers, it is assumed, are interested only in the explicit, hence the weekend gross will be anemic and the industry, while cognizant that films can be art, is, after all, in the business of making money. The film opens with a French clan having their yearly summer reunion at the country home of the family matriarch, Helene Bertheir (Edith Scob), 75. She has three children, Frederic (Charles Berling), Adrienne (Juliette Binoche) and Jeremie ( Jeremie Renier). Alone with Frederic, the oldest, they have a difficult though prescient conversation about what should happen in the event of her death. She possesses museum quality art and furniture along with a magnificent house she inherited from a long ago deceased uncle, also a famous artist in his own right. Shortly after the summer gathering, Helene passes away unexpectedly. Now the siblings and their wives are left with sorting out what they should do with the house where they grew up and disposing of their mother’s elegant and treasured possessions. And so, by the end of act one – the film is wonderfully constructed in three acts with a nice, unexpected denouement – it is clear that Summer Hours is about relationships and the subtle contrasts between brothers and sister. It is also about how families fragment when the glue that binds them together ceases to be, in this case Helene. She was the catalyst for their gatherings, as was the house, the gardens, the lovely grounds, all of it representing the essence of them as a family. While negotiating the many decisions confronting them, the siblings make choices that say a great deal about them as people and about their values and about how much they care for one another. Those conversations, negotiations really, and the occasional flare up essentially summarize the film. Yet, there is so much that is deeply human and recognizable in every scene: Frederic’s sentimental attempt to keep things as they are; Jeremie and Adrienne, whose lives have moved on beyond France, argue for change. It’s time to move on – Jeremie, lives in China with his family where he heads a shoe factory, and Adrienne resides in New York where she is a designer. Both have stepped outside the circle that was once so familiar. And without Helene, the center cannot hold. French films are different. Part of it is cultural. Consider but one example from the film: a long, lovely scene where family members are seated at a table in the garden. Talking. Eating. The sun giving everything a patina of gold, the foliage so deeply green its almost purple, the languid space between conversations punctuated by laughter and interrupting children, the universality of imperfect relationships, deep love, and long held grievances gently revealed. That’s life in a microcosm, all of it captured in a garden, in a moment that portends great change and wrenching sadness. Is that the difference? Is it the belief that such moments possess a relevance and import and will, indeed, resonate with the audience? Perhaps. Summer Hours. Directed by Oliver Assayas. Starring Juliette Binoche, Charles Berling, Jeremie Renier and Edith Scob. French with English subtitles. 1 hr., 42 min. Released in 2009. Streaming on Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Luca, the 24th animated feature from Pixar, opened absent a wide theater release and is therefore now streaming. It is a comingof-age story set in the Italian seaside village of Portorosso, on the sun-washed Riviera. It’s a place of dreamy blues, soft oranges, and inviting yellows. The time is in the 1950s and 1960s. At the center of the tale is Luca Paguro (Jacob Tremblay), a restless tween-teen who is a sea monster. He lives with his extended sea monster family in an underwater world. There’s Daniela, his mom (Maya Rudolph); Lorenzo Paguro, his dad (Jim Gaffigan); Grandma Paguro (Sandy Martin); and Uncle Ugo (Sacha Baron Cohn). Plus Luca’s new best friend, also a sea monster, Alberto Scorfario (Jack Dylan Grazer). The interesting twist is that when Luca and Alberto venture on shore they turn into regular boys who look like everyone else. And it’s on land where they discover that though they were warned by their families that the town of Portorosso could be dangerous, the boys find it filled with interesting, eye-widening possibilities. And so, the two set off on an irresistible adventure in where they meet a cast of interesting characters, to include a feisty girl, Giulia Marcovaldo (Emma Berman), and her good-hearted fisherman/cook father, Massimo Marcovaldo (Marco Barricelli). They enter an annual Vespa race, take countless Vespa rides around town, confront the town bully, Saverio Raimondo (Ercole Visconti) – he was the previous winner of the Vespa race medal – and, along the way, learn the meaning of true friendship. The animation is delightful, the palette of detail and colors extraordinary. And the filmmakers acknowledge the influence of the iconic Japanese Studio Ghibli and the creative genius of animator and storyteller Hayao Miyazaki. Luca is a wonderful, imaginative story that should engage a wide audience of kids who will find Luca, both the sea monster and the boy, compelling. Luca. Pixar/Disney animation. Directed by Enrico Casarosa. Voices by Jacob Tremblay, Jack Dylan Grazer, Emma Berman. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Disney+/Apple tv. A scene from Pixar’s Luca

articles.text: Bolt is a family friendly, Disney animated, comedy adventure that features a fearless pooch named Bolt (John Travolta), and his feisty teen owner Penny (Myley Cyrus). They star together on a top-rated TV show filled with villains and intrigue and action. Bolt, a white Swiss shepherd, is cast as a canine superhero with special powers who weekly saves the day – and Penny. The only problem is that Bolt so inhabits his character that when the director (James Lipton) yells “cut!”, and the cameras stop rolling, the pooch comes to believe that he does possess extraordinary powers (a super bark, beaming heat rays flash (Susie Essman) and a hamster named Rhino (Mark Walton). They become fast friends, and since the surroundings are not user-friendly, the three amigos decide to set out on a long journey back to Los Angeles. After a number of close scrapes, mishaps, and adventures on the road, Bolt gradually comes to fully understand that he truly doesn’t have super powers. After having lived his life on the set of a TV show, filled with movie magic, this is a surprising revelation. Grudgingly. he realizes that he an ordinary dog. Meanwhile back on the TV show set, Bolt is replaced with a stand-in pooch allowing the show to continue. Finally Bolt and his now best buds arrive in L.A. where, displaying no extraordinary powers, Bolt saves Penny from a fire. It’s his less than super barking that leads the firefighters to Penny, who is trapped and in danger. This time, Bolt simply commits an act of bravery. As stories go, Bolt does have a right ending, involving Penny and Bolt and Mittens plus Rhino who happily set up housekeeping together. Kids will love Bolt and will likely lobby for a pooch of their own. Good luck. mom and dad. Bolt. Disney Entertainment. Directed by Byron Howard and Chris Williams. It is a comingof-age story set in the Italian seaside village of Portorosso, on the sun-washed Riviera. It’s a place of dreamy blues, soft oranges, and inviting yellows. The time is in the 1950s and 1960s. At the center of the tale is Luca Paguro (Jacob Tremblay), a restless tween-teen who is a sea monster. He lives with his extended sea monster family in an underwater world. There’s Daniela, his mom (Maya Rudolph); Lorenzo Paguro, his dad (Jim Gaffigan); Grandma Paguro (Sandy Martin); and Uncle Ugo (Sacha Baron Cohn). Plus Luca’s new best friend, also a sea monster, Alberto Scorfario (Jack Dylan Grazer). The interesting twist is that when Luca and Alberto venture on shore they turn into regular boys who look like everyone else. And it’s on land where they discover that though they were warned by their families that the town of Portorosso could be dangerous, the boys find it filled with interesting, eye-widening possibilities. And so, the two set off on an irresistible adventure in where they meet a cast of interesting characters, to include a feisty girl, Giulia Marcovaldo (Emma Berman), and her good-hearted fisherman/cook father, Massimo Marcovaldo (Marco Barricelli). They enter an annual Vespa race, take countless Vespa rides around town, confront the town bully, Saverio Raimondo (Ercole Visconti) – he was the previous winner of the Vespa race medal – and, along the way, learn the meaning of true friendship. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays walkers knew the temperature would be high as they assembled on August 23. A hearty group of 45 walkers and one K-9 best friend were on hand to see something special. Retired architect Chuck Oraftik had offered the group an opportunity to see the large and highly detailed model railroad he has built in the basement of his Oakland Avenue home. This visit would be a shorter walk and offer a fun activity on a hot day. The walkers headed off going down Magnolia Avenue past the construction for the new Piedmont Aquatics Center. Peak holes in the construction fence allowed walkers to make inspections. The group continued down Magnolia past El Cerrito Avenue where EBMUD has been repairing a critical water pipeline leak. The group turned down Oakland Avenue and quickly came to Chuck’s house, which had a temporary railroad crossing sign in front. Chuck came out to greet them and a group photo was taken. They went down the driveway to a garage area where Chuck had chairs and beverages waiting for them. In response to a question, Chuck recounted the origins of both his train fascination and his architectural career. When he was a young boy most of his earliest toys were building/construction related, starting with tinker toys. , over the years they became more complex and sophisticated - slowly developing the technological, research, construction, artistic and planning skills required for an architectural career and for a historically accurate scale model railroad. His basement is a “time machine” from the 1950s in upper New York state. There is heavy freight and passenger train traffic on his HO scale version of the Boston & Albany Division of the New York Central railroad. The trains pass through the Berkshire Hills in route to Pittsfield, Mass. Chatham, N.Y. and, eventually, Albany N.Y. Along the way are small villages, industries, downtowns, swiftly moving rivers and hillsides forested with some 4,000 detailed trees. All locomotives have been equipped with sophisticated integrated circuits that control locomotive sounds, momentum, and speed. The steam locomotives have synchronized smoke effects. In addition, all locomotives, rolling stock, buildings, automobiles, and scenery are “weathered” to create a realistic, muted appearance and to eliminate a resemblance of toy trains. To ensure his work not be destroyed if it ever needs to be moved, his model railroad is built in large modules that can be separated with minimal damage. Chuck has been working on his model railroad for some 20 years. This phase one measures about 400 square feet. He has recently begun planning a second phase which will almost double its size. The large number of walkers and the confined aisle space allowed only a dozen at a time to view his trains. It took about 40 minutes for everyone to see his elaborate layout. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: World famous anthropologist and conservationist Jane Goodall will appear in discussion at the Golden Gate Theatre on Friday, September 15. For one night only, world-renowned ethologist and activist Goodall will discuss her decades of work in conservation and as a pioneer in the study of chimpanzees. She began her landmark studies in Africa in 1960. Her research continues to influence scientists and environmentalists today. The Jane Goodall Institute, which she founded in 1977, is widely recognized for creating innovative conservation and development programs in Africa. Goodall’s global Roots and Shoots program also supports tens of thousands of young people in nearly 100 countries with projects that help environment preservation and animals. Goodall will answer audience questions at the conclusion of the evening. Visit https://www.broadwaysf. com/events/jane-goodall/golden-gate-theatre/calendar/ to purchase tickets. articles.text: Piedmont’s Commercial Center, 1912-1970 The Piedmont Commercial Center was built in 1913 and housed the first stores in Piedmont. This 1970 photo shows Wells Fargo Bank on the left, Hamby’s Market, Springman’s Pharmacy and the Highland Sweet Shop. design the commercial building. Farr did not design a square box for Piedmont’s stores. He designed three storefronts that gracefully followed the curve of Highland Avenue. A mission tile pent roof spanned the three stores, and tall transom windows and bold columns framed the storefronts. Farr claimed his design would “rival in tone and architecture, the enormous mansions which are to surround it on every side.” The building was completed in 1913. Over time, Farr’s building would fondly be called “The Stores.” Hamby’s Market The first grocery store opened in 1915 and was run by the Ainsworth Brothers. By 1921, Walter Hamby was running the grocery that became the popular Hamby’s Market. For decades, Piedmont shoppers often met and caught up on local news while they bought their groceries. Hamby’s was a full service grocery and later offered delivery service. After school, high school boys delivered groceries in collapsible wood crates to homes throughout Piedmont. One of those wood crates is in the Piedmont Historical Society collection. Hamby’s thrived for almost 50 years until the building was sold and slated to be demolished in 1970. Before closing, then owners Mary and Harry Sund, threw a ”Goodbye to Hamby’s party” with champagne, cake, and coffee for their customers. Piedmont’s Drug Store In 1921, W. L. Ferard opened the first drug store in Piedmont, the Piedmont Drug Company. From at least 1931 to the late 1960s, Gustav Springman operated the successful Springman’s Pharmacy. Also, a full service store, the pharmacy delivered prescriptions and goods to their customers. Highland Sweet Shop In 1921, Joseph H. Cheatham opened the Highland Sweet Shop with a candy store, soda fountain, and tea room. Originally, this candy store was to have housed George Merra’s candy shop in Piedmont Park before his untimely death in 1920. The Sweet Shop was popular with old and young alike. Piedmont matrons enjoyed lunch and tea in the small tea room at the back of the shop, and students often stopped for candy or a soda on the way home after school. Also, in 1921, the Standard Oil Company built the first serCrowds of Piedmont shoppers attended the Hamby’s Market closing party in 1969. vice station on Highland Avenue, opposite Vista Avenue. American Trust Bank In 1928, Albert Farr added the American Trust Bank building to the original three stores. His design included a deeply arched entrance with Churrigueresque relief and a decorative niche to the left. American Trust operated this branch until the 1960s when it became part of Wells Fargo Bank. A small office building behind the bank was the Alexander Allen realty office and later the Robert F. Atkinson realty company. Later, it became the local barber shop, which served generations of Piedmonters. Piedmont’s beloved stores were demolished in 1970 to make way for the current Wells Fargo Bank Building.

pages.text: Wednesday, August 30, 2023 25 The History of Piedmont Piedmont’s Commercial Center, 1912-1970 By Gail G. Lombardi Previously published in the Piedmont Post on February 27, 2019. Until 1912, Piedmont was known as the “store-less” city. With just over 1700 residents and 700-plus houses, the closest grocery store was the H. F. Sacks grocery on Piedmont Avenue, now the Piedmont Grocery. While residents enjoyed living in a completely residential city, they began to feel the need for a commercial center. To protect the city from what the Oakland Tribune called “an invasion of cheap and unsightly stores,” a group of residents, headed by Wallace Alexander, formed the Piedmont Commercial Association. articles.text: During a brief respite from the intense summer heat, 14 members of the Piedmont Seniors took an excursion to the picturesque town of Saratoga to visit the breathtaking Villa Montalvo estate. Built in 1912 by Senator James Phelan, who was also a three-term mayor of San Francisco, this 177- acre gem is an Italian Mediterranean Revival mansion. It was Phelan’s favorite home and became a center of artistic, political, and social Pictured are (clockwise from left): Yorkman Lowe, Carol Warren, Madeline Moore, Mona Jamieson, Penny Robb, Diane Frost, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska life in Northern California. Some of Phelan’s well-known guest celebrities included Jack London, Ethel Barrymore, Mary Pickford, and Douglass Fairbanks. Montalvo sits near the Santa Cruz mountains surrounded by exquisite gardens and an arboretum. Since 1939 Montalvo opened as a public arts center and is part of the County Park System, so it is available for visitors to explore. Montalvo is home to the oldest artists residency program of its kind west of the Mississippi. The organization hosts more than 60 artists from over 17 countries active in the visual arts, dance, literature, music, and the culinary arts. Montalvo also has a small gallery in the Villa. It is now a park with hiking trails, in addition to being a very popular venue for weddings and other events, complete with an outdoor 1600- seat amphitheater for concerts and other cultural events. As the Villa is quite expensive to maintain, the Montalvo Service Group offers catered “summer luncheons” as a major charity benefit to continue the preservation of this magnificent property. The Montalvo Organization also hosts a Mother’s Day Brunch, Yuletide, Madhatters Tea for children, and Gourmet Dinners at the Villa. On this occasion, the Piedmont Seniors were treated to a gourmet lunch consisting of a crispy polenta appetizer with ricotta and truffle honey, the entrée of Tuscan roasted chicken stuffed with spinach, herbs, and cheese., and a lemon raspberry trifle consisting of layers of fresh lemon curd, baked shortbread cookies and raspberry whipped cream! While the Seniors were enjoying their luncheon under the shade of a large front veranda, Montalvo volunteers hosted an informal fashion show by Chicos’ women’s apparel. Never one to miss a shopping experience, the Seniors At the luncheon table on the veranda at Villa Montalvo are (clockwise from the left): Sue Getreuer, Marianne Gunther-Murphy, Edith Hereso, Janice Subotnick, Janet Epstein, and Nava Shaham. Missing is Jim Ayotte, who is the group’s photographer. group also took advantage of the lovely boutique consisting of a variety of hand-made crafts and jewelry created by the volunteers themselves. This outstanding property is a “must-see” for anyone interested in natural beauty and historic architecture. Needless to say, the Piedmont Seniors were most impressed by this “hidden gem” tucked away in the hills of Saratoga. The Piedmont Seniors holds monthly meetings on the third Wednesday of each month at Piedmont Community Hall. If you would like to participate in some of the Piedmont Seniors programs and excursions, e-mail Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to join.
articles.title: Piedmont Seniors visit beautiful Villa Montalvo in Saratoga

articles.text: On Saturday, August 12, a gorgeous summer day, 22 excited seniors took a three-hour cruise aboard the historic USS Potomac on San Francisco Bay. The tour began with a 20-minute video giving a brief history of the USS Potomac. The tour included a box lunch and allowed time to leisurely explore the famous presidential yacht. Shorter two-hour tours without lunch are also available to the public. The USS Potomac, which is docked conveniently in Jack London Square at the Oakland Estuary, encourages visitors to come aboard and learn the history of this famous vessel. On the day the Seniors arrived there was a special narration about World War II. The Seniors were fortunate enough to have a docent explain some of the areas of the presidential yacht, such as the private quarters of FDR, the engine room, and officers’ quarters. The vessel was President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s yacht on which he was able to relax and entertain visitors, including kings and queens, until his death in 1945. This yacht is a living memorial to President Roosevelt and a testament to the challenges he overcame as a polio victim and during one of the most stressful times in American history. As Secretary of Navy prior to becoming President, he had a special affinity for the sea, unlike his wife, Eleanor, who rarely accompanied her husband on his sailings. The USS Potomac has an unusual history. It was initially commissioned as a Coast Guard Cutter in 1934 and was renamed in 1936 as the USS Potomac. Elvis Presley owned the ship briefly. He transferred ownership to Danny Thomas for St. Jude’s Foundation. Later it fell into disrepair when the next group of owners were using it to smuggle drugs. Soon it was seized by the federal government, but sank in the cove at Treasure Island. Fortunately, the vessel was rescued and purchased for $15,000 by the Port of Oakland at auction, with no other bidders. After the purchase, the process of restoration began by the Potomac Association, a 501c3 non-profit organization, to turn the yacht into a floating museum. An interesting sidenote of the yacht is its simplicity. It is nothing fancy or luxurious that one might expect a President to own. You can visit FDR’s bedroom, bathroom and the quarters for the crew and executive officers as well as the dining room. The recently hired Executive Director of the USS Potomac is Ford Roosevelt, son of Elliott Roosevelt and grandson to FDR. Ford brings a special knowledge of the family history and a dedication to see that this presidential yacht retains its integrity. Today the USS Potomac is used for Bay cruises, dockside tours on specific Saturdays and Sundays, private charters, and student cruises. For more information, see usspotomac.org or call (510) 627-1215. After disembarking the USS Potomac the Piedmont Seniors posed for a group photo. articles.title: Piedmont Seniors explore FDR’S “Floating White House”

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, August 30, 2023 Seniors During a brief respite from the intense summer heat, 14 members of the Piedmont Seniors took an excursion to the picturesque town of Saratoga to visit the breathtaking Villa Montalvo estate. Built in 1912 by Senator James Phelan, who was also a three-term mayor of San Francisco, this 177- acre gem is an Italian Mediterranean Revival mansion. It was Phelan’s favorite home and became a center of artistic, political, and social Pictured are (clockwise from left): Yorkman Lowe, Carol Warren, Madeline Moore, Mona Jamieson, Penny Robb, Diane Frost, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska Piedmont Seniors visit beautiful Villa Montalvo in Saratoga life in Northern California. Some of Phelan’s well-known guest celebrities included Jack London, Ethel Barrymore, Mary Pickford, and Douglass Fairbanks. Montalvo sits near the Santa Cruz mountains surrounded by exquisite gardens and an arboretum. Since 1939 Montalvo opened as a public arts center and is part of the County Park System, so it is available for visitors to explore. Montalvo is home to the oldest artists residency program of its kind west of the Mississippi. The organization hosts more than 60 artists from over 17 countries active in the visual arts, dance, literature, music, and the culinary arts. Montalvo also has a small gallery in the Villa. It is now a park with hiking trails, in addition to being a very popular venue for weddings and other events, complete with an outdoor 1600- seat amphitheater for concerts and other cultural events. As the Villa is quite expensive to maintain, the Montalvo Service Group offers catered “summer luncheons” as a major charity benefit to continue the preservation of this magnificent property. The Montalvo Organization also hosts a Mother’s Day Brunch, Yuletide, Madhatters Tea for children, and Gourmet Dinners at the Villa. On this occasion, the Piedmont Seniors were treated to a gourmet lunch consisting of a crispy polenta appetizer with ricotta and truffle honey, the entrée of Tuscan roasted chicken stuffed with spinach, herbs, and cheese., and a lemon raspberry trifle consisting of layers of fresh lemon curd, baked shortbread cookies and raspberry whipped cream! While the Seniors were enjoying their luncheon under the shade of a large front veranda, Montalvo volunteers hosted an informal fashion show by Chicos’ women’s apparel. Never one to miss a shopping experience, the Seniors At the luncheon table on the veranda at Villa Montalvo are (clockwise from the left): Sue Getreuer, Marianne Gunther-Murphy, Edith Hereso, Janice Subotnick, Janet Epstein, and Nava Shaham. Missing is Jim Ayotte, who is the group’s photographer. group also took advantage of the lovely boutique consisting of a variety of hand-made crafts and jewelry created by the volunteers themselves. This outstanding property is a “must-see” for anyone interested in natural beauty and historic architecture. Needless to say, the Piedmont Seniors were most impressed by this “hidden gem” tucked away in the hills of Saratoga. The Piedmont Seniors holds monthly meetings on the third Wednesday of each month at Piedmont Community Hall. If you would like to participate in some of the Piedmont Seniors programs and excursions, e-mail Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to join. By Janet Epstein On Saturday, August 12, a gorgeous summer day, 22 excited seniors took a three-hour cruise aboard the historic USS Potomac on San Francisco Bay. The tour began with a 20-minute video giving a brief history of the USS Potomac. The tour included a box lunch and allowed time to leisurely explore the famous presidential yacht. Shorter two-hour tours without lunch are also available to the public. The USS Potomac, which is docked conveniently in Jack London Square at the Oakland Estuary, encourages visitors to come aboard and learn the history of this famous vessel. On the day the Seniors arrived there was a special narration about World War II. The Seniors were fortunate enough to have a docent explain some of the areas of the presidential yacht, such as the private quarters of FDR, the engine room, and officers’ quarters. The vessel was President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s yacht on which he was able to relax and entertain visitors, including kings and queens, until his death in 1945. This yacht is a living memorial to President Roosevelt and a testament to the challenges he overcame as a polio victim and during one of the most stressful times in American history. As Secretary of Navy prior to becoming President, he had a special affinity for the sea, unlike his wife, Eleanor, Piedmont Seniors explore FDR’S “Floating White House” who rarely accompanied her husband on his sailings. The USS Potomac has an unusual history. It was initially commissioned as a Coast Guard Cutter in 1934 and was renamed in 1936 as the USS Potomac. Elvis Presley owned the ship briefly. He transferred ownership to Danny Thomas for St. Jude’s Foundation. Later it fell into disrepair when the next group of owners were using it to smuggle drugs. Soon it was seized by the federal government, but sank in the cove at Treasure Island. Fortunately, the vessel was rescued and purchased for $15,000 by the Port of Oakland at auction, with no other bidders. After the purchase, the process of restoration began by the Potomac Association, a 501c3 non-profit organization, to turn the yacht into a floating museum. An interesting sidenote of the yacht is its simplicity. It is nothing fancy or luxurious that one might expect a President to own. You can visit FDR’s bedroom, bathroom and the quarters for the crew and executive officers as well as the dining room. The recently hired Executive Director of the USS Potomac is Ford Roosevelt, son of Elliott Roosevelt and grandson to FDR. Ford brings a special knowledge of the family history and a dedication to see that this presidential yacht retains its integrity. Today the USS Potomac is used for Bay cruises, dockside tours on specific Saturdays and Sundays, private charters, and student cruises. For more information, see usspotomac.org or call (510) 627-1215. After disembarking the USS Potomac the Piedmont Seniors posed for a group photo. articles.text: Consideration of Amendments to Piedmont City Code and to Piedmont Design Guidelines to Implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards and Accessory Dwelling Unit Incentives Notice is hereby given that the City of Piedmont City Council will conduct a public hearing at a regular meeting at 6:00 pm on Tuesday, September 5, 2023 in Council Chambers, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA, to consider the following actions: (1) consideration of an ordinance amending the Piedmont City Code to add a Pre-approved Plans incentive for Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS), add ministerial review procedures, and make other conforming changes; and (2) consideration of amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code include amendments to Division 17.38, Accessory Dwelling Units, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use, including new incentives for rent-restricted ADUs for applicants using new City-approved plans for ADUs. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code also include the establishment of a new Division 17.67, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use to establish procedures and standards for ministerial review of multifamily and mixed-use building types, and other conforming changes. Proposed amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines include: (1) new objective standards for architectural elements to be used by City staff to review development applications for multifamily and mixed-use building types; (2) pre-approved plans for accessory dwelling units (ADUs); (3) renaming the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines as to “Piedmont Design Standards and Guidelines”; and (4) other conforming changes. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are exempt under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The amendments to address pre-approved architectural plans for ADUs are statutorily exempt from CEQA pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21080.17 and CEQA Guidelines section 15282(h) which exempts adoption of ordinances to implement Government Code section 65852.2 regarding accessory dwelling units. These amendments are also exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303.The amendments related to Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) are exempt because it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the adoption of MODS may have a significant effect on the environment. (Public Resources Code section 21065; CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Sections 15061(b)(3), 15378.) Further, these amendments are exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303. On August 14, 2023, the Planning Commission recommended City Council adoption of the amendments to the City Code and to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are available for public review on the City’s webpage at https://piedmont.ca.gov as well as https://piedmontishome.org. They are also available at City Hall located at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. INTERESTED PERSONS MAY be heard at the public hearing, and written comments may be submitted prior to the public hearing(s). Written comments will be made a part of the public record. If you challenge this matter in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you or someone else raised at the public hearing, described in this noticed, or in written correspondence, delivered to the City of Piedmont at or prior to the public hearing. You may choose to write your opinion and address the response to the Piedmont City Council via email at citycouncil@ piedmont.ca.gov or via U.S. Mail at Piedmont City Council, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. All City Council meetings are televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and will be available through streaming video on the City’s website https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/meeting_videos The City of Piedmont will publish the meeting agenda not less than 72 hours prior to the meeting. The agenda will be posted at City Hall and Police Department bulletin boards. The agenda will be available online at: https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/ city_council/meeting_information___agendas QUESTIONS AND INQUIRIES regarding this matter, or to review information for the project described above, can be directed to: Pierce Macdonald Senior Planner pmacdonald@piedmont.ca.gov • (510) 420-3050 Originally Posted on August 18, 2023 Piedmont Post newspaper Routes currently available for weekly & monthly routes. articles.text: part, describe our lives as well? We too get lonely, catastrophe seems to be ever present, we don’t have the luxury of being stupid, massive change buffets us, we need adequate rest, media seems to dominate us and it all adds up. In her essay, “Why Does Everyone Feel So Insecure All the Time?”, Astra Taylor put it this way. “We are all, to varying degrees, overwhelmed and apprehensive, fearful of what the future might have in store. We are on guard, anxious, incomplete and exposed to risk. To cope, we scramble and strive, shoring ourselves up against potential threats. We work hard, shop hard, hustle, get credentialed, scrimp and save, invest, diet, self-medicate, meditate, exercise, exfoliate. And yet, security, for the most part, eludes us.” Jesus, seemed to know that like us, the people of his world were burdened by rampant insecurity. His answers were to “do unto others as you would they do unto you,” to love our neighbors as ourselves, to seek forgiveness as well as to be forgiving and to set aside time for prayer. He urged all who were “weary and heavy laden” to come to him. He promised that his burden would be light.
articles.title: Religion Corner

articles.text: Youth Leadership — The Crew has monthly meetings where crew officers plan future events. All crew members and parents are invited to contribute. Each spring at a weekend retreat, members receive formal leadership training, PCSC is a youth-run organization. All crew parents are invited to sit in on Crew Committee meetings. Serving on the crew committee is a great way to witness how much teens can do. Open House on Sept. 11 PCSC is excited to be hosting its annual fall kickoff, an open house on September 11, from 4-6pm in central Piedmont. Non-members and parents can mingle with current crew members and learn why PCSC is an amazing resource for local youth. Although new members can join at any time of the year, the Kickoff is one of the best times to be introduced to the crew. We welcome middle school through high school aged youth, but the Open House is especially perfect for freshmen to start to get involved in their first year of high school. Please pre-register at https:// forms.gle/h5ooAS5iv5kMP9E46 to attend the Kickoff, where parents may register their teens. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, August 30, 2023 Religion Corner Continued from page 2 part, describe our lives as well? We too get lonely, catastrophe seems to be ever present, we don’t have the luxury of being stupid, massive change buffets us, we need adequate rest, media seems to dominate us and it all adds up. In her essay, “Why Does Everyone Feel So Insecure All the Time?”, Astra Taylor put it this way. “We are all, to varying degrees, overwhelmed and apprehensive, fearful of what the future might have in store. We are on guard, anxious, incomplete and exposed to risk. To cope, we scramble and strive, shoring ourselves up against potential threats. We work hard, shop hard, hustle, get credentialed, scrimp and save, invest, diet, self-medicate, meditate, exercise, exfoliate. And yet, security, for the most part, eludes us.” Jesus, seemed to know that like us, the people of his world were burdened by rampant insecurity. His answers were to “do unto others as you would they do unto you,” to love our neighbors as ourselves, to seek forgiveness as well as to be forgiving and to set aside time for prayer. He urged all who were “weary and heavy laden” to come to him. He promised that his burden would be light. I don’t profess to understand all that his invitation means. At the very least I think it means that Jesus sees our insecurity both as a threat to our well-being and as an opportunity – an opportunity to be vulnerable, to be honest about our situation and to recognize that the better way we seek was lived by a Palestinian Jew residing in the shadow of the Roman Empire in a time long ago. A time when people like him did not have the luxury of being stupid. Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at 3534 Lakeshore Avenue at Mandana Boulevard in Oakland. jim@labcoakland.org. Phone: (510) 893-2484.
