articles.text: Since Saturday, August 12, East Bay Municipal Utilities District (EBMUD) workers have been involved in repair work related to a critical water pipeline leak at the corner of Magnolia and El Cerrito Avenues. While the leak was identified, the holes backfilled, and the pipeline repaired by Tuesday, August 15, street repair work is expected to continue through August, with traffic impacts to residents. During working hours (9 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.), cars on Magnolia will be redirected around the site, which will be repaved with asphalt. “The city first received reports of a water leak in late July,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, “when city crews removed a tree by the intersection so utility workers could study the leak.” The pipeline is the Sequoia Aqueduct, built in 1928. The steel pipe, which is among the largest in EBMUD’s system, is 20 miles long, 48 inches wide, and delivers water to 300,000 residents from Oakland to Castro Valley. EBMUD performed emerStaff photo Although work to repair an EBMUD water pipe leak at Magnolia and El Cerrito Avenues has finished, repairs to the pavement at the intersection are expected to continue through August.
articles.title: EBMUD pipe leak fixed at Magnolia and El Cerrito; street repairs continue

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School observed a minimum day on Monday, August 21, opening up the afternoon for the 6th grade Carnival hosted by parents, and including carnival games, sports, food and a raffle. The move from elementary school to middle school is one of the biggest changes for students. To help the transition, PMS hosts many 6th grade specific events to start the year, including Ted Scherman’s 6th grade boot camp, Scots Camp, and the 6th grade carnival. The optional afterschool event put to use the newly resurfaced Bern courts on the PMS campus. Although the students are not in elementary school anymore, the atmosphere resembled that of recess, with kids running around entrenched in games and play.
articles.title: 6th grade Carnival celebrates transition to middle school

articles.text: In the most recent Piedmont School District newsletter, Superintendent Jennifer Hawn delivered a week three update on topics of interest to parents, community members and students. Staffing Update Parents, here is the latest update on staffing at PHS, MHS and PMS: We are currently finalizing two part time science teachers to take three courses at PHS and MHS. We hope to have these individuals in the classroom teaching by next Monday, 8/27. Thank you to our students and parents for their patience while we worked through these challenges. A special thanks to our PHS Science teachers for their effort to get creative and offer all courses to our students. Unfortunately, we also now have a counseling vacancy at PMS. We will update you when we have additional information about filling this position. A special thanks to the PMS team for getting creative in how they support our students. And finally, we also have several open positions in our Special Education department that we have posted. articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Four Seasons Arts Four Seasons Arts, a classical music recital and chamber series in Berkeley, needs volunteer drivers to provide door-to-door transportation for subscribers in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Concerts are held on Saturday afternoons at 3 p.m., and subscribers who use the transportation service attend 5 concerts per season. Volunteer drivers are given a pair of complimentary concert tickets and complete directions to one or two convenient stops. Volunteers can drive once or to several concerts, depending on their availability. Drivers must use a reliable, safe, and insured vehicle, have a good DMV driving record and pass a basic background check. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has announced the September schedule of its “Cop on the Block” program, a yearlong series of community outreach events which launched in June. It is the first scheduled walking patrol. The following patrols are scheduled through September: Monday, September 4, 8 pm Jerome Avenue between Magnolia and Keefer Court Tuesday, September 12, 1 pm Sea View Avenue between Lincoln and Hampton Sunday, September 17, 7 pm Monticello Avenue between Park and Moraga Thursday, September 28, 6:30 pm Cavenagh Court & Trestle Glen Described by the department as a program designed to bring officers out of cars and into neighborhoods, neighbors are invited to bring their questions, comments and concerns to officers as they patrol the city’s blocks on foot at selected locations and times, announced by PPD monthly. Police Captain Chris Monahan, who oversees the program, said, “We rolled out Cop on the Block as a way to encourage more non-enforcement contact with the community. It’s very casual. We plan that each week with a member of the department walking up and down the block for a minimum of half an hour and for as long as people want to chat. “We plan to keep going with the program until we cover the whole city,” he added. “Piedmont has about 145 streets and once we cover them all, a block at time, we’ll start over again. We currently plan to keep it at one officer a week. So far, the program has been very well-received; I’ve even had people call me and ask to schedule a time and date for us to visit their block.” Monahan encourages those interested in bringing Cop on the Block to their street (block patrols are scheduled 90 days in advance), or who have questions about the program, to contact him by phone at 520-3012 or by email at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov. More information on Cop on the Block events, including an interactive map of the blocks where PPD police officers will go and where they’ve been, can be found through the Piedmont Police Department’s website at bit.ly/42yYRTu. articles.text: Four student representatives to Piedmont School Board were officially appointed at the August 9 board meeting. In May, Piedmont High and Millennium High students voted for two representatives each to serve on the board this year. Attending board meetings in the fall semester will be PHS senior Siddharth Bhatia and, MHS senior Orla Cohen. In the spring, PHS senior Elena Stevens and MHS junior Shakila Zuberi will take be the student reps. The positions were created in 2022 and Bhatia was one of the three students appointed in the inaugural year. “I’m looking forward to continuing our work from last year in bringing much needed student voices to the board,” said Bhatia. “This is an absolutely amazing opportunity, and I’m so honored to be welcomed as part of the PUSD board,” said Cohen. Board member Ruchi Medhekar participated in candidate screening prior to the student vote, which allowed for some oversight. “I remember when I was in high school talking with adults around me and thinking they didn’t always understand the big picture. I think the best way to have change driven is by listening to folks your age,” said Medhekar. Piedmont School Board members and Supt. Hawn welcome the 2023-24 student board members. Pictured are Cory Smegal (left), Shakila Zuberi, Ruchi Medhekar, Hilary Cooper, Lindsay Thomasson, Veronica Anderson Thigpen, Siddharth Bhatia, Elena Stevens, Orla Cohen and Jennifer Hawn.

articles.text: Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center’s first Week of Wellness will run from September 20 to 27. During the week supporters who purchase an event ticket or sponsorship have access to events ranging from fitness classes at local studios to walks and outdoor activities led by Piedmont parents. The Week of Wellness is the center’s largest annual fundraiser and helps ensure that Piedmont students continue to receive the mental health support they need. articles.text: The Beach Dads Club will host its largest annual event on Sunday, September 10, the 18th Annual Beach Dads Pancake Breakfast at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. The club’s new president Michael Gross helped kick off the school year with a welcome event on Thursday evening, August 17, held in Eric Pinsky’s backyard. The get together, which included beer on tap, lumpia, chicken wings and homemade cookies, brought together 50 dads to catch up after the summer and plan for the year. “A lot of these people are new to Piedmont; some just moved in last week,” said Gross. “Especially for the TK parents, we’re all going to be together for the next 14 years, so it was a good way to get to know people.” In addition to the Pancake Breakfast, the Dads Club also hosts an end-of-year BBQ and coordinates volunteering for the school. Gross was a bacon griller last year at the Pancake Breakfast, and this year he takes over as the “Padre Grande.” “Last year I looked over and saw Beach dad James Syhabout flipping pancakes and grilling bacon. He’s the owner of the restaurant Commis, and a Michelin star chef,” said Gross. Hundreds of pancakes from six grills will be flipped at the event which requires more than 40 volunteer dads, along with the help of Scout Troop 4 and music by the Carmel Quartet jazz band consisting of Beach school alums. The pancake party runs in conjunction with the Chalk Art Festival, also on the Beach Blacktop. The Beach Dads Club hosted a Welcome event on August 17. 8 Wednesday, August 23, 2023 POSTCARDS FROM CAMP POSTCARDS MAIN Postcards from Camp Postcards from Camp In “Kitchen Sink Week” for Session 6, instead of cabin act we had an oatmeal versus slime fight to see which product, once and for all, is better. Letters to home by kids at Camp Augusta Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of photos of kids’ activities at Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. As summer comes to a close at Camp Augusta, the staff members were ready to give it their all one last time. The evening programs were doubled, mega play stations scheduled, and during cabin acts we had the first ever oatmeal versus slime fight. With over 60 first-year campers, we were able to wow all of them with the wish, wonder, and surprise Augusta has to offer. We are trying to do as much as we can in as little time as possible. Mega playstation was brought back this year, with everything bigger, better and having never run before. We are sad that these campers have only been here a short time and have to leave, but we are glad that we made their camp time as fun as possible. Campers solved a series of puzzles, ran from rogue pirates and played games of Liar’s Dice to complete the game of Arrrrrcapelago. Campers fill up water balloons with paint to throw at each other on the wheel of doom. For cabin act, this cabin decided to destroy their counselor’s shoes by running a gauntlet on the lake field and ending with the rope swing into the lake. A pine cabin wanted to throw flaming pine cones into buckets filled with smoke bombs. As a special birthday celebration, Manzi 1 made cupcakes for their cabin members. A good cabin bonding time on the first day of the session, low ropes allows campers to have fun while also working on their team-building skills. Evening programs bring campers together, especially when completing stations as a cabin group.

articles.text: Piedmont High graduate Alexandra Clayton (2005) co-directed her first feature length film, Unpacking, in Bali in 2019. The film is showing in Mountain View on August 25 and 30 part of the Cinequest Film & Creativity Festival. Clayton also wrote, produced and acted in the indie film, with the help of PHS alums Chelsea Bangert as Graphic Designer, and Mitchell Manburg as Music Composer. Synopsis: “Six women, sold on the promise of radical transformation, travel to Bali into the hands of an influencer guru and get slapped with reality: change is messy AF. It’s awkward and earnest. It’s humor where people are taking themselves so seriously, that it’s comical – almost a cringe comedy,” said Clayton. To make this film, co-directors Michal Sinnott and Clayton asked 40 friends in the acting world if they would take two weeks to fly to Bali for filming. A dozen accepted the offer and the movie was shot in 13 days. “It’s been such a journey. I thought it was going to be something small with our friends for no money but it has been a big undertaking,” she said. After graduating from Piedmont High, Clayton went to community college and then finished her undergraduate degree at Columbia. In New York she realized that film was her passion. The Cinequest Film & Creativity Festival runs until the end of the month. To watch the trailer 2005 Piedmont High graduates Alexandra Clayton (left) and Chelsea Bangert in Bali. of Unpacking visit Youtube.com/ watch?v=B4kAW6F9zrw. ShowPlace ICON Theatre & Kitchen in Mountain View is located at 2575 California Street. Show times are Friday, August 25 at 9:00 p.m. and Wednesday, August 30 at 2:30 p.m. For tickets see: Tickets.cinequest.org/websales/pages/info. aspx?evtinfo=292622~a12ee803- 7 e a e - 4 3 7 e - 8 2 0 8 - 1 c 4 d - 52da2020&epguid=330ab4d6- 45cd-4e3a-a87e-02c739b12dbb&. “Directing is 85% ego management for a really wide variety of people,” explained Clayton. “For me, the director gets to set the tone of how the cast and crew treat one another and collaborate. It’s an incredibly collaborative art form.” Art Director/Graphic Designer Chelsea Bangert has remained best friends with Clayton since Piedmont Middle School. “It was a ‘pinch me’ moment to have her as my right hand while filming my first feature in Bali, Indonesia all these years later,” said Clayton. Unpacking hit the festival circuit in Fall 2022 and has received several accolades: • Best Narrative Feature - Valkyrie International Film Festival (VIFF) • Excellence in Comedy - WRPN Women’s International Film Festival • Best Script (Produced) - Austin Revolution Film Festival 2023 • Audience Award - Best Feature - NYC Indie Theatre Film Festival 2023 A scene from the film shows co-Director Alexandra Clayton (left), who also acted in the film Unpacking You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: On July 27 Piedmont Council Scouts Jack Langowski, Simon March-Cunningham, and Naomi Treichler packed their Scouting gear into duffle bags and backpacks to join other U.S. Scouts at the 25th World Scout Jamboree in South Korea from August 1 to 12. The World Jamboree is held every four years. This year South Korea hosted over 40,000 Scouts representing more than 153 countries at Saemangeum in the North Jeolla province. During the first few days Piedmont Scouts spent time making friends with Scouts from all over the world through activities and meals. “We helped a Kenyan unit set up their camp next to us, had dinner with Scouts from Taiwan, the UK, and Sweden, and I had lunch with a group of Irish Scouts,” said March-Cunningham. “In fact, I just spent time this weekend talking online with a Scout from Ukraine who I met at the Jamboree.” Langowski spent time meeting Scouts and trading U.S. neckerchiefs (neckers) from other countries – a tradition at all Scout Jamborees. He used the trading as an opportunity to meet Scouts from all over the world including Peru, Namibia, Kenya, Israel, Hong Kong, the United Kingdom and Latvia, where his grandmother grew up. He also collected a necker and belt from Poland, his grandfather’s native country. Each item he brought home had its own story and special memory. Treichler’s favorite necker trade was with a Korean Scout when she went in the Korean unit camps looking for someone to trade with. “One of the Scouts seemed almost as excited as I was to trade, and the smile on his face when I gave him my necker and he gave me his was something that I think I’ll always remember,” she said. Unfortunately, a combination of a massive heat wave and logistical and sanitation problems led to the UK, U.S. and Singapore Scouting contingents pulling their Scouts from the event after only a few days. U.S. Scouts decamped to Camp Humphreys, a U.S. Army camp about an hour away from Saemangeum on August 5. Then the arrival of Typhoon Khanun led to the evacuation of the remaining tens of thousands of Scouts starting on August 7 to various locations in South Korea. After arriving at Camp Humphreys, the California Scouts persevered in making the most of their experiences. They embarked on trips to local sights, communities, and events, including seeing Photos by Steve Parris, Melissa Schreiner, and Crew 16 Scouts Venturers from Crew 16, including Naomi Treichler (left), explore Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul. Naomi Treichler (bottom) eats bibimbap with the rest of Venture Crew 16. Piedmont Troop 15’s Simon March-Cunningham (second from left) and Jack Langowski of Troop 6 (far right) with U.S. and Australian Scouts at the World Scouts Jamboree in South Korea a baseball game by local Korean team. A few groups of US Scouts were able to tour parts of the Samsung headquarters in Suwon. “I really enjoyed the Samsung employees’ presentations on the technology that they’ve developed there,” said Treichler. All Scouts were able to come together again for a closing ceremony on August 11, which finished with a K-pop concert at the Naomi Treichler (center) meets Scouts from Hong Kong. articles.text: 1-0 upset victory vs. England a game for the ages How amazing was this year’s Women’s World Cup? In the end, Spain took a 1-0 win over the favorites, England, to capture its first title in the team’s 43-year history. With both England and España fighting as first-timers in the finals, perhaps there is a changing of the guard in the women’s game, which the United States know the field has quickly risen against them. England was bigger, stronger, more experienced, and winner of last year’s Euro Championship. Spain was talented but endured a year of turmoil when more than half of the team chose not to play under coach Jorge Vilda. There were so many illustrious and awe-inspiring moments from this year. Here’s a recap of some of our favorite moments. Spain wins 1-0 over England on Olga Carmona’s goal It’s hard not to view Olga Carmona’s goal in the 29th minute as the pinnacle of the tournament. Spain played fantastically, showing the classic “tiki-taka” style that encapsulates the Spanish-football style. Looking back at Carmona’s game-winner now a few days later, it’s a certain tear-jerker moment. Following the match, she was told by gamily members that her father, Tomas Carmona Mena, had died. When Carmona scored from her left fullback position, the 23-year-old had a separate message, lifting her jersey to reveal “Merchi” written onto her undershirt. She explained it was in honor of a close friend’s mother who had passed away recently. Little to Carmona’s knowledge at the time, her father also had passed. Her shot in the 29th was as perfect as could be to narrowly get past the outstretched arms of England goalkeeper Mary Earps. It was almost as if an angel lent a hand in pushing it into the net. Olga left an emotional message on social media after learning of her father’s passing: “And without knowing it, I had my Star before the game started. I know that you have given me the strength to achieve something unique. I know that you have been watching me tonight and that you are proud of me. Rest in peace, papa… Yesterday was the best and the worst day of my life. I know that you would like to see Photo courtesy of Goal.com Olga Carmona scored Spain’s game-winning goal in the 29th minute. She learned after the game that her father passed away. me enjoy this historic moment, that is why I will be with my teammates, so from wherever you are know that this star is also yours, papá.” Heartbreak, shock for the U.S. Waking up a week earlier on Sunday morning to see the United States lose to Sweden 5-4 in penalty kicks after ending regulation and overtime in a 0-0 deadlock left U.S. supporters in disbelief. The mighty United States just suffered its earliest exit in history after seeing Megan Rapinoe and Sophia Smith and Kelly O’Hara all miss their penalty kicks. It was a sad ending for Rapinoe’s illustrious professional career. celebrates her goal. Bronze. Spain’s players celebrate after winning the Women’s World Cup.

articles.text: Richey recounts attaining No. 1 in the U.S. and subsequent work in mental health awareness Originally printed in October 2020. With the French Open now concluded, we take a look back to a former headlining tennis tournament in the Bay Area, the Pacific Coast Championships. in the ‘50s through the early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world played at the Berkeley Tennis Club in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the start of October. The Pacific Coast Championship was held from 1889 to 2013. it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States and is predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of tennis’ Open Era beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championships were in Berkeley from 1968 to 1971. Many influential matches took place for endof-year rankings, given an October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. In 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States. It was a semifinal match at the Pacific Coast Championship that was one of the most breathtaking matches ever played. Their match ran over four hours. and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point the end-all, win-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey, now 73, from his home in San Angelo, Texas. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, which was famously the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix,” Richey said. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals in London. I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my tail was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified in the previous round. “All the players and officials knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an activist for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. In his book, Acing Depression, Richey describes his challenges with the disease in the years following his tennis career. “It’s been a good book from the standpoint of what I wrote it for; if I could help just one person. Clinical depression has 10 or 12 criteria that lasts a various amount of time. It is a bonafide medical illness; it’s like in America we’re allowed to be sick from the Adams Apple down but not the Adams Apple up. It can happen to anybody,” Richey explained. He recounted some of his experiences with depression and what led to him writing the book. “I had episodes throughout my life. In tennis, my last six years of the tour, I had lost my game; I couldn’t get my backhand back,’ he said. “That’s why I got depressed; I had lost what was most valuable to me: my skill… I had a three-year breakdown at my worst,” said Richey, describing some situations from his book. “I’ve spoken at 60 or so events over the last 10 years and hosted some golf events. I wrote the book as a mental health book. The desire was to help others who suffered like I did. It just so happened that my daughter had a year off from being a professor at Texas A&M. She did a wonderful job of Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. putting it together,” he added. Pacific Coast Championship history In 1971, the final year at Berkeley, Australian legends Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall squared off in what became “Rocket” Laver’s sixth singles title of the year. The doubles’ title in ‘71 was another all-Australian exhibit with Laver and Roy Emerson defeating Rosewall and Fred Stolle. It was held in multiple venues starting at the Old Del Monte Lodge in Monterey in 1889, moving to the Hotel Rafael in San Rafael from 1890 to 1899, and then to Berkeley from 1900 to 1930 for its initial stay. From there, the PCC played in Alamo from 1931-1933, returned to Berkeley from 1934-1941, went to San Francisco in ’42-’48, then back to Berkeley from 1949 through 1971. The Cow Palace and Bill Graham Civic Auditorium hosted the tournament from 1973 to 1993; then moved to San Jose with the opening of the HP Pavilion. That was its downward phase when it was classified as an ATP 250 series tournament. During its time in San Francisco, John McEnroe dominated the event with 14 combined singles and doubles titles, five in singles. Photo courtesy of World Tennis Magazine Cliff Richey talks with the Post about his tennis career and mental health activism.

articles.text: Staff Photos The Post visited an elephant sanctuary on the outskirts of Chiang Mai, Thailand. When visiting Chiang Mai and the northern province of Thailand, it’s clear to see the region’s cultural ties to elephants. Countless merchants have elephant-based trinkets, clothing, and jewelry on display. If you’re visiting Chiang Mai, travelers are bound to run into businesses looking to lure in tourists, so it is important to do your research to ensure you’re investing your experience with the right company. With that, the Post visited Into The Wild Elephant Camp on the outskirts of Chiang Mai. In Thailand, elephants are tied to the nation’s history in religion and royalty. They are considered guardians of Buddha, Earth and Thailand’s temples. They were also used in ancient wars to defend the country. Ownership of them was considered a sign of status. However, the species has decreased from the 300,000 wild elephants in the 20th century to an estimated 3,084-3,500 now with an estimated 4,000 in capOne of Into The Wild Elephant Camp’s seven elephants Elephants coating themselves with dirt while on the trail

pages.text: 14 Wednesday, August 23, 2023 HIKING WITH JON Hiking with elephants in Thailand Staff Photos The Post visited an elephant sanctuary on the outskirts of Chiang Mai, Thailand. By Jonathan Comeaux When visiting Chiang Mai and the northern province of Thailand, it’s clear to see the region’s cultural ties to elephants. Countless merchants have elephant-based trinkets, clothing, and jewelry on display. If you’re visiting Chiang Mai, travelers are bound to run into businesses looking to lure in tourists, so it is important to do your research to ensure you’re investing your experience with the right company. With that, the Post visited Into The Wild Elephant Camp on the outskirts of Chiang Mai. In Thailand, elephants are tied to the nation’s history in religion and royalty. They are considered guardians of Buddha, Earth and Thailand’s temples. They were also used in ancient wars to defend the country. Ownership of them was considered a sign of status. However, the species has decreased from the 300,000 wild elephants in the 20th century to an estimated 3,084-3,500 now with an estimated 4,000 in capOne of Into The Wild Elephant Camp’s seven elephants Elephants coating themselves with dirt while on the trail Walking through a thick jungle in Doi Inthanon National Park A look at Into The Wild Elephant Camp’s valley and river. tivity. When choosing an elephant sanctuary to visit, it’s important to decide against places that host rides and keep their elephants in enclosed areas, considered animal cruelty. Elephants, which have a typical lifespan of 60-70 years, can have a severe drop in life expectancy when kept in enclosed areas. Into The Wild Elephant Camp have seven elephants in a large encampment about 40 miles outside of Chiang Mai in the Doi Inthanon National Park. Their elephants are in an open space along the Mae Tian River, allowing visitors to learn about the species, their history, and natural habitat. As the guides at Into The Wild explained, it is difficult to release domesticated elephants back into the wild given that they are intelligent creatures with good memories. They will seek out humans in order to get food. Into The Wild specializes in finding other domesticated See Hiking with Jon on page 30 An elephant searches to see if I had any treats. A torrential downpour overtook the camp. The elephants scamper into the river while the rain pours down.

articles.text: Your child’s path in school might take many twists and turns. It’s back to school time! A time when parents are taking a deep breath. While summer can be super fun, it can also be exhausting because there is so much less structure to the schedule. So, back to the day to day it is for kids and their anxious parents. Get up, get ready, shoes on, out the door and into the classroom on time and ready to learn, As school begins, it can become easy to think that the year needs to follow a specific path and have one set outcome for kids. Of course, we all want our kids to do well in school. But, the definition of “do well in school” can be looked at from different perspectives. It could be a prescribed concept that means one specific path, or it could be a developing idea that shifts and changes daily. School is all about learning. And, as a parent, we can get stuck in believing that the learning journey has a set outcome goal– get good grades, do the right activities, and eventually, get into the right college. This is typically how we all think about school. Every day is one more step towards a set outcome. Therefore, if on any given day your child is struggling with an element of the school process, that becomes a problem. The steps are predetermined, so the path is already made and the child must follow that path. Or, we can see the day to day of growing up and developing, and therefore school, as a creative process. The creative path doesn’t know its end point. It’s the process itself that creates and reveals the end point. If there is no already-predetermined outcome goal, the child is creating the path every day. All of a sudden, a struggle is not a moment where we are fearful of a bad grade, but instead becomes a gift because an opportunity for learning has presented itself. A child’s passions can lead the way, and if those passions change, that’s ok too because the passions are also determining the path. as a creative process, it allows the child’s experience to formulate the path one day at a time and it releases the parent from stressing about every setback. It’s the process of attending school that creates the endpoint. As a result, each step the child takes, even if it is a tiny step or a sideways step or, even a step backwards, is creating the path and the outcome. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Speaker, Consultant and Coach. https:// gocreate.zone.

articles.text: I went through Piedmont schools and my emotions about going back to school fluctuated over the years from so excited to see my friends to begging my mom to let me stay home. Does that sound familiar? As summer comes to an end and the hustle and bustle of fall begins, I want to introduce a concept called “negativity bias”. This is the idea that our brains are wired for survival and therefore wired to see the negatives of a situation much more easily than the positives. This was optimal in our primal days where we needed to be aware of danger and threats, but in our current environment it can lead us to unnecessary negativity. Even though there are both negatives and positives about summer ending, it’s so much easier to focus on the negatives. We might think about vacation ending, shorter days, and less free time but forget about the friends we’ll see or the return of the Pumpkin Spice Latte. Understanding that our brains have this bias is the first step to changing it, but simply being aware of it is not enough to become happier. Using Positive Psychology, we can actually rewire our brains to be happier and more productive. Through tools like mindfulness, gratitude, and goal setting, we are able to train our brains to see the positives more often and more easily. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and experience to coach people one-on-one and facilitate workshops on different concepts from Positive Psychology. I found my passion in helping others figure out what they want, who they are, and how to show up more authentically in their lives. Learning these tools from Positive Psychology has completely transformed my life, and I feel so lucky to be able to help other people find that joy. If you have been waiting for a sign to do something different this year, this might be it. Positive Psychology is not the idea that we need to be happy all the time but instead the concept that we are happy a lot of the time and just need a little help noticing it. Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. She can be reached at 415-680- 6990 or mindsglowing@gmail. com. A free consultation session is offered if interested in hiring a Positive Psychology coach.

articles.text: The Atelier programs at California College of the Arts offer accessible, flexible, and immersive learning experiences in art and design studios for current high school students. Students learn new concepts and techniques while meeting other students from around the Bay Area. This fall, our weekend intensive workshop topics include animation, illustration, and industrial design. Extended 8-week classes in figure drawing and screen-printing are offered. Registration opens August 18 and courses run in October and November. The CCA Pre-College program is the comprehensive college experience for high school students. The program is open to students ages 15-18. Students live and learn on CCA’s campus in the heart of the Design District. Guest speakers, field trips, and interdisciplinary workshops complement the curriculum, where students learn new skills and build portfolios towards college admission while earning 3 college credits. CCA hosts the Bay Area chapter of the national Scholastic Art & Writing Awards, which are a prestigious opportunity for middle and high school students to share their vision, earn important recognition, and jumpstart a pathway toward art and design careers. Regional awards happen all over the United States, and this year’s Pre-college students at Oakland’s California College of the Arts create artwork as part of a summer program. Students work independently on projects in drawing and painting studios. Fashion Design is one of the CCA’s Young Artist Studio Program. Students explore what it means to be a fashion designer, learning how to communicate their ideas while designing their own fashion collection. Bay Area competition opens for submissions on September 1. This year CCA is hosting National Portfolio Day on November 19. More than 40 leading art and design colleges accredited by the National Association of Schools of Art and Design will participate and offer portfolio reviews. Representatives are there to answer your questions about their institution’s programs and application requirements and help you put together your best portfolio. To learn more about California College of the Arts Youth Programs & continuing Education, see the website at cca.edu/you, e-mail youthprograms@cca.edu, or call 415-610-7004.
articles.title: Exploring art & design at California College of the Arts

articles.text: Kronos Quartet will perform at the bandshell in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park this Saturday, August 26, at 5:30 p.m. The concert,, which is free, is the beginning of “Kronos Five Decades,” a yearlong celebration of San Francisco’s Kronos Quartet, now in its 50th year. The string quartet, founded by violinist David Harrington, covers a broad range of musical genres, including contemporary classical music. The quartet has had a rotating set of musicians since its inception in 1973. More than 1,000 works have been written for the group, which has been praised for the inclusiveness of its repertoire. Kronos Quartet is the best known and nationally recognized string quartet that hails from San Francisco. The program will include music by Bob Dylan, Angélique Kidjo, Nicole Lizée, Clint Mansell, and Sigur Rós. Visit https://kronosquartet.org/ events/detail/san-francisco-california-96/ for more information. The event is free and open to the public, no reservations are required. The concert begins at 5:30 p.m. The internationally renown Kronos Quartet: David Harrington and John Sherba (violin), Hank Dutt (viola), and Paul Wiancko (cello).
articles.title: Kronos Quartet performs free at Golden Gate Park on Saturday

articles.text: The story of a pair of sturdy stilettos Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2023-24 season with the Tonyaward winning musical Kinky Boots opening on September 8. Kinky Boots protagonist Charlie Price inherits his father’s beleaguered and nearly bankrupt shoe factory. He finds inspiration in customer Lola, a provocative entertainer, who wants to purchase a pair of sturdy stilettos. An unlikely pair, Charlie and Lola find they have more in common than they initially thought. The uplifting play features music and lyrics by Cyndi Lauper and is based on the 2005 British film of the same name, written by Geoff Deane and Tim Firth and mostly inspired by true events. “It’s just a heartfelt, heartwarming show about community and that’s exactly what Berkeley Playhouse is about. It’s perfect,” Director William Thomas Hodgson said. “The vision is a celebration of queerness, a community in queerness. Tshow has been on Broadway, on the West End, and around the world, I feel like we have our own special sauce in Berkeley.” The cast includes B Noel Thomas playing both Lola and Simon, Seth Hanson as Charlie Price, Grace Margaret Craig as Nicola, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Lauren, Danny Cozart as Don and Maia Campbell as Pat. The musical will be performed through October 15. Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, beginning September 8. For tickets, visit https://tickets. berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/ default.asp. Seth Hanson in the role of Charlie Price in the Berkeley Playhouse production of Kinky Boots.
articles.title: Musical Kinky Boots opens Sept. 8 at Berkeley Playhouse

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now exhibiting Hell: Arts of Asian Underworlds through September 18. The new exhibition displays how different Asian cultures view the afterlife of the condemned over time. Hell exhibits over 40 paintings, sculptures, maps, puppets, and religious objects from India, Tibet, China, Korea, Japan, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, and the Philippines. “There is a presumption that all representations of Hell across Asian cultures are the same or continuous,” said Jeff Durham, Curator of Himalayan Art at the Asian Art Museum. “But in fact, whether they appear in ancient traditions or the work of contemporary artists, depictions of Hell have been extraordinarily diverse: some are terrifying and gruesome, but many are humorous and playful.” The majority of artworks on view are on loan from other institutions and collections. articles.text: Part 67 In a biweekly series At the heart of all viable, functioning, well designed cities, towns and even villages is a central outdoor public space referred to by various names including City Square, Town Plaza, or Village Green. These vary in size from immense paved open spaces to planted park-like piazzas. At the scale of the biggest, the spaces are mostly suited for ceremonial or ritual activities involving large numbers of people, and are surrounded by mostly civic buildings. The smallest scale found in most intimate town or village plazas typically contains more interactive civic spaces surrounded by restaurants, shopping and some smaller government functions. There exist important and even critical requirements for all these different essential places to be successful: these are essential design concepts that must be adopted to the specific layout, use, orientation, geography, size and culture of a place. There are no pat examples that can be copied indiscriminately. The concept of “enclosure” (forming “outdoor rooms”) that we have discussed before applies at all scales. Without surrounding buildings, or trees, or geographical features that define the limits or edges of these outdoor plaza spaces it is difficult to really mark them as the heart of the municipality. There also seems to exist a sense of order and even comfort to the spaces that are clearly bounded. Attractions and destinations Now a museum and tourist attraction, the Forbidden City in the heart of Beijing was the ceremonial and political center of the Chinese government. The preserved wood buildings are marvelous in stature and detail; they were and do inspire awe. But to my mind the place is compromised by the excessive undefined open space around them – a lack of urban design.
articles.title: Urban design components: large scale city squares

The alignment and shapes of the series of large spaces creates heightened perspective leading up to the featured St. Peter’s Basilica (out of photo). It is interesting, too, that this work is largely an intelligent, creative response to existing site constraints over the centuries of its evolution. Note the buildings tight to the curved colonnade in the lower left of the photo. The obelisk, fountains, paving, and “enclosure” of the colonnade make this a masterpiece of urban design. By contrast, the huge (14-acre) Zócalo (main square) in Mexico City, while offering plenty of space for the frequent exhibitions and events, is lacking. Surrounded by numerous wonderful buildings, a responsive, exciting urban design treatment is missing in the square itself. Unlike dozens of other wonderful plazas and squares in Mexico, there is no character or spirit to this huge place. of various kinds must be a part of the square as well: things such as important anchor buildings, fountains, bandstands, sitting areas and special landscaping. And these elements must be designed to be flexible to handle the different types of activity that inevitably occur with a large mix of people coming together. articles.text: Part 2 of a 2-part series While some wine was produced in Oregon before prohibition the real beginning for the Oregon wine industry was the 1960’s when California winemakers opened several wineries in the Willamette Valley. By 1970 there were five commercial wineries with 35 acres. Most of the activity included planting Pinot Noir grapes in the Willamette Valley, a region long thought too cold to be suitable for viticulture. In the 1970’s more out of state winemakers migrated to the state and started to organize as an industry. In 1979 The Eyrie Vineyards entered a 1975 Pinot Noir in the Wine Olympics; the wine was rated among the top Pinots in the world, thus gaining the region its first international recognition. Willamette Valley is huge. Its 150-mile length runs from just south of Portland all the way down to Eugene and today it is synonymous with “Oregon Wine Country” and contains more than 19,000 acres of vineyards and over 500 wineries. Several things struck me as I toured the region for the first time. First was the beauty. Compared to California everything was so GREEN. The rolling hills were lush with evergreen and deciduous trees and the vineyards were perfectly manicured. Second there was a relaxed vibe that reminded me I was far from Napa Valley where wine tasting now seems to be a contact sport. We never encountered a winery that was overcrowded with tourists and the roads were free of traffic. Third my friend Kent who has spent his life in the wine business remarked on the professionalism and extreme hospitality of every wine industry worker we met. At every stop the staff was well trained and anxious for you to have the best possible tasting experience and the owners and winemakers were generous with their time. The luxurious tasting room at Domaine Serene. Jill A. Martenson, DDS
articles.title: The Best of Willamette Valley

The winemaker is Veronique Boss-Drouhin and the Estate manager is her brother Philippe Drouhin. Today the estate consists of 235 acres of gentle slopes planted to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. articles.text: It’s still summer, so enjoy the freshness of tomatoes Photos by Deborah Quok Pan con tomate is an ideal summer snack for any time of the day. Throughout Spain is eaten throughout the day – breakfast through tapas time. The dish is simply plated – fresh tomato on toasted bread; with a rub of fresh garlic, a splash of extra-virgin olive oil, and a sprinkle of salt for additional flavor. Regular readers have likely noticed what a fan I am of Spanish cuisine. I’ve had the good fortune to visit the diverse country many times, starting back in the late ‘90s. I’ve experienced pan con tomate set-ups at breakfast buffets, on lunch, tapas and dinner menus, and my personal favorite, at the beachside restaurants in Menorca. This dish makes an appearance from humble to haute settings. For such a simple recipe, I have had the misfortune of subpar offerings. Here’s my technique that ensures crusty bread and supreme tomatoey-ness with unctuous textures and popping flavor. Since there are so few ingredients, quality is key: select the tastiest bread and tomatoes you can find; and the best extra-virgin olive oil whose flavor will enhance the tomatoes. The Bay Area and Central Spain share a similar latitude, so farming crops are similar. Think citrus, olives, nut trees, grapes, and the star of this dish – tomatoes. It’s peak tomato season now and since my paltry container tomato crop doesn’t fill our needs, I’m taking full advantage of what our farmers’ markets have to offer. Advance note: The resulting recipe quantity will vary depending on the size of your tomatoes, their juiciness and the size of the bread used. Scale the ingredients to suit your situation. Pan con Tomate – Spanish Style Bread with Tomatoes Makes about 1/2 cup of tomato topping, good for about 8 pieces INGREDIENTS • 2 medium-large tomatoes, select firm-ripe ones at peak flavor • 1 large clove garlic • 2 - 4 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil • 1 teaspoon sea salt • 1 loaf baguette, or other firm, crusty bread INSTRUCTIONS Cut the tomatoes in half crosswise. Using the large holes of a box grater, carefully grate the fleshy side into a bowl. You should only have the thin skin remaining. This will yield about one cup of grated tomato. Pour the grated tomato through a fine mesh strainer into another bowl, reserving the juice to add back as needed to create a tomato spread with the viscosity of a jam or jelly. Cut the baguette into 3-inch lengths, then slice each piece in half crosswise. Place the sliced pieces cut side up and broil until lightly toasted, about 4 minutes. (A toaster oven is ideal here.) Rub the clove of garlic across the toasted bread. Start on the crispier edges to break through the garlic. Go lightly as this method imparts a lot of garlickiness, and you want to have the tomatoes shine here. Spread the jammy, fresh tomato onto each piece. Drizzle each piece with extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with sea salt. Serve immediately. Some absorption of the tomatoes into the bread is desired, but you want to avoid soggy bread.

articles.text: A Walking on Wednesdays group 30 walkers and one k-9 best friend headed out on another uphill trek, this time to see the EBMUD’s Piedmont “Reservoir Number 2” at the top of Dudley and Blair Avenues. There was some elevation going up Dudley, but it is a long, slow climb. The group started out taking shortcut path from Piedmont Court to Mountain Avenue. They passed a front yard with a life-size sculpture of a distinguished looking gentleman in a leaf-like coat, something like the Stanford Tree. The walkers continued on, and turned up the long, steep Dudley Avenue. They took a side trip onto the Dudley Court cul-de-sac to catch their breaths, and arrived at the reservoir one block away. It is far above Blair Park and occupies more than nine acres straddling the Oakland-Piedmont border with 8.3 acres of in Piedmont. A 22.8 million gallon water storage tank provided water for Piedmont from 1905 to 2003. The facility was decommissioned and drained in 2003 as part of EBMUD’s facility modernization program. Piedmont’s water now comes from other large tanks in the Oakland Hills. Jim Kellogg told the group that the land was once considered for residential development, but with parts of it in Piedmont and Oakland, the approval process was too complicated. A shelter and bench provided a respite from the rising temperature, and the backdrop for a group photo. There were more streets nearby that could have been explored, but the group chose to save those for a future day. They descended to the middle of town on Mountain and Hager, with spectacular views of the Bay. A breeze was welcomed too. It was about a two mile walk over about one hour and offered some good exercise. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. More than 30 walkers showed last week with the Walking on Wednesdays group. Among those participating were: Woody Baily, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mike Gallant, Sherry Jacobs, Albert Chen, Phil Witt, Jasmine Cai, Rick Eigenbrode, Chuck Oraftik, Quincy Don, Nancy Henn, Bob Wong, Priscilla Wanerus, Jim Kellogg, Judy Love, Martin Levy, Lois Price, Swee Ling Chen, Elizabeth Richter, Christine Calliste, Kat Lang, Helen Dong, Mike Henn, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Ken Hubbert, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Peggy Shultz and her friend Carrie Krehlik. GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2023 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2023 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2023 GOOD THROUGH SEPTEMBER 2023

articles.text: Don Parachini, a longtime Piedmont resident passed away on July 1, 2023. Born Donald Gene Parachini, he was the son of Victor and Elma Parachini of Antioch, CA. He attended school in Antioch and was on the high school football, track, and wrestling teams. While growing up he developed a great love of the outdoors, especially hunting ducks and pheasants and fishing in the Delta. His interest in the outdoors led him to enroll at Washington State University in Pullman as a forestry major, eventually changing to a major in business and economics. He continued to wrestle and was co-captain of the team his senior year. Don had a lifelong love of learning on wide-ranging topics and was an avid reader. He maintained his college friendships and later served as a member of the Board of Governors and Gift Acceptance and Management committee of the WSU Foundation. Following graduation from college, Don and his father took a lengthy tour through Europe. While there, they made contact with cousins for the first time since WWI. This experience heightened his interest in his Italian heritage and a desire to further expand his Italian language skills. He read many of the Italian classics and the local San Francisco Italian newspaper. He cultivated friends often over a long meal or a glass of wine in North Beach. Upon returning from his trip to Europe Don received an invitation from the Army to report for duty at Fort Ord. Don entered as a private but liked the military life and enrolled in the Officer Candidate School in Fort Sill, Oklahoma. As a freshly minted lieutenant in the artillery, he was sent back to Fort Ord where he spent much of his time at Hunter Ligget. Although he could sleep at the BOQ, he and a friend preferred to live in a Volkswagen Van in the woods. They had wonderful days exploring the vast area of the Santa Lucia mountains. On weekends they would go to the coast for long bike rides and diving for abalone which they cooked on their hibachi on the beach. While it was a great experience and he made close friends, he decided to go in a different San Francisco. The Agency was formed in 1916 by A.P. He was a member and Director of the ItaLingua Institute, an Italian language school, and a member of Il Cenacolo, an Italian cultural club in San Francisco. A resident of Piedmont for 52 years. He was a member of the Piedmont Community Church and held various board positions including President. In the early days of the Oakland Museum, he trained and worked as a docent on the Natural Science floor. A strong hiker, he led Sierra Club Highlight backpacking trips for several years, sharing his love of the mountains and the high country. An avid bicycler, Don took each of his children on a bike tour in Italy upon their college graduation. He hiked in the Dolomites, around Monte Bianco, and the Haute Route on Mt. Blanc. In the fall he spent time duck hunting with friends near the Sutter Buttes. The majesty of the marsh wildlife when the sun came and the sounds in the dark of night never ceased to bring him joy. Don fished for trout in the Sierra but also had angling adventures in Alaska and Africa. During his lifetime, three of Don’s interests came together: gardening, cooking, and wine. He was a vegetable gardener and enjoyed the hours in his garden as well as turning his harvests into fine Italian dishes. Any Italian meal would not be complete without good wine which involved a lifetime of tasting. Don’s extraordinary mind, devotion and gracious presence will be missed by all. He is survived by his wife of 62 years, Mary Ann, his son Michael Parachini and daughterin-law Youngmi, his daughter Sara Aumuller and son-in-law, David, as well as his grandchildren Joseph Aumuller, Kathryn Aumuller, Teresa Aumuller, Emma Parachini, Samuel Parachini and Olivia Parachini. In addition, Don is survived by his brother Victor Parachini and wife Anne and his nephew John Parachini and niece Lesley Parachini-Patten, nieces Susan Biggins and Ann Downey and their families and countless friends. Her musicianship is limited only by her imagination. French impressionism encourages imaginative, musical painting… actually it demands this imagination, and Kasahara’s concert was a lesson in many respects. Hawn Continued from page 1 have some large classes this year. Last week, I began reviewing the high school master schedule for enrollment and class size. Having served as a high school principal in a similar sized district, I know the challenges of building a master schedule of classes that meets the needs of all students. In my review of the master schedule, what I can see is that the combination of our small size (about 800 students), the large number of specialty courses, along with our effort to accommodate the courses students request can result in a lot of classes that have higher than usual enrollment. However, you may also want to ask why so many classes are so low in enrollment. We currently have 21 classes that are enrolled with over 30 students, and we have 40 classes with 21 or fewer students (excluding PE, ELD, Special Education and combined courses). I suspect most of us would agree that small class sizes are a benefit; however, there are several factors to consider. Here are some factors that impact class size: 1. N u m e r o u s S p e c i a l t y Courses: We have a very large number of specialty courses, including electives and AP courses, which can skew very large or very small, depending on student interest. For example, if your child is taking AP Music Theory, that class currently has 16 students enrolled. However, if your child is taking Journalism, there are 32 students enrolled. Both of these courses are only offered one period. PHS has a range of fabulous courses, but we are unable to offer all courses every period. To view the high school master schedule of classes see: Docs.google.com /spreadsheets/d/10RgJzX1f4SWv-vsxC6ZxlHfp3Uh4szamfmBzz-326N8/edit#gid=0 2. Limited Sections of Specialty Courses: Because we have so many specialty courses, with only one or a few sections offered each period, students can get locked into a schedule. For example, if I want to take AP Music Theory (only one section offered), Guitar Engineering (only one section offered) and AP Calculus AB (only two sections offered, but one is the same period as Guitar Engineering), I now have three classes that are locked into specific periods. This happens to many students, which skews class size, sometimes high or low. 3. Small School: You may be wondering why we cannot offer more sections of each course. There are several reasons, but most significant is that we are a small high school with a limited number of teachers and facilities. And so, we offer one or several sections of specialty courses and sometimes even combine courses into a single period when it makes sense to do so (e.g., Applied and Visual Arts courses). How do we solve for this dilemma? Solving for classes that are large could mean adding sections. However, this means additional costs not currently in our budget, and it also requires teachers to pick up a section (or we try to hire a teacher for 1-2 periods), which may be challenging or not viable. Another way to balance course loads is by reducing the number of specialty courses we offer; however, we would need to involve students, teachers, families and staff in a discussion of our course offerings to see if we should reduce offerings. Part of what is special about PHS is the robust number of course offerings. In the end, building a master schedule that meets the needs of all students and does not result in large or very small classes can be challenging. A special thanks to our PHS counselors for their tireless efforts to schedule students into the classes they need. articles.text: elephants that may not have had good living conditions. “Elephants have been living with people for many generations, so they generally rely on people. It’s really difficult for them to return to the wild by themselves. They have a really big brain, so when they are used to being fed by people, it’s hard for them to find their own food because they know humans will feed them,” explained Mike, a guide at Into The Wild. After feeding the elephants, visitors were offered a brief hike through the jungle alongside the elephants, observing how they naturally live in the wild—finding dirt pits to throw on themselves and trees to topple as they scratch their backsides. Guides also pointed out edible foliage for foraging and how local tribes have used different species of plants for uses as medicine, insect repellent, and cuisine. This hike put us in close quarters with the Thailand wilderness. Getting back to Into The Wild’s camp, a typical July-monsoon swept over the area. It was breathtaking to watch and listen to the downpour of rain slam on the metal roof of out platform. When the rain passed, our group made medicine balls to help the elephants’ digestive systems using the camp’s mortar and pestle system before jumping into the Mae Tian River to coat the elephants with mud. After a brief swim in the river without the elephants, it was time to call it a day and make the trek back to Chiang Mai.
articles.title: Hiking with Jon

Gran Moraine Taking its name from the glacier movements in the last Ice Age, the Missoula Floods deposited glacial sediment (moraines) in the northern Willamette Valley. Located in the heart of the Yamhill-Carlton AVA in the Willamette Valley, Gran Moraine produces Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from a 190-acre estate vineyard. The winery which is part of the Jackson Family of wineries purchased the Zena Crown vineyard in the Eola-Amty Hills AVA in 2013. We met winemaker Shane Moore there one bright, sunny morning for a tour of this exquisite property. The perfectly manicured hills of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are cooled by Pacific Ocean air that comes through the Van Duzer Corridor, a gap in the coastal mountain range. Back at the Gran Moraine main tasting room we worked our way through three sparkling wines, concluding with the 2015 Gran Moraine Blanc de Blanc, a magnificent sparkler with great beauty and depth. It was the best sparkling wine of the trip. They also poured a now seriously trendy “orange wine” – the 2021 Flavorscape Pinot Blanc. Orange wines are white wines made in the style of red wines with extended skin contact during the fermentation. The wine was perky and fresh with intriguing earthy flavors. We had three of the Zena Crown Pinot Noirs – all were big, intense wines with a Burgundian complexity to the nose and the capacity to age for decades. Gran Moraine also produces a lovely Chardonnay, the 2019 Yamhill/ Carlton Chardonnay, which had the perfect touch of sweet vanilla oak on the nose and a long savory finish. The entire experience at Gran Moraine from the wonderful tour of Zena Crown that Shane Moore gave us to the charming friendly hospitality of the tasting room staff made our visit a truly pleasant one. FAVORITE WINE 2019 Gran Moraine Dropstone Pinot Noir The wine offers layered scents of cherries, cranberries, licorice and underbrush. Medium bodied, its concentrated berry fruit boasts layer after layer of spicy, earthy accents with a seamless frame and impressive length. something that would not only serve consumers, but also the longevity of the state he calls home. Utilizing organic farming methods and gravity flow production, Lemelson crafts estate grown Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Riesling. Lemelson owns and manages multiple sites in the Northern Willamette Valley, with vineyards that span three AVAs with numerous soil types, exposures, and elevations. The Lemelson tasting room is comfy and cozy with tastings also offered outdoors. We were hosted by Sales and Operations manager Devon Elstun who was extremely knowledgeable about the winery history and current practices in addition to the wines. After a week of drinking almost exclusively Pinot Noir and Chardonnay it was refreshing to get to try the Lemelson 2022 Riesling, a dry wine from the Dundee Hills. The nose was all grapefruit and pineapple with medium body and good fruit. It could use a touch more acid. I also enjoyed their 2022 Chestnut Hill Pinot Gris which was floral, soft and round with apricot and peach flavors. The 2021 Lemelson Chardonnay had some vanilla oak in the nose alongside apple and pear flavors with great balance and structure. The tasting experience at Lemelson is very laid back with warm hospitality from the entire staff. Highly recommended. FAVORITE WINE 2016 Lemelson Pinot Noir Jerome Reserve Named for Eric Lemelson’s father, the noted American inventor Jerome Lemelson, this cuvee is a selection of the very best barrels from a variety of vineyards. It has layered aromas; cranberries, blueberries and earth are complemented by shifting tones of sage, lilac and black pepper. The medium-bodied palate is just as alluring, with powerful layers of spicy fruit. It has great structure and a long finish. Gran Moraine is one of the flagship wineries of the Willamette Valley in Oregon. The adult leaders were great examples to follow. They were tireless and enthusiastic. I think our youth leaders had lots of issues controlling a group that size, but we still managed to push through and have a great time,” said Treichler. World Cup Continued from page 12 Australia’s arrival Host-nation Australia battled it way to the semifinals after entering the tournament as the No. 10 ranked nation after winning Group B. They upset No. 5 France in an epic 7-6 penalty kick shootout after ending regulation in a 0-0 deadlock and shut out No. 13 Denmark 2-0 in the Round of 16. Their Group Stage opener against Ireland was a magnificent event, where Australian fans packed 75,784 into Stadium Australia to watch the Matildas win 1-0 win. And they did most of their work without star player, Sam Kerr. Although Australia lost 3-1 to England in the semis, Kerr scored in the 63rd minute on a magnificent 40-yard run before unleashing a shot from the atop the penalty area, erupting their fans in Stadium Australia. Linda Caicedo master class Colombia’s 18-year-old phenom Linda Caicedo proved to be one of the most entertaining playPhoto courtesy of Goal.com Mary Earps, named the tournament’s outstanding goalie, blocks a penalty kick by England in the finals. ers of the tournament. Caicedo, took the event by storm with her technical footwork and slick playmaking ability. Her goal in Colombia’s 2-1 upset of Germany in the Group Stage was brilliant as she weaved in between two defenders before curling a shot from the left side of the net to the far post – truly a thing of beauty. Japan’s early dominance Japan came in as the No. 11 ranked team but arose from the Group Stage as a favorite to win the tournament after scoring 11 goals and conceding none through the opening stage, including a mighty 4-0 win over Spain on their way to winning Group C. They handled Norway 3-1 in the Round of 16, but didn’t have the same fluidity in a 2-1 loss to Sweden. Philippines wins first-ever World Cup game Despite finishing at the bottom of Group A, Philippines made history by achieving their first World Cup win, a 1-0 victory over tournament co-host New Zealand. Midfielder Sarina Bolden scored her country’s first World Cup goal in the 24th minute. Civic squares surrounded by lanes of fast-moving traffic will be impeded or even cut off from pedestrians and thus deprived of their most essential element: people! As valuable as these places with so much historic precedent are, they are unfortunately lacking or insignificant in many towns and cities in much of our country. One measure of success of a city square is that at first glance it is obvious what it is: a place for interaction among people for various activities—the heart and identity of an entire community. Next: Small town plazas Editor’s Note: Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com This secondary square in the university town of Coimbra, Portugal is interesting, attractive and wonderfully proportioned. Five- and sixstory buildings “enclose” and define the “outdoor room” of a square filled with shops and eateries, punctuated by a small church. Relatively small buildings with their individual detailing give a vitality and rich texture to the place. Not so nice is the new secondary plaza close by in Porto, Portugal. Just a big empty space is the result begging the question, what was the urban design concept here? Where in the World Are We? articles.text: Seriously? We Just Got Cancelled!? Last month, like a number of our neighbors and clients, my husband and I found a cancellation notice in the mail from our home insurance provider. In our case, the reason for the cancellation was not clear. Is it the type of roof on our home? Is it the size of our home? Are there too many trees on our parcel? Prompted by this notice, I reached out to a seasoned insurance broker, Steven Klein of Greystone Insurance, seeking more information on the primary reasons for cancellations in the marketplace. Steven’s insight can be found in the side bar. What should you do if you received a notice of cancellation? First, contact the company or Broker that you worked with on the policy and see if they can assist in preventing the cancellation. Keeping your current insurance may be the best path forward because if you go to a different company, they may require an inspection of your home and decide not to offer a policy because of the four items listed. Nonrenewal rate of all homeowner policies Old Home Systems or Systems in Disrepair Condition is important. Having the major systems in your home relatively updated can be critical. Some insurance companies are using artificial intelligence (AI) and drawing from public records to determine the age of, say, a roof. If they see that the last permit for a roof replacement was 40 years ago, they may ask for proof that the roof has been replaced recently or cancel the policy if the roof is not replaced. Neighborhood Risk Designations Changing Insurance companies are changing their mapping for risks like fire. Steven has a client in the Berkeley Hills whose home was not originally considered high-fire risk, now it is. Some insurance companies are working to move out of areas considered higher risk and may either raise the cost of policies annually or cancel them altogether. Defensible Space and Brush Clearance For policy renewal, some companies are requiring that brush and trees around the subject property be cleared. Of course, in several of our local cities certain types of trees are protected, like oak trees in Berkeley, which creates a challenge for the homeowner if the insurance company requires the tree to be cut down but the local city will not permit its removal. Submitting a Claim Exercise caution when making a claim on your home insurance. Companies can increase your rates or drop you for making even one claim. Consider whether the consequences of making the claim merit the financial burden of the item for which the claim is being made. This includes nonrenewals and cancellations initiated by the consumer or the insurer. Chart: Sriharsha Devulapalli/The Chronicle. Source: CA Dept of Insurance. Second, if you worked directly with a company like State Farm or Allstate and they are going to cancel your policy, try reaching out to an insurance broker. Insurance brokers are different in that they often sell policies for 10-20 different companies and can look for one who insures homes in your neighborhood and will do so at the lowest cost. In the end, our insurance broker worked with the company to maintain the policy on our home. The rate increased by nearly 25%, however, in this insurance environment, keeping the policy we have on the home seems like the prudent choice. Thank you to Steven for taking the time to share his knowledge and insights about insurance with us. can be found at https://www.greystoneinsured.com. He Some homeowners and homebuyers have resorted to the California Fair Plan, which is generally more costly, but unless the state’s insurance commissioner can get more private insurers to write policies in high risk areas, it may end up being the only property insurance available. pages.text: Piedmont Real Estate Update August 2023 Seriously? We Just Got Cancelled!? Last month, like a number of our neighbors and clients, my husband and I found a cancellation notice in the mail from our home insurance provider. In our case, the reason for the cancellation was not clear. Is it the type of roof on our home? Is it the size of our home? Are there too many trees on our parcel? Prompted by this notice, I reached out to a seasoned insurance broker, Steven Klein of Greystone Insurance, seeking more information on the primary reasons for cancellations in the marketplace. Steven’s insight can be found in the side bar. What should you do if you received a notice of cancellation? First, contact the company or Broker that you worked with on the policy and see if they can assist in preventing the cancellation. Keeping your current insurance may be the best path forward because if you go to a different company, they may require an inspection of your home and decide not to offer a policy because of the four items listed. Nonrenewal rate of all homeowner policies Old Home Systems or Systems in Disrepair Condition is important. Having the major systems in your home relatively updated can be critical. Some insurance companies are using artificial intelligence (AI) and drawing from public records to determine the age of, say, a roof. If they see that the last permit for a roof replacement was 40 years ago, they may ask for proof that the roof has been replaced recently or cancel the policy if the roof is not replaced. Neighborhood Risk Designations Changing Insurance companies are changing their mapping for risks like fire. Steven has a client in the Berkeley Hills whose home was not originally considered high-fire risk, now it is. Some insurance companies are working to move out of areas considered higher risk and may either raise the cost of policies annually or cancel them altogether. Defensible Space and Brush Clearance For policy renewal, some companies are requiring that brush and trees around the subject property be cleared. Of course, in several of our local cities certain types of trees are protected, like oak trees in Berkeley, which creates a challenge for the homeowner if the insurance company requires the tree to be cut down but the local city will not permit its removal. Submitting a Claim Exercise caution when making a claim on your home insurance. Companies can increase your rates or drop you for making even one claim. Consider whether the consequences of making the claim merit the financial burden of the item for which the claim is being made. This includes nonrenewals and cancellations initiated by the consumer or the insurer. Chart: Sriharsha Devulapalli/The Chronicle. Source: CA Dept of Insurance. Second, if you worked directly with a company like State Farm or Allstate and they are going to cancel your policy, try reaching out to an insurance broker. Insurance brokers are different in that they often sell policies for 10-20 different companies and can look for one who insures homes in your neighborhood and will do so at the lowest cost. In the end, our insurance broker worked with the company to maintain the policy on our home. The rate increased by nearly 25%, however, in this insurance environment, keeping the policy we have on the home seems like the prudent choice. Thank you to Steven for taking the time to share his knowledge and insights about insurance with us. can be found at https://www.greystoneinsured.com. He Some homeowners and homebuyers have resorted to the California Fair Plan, which is generally more costly, but unless the state’s insurance commissioner can get more private insurers to write policies in high risk areas, it may end up being the only property insurance available. articles.text: The calendar may still read August, but in Piedmont, school is back in full force. Classes began throughout the school district on Wednesday, August 9, the earliest opening day in the city’s history. Piedmont’s identity waxes and wanes with the rhythms of its three elementary schools, middle school and high school. Back to school is always a time of rebirth and looking to the future. It’s a time of change for parents too as their kids get back to their normal rhythms of academia. With the end of summer, mornings now include packing lunchboxes, cooking breakfast and walking to school. Afternoons are now all about school pickup, snack and homework time, and questions of “What did you learn today at school?” A change in schedule occurred in the 2022-23 school year for middle and high school students with slightly later start times. “I know from long experience that amazing things are going to happen for all those kids that are swarming the playgrounds and hallways. It’s going to be a great year,” stated PHS English teacher Elise Marks at the August 9 School Board meeting. Wildwood has a new principal for the first time since Carol CraHavens students are quick to remember how to get in line in an orderly fashion on the first day of the school year.

articles.text: New Superintendent of Piedmont Unified School District Jennifer Hawn wasted no time in giving herself a crash course to learn as much as possible about the schools and the community. She officially began her tenure with the district on July 1, and chose August 9, the first day of classes, as the time to begin a tour of all campuses. First stop was Beach School at 8 a.m. and the last stop was at City Hall 13 hours later after presiding over her first school board meeting. “We had our first day back, and it was super exciting. I’d like to thank the board, staff and families for such a warm welcome,” said Hawn. In her first board meeting, Hawn spoke briefly about the state’s new math framework, a subject that is a hot topic for many parents of secondary students. “While we are excited to see the state is giving greater attention to mathematics, we have many questions about the new framework and we have no plans or timeline for any changes to our mathematics program… at this time,” she said. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved on August 7 the formation of a “working group” to review concerns from pickleball players who want the Linda Beach courts restriped for permanent play with extended hours, and concerns from Linda Beach neighbors who have complained about the noise from pickleball play. The group will be composed of a representative of pickleball players; a representative of neighborhood residents; and two City Council members to review the concerns and suggestions of players and court neighbors. The Council has not yet declared who these members will be. A five-month trial of exclusively pickleball play at the Linda Beach courts began on February 27 and ended on July 31. The city planned to repair and re-stripe the Beach courts after the trial. Depending on public feedback and a Recreation Commission recommendation the council likely will choose to re-stripe the courts for pickleball use only. During a July 21 meeting, the Recreation Commission recommended restriping for permanent pickleball use and limiting daily future play from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Some players, like Piedmont High School senior Ruby Guzdar said that even shortening the hours of play to end at 6 p.m. rather than 9 p.m. would impede their experience. “Students need a release from the stress of schoolwork, college applications, intense sports teams, and jobs,” said Guzdar. “Pickleball provides an opportunity to not only relieve stress and be outdoors, but connect to members of our community and be social outside of school.” Other speakers who lived close to the Beach courts, however, described the 12 hours of daily noise they experienced during the trial as no less than torture.
