articles.text: The Piedmont Public Works Department suffered the loss of $20,000 in equipment at the Corporation Yard in a burglary committed between midnight and 6 a.m. on Sunday, August 6. Three vehicles had tools removed, and several other vehicles were rifled through. The stolen items included heavy-duty tools, including chainsaws and drills. Damage to cabinets and storage lock mechanisms on the trucks will require repairs. An alarm and camera defense system will be added to the area. Police Captain Chris Monahan said the burglary is part of a “troubling pattern that’s occurring in our city. It seems that every year or two someone breaks into the Corp Yard, and property is either taken or broken.” Those with questions or information regarding the burglary may contact the Police Department at 420-3000.
articles.title: $20,000 Burglary at Corporation Yard

articles.text: A full-size sedan lost control while driving south on Grand Avenue on Wednesday afternoon, August 9, and crashed into a City tree. According to the police, the driver swerved over a double yellow line, into the north lane and hit the opposite curb line near Arroyo and Lower Grand. The vehicle, a white 1999 Dodge Intrepid, sustained major damage and came to a dead stop at the base of the tree. The entire front engine compartment was pushed back, the doors rippled in, and the windshield broken. The driver was trapped inside the vehicle which ultimately caught on fire. Police were notified of the accident around 4:42 p.m., and the driver was extracted by the Piedmont Fire Department using the jaws of life. The fire was extinguished, and the driver transported to Highland Hospital with no obvious physical injuries. Police closed traffic briefly to investigate and have the car towed. Piedmont Police obtained a blood sample from the driver, who was driving with a suspended license. A Dodge Entrepid collided with a large tree around 4:42 p.m. on Wednesday, August 9, near the intersection of Grand and Arroyo Avenues.
articles.title: Car totaled in collision with tree

CRIME REPORT Car totaled in collision with tree By Jay Russell A full-size sedan lost control while driving south on Grand Avenue on Wednesday afternoon, August 9, and crashed into a City tree. According to the police, the driver swerved over a double yellow line, into the north lane and hit the opposite curb line near Arroyo and Lower Grand. The vehicle, a white 1999 Dodge Intrepid, sustained major damage and came to a dead stop at the base of the tree. The entire front engine compartment was pushed back, the doors rippled in, and the windshield broken. The driver was trapped inside the vehicle which ultimately caught on fire. Police were notified of the accident around 4:42 p.m., and the driver was extracted by the Piedmont Fire Department using the jaws of life. The fire was extinguished, and the driver transported to Highland Hospital with no obvious physical injuries. Police closed traffic briefly to investigate and have the car towed. Piedmont Police obtained a blood sample from the driver, who was driving with a suspended license. A Dodge Entrepid collided with a large tree around 4:42 p.m. on Wednesday, August 9, near the intersection of Grand and Arroyo Avenues. articles.text: At the earliest start of school in Piedmont history, students and parents shifted gears on Tuesday, August 8, with walkthrough registration at Piedmont Middle and High Schools. Students at both campuses were given their class schedules for the year. The ambiance could not have been more different. At 1:30 p.m. on Tuesday, the middle school’s walkthrough registration in the Buzz Redford Gym was jam packed. In contrast, in Sukanya Goswami’s second year as principal of Piedmont High School, parent volunteers and high school clubs were well spaced out on the campus. Walkthrough registration is more than just getting your planner and finding out if you got your desired electives. It is also a day for students to see long lost friends after the summer break and to rekindle the back-to-school excitement. Middle schoolers, many of whom were accompanied by parents or guardians, shuffled in line for photos in the gym, then headed to the library to pick up their schedules. Last year, middle school registration was spread out more, with photos being taken in the John Morrison Gym. Long lines didn’t seem to concern students though as they happily socialized inside and on the patio.
articles.title: Walkthrough registration signals start of school year

articles.text: As the project to replace turf and irrigation at Witter Field continues, neighbors are increasingly concerned about flooding impacts. In 2007, when new synthetic turf was last installed at Witter, it cost $219,000 and was installed in two weeks by FieldTurf, the company manufacturing the product of the same name. When the current project began on June 6, 2023, the turf was eight years past its eight-year life span. Since then, the field has often flooded and been unplayable for sports due to an apparent insufficient drainage system. The project now has a $4,150,000 price tag and a sixmonth project span. The proposed new irrigation system involves rerouting a storm drain from its current location under the field, to a Bushy Dell Creek manhole. However, some neighbors on Palm Drive, by the base of the field, raise questions not yet sufficiently answered by the Piedmont Unified School District. They maintain that the district, responsible for overseeing the renovation, has not adequately studied flood risks that this project may present to their homes. At a community meeting held by the district at Wildwood School on May 22, two weeks before the six-month, $4.1 million project began, many among approximately 30 attending neighbors raised the concern of Staff photo As turf is replaced on Witter Field, many neighbors on the nearby streets worry that the storm pipes meant to drain the field will flood their own backyards.
articles.title: Witter Field neighbors raise concerns of flooding

articles.text: Editor: In “City awards $588,000 to consultant for Moraga Canyon housing plan” (Piedmont Post July 19, 2023), Councilmember Tom Ramsey is quoted as stating that the City “is not producing a design … to build something that we’re going to pay for.” Perhaps the Post can ask Mr. Ramsey whether he will promise, in addition, that the City will not give away land, or make land available at less than fair market value, for the Moraga Canyon project, because such a giveaway would constitute the City paying for part, albeit not all, of the project. –Dana H. By Pastor Jim Hopkins If you are a Facebook friend or an X (formerly Twitter) follower of mine you know that for almost a decade I have shared my daily spiritual practice publicly. That practice is quite simple. After offering a prayer I read a portion of scripture and write a short response. Here are some my most responded to postings from the month gone by. Exodus 2:19 “An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they answered, “and he even drew water for us and watered our animals.” There is much irony in this verse. Moses is identified as an Egyptian. Jethro’s daughters need to he rescued from shepherds, a term that often described political and religious leaders. Moses, who was pulled from the water, now provides water. Luke 18:13 But the tax collector stood at a distance and would not even raise his face to heaven, but beat on his breast and said, ‘God, have pity on me, a sinner!’ In Jesus’ vision of the world put right, he called it the Reign of God, widows win justice from corrupt judges and tax collectors are praised for their spiritual insight. Matthew 18:20 [Jesus] For where two or three come together in my name, I am there with them. As churches gather in Jesus’ name this 4th of July weekend, may we pray for the country rather than to it. articles.text: At a public hearing on Monday, August 14, at 5:30 p.m., the Planning Commission will consider two proposals to make new housing easier to build in Piedmont: pre-approved design plans for affordable ADUs and objective design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings. If the Commission approves the proposals, they will advance to the City Council for adoption. Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs - which are three Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont - can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (though construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). This proposal would allow Piedmont property owners who submit these preapproved designs as-is to receive a planning permit, giving applicants a head start on the development process. ADUs that use the City’s pre-approved designs would be rent-restricted for 10 years. During this period, if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet “very low income” affordability thresholds for the Alameda County area set by the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. However, the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing for homeowners to submit ADUs larger than the city’s standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Both the permit-ready ADU styles, and information on building larger ADUs, is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Multifamily objective design standards (MODS) Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The MODS don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. generally urban infill areas, which comprise less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking - they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Community members can submit comments on the proposals ahead of the meeting by email to PiedmontIsHome@piedmont. ca.gov; by mail to the Piedmont Planning Commission, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611; or speak on the topic at the 5:30 p.m. August 14 meeting in-person or via Zoom. The agenda report for both items is available for download on PiedmontIsHome.org. articles.text: Westside Joe’s Bikes is opening its second location at 4319 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. Westside Joe’s Bikes has been a staple in Alameda since the 1930’s. The current owner, Vivian “Vivee” Young-McDonald, a previous resident of Piedmont, had been looking to expand after the height of the pandemic. She met Dan Hensley, an industry veteran who has owned and managed bike shops and bicycle nonprofits. Vivee and Dan realized they shared many of the same goals, so they teamed up with a plan to relocate and grow Westside Joe’s Bikes of Alameda. With the recent closures of multiple bicycle shops in Oakland, they decided to keep the current location in Alameda and open a second location in Oakland to help better serve the East Bay Cycling Community. Westside Joe’s Bikes is creating an environment that is open, comfortable, and all inclusive to anyone interested in bicycles. Coupled with this is offering bicycle retail and service professionals a career path along with a living wage and work / life balance, something they see the industry is lacking. A near term goal that is important to the business is to create or partner with a youth based non-profit that offers mechanic training with a path that leads directly to working in a bike shop. The dream is to have an aspiring youth begin at the non-profit that can lead them to a job at the retail and service shop with a distinct career path to management, and eventually franchise ownership. Vivee is very excited for the future and to be able to better serve a community she loves so much. If you would like to speak with Dan or Vivee feel free to contact them at 510-407-6950, or simply stop by either location. Westside Joe’s Piedmont will have their Grand Opening August 11th.
articles.title: Westside Joe’s Bikes expanding to Piedmont Ave.

articles.text: Registration opens Monday, August 14 for Piedmont Adult School’s fall session. The session will begin September 11 and run through December 17. New classes this session include courses in gardening, wreath-making and poetry, as well as many new cooking, computer and iPhone classes. The school also continues to offer popular art, language, music, exercise and business courses. “We are very excited for the upcoming year,” said Shannon Fierro, director of Piedmont Adult School. “Our motto is ‘Education for Life’ and we are committed to providing a wide range of classes to meet the needs of the community.” Through the Adult School’s Creative Retirement program, special classes are offered to senior citizens (age 55 and over) at no cost. Courses include Exercise for Seniors, Fine Arts Media, and Needlework. These classes are held on Thursday mornings at the Veterans Hall in Piedmont and registration is required. In addition to its wide range of community classes, Piedmont Adult School offers a high school diploma program, English as a Second Language (ESL) classes, and short term Career Technical Education computer courses. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over. Course offerings and registration may be found at www.piedmontadultschool.org or through the Moonlighter catalog, which is mailed to households in Piedmont and surrounding areas. For more information, contact the Piedmont Adult School office at (510) 594-2655 or pas@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: Fire Dept. asks residents to eliminate fire hazards As summer heat continues and vegetation dries out, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to prepare their yards for fire season by trimming trees and shrubs, clearing flammable materials, and removing dead vegetation around their property. Recent wildfires across California have taught us that our communities are best protected when everyone takes steps to manage the vegetation around their homes, which helps to reduce the spread and severity of fires when they start. Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said that homeowners’ responsibility for fire prevention “is whatever is on your property. Cities take care of the trees and vegetation in the public rights-of-way and the parks.” “Ideally,” he said, “people should leave at least five feet of room between vegetation and flammable property (like homes, fences and decks), and 10 feet between tree limbs and roofs or chimneys.” To prevent ladder fuel – a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the ground upward to tree or shrub canopies – Brannigan said “for the height of the fuel, you want three times the amount of space above it, so if you have one foot of grass, try to have three feet between whatever is above it.” Although property owners may find their yards in particularly dangerous situations this fire season due to high vegetation growth after last winter’s rainstorms, Brannigan said “We have a saying that every year is going to be the worst fire season, whether its dry and drought or whether it’s wet and a lot of growth.” He urged Piedmonters to clear their yards of dead and excess vegetation as soon as possible, ahead of the dryer months of September and October. In Piedmont particularly, he said, “We have a lot of beautiful old homes; some have wood siding and wood shingles. Having vegetation right up against that or overhanging with debris falling down” presents a particular danger in lieu of regular tree and shrub maintenance. In the Bay Area more broadly, he continued, “when you look at statewide [fire] guidance, it often involves five feet, thirty feet, a hundred feet, but we just don’t have that kind of space. We are trying to come up with practical, realistic guidelines to keep your property safe as well as the adjacent properties and prevent fire from spreading.” Just as crucial is the knowledge of evacuation routes, “Know, from where you live, work, go to school, at least two ways out of your neighborhood, Also know multiple ways you can get yourself out, whether by car, by walking, whether you’re in a wheelchair or on a bicycle. Talk with your neighbors and find out if there are people around you who might need a little bit of extra help.” In short: to increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire, create space between plants and your home, and clear your yard of any debris or flammable materials like dead vegetation. If you need help with firesafe landscaping or with identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Piedmont Fire Department at 420-3030 to request an inspection. If you’d like to get a head start on preparing your household, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ wildfire and piedmont.ca.gov/ vegetation for more recommendations on preparing your household. A checklist for preparing your yard is available at piedmont.ca.gov/YardChecklist.
articles.title: Time to prepare for wildfires

articles.text: Kerry Persichitte has been selected to lead PCC’s new NextGen ministry program. Piedmont Community Church will host a community picnic in Piedmont Park on Sunday, August 20, at 11 a.m. The event will have food, live music and children’s games as part of the church’s celebration of a new youth ministry, NextGen. Kerry Persichitte, who has been hired to lead the program, said the church is starting the new ministry “to find out how we can best serve kids — from the ages of three months all the way through 18 — so they can build their faith, develop fun relationships with friends, and feel supported by their parents. I’m excited for the picnic on the 20th, when NextGen officially launches, to reflect that combination of safety, community, faith, fun, and a sense of belonging.” The ministry will involve age-divided groups - including a nursery, a pre-kindergarten program, and respective programs for elementary, middle school and high school students. “Worship will involve largegroup communicators that really bring the Bible stories to life, and what we call ‘life groups,’ which will be smaller spaces to give the kids a chance to discuss or share whatever they’d like, with a trusted adult or fellow student,” Persichitte said. A veteran of 17 years developing youth ministry in churches across the country, from Illinois to New jersey to California, has affirmed the importance of student leadership and parent collaboration in helping shape worship programs. “Kids today want to have a lot of agency in their environments and know best what’s going on in their worlds,” she continued. “With NextGen, we’ll always be asking the kids involved: ‘What is it you need?’ We want them to help create a space they’re proud of, feel safe in, and that they want to invite their friends to.” On Sunday, Aug. 20, at 11 a.m., Piedmont Community Church will hold a family picnic in Piedmont Park celebrating the launch of its new NextGen youth ministry program, directed by Kerry Persichitte (above). Furthermore, she added, “Despite how overconnected we all are with social media, I think there’s an overwhelming sense of loneliness in our culture. Staying culturally relevant is an issue that is important for anyone who wants to create that sense of belonging. We’ll focus on bringing the Bible to life for these kids in relevant ways that can impact their everyday lives, and developing safe relationships where they can share struggles they’re facing in their lives. A key part of that, too, will involve partnering with parents, and offering support to them in dealing with these struggles that kids face, like anxiety and the place of social media.” “The heart of what we want kids and parents to take from NextGen,” she concluded, “is a sense of purpose and connection. We want kids to know that we believe in their future. They are the world changers, they are the future of this world, and we want to do everything that we can to support them through the church.” For more information visit PiedmontChurch.org or call the church at 547-5700. articles.text: Vegetation management plays a critical role in reducing wildfire risk to our community. It is important to take time every year to prune plants and clear debris before fire season. Use this checklist to prepare your property in early summer, then review it again in September. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! If you have questions or need assistance, call us at (510) 420-3030.

In the Bay Area more broadly, he continued, “when you look at statewide [fire] guidance, it often involves five feet, thirty feet, a hundred feet, but we just don’t have that kind of space. We are trying to come up with practical, realistic guidelines to keep your property safe as well as the adjacent properties and prevent fire from spreading.” Just as crucial is the knowledge of evacuation routes, “Know, from where you live, work, go to school, at least two ways out of your neighborhood, Also know multiple ways you can get yourself out, whether by car, by walking, whether you’re in a wheelchair or on a bicycle. Talk with your neighbors and find out if there are people around you who might need a little bit of extra help.” In short: to increase your home’s chance of surviving a wildfire, create space between plants and your home, and clear your yard of any debris or flammable materials like dead vegetation. If you need help with firesafe landscaping or with identifying what needs to be done on your property, call the Piedmont Fire Department at 420-3030 to request an inspection. If you’d like to get a head start on preparing your household, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ wildfire and piedmont.ca.gov/ vegetation for more recommendations on preparing your household. A checklist for preparing your yard is available at piedmont.ca.gov/YardChecklist. PREPARE YOUR YARD FOR FIRE SEASON Vegetation management plays a critical role in reducing wildfire risk to our community. It is important to take time every year to prune plants and clear debris before fire season. Use this checklist to prepare your property in early summer, then review it again in September. CREATE SPACE Maintaining adequate space between plants, structures, and other objects on your property makes it harder for a fire to spread. Trim trees so that the lowest branches are at least 6 feet from the ground, or 3 times the height of any shrubs beneath the tree. Trim trees so that branches are 10 feet apart from other trees. Remove branches within 10 feet of your chimney. Remove branches that hang over your roof. Remove or prune plants and shrubs near windows. Move patio furniture, wood piles, etc. away from plants. CLEAR DEBRIS & FLAMMABLE MATERIAL Clear leaves, pine needles, and other debris from roofs, gutters, and the ground. Remove all dead plants, grass, and weeds around your property. Remove plant debris and other flammable materials, such as propane containers and paint from under decks. KEEP PLANTS WELL MAINTAINED Whether you have natives or non-natives, the most important thing is to keep all plants in your yard watered and well-maintained. Trim any dead or dying material from plants. Keep plants watered - especially any plants located within five feet of your home. If you have Eucalyptus trees, remove any shedding bark and leaves. Minimum Vertical Clearance: Avoid Fire "Ladders" Lack of vertical space between shrubs and trees allows fire to move from the ground to treetops like a ladder, leading to more intense fires. 3X X Trim trees so the lowest branches are 3 times the height of shrubs below. For example, if a 5 foot shrub is growing near a tree, the lowest branch should be be 15 feet above it - 20 feet from the ground. We're here to help! If you have questions or need assistance, call us at (510) 420-3030. ADVERTISE IN THE POST Piedmont Church family picnic on Aug. 20 Kerry Persichitte has been selected to lead PCC’s new NextGen ministry program. By Selen Ozturk Piedmont Community Church will host a community picnic in Piedmont Park on Sunday, August 20, at 11 a.m. The event will have food, live music and children’s games as part of the church’s celebration of a new youth ministry, NextGen. Kerry Persichitte, who has been hired to lead the program, said the church is starting the new ministry “to find out how we can best serve kids — from the ages of three months all the way through 18 — so they can build their faith, develop fun relationships with friends, and feel supported by their parents. I’m excited for the picnic on the 20th, when NextGen officially launches, to reflect that combination of safety, community, faith, fun, and a sense of belonging.” The ministry will involve age-divided groups - including a nursery, a pre-kindergarten program, and respective programs for elementary, middle school and high school students. “Worship will involve largegroup communicators that really bring the Bible stories to life, and what we call ‘life groups,’ which will be smaller spaces to give the kids a chance to discuss or share whatever they’d like, with a trusted adult or fellow student,” Persichitte said. A veteran of 17 years developing youth ministry in churches across the country, from Illinois to New jersey to California, has affirmed the importance of student leadership and parent collaboration in helping shape worship programs. “Kids today want to have a lot of agency in their environments and know best what’s going on in their worlds,” she continued. “With NextGen, we’ll always be asking the kids involved: ‘What is it you need?’ We want them to help create a space they’re proud of, feel safe in, and that they want to invite their friends to.” On Sunday, Aug. 20, at 11 a.m., Piedmont Community Church will hold a family picnic in Piedmont Park celebrating the launch of its new NextGen youth ministry program, directed by Kerry Persichitte (above). Furthermore, she added, “Despite how overconnected we all are with social media, I think there’s an overwhelming sense of loneliness in our culture. Staying culturally relevant is an issue that is important for anyone who wants to create that sense of belonging. We’ll focus on bringing the Bible to life for these kids in relevant ways that can impact their everyday lives, and developing safe relationships where they can share struggles they’re facing in their lives. A key part of that, too, will involve partnering with parents, and offering support to them in dealing with these struggles that kids face, like anxiety and the place of social media.” “The heart of what we want kids and parents to take from NextGen,” she concluded, “is a sense of purpose and connection. We want kids to know that we believe in their future. They are the world changers, they are the future of this world, and we want to do everything that we can to support them through the church.” For more information visit PiedmontChurch.org or call the church at 547-5700. articles.text: August 3, 2023 Dear Piedmont USD Families: I would like to take this moment to express gratitude and appreciation for our families at the start of the 2023-2024 school year. Piedmont Unified School District faculty and staff are committed to delivering the finest educational experience available. I have a firm belief in the potential of every one of our students, and I look forward to collaborating with our staff, families and students to help every student belong and thrive. I have a number of items to share with you as we approach the start of school on August 9th. Below you will find information on the following topics: • COVID Safety Protocols • Access to Campuses - Wildwood/Witter Field • Access to Campuses - City Pool Project/PHS/MHS/PMS • Staffing Update • New Leadership Team • Future Communication Topics COVID Safety Protocols First, please note that we are still taking health and safety precautions according to guidance from the Alameda County Public Health Department. We will update families as new information becomes available. Docs.google.com/ d o c u m e nt /d /1n D q Q e 8 c pWvtMUC-8DZsRb1sCGP5_ OH7f-Ao7GHJRRc0 Access to Campuses Wildwood School/Witter Field I would also like to share safety measures/protocols regarding access to and around our campuses as work is completed on the Witter Field Renovation Project. These changes to the path of travel will be strictly enforced and adhered to by the Witter contractor: 1. All drop off and pick up activity will need to take place on Wildwood Ave via the front door entry, directly in front of the campus. The City has extended the white curb drop off area on Wildwood Ave to help accommodate a few more vehicles in the drop off/pick up queue. And, thanks to the gracious donations via the Wildwood parents/Dads club, students can now wait to be picked up on the newly installed benches located in the front of the school. 2. Drop off or pickup via the Winsor Ave driveway or rear stairs will not be permitted. All gates leading to the rear of the school and to the lower Wildwood playground will be locked. Refer to the site map/path of travel showing the entry points on Wildwood Ave. (See photo above or click for the map) Drive. google.com/file/d/1xON7AcZ lo12 m x NJ H K-yH i RTCzeHmCzRI 3. Parents and students who typically walk from the El Cerrito/Jerome Ave neighborhood will need to walk up the left side of PE Hill, past the yellow gate, past the softball field and walk up the stairs or wood ramp to Wildwood Ave. (See photo or link above.) 4. PHS and PMS students will not be able to travel through Witter Field from Winsor Ave. All students walking from the Palm Drive-Winsor neighborhood will need to walk to Magnolia Ave. and then access the schools via El Cerrito Avenue and walk up the left side of PE Hill. 5. Via Piedmont Police, a crossing guard will be stationed at the front of the school for drop-off and pick-up every school day. 6. A double fenced traffic lane has been constructed on the Wildwood lower playground to allow a safe path of travel for all construction vehicles to and from the Witter Field construction site. The traffic lane will be staffed with a monitor during the school day. 7. Regarding the Witter Field Renovation Project, refer to the technical reports: Drive. google.com/drive/folders/1LTeahsKNA38aRj0aayw6vPILu49Jq58g, from the PUSD environmental consultants. We will closely monitor Bothman Construction, the Witter Field contractor, to ensure strict adherence to all of the guidelines and recommendations set forth in the technical reports. We will be holding regular Wildwood Elementary/Witter Field Renovation Project Committee meetings. The committee meeting schedule will be forthcoming. City Pool Project – PHS, MHS, & PMS The City notified us that on Thursday and Friday, August 10th and 11th, there will be the pouring of concrete for the perimeter foundation along Magnolia and Bonita Avenue. This work will involve multiple trucks starting at 7 a.m. and finishing at 7 p.m. on both days. Flaggers will be onsite to direct traffic traversing along Magnolia Avenue and Bonita Avenue, directing concrete trucks and cars to avoid delays and facilitate the flow of traffic. There will also be a crossing guard at Magnolia and Bonita for the entire duration of the City pool construction project. We recommend avoiding driving in this area on these days, if at all possible. Staffing Update I would also like to share some updates on matters related to our schools. First, I must share that we are still in the process of hiring staff for our schools. We have experienced some late summer resignations, which has challenged us to fill some positions at the last minute. One vacancy that we may have to start the school year with is high school Chemistry. Please know that we have posted the position and leveraged our connections to find a teacher; however, I believe we can do more. Although new to PUSD, I have already felt the remarkable support our families have offered, and I am wondering if we have families with connections in our local colleges and universities, in particular in schools of education. Parents/ Guardians, I can certainly make calls myself; however, having a direct connection would be ideal as I build a more robust pipeline of teachers. Gates leading to the rear of Wildwood Elementary School will be locked during the current renovation of Witter Field.

articles.text: Schoolmates registration for the coming 2023-2024 school year is open while spots in each program remain. Starting this fall, Schoolmates, Piedmont Recreation Department’s popular afterschool program will have increased capacity and new, flexible scheduling options. Registration began on Wednesday, July 19. This year’s Schoolmates offers three choices: • Block Booking – a full year of traditional, full afternoon care • Flexi-Care – Families may register in hourly increments and pay only for the care they need. Schedules can be adjusted each month based upon available space. • Camp Kaleidoscope – expanded care options to accommodate early dismissal for grades K-3 during the first few weeks of school. Registration can be made online with a Community Pass at bit.ly/3K43zlM. Detailed information on program options, dates, registration, scheduling, tuition, withdrawals, adjustments, and waitlists is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ schoolmates. Block Booking The Schoolmates “Block Booking” option offers predetermined time slots for families needing consistent weekly care throughout the year: • Register once for the full school year September 5 to May 24 • Sign up by day of the week for full afternoon care (3-6 p.m. most weekdays, 1:45-6 p.m. on Wednesdays) • A waiting list is available Tuition: $11.20/hour, billed monthly. Flexi-Care The new Flexi-Care program offers registration in hourly increments, allowing families to select only the days and times they need: • Separate enrollment periods for fall (September 5 to December 21) and spring (January 8 to May 24) • Option to adjust schedule monthly, pending availability Tuition: $13.40/hour, billed monthly. Camp Kaleidoscope Camp Kaleidoscope, provides expanded care availability during the first few weeks of school, when demand is the highest. Camp Kaleidoscope offers weekly flexibility and enrichment activities ranging from sports and scavenger hunts to cooking and arts & crafts. Camp Kaleidoscope runs from 2 to 6 p.m., August 14 to September 1. Sports openings currently exist at Beach and Havens Elementary locations. Minimates The Minimates program offers transitional kindergarten students opportunities to learn, grow, and have fun with age-appropriate games, crafts, and sports. • Register once for the full school year. August 14 to May 24 • Sign up by day of the week for full morning (8:30 a.m. start) or full afternoon (class release to 3 p.m. start) • Waitlist available Tuition: $11.20/hour, billed monthly. For questions, contact Chelle Putzer at 420-3070. Schoolmates registration is now open for the 2023-24 school year.

articles.text: Highlander Robotics, an FRC team in the FIRST Robotics program, is hosting an Open House at Piedmont High School on Friday, August 11, at 6 pm. The team encourages interested 9th to 12th grade students and their parents to learn more about the team and this season’s robot “Paddo the Frog,” who just returned from the Houston World Championships. The event will include a presentation of the program as well as a demo of the robot. Working under the mentorship of experienced industry professionals, members are guided through the build process with full support. Team members gain real-world engineering experience and get to work in a constructive learning environment amongst other like-minded and passionate team members. When prompted with a fieldgame challenge at the start of each build season, student members get an opportunity to learn and apply the fabrication, design, prototyping and coding skills learned during the off-season training that takes place each fall. Highlander Robotics welcomes all students regardless of experience. “Our program expects to train students from scratch. We believe that anyone can become a leader on the team if they have the interest and can dedicate the time,” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark. The Highlanders provide training in programming, CAD (computer aided design), and general mechanical work. Outside of more traditional robotics work, Highlander Robotics also seeks members with other diverse interests including community outreach, visual and industrial design, marketing, branding, video production and other roles needed to display a well-functioning robotics team. To learn more, come meet the team this week, August 11, in the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab in the STEAM Building. For more information, visit frc8033.com, or contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.org. Piedmont’s Highlander Robotics team at the World Championships in Houston, Texas.

articles.text: PRAISE (Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy and Information in Special Education) announced this week that it has changed its name to PIE (Piedmonters for Inclusive Education). Why change our name? We believe that Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) best reflects who we are at this time in our organizational history,” said board president Iris Warchall. We are parents who support inclusion in PUSD for all students with disabilities and learning differences. We believe that all learners have the right to full participation and inclusion in our classrooms and in our community, and that for us to do so as a community we must work to meet the needs of students with all neurotypes, abilities, and learning styles. We strive to ensure that the Piedmont Unified School District provides all students with an excellent education in a nurturing environment. “We will continue to advocate for resources to help meet students’ access needs, provide educational resources in the form of our well-loved Neurodiversity Speaker Series and provide grants to PUSD teachers and Piedmont Recreation Department programs that help make Piedmont a welcoming community for all,” added Warchall.

pages.text: 8 Wednesday, August 9, 2023 Schoolmates registration opens Schoolmates registration for the coming 2023-2024 school year is open while spots in each program remain. Starting this fall, Schoolmates, Piedmont Recreation Department’s popular afterschool program will have increased capacity and new, flexible scheduling options. Registration began on Wednesday, July 19. This year’s Schoolmates offers three choices: • Block Booking – a full year of traditional, full afternoon care • Flexi-Care – Families may register in hourly increments and pay only for the care they need. Schedules can be adjusted each month based upon available space. • Camp Kaleidoscope – expanded care options to accommodate early dismissal for grades K-3 during the first few weeks of school. Registration can be made online with a Community Pass at bit.ly/3K43zlM. Detailed information on program options, dates, registration, scheduling, tuition, withdrawals, adjustments, and waitlists is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ schoolmates. Block Booking The Schoolmates “Block Booking” option offers predetermined time slots for families needing consistent weekly care throughout the year: • Register once for the full school year September 5 to May 24 • Sign up by day of the week for full afternoon care (3-6 p.m. most weekdays, 1:45-6 p.m. on Wednesdays) • A waiting list is available Tuition: $11.20/hour, billed monthly. Flexi-Care The new Flexi-Care program offers registration in hourly increments, allowing families to select only the days and times they need: • Separate enrollment periods for fall (September 5 to December 21) and spring (January 8 to May 24) • Option to adjust schedule monthly, pending availability Tuition: $13.40/hour, billed monthly. Camp Kaleidoscope Camp Kaleidoscope, provides expanded care availability during the first few weeks of school, when demand is the highest. Camp Kaleidoscope offers weekly flexibility and enrichment activities ranging from sports and scavenger hunts to cooking and arts & crafts. Camp Kaleidoscope runs from 2 to 6 p.m., August 14 to September 1. Sports openings currently exist at Beach and Havens Elementary locations. Minimates The Minimates program offers transitional kindergarten students opportunities to learn, grow, and have fun with age-appropriate games, crafts, and sports. • Register once for the full school year. August 14 to May 24 • Sign up by day of the week for full morning (8:30 a.m. start) or full afternoon (class release to 3 p.m. start) • Waitlist available Tuition: $11.20/hour, billed monthly. For questions, contact Chelle Putzer at 420-3070. Schoolmates registration is now open for the 2023-24 school year. Highlander Robotics Open House tomorrow By Kevin Clark Highlander Robotics, an FRC team in the FIRST Robotics program, is hosting an Open House at Piedmont High School on Friday, August 11, at 6 pm. The team encourages interested 9th to 12th grade students and their parents to learn more about the team and this season’s robot “Paddo the Frog,” who just returned from the Houston World Championships. The event will include a presentation of the program as well as a demo of the robot. Working under the mentorship of experienced industry professionals, members are guided through the build process with full support. Team members gain real-world engineering experience and get to work in a constructive learning environment amongst other like-minded and passionate team members. When prompted with a fieldgame challenge at the start of each build season, student members get an opportunity to learn and apply the fabrication, design, prototyping and coding skills learned during the off-season training that takes place each fall. Highlander Robotics welcomes all students regardless of experience. “Our program expects to train students from scratch. We believe that anyone can become a leader on the team if they have the interest and can dedicate the time,” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark. The Highlanders provide training in programming, CAD (computer aided design), and general mechanical work. Outside of more traditional robotics work, Highlander Robotics also seeks members with other diverse interests including community outreach, visual and industrial design, marketing, branding, video production and other roles needed to display a well-functioning robotics team. To learn more, come meet the team this week, August 11, in the Mary G. Ross Engineering Lab in the STEAM Building. For more information, visit frc8033.com, or contact frc8033@piedmontmakers.org. Piedmont’s Highlander Robotics team at the World Championships in Houston, Texas. Kids bouncing off the walls at home? Take them somewhere where they can literally climb the walls. Check out the 100 year establishment that celebrates the variety of all life forms. PRAISE gets a new name PRAISE (Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy and Information in Special Education) announced this week that it has changed its name to PIE (Piedmonters for Inclusive Education). Why change our name? We believe that Piedmonters for Inclusive Education (PIE) best reflects who we are at this time in our organizational history,” said board president Iris Warchall. We are parents who support inclusion in PUSD for all students with disabilities and learning differences. We believe that all learners have the right to full participation and inclusion in our classrooms and in our community, and that for us to do so as a community we must work to meet the needs of students with all neurotypes, abilities, and learning styles. articles.text: The oldest rowing club in the East Bay is launching a new rowing program for competitive high schoolers. Lake Merritt Rowing Club, founded in 1962, is starting a team that will be capped in size and will focus on individualized coaching for aspiring high school rowers. Lake Merritt’s competitive program is geared to accommodate young athletes who want to compete at a high level without sacrificing on family, academic and other obligations. Lake Merritt Rowing Club has its boathouse in the Lake Chalet building directly on Lake Merritt. Although the club has trained recreational youth rowers for decades, this is its initial foray into youth competitive teams. Rick Gallagher, a Piedmont resident and President of the Club, explained the motivation behind the new program. “We have amazing coaches and a boathouse in one of the best spots in the Bay Area. We have all the ingredients for a top high school program. We felt that the community needed a program for kids who want to row fast, but who also need a more flexible approach given family and academic pressures.” The head coach for Lake Merritt’s competitive youth team will be Heather Krakora, a former Division I rower for the University of Minnesota who is still a top rower in the adult competitive ranks. “My own rowing journey began on a small, tight-knit squad. I was forever shaped by my rowing team that was like family – together we pushed one another to be our best while building strong bonds,” said Krakora. “That unforgettable experience sparked a lifelong love of rowing that I can’t wait to instill in Lake Merritt’s Competitive Youth team.” In addition to offering a small team environment, Lake Merritt’s program will offer more scheduling flexibility for high school rowers who also need to focus on academics, family and other sports. The key to flexibility is its Heather Krakora recently was named head coach of Lake Merritt Rowing Club’s new youth competitive crew. small team and a focus on smaller boats. “We’re focused on creating an environment where driven young athletes can thrive on their own terms,” said Krakora. “By keeping the team small and flexible, we empower each rower to balance the sport with the other important parts of their lives.” Lake Merritt is limiting its team to only 16 participants. This is a departure from the traditional approach, in which young athletes are separated into larger boats and ranked. “On a small team, each athlete’s individual progress helps motivate the entire crew.” Krakora added, “There’s a special sense of trust and friendship that develops when a group is focused, driven, and working toward the same goals.” Lake Merritt’s boathouse is located directly under the Lake Chalet restaurant. It docks in the historic 100-year-old pump house renovated by the City of Oakland in 2004. Gallagher noted that Lake Merritt’s rowers get the benefit of some of the safest and flattest water in the Bay Area. “Rowing out in the Bay can be rough with all the wind and boats moving around. We’re lucky that the only obstacle in the Lake comes from ducks from the bird preserve.” Lake Merritt’s team, once filled, will start practices in September and will compete in regattas this Fall and Spring. Practices will run Mondays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from 4:15 pm to 6:30 pm and on Saturdays from 9:30am to noon. One practice per week will be on land and focused on strength and fitness. Athletes will be permitted to choose whether to participate in weekend regattas based on their individual academic and other commitments and their desire to compete in events. Registration is now open on Lake Merritt Rowing Club’s website and will remain open until 16 team member slots are filled. Interested families may contact the Club’s President (Rick Gallagher) or Youth Competitive Coach (Heather Krakora) by emailing President@LakeMerrittRowingClub.org or CoachHeather@LakeMerrittRowingClub.org.

articles.text: The fall of 2023 marks a first for many high schools in California to introduce girls’ flag football to go from being a club sport to official status. Entering its inaugural season as an official Piedmont High sport is the Highlanders’ girls’ flag football team, currently training at Humphries Diamond’s ahead of Week 1 in September. “I see a lot of girls who are hungry to play football and are so excited to be out here. We are making sure it’s real football. They have more skills than we expected, we’ve been impressed from Day 1. I like their hustle, their mindset, and they’re smart. We have intelligent girls, I think that will make a big difference for us,” said head coach Beth Black, who in her spare time moonlights as the head of the school’s English Department. Piedmont will be a part of an 8-team league competing in the Western Alameda County Conference with Alameda, Berkeley, Encinal, Hayward, San Leandro, and Tennyson. The season opens with a League Jamboree featuring all eight schools on Saturday, September 9 at Mt. Eden (Hayward) , followed by Piedmont playing a seven-game schedule before the WACC’s Championship Tournament on October 28 at Hayward High. No Section playoffs are being offered in its first year of competition. For PHS student athletes takStaff Photos Friedie Schickedanz throws a pass in Piedmont’s girls’ flag football practice ahead of its inaugural season. ing part in the team, it marks an exciting time as the players help build a program from its ground-level. They’ll represent the trend-setters for a completely new sport, being a major part of creating traditions like the other established sports at the school. “This is the first year, where no one has really played as a team, so we’re all learning together. We’re sort of like the guinea pigs, we’re setting the trend,” said Dahlia Osman. Day 1 of its season started this week on Monday, August 7. With Witter Field unusable to a major renovation project, the team is practicing on Humphries Diamond, the baseball field. Students Head coach Beth Black directs defensive drills at a practice. Mia Leggett gets ready to receive a long pass during offensive drills. took part in flag-pulling drills, running routes, and worked on their defensive and offensive formations. Piedmont is still in the phase of determining who plays what positions and hammering home the fundamentals of the game. “I really don’t know a lot about football, but I came in excited. I play soccer, but I wanted to try something new. I’ve always just watched football, like on TV or at the high school games, so it’s really interesting to learn the positions and nuances of the game,” said Elspeth Grippando. It’s difficult to say who is emerging as leaders, but making their presence felt were multisport athletes such as Friedie Schickedanz (water polo and lacrosse), Ella Yasar (track), Juliana Thornborrow (soccer), and Mia Leggett from the softball team. Leggett has been a member of the softball team and was on the varsity basketball team in 2022. At Monday’s practice, Leggett was proving herself as a playmaker with sure-hands, agility, and an understanding of route-running, making a clean over-the-shoulder catch on a fade route. She credits her knowledge of football to her time throwing the ball around the yard with her father and being in a family of devout Raiders fans. Leggett, a senior at PHS, now has an opportunity to play the game she loves in an organized league. “Football has always been a part of my life. I played softball and basketball, some of the same mechanics apply here, like with route-running, so it’s kind of been easier to adjust in practice. My family has been Raiders fans through thick and thin, they still are. I grew up with the game, just throwing the football with my dad. Sports have always been a big part of my life,” said Leggett. Piedmont’s current schedule isn’t yet official. A s it stands, following the season-opening jamboree on September 9, Piedmont will play games at Alameda on September 15, Mt. Eden on September 22, Encinal on September 28, and host its first flag football game on October 5 versus Berkeley.
articles.title: PHS girls’ flag football off and running

articles.text: Staff Photos Finn Burke received honorable mention All-League honors last season. With the new school year underway, the Class of 2024 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. FINN BURKE Water Polo Finn Burke returns to the water polo team after helping lead it to a Western Alameda County Conference title last fall. He earned honorable mention for All-League honors after Piedmont’s 20-7 season. Burke scored once in Piedmont’s 13-4 WACC Finals win over Alameda, two goals in the semifinals 11-6 win over Lick Wilmerding, and two scores in their 20-3 first-round win over San Leandro. He also scored twice in Piedmont’s 15-12 win over No. 6 Novato in the North Coast Section quarterfinals. AMY DERR Soccer Amy Derr is a defender on Piedmont’s North Coast Section winning soccer team. departing at graduation, Derr will be a key leader of the returning cast alongside striker Miranda Liu, midfielders Arden SorensenWald, and Lola Biehn, and defenders Charlotte Davies and Elle Ruegg. Amy Derr is a defender on Piedmont’s Division 4 North Coast Section championship team. The strength of Piedmont’s back line shined throughout last winter, helping the team go 13-1-6 (W-T-L) including 10 shutout victories. During Piedmont’s run to an NCS title, the Highlanders limited their opponents to two goals in four matches and compiling an 11-2 goal differential. Despite being a defender, Derr still made her presence felt on offense. She scored in a 5-0 win over Castro Valley and scored a goal on a 35-yard free kick in a 1-1 tie against Alameda. With 10 members of the team SEVE SANCHEZ Baseball Seve Sanchez was a key player in Piedmont’s 14-11 season, helping them battle to the NCS Semifinals, where they narrowly lost 11-10 to No. 5 Justin-Siena. Sanchez was Piedmont’s winning pitcher in their 5-2 upset of No. 1 Fortuna in the NCS Quarterfinals, throwing two innings and two strikeouts. In 2023, Sanchez had 15 appearances and four starts, totaling a team-leading 32.1 innings pitched with a 4-2 overall record. He recorded 20 strikeouts and carried a 4.33 ERA. Seve Sanchez led Piedmont in innings pitched last season.

articles.text: After waking up early Sunday morning, I kept rubbing my eyes to grasp the reality of seeing the U.S. Women’s Soccer Team, the two-time World Cup champion, losing in the Round of 16 to Sweden 5-4 in penalty kicks after ending regulation and overtime in a 0-0 deadlock. USWNT supporters likely experienced all the stages of grief: denial, anger, depression, and a harsh dose of reality. Much like their earlier three matches in the Group stage, the United States just couldn’t find the finishing touch despite having its chances. They outshot the Swedes 22 to nine, including 11 shots on target to Sweden’s one. Sweden’s goalkeeper Zecira Musovic was amazing, standing on her head to make 11 saves with five by dives, stopping nine shots from inside the box. Each stop by Musovic seemed to take the life out of the United States, which were uncharacteristically inconsistent on open situations. The nerves perhaps carried into penalty kicks. The U.S. was up 3-2 after Nathalie Björn skied a shot for Sweden. However, what followed was unimaginable. Megan Rapinoe, Sophie Smith, and Kelley O’Hara, three of the team’s best goal scorers all went wide-right, allowing Sweden to march back to a 4-4 deadlock and just needing to convert the winner. It couldn’t have been more dramatic with Lina Hurtig’s shot initially stopped by U.S. goalkeeper Alyssa Naeher, only for it to loop in the air and cross the goal line for the winning goal. It was a result many soccer fans felt was coming after the United States finished second in the 3-team Group E. Photo courtesy of NBC Sports The United States took its earliest exit from the World Cup in team history after falling 5-4 to Sweden in penalty kicks. Japan will face Sweden in the Quarterfinals and are the favorites despite having a lower world ranking. England is the current favorite to win the entire World Cup. They were the recent UEFA 2022 European Champion but are without their lead player. Photo courtesy of AP News Sweden celebrates after defeating the United States in penalty kicks. Hinata Miyazawa of Japan is the Golden Boot leader with five goals, while Mina Tanaka has been instrumental with three assists and two goals. It’s hard to pick against Japan, so I’m going with a 2-1 win for the Japanese. No. 4 England vs. No. 25 Colombia England is currently favored to win the entire World Cup which is somewhat surprising after going to penalty kicks against Nigeria, winning 4-2 after ending overtime in a 0-0 tie. Key player, Lauren James, was red carded and will miss the quarterfinals against Colombia. But England gets their favored status after winning the 2022 European Women’s Championship, so their praise despite losing James and barely getting by Nigeria is well-deserved. They should still get the job done against lowly ranked Colombia. I’m not going with an upset, 2-0 Three Lions of England. No. 5 France vs. No. 10 Australia The French are coming in on a strong run of form after defeating No. 72 Morocco and winning a difficult Group F over Jamaica and Brazil, but Australia, the host country will have a large rooting section. . France boasts Kadidiatou Diani, who has four goals and three assists thus far. I’m going France 3-1. No. 6 Spain vs. No. 9 Netherlands Spain is another favorite to win it all by beating the Netherlands. The Spaniards demolished Switzerland in the Round of 16, while the Dutch had a strong 2-0 win over South Africa. The Netherlands won Group E over the United States and are led by Jill Roord, who has four goals thus far.

TAYLOR ROLEFSON Swimming Piedmont High Class of 2024 Taylor Rolefson was an AllLeague swimmer on Piedmont’s league championship swimming relay team. PHS’ 200 medley relay and 400 freestyle relay teams finished its regular season undefeated and won the WACC title in both events. Their 200 medley team featured Josie Oesterer on backstroke, Abigail Jacoby on breaststroke, Rolefson on butterfly, and sophomore Sonja ten Grotenhuis as the anchor leg for the relay team. They won the league title with a time of 1:54.74. The 400 free relay team included freshman Sydney Olson in place of Jacoby, and ten Grotenhuis swimming the second leg. They won a second league title in 3:44.42. Rolefson qualified for the North Coast Section Finals in the 200 meter freestyle. She finished 16th in the Finals with a time of 1:59.67. To get there, Taylor finished the preliminary round in 1:58.03 to finish 13th of 39 swimmers. In the Far Westerns Championship on July 27-30, Rolefson was 16th of 36 in the 50 freestyle, clocking a time of 28.54. She was also 35th of 48 in the 100 freestyle in 1:03.56, while she was 17th of 27 in the 100 butterfly in 1:09.51. She also competed in the 200 freestyle, finishing in 2:19.19. What is your workout program this summer? This summer I’ve had to stick around to attend my eight practices a week. This consists of two doubles on Tuesday and Thursday where I’ve had to attend 6 a.m. practice and afternoon practices. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My main goal was to achieve a Sectionals time so that I could attend the winter sectionals meet in Huntington Beach in December. How are you measuring your development? Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I rely on my coach for sets crafted around my needs and areas for improvement and I rely on my teammates to push me in the pool and in the gym. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? At my last meet at long course Far Westerns, I reached my goal of getting a Sectionals time in my 50 freestyle. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? If you have a goal you want to achieve make sure you keep your head straight and stay focused. It is a part of being an athlete to not always do your absolute best every meet but through hard work and surrounding yourself with the right people you can achieve anything. TOM ROLEFSON Swimming Swimmer Taylor Rolefson was a member of Piedmont’s undefeated 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams. She also qualified for NCS Finals in the 200 freestyle. Piedmont High Class of 2024 Tom Rolefson, the twin brother of his swimming sister Taylor, is entering his senior year at Piedmont High and recently competed in the Far Westerns Championship from July 27-30 with Hills Hurricane Swimming. Rolefson finished third of 31 in the WACC’s 50 freestyle finals with a time of 21.89. He was also fourth of 34 in the 100 free with a time of 49.21. He helped lead the 200 medley relay team to a third place finish out of eight teams with a time of 1:44.69. The 200 freestyle relay team was fourth of eight in 1:31.97. He qualified for NCS individually in the 50 free, where he was 34th of 40 in 22.26—a tight field where a one second improvement would’ve gotten a top-6 time. At Far Westerns, Rolefson finished the 50 freestyle preliminary round in 13th of 61, clocking a time of 25.24. He also raced the 100 freestyle, finishing 39th of 62 with a time of 57.50. In the 200 freestyle, he was 36th of 53 in 2:09.12. He placed 24th of 34 in the 100 breast in 1:14.74. In the 200 freestyle relay, his team was 19th of 26 in 1:43.08. His 400 freestyle relay team was 16th of 19 in 3:55.49 in the Boys 15-18 category. He was the third leg of the mixed 18 and under 400 freestyle relay team that placed second of six in 3:55.49. What is your workout program this summer? Our workout program was to go to seven practices a week approximately two hours each, and we would do 3,000-5,000 yards a practice. We would also lift three days a week, splitting it up into three separate days of chest back, legs, and arms. We did a lot of sets that were high intensity, getting our heart rates way up, and going fast on right intervals. We did this to prepare for Sectionals and Far Westerns at the end of the summer. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Goals were to try and beat our best times for our races, and to try and put on some more weight in the gym as weight is needed to be able to get faster at sprinting. How are you measuring your development? We measure our development in our times in the pool at faster qualification meets, like Far Westerns. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Taylor and I are on the Hills Tom Rolefson is a member of Piedmont High’s varsity boys’ swim team, competing in the freestyle and breaststroke. Hurricane Swim Team, where we are on a team with 20 other people in our “Senior 2” training group under our coach Shad Wojtala. We do all the training together; being with other people on a swim team, pushes you to train harder, and go faster in practice. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A milestone we each accomplished was achieving a Sectionals cut in our 50 Frees. We will be attending the CA/NV Winter Sectionals meet December 14-17. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Value your teammates. Your teammates are the ones who you practice with every day and who push you harder. The best way to improve is constantly trying to beat our teammates in practice. Teammates push you to be better and want you to be best you possibly can be, so value those relationships—they can last lifelong. SONJA ten GROTENHUIS Swimming Piedmont High Class of 2025 Sonja ten Grotenhuis was the Piedmont Post’s Sophomore of the Year, and its Freshman of the Year in 2022. She was a key member of both the 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams that went undefeated against WACC teams on their way to league championships in both events. She was an All-League selection alongside her other relay teammates. Sonja ten Grotenhuis was the Post’s 2023 Sophomore of the Year after helping the 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay teams going undefeated against league competition.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre in San Francisco premieres Hippest Trip – The Soul Train Musical on August 25. Soul Train is based on the iconic TV show that originally aired on Chicago airwaves in the 1970’s. For over 30 years, it brought Black music, dance, and style into living rooms in America and was a celebration of black youth culture. The show’s self-proclaimed reputation was “the hippest trip in America,” hence the musical’s title. The creative team behind ACT’s reimagined Soul Train includes Tony Award–nominated playwright Dominique Morisseau known for The Detroit Project, Tony Award–nominated choreographer Camille A. Brown, and Apollo Theater’s executive director Kamilah Forbes. Playwright Morisseau said she is looking forward to partnering with an all-female creative team to celebrate “the history and unsung heroes of our nation’s longest running televised music and dance series.” ACT’s Hippest Trip - The Soul Train Musical “I am so excited to help bring the narrative of one of our culture’s most influential and legend-making endeavors to the stage. Having grown up on this series and being immersed in the culture around it, I never knew what it took to make it the iconic staple that it is,” she said. The cast includes Angela Birchett as Delores, Quentin Earl Darrington as Don Cornelius, Amber Iman as Pam Brown, and Kayla Davion as Jody Watley. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/2023-24-season/soul-train/. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is now exhibiting Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966–1975, the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in 40 years. The exhibit will be on view through September 10. Sir Richard Sheridan Patrick Michael Aloysius Franklin Bowling, known as Frank Bowling, was born in British Guiana, now Guyana, and moved from London to New York. He is best known for his large-scale, abstract and colorful paintings, color field painting and lyrical abstraction; sometimes referred to as ‘abstract expressionism.’ SF MOMA’s exhibition features 45 vibrant and largescale paintings, and a selection of archival materials such as recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. “The exhibition offers an oppor tunity to experience Bowling as a scholar and teacher committed to elevating the voices of Black artists and expanding the understanding of art history as it unfolded,” said Christopher Bedford, Art Director at SF MOMA. “This very much aligns with our institutional vision to share significant, if perhaps lesser-known, facets of artists’ careers and to explore artistic achievement through a spectrum of lenses and perspectives.” For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit www.sfmoma.org.
articles.title: Frank Bowling exhibit at SF MOMA through September 10

articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco continue to offer an exhibit titled The Tudors: Art and Majesty in Renaissance England. The exhibit will be on view through the end of September. It is the first major exhibition in the United States of portraiture and decorative arts of the Tudor courts. It includes works from the museum’s collection, including a late 16th century panel painting, as well as tapestries commissioned or acquired by Henry VII and Henry VIII. “The Tudors reunites scores of sumptuous paintings, precious jewels, rich tapestries and rare artifacts from collections around the world to bring the Tudor dynasty vividly to life–from the bloody founding of the dynasty in 1485 by Henry VII on the fields of Bosworth, to the final moments of Queen Elizabeth in 1603,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. The Tudors exhibit will be on view through September 24. For more information and tickets, visit https://www.famsf.org. That revelation occurred recently. The Saint Paul Suite by Holst phony, conducted by Richard The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Studt. Who are these folks? The names were completely new. A little research was required. Orchestra conducting is a very misunderstood art. When the concert is good, the conductor takes all the credit. When the concert is bad, the conducFront and center tor blames the musicians. When concerts began to be televised, conductors mugged for the camera. That was the beginning of the end for really good orchestra conducting. The basics are really quite simple. The conductor needs to marshal the musicians and inspire them to a unified interpretation of the music. Then, using a good stick technique, the conductor controls the line of scrimmage. All instructions, whether verbal or visual, must be communicated clearly and simply. Those are the basics. Visual histrionics are not needed. With these things in mind, it was a pleasure to discover a true exemplar of great conducting in Richard Studt. He is not only an all-inspiring conductor, he is also an outstanding violinist. I urged him to write a book on conducting. He responded enthusiastically, and then added that his book would probably be more entertaining than erudite. Perhaps that is as it should be. articles.text: Sept. 8 benefit at Center for the Arts for Family Sanity’s 10th Anniversary Can talking about mental health be funny? They say laughter is good medicine. Come find out September 8. What started as an idea in a Piedmont living room a decade ago is celebrating with a very special Family Sanity event at Piedmont Center for the Arts, Friday, September 8, beginning at 7 p.m. Comedian/TV Reporter/Podcaster/Talk Radio Host Brian Copeland will present his one-man show, The Waiting Period. Tickets are available now at www.familysanity.org. Brian is a Bay Area native. Like Robin Williams and other funny men and women, he has suffered from depression throughout most of his adult life. In the early 2000’s he felt so down that he considered buying a gun and ending his life. The Man and Grandma and Me that have been performed throughout the Bay Area. The evening in Piedmont will begin with original jazz piano compositions played by California Jazz Conservatory graduate Michael Echaniz. Family Sanity was founded by Lisa Scimens, a former longtime Piedmont resident. The nonprofit organization helps parents of older teens and young adults coping with mental illness. Over the years, the group has helped hundreds of families in the Bay Area and beyond. Monthly online support groups and a robust website of resources are available. To find out more or to sign up for a support group, visit www.familysanity.org. This play is not appropriate for children or younger teens. Parental discretion is advised. East Bay comedian and playwright Brian Copeland brings a one-man show to the Piedmont Center for the Arts on September 8. play shows how he persevered and lifted himself out of his dire state. Copeland is the genius behind several other one-man shows, including Not a Genuine Black Resources in mental health for parents of older teens and young adults.

articles.text: To call Quentin Tarantino’s film, Inglourious Basterds, a solid B-movie may seem a bit cranky. After all, it does have its A-movie moments. The opening of the film demonstrates Tarantino’s unassailable talent as a writer-director. It’s a set piece in which a German SS Colonel., Hans Landa (Christop Waltz), arrives at a French dairy farm to interview the farmer. The year is 1941 and the words, “Once upon a time in Nazi-occupied France…” flash on the screen. Landa, known as Hitler’s Jew Hunter, arrives at the farm because he suspects the farmer is hiding a Jewish family. The scene, wonderfully framed inside the farmhouse, is filled with menace, even more chilling because of Landa’s exaggerated civility and calm. In that moment, the Col. is a distillation of the evil perpetrated by the Nazis as they set about finding and then exterminating a people. As Landa slowly drinks a cold glass of milk, while discoursing on Jews as rats, the camera pans to the cracks in the floorboards. It’s quickly apparent that a family is lying just below, listening and watching, hands held over their mouths, as the moment unfolds. They are clearly terrified. This scene and its outcome could easily be a remarkable, stand alone short possessing an intense arc and a perfect, if unexpected, denouement. But because the film is divided into chapters, a new scene quickly begins which introduces the inglourious Basterds, a small group of American Jewish G.I.s, led by Lt. Aldo Raines (Brad Pitt), a Tennessee good old boy who wants not only to kill Nazis but take their scalps as well. Pitt’s over the top portrayal approaches caricature and the film flirts with farce. It’s a surprising decision by Tarantino, for this group of behind the lines commandos (OSS) should be quietly lethal and profoundly serious about what’s a stake, not simply a congregation of idiosyncratic psychopaths unleashed on the Third Reich. It soon becomes evident that the hunt for Jews by Col. Landa will not be the contextual backdrop of the film, but merely an isolated vignette. And so the film abruptly jumps to 1944, the story now focused on Shoshana Dreyfus (Melanie Laurent), owner of a small Paris cinema (inherited from her aunt and uncle), and pursued romantically by a German war hero, Frederick Zoller (Daniel Bruhl). The film then cuts to the second nicely constructed scene that takes place in a Parisian bistro, involving British and American soldiers dressed in Nazi uniforms, their mission being to contact German movie star Bridget von Hammersmark (Diane Kruger), a British undercover agent. Like the opening, this set piece is fraught with tension, is wonderfully shot, and even with its concluding Mexican standoff represents Tarantino at his best. But where the film falls away is in its inability to tell a fully coherent story with compelling characters that connect with each other and with the audience. Ultimately, despite the vignettes, or because of the disparate vignettes, there is no there there; the film has no sustaining center. Tarantino can almost blithely skirt the horror of the extermination of the Jews, perpetrated by monsters like Landa, and turn Landa, decked out in his tailored SS uniform and gleaming black riding boots, into the most attractive and authentic hustler in the film. This is not a film about distilled evil but about scenarios leading to a blazing climax where revisionist history takes place inside a burning cinema in Paris. If Schindler’s List is the yin, then Inglourious Basterds is the yang. Regarding the unusual spelling of the film’s title – Inglourious Basterds – apparently it’s an obscure reference to an Italian knock-off film of The Dirty Dozen, reflecting nothing more than Tarantino’s quirky style and no more. Inglourious Basterds. Starring Christop Waltz, Brad Pitt, Diane Kruger, and Melanie Laurent. Directed by Quentin Tarantino. 2 hrs., 32 min. Rated R. Released in 2009. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Quentin Taratino’s Inglourious Basterds

articles.text: It’s possible that Gran Torino will be Clint Eastwood’s last film as an actor, so it seems appropriate that his role in this film seems a solid reprisal of his earlier, now iconic characters. Over the last 30 years Eastwood has cut a wide swath through Hollywood and our popular culture. Beginning with spaghetti westerns made in Italy, such as A Fistful of Dollars and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, he went on to create Dirty Harry, the rogue, jaw-clenching cop who grimaces, squints and asks the bank robber, “You feel lucky? Well, punk, doya?” And of course there were those five words that made their way into our language, “Go ahead, make my day.” In fact, watching Eastwood in Gran Torino portraying Walt Kowalski, a retired auto worker who has just lost his wife, his face deeply lined, his grizzled hair thinning, the rude, gruff mannerisms so familiar, well, it is clear that Eastwood has always played a variation of himself. Kowalski is Dirty Harry. But he’s also the Carmel DJ in Play Misty for Me, and Clint Eastwood stars in Gran Torino Rowdy Yates in the television series Wagon Train, the righteous western homesteader in Unforgiven, or the WWII G.I.in Kelly’s Heroes. Fearless as an actor, Eastwood has never been averse to stepping away from the hard-shelled persona he perfected with Harry and starring in Paint Your Wagon, Anyway But Loose (recall one of the supporting actors was an orangutan), and The Bridges of Madison County. What has surprised his audience the most, perhaps, is the fine work Eastwood has produced as a director, making such remarkable films as Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, The Changeling, and the two-film saga about Iwo Jima from the American and Japanese points of view. In Gran Torino, Eastwood inhabits the character of Kowalski and then some. The man is bigoted, ever growling, narrow of mind, without patience or tolerance; yet, he is also decent,
