articles.text: Whether it’s men in tights or Gladiator haute couture, the legend of Robin Hood is mythic, the stuff of high adventure. Hollywood has been enamored of this character for decades, always eager to give the tale a new twist, or give the actor du jour an opportunity to don costume and take up residence in Sherwood Forest. One incarnation of Robin Hood searches for originality with Ridley Scott (Alien, Blade Runner, Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, and Kingdom of Heaven) directing and Brian Hegeland (L.A. Confidential) writing the script. Scott and Hegeland, deciding to add to the legend, set about answering the central backstory question: who was Robin before he was, well, Robin, prior to the time when he and he and his band of outlaws were ensconced in Sherwood Forest from whence they stole from the rich and gave to the poor (called wealth distribution today). Because Hollywood practices revisionist history with conviction and insouciance, the year, instead of 1185, is 1199. But who’s counting? Robin (Russell Crowe), we are told, is Robin Longstride, a commoner and master archer with the army of King Richard the Lionheart, who, after a decade-long crusade in the Holy Land, is on his way back to England. Crossing France, he lays siege to a well-defended castle. It is during that battle that the film opens and where we meet Longstride and what will eventually be his crew of Merry Men – Little John (Kevin Durand), Will Scarlett (Scott Grimes) and Allan A’Dayle (Alan Doyle). Longstride and his crew conclude, after King Richard is killed when a French castle cook drops a pot of stew and takes random aim with a crossbow, that they have served the crown long enough and decide to make their own way back to England. It is Russell Crowe stars in Ridley Scott’s Robin Hood on that trip that Robin’s future is changed forever. It’s tempting to recount what proves to be a convoluted tale. Suffice it to say that he lands in London under an alias, Robert of Loxley, and makes his way to Nottingham where he returns a sword to Sir Walter Loxley (Max von Sydow), father of Robert. He also meets Robert’s widow, Marion (Cate Blanchette). Chemistry is afoot. Thus far, the story of how Robin Longstride becomes Robert of Loxley/Robin of Loxley is appealing; however, it lacks a sharp edge. There is, eventually, palace intrigue, perpetrated by the newly crowned John, Richard’s brother. And there is the duplicitous Sir Godfrey (Mark Strong), newly anointed chancellor and tax collector, who prepares, surreptitiously, to betray England to France for power and fortune. Nevertheless, even with the signature battle scenes, for which director Scott is famous, the film is missing something at its center. Crowe, always a bit distant and laconic, now all but middle-aged and beefy, never conveys jeopardy or urgency as he did in Master and Commander and L.A. Confidential. Even with the epic battle on the English shore, fending off a French army prepared to invade England once again, there is an absence of the tension that Scott is so brilliant at creating, examples being Gladiator and Black Hawk Down. That isn’t to say that Robin Hood lacks a certain intensity. It is, after all, a Ridley Scott film, one brought to life by some of the finest actors working today. And keep in mind that as this story ends, King John declares Robin an outlaw prompting Robin to retreat to Sherwood Forest where he will take up his bow and his sword against King John and cohorts. Robin Hood. Directed by Ridley Scott. Starring Russell Crowe, Cate Blanchette, Mark Strong, Oscar Isaac. and Max von Sydow. 2 hrs., 19 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2010. Streaming on VUDU/Prime.
articles.title: Robin Hood – What we always wanted to know

articles.text: Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E, Up will delight and entertain audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail. Written and directed by Piedmont resident Pete Docter, it won an Academy Award, among many awards. It is breathtaking, and the story is a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, square-faced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed: years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. All that is absent from this touching retrospective is that one, magnificent adventure. Sadly, having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties some 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning floats away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, wellequipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of lift-off. And so the journey begins with the unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. You can’t make this stuff up. Well, actually, in the case of Pixar, you can, and that is exactly what these filmmakers do with unbridled imaginations and an inexhaustible well of stories that captivate and entertain. In Up they even manage to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell, Carl’s being that poignant aphorism about how life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). UP. Directed by Pete Docter. Animated with the voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated PG. Released in 2009. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+/Apple tv. A scene from Pixar Animations’ UP.
articles.title: UP – Pixar’s all-time winner

articles.text: Over the past 20 years of writing about wine I have had the opportunity to visit some amazing wine regions around the world – Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, much of Europe. The one region I had yet to visit was the one closest to California – Oregon. Since I have had many outstanding wines from Oregon, I knew I had to correct this oversight. I planned a trip with my buddies Mike Osborn, an Oregon native son, veteran of the Oregon wine industry, and Founder of Wine.com. and Kent Rasmussen a veteran California winemaker and winery owner who specializes in Pinot Noir. In June we made a trip focusing on the Willamette Valley to visit some of the most iconic producers. While some wine was produced in Oregon before prohibition, the real beginning for the Oregon wine industry was the 1960’s when California winemakers opened several wineries in the Willamette Valley. By 1970 there were five commercial wineries with 35 acres. Most of the activity included planting Pinot Noir grapes in the Willamette Valley, a region long thought to be too cold to be suitable for viticulture. In the 1970’s more non-Oregon winemakers migrated to the state and started to organize as an industry. In 1979 The Eyrie Vineyards entered a 1975 Pinot Noir in the Wine Olympics; the wine was The magnificent WillaKenzie Estate is one of the leading lights of the Willamette Valley. Jill A. Martenson, DDS
articles.title: The Best of Willamette Valley – Part One

In 1979 The Eyrie Vineyards entered a 1975 Pinot Noir in the Wine Olympics; the wine was Domaine Willamette has a state-of-the-art tasting room and restaurant. rated among the top Pinots in the world, thus gaining the region its first international recognition. First of all, Willamette Valley is huge. Its 150-mile length runs from just south of Portland all the way to Eugene. Today it is synonymous with “Oregon Wine Country” and contains more than 19,000 acres of vineyards and over 500 wineries. Several things struck me as I toured the region for the first time. First was its overall beauty. Compared to California everything was so green. The rolling hills were lush with evergreen and deciduous trees and the vineyards were perfectly manicured. Second, there was a relaxed vibe that reminded me I was far from Napa Valley where wine tasting now seems to be a contact sport. We never encountered a winery that was overcrowded with tourists and the roads were free of traffic. Third. my friend Kent who has spent his life in the wine business, remarked on the professionalism and extreme hospitality of every wine industry worker we met. At every stop the staff was well trained and anxious for you to have the best possible tasting experience and the owners and winemakers were generous with their time. The magnificent WillaKenzie Estate is one of the leading lights of the Willamette Valley. The Syrah was deep, rich, full-bodied, and voluptuous, reminding me of the Syrahs from Rhone Valley’s Hermitage region. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, August 9, 2023 AMERICANS IN PARIS By P K Forsyth The most visited necropolis in the world is Père Lachaise cemetery. This is a bucolic place, perched under several thousand trees, where the air is cooler than the tangent city streets of the 20th arrondissement toward the east. The cemetery slopes gently on a hillside, while some terrain is rocky, and sidewalks wander off into pathways. Resting stones give way over time and into a slapdash array, especially, it seems, when one is in search of a famous gravesite. There are hundreds of famous gravesites, and so, expect a hike – and a search. Père Lachaise is The gravesite monument of Héloise and Abélard as they lie together in eternity. Whether their remains exist at this site, is disputed. Héloise and Abélard, as they may have appeared when they fell in love during the 12th C. in Paris. A visit to Pere LaChaise Cimetaire one of 20 cemeteries in Paris, and the largest and best known. Composer Fréderic Chopin, writers Honoré de Balzac, Marcel Proust, Oscar Wilde, and Gertrude Stein, banker James Rothschild, jeweler René Lalique; singer Edith Piaf, rock star Jim Morrison, painters Amadeo Modigliani, Camille Pissarro, Eugène Delacroix; actresses Simone Signoret and Sarah Bernhardt, and mime Marcel Marceau are buried here. The burial business grew. The 12th Century Héloise and Abélard were among the most famous star-crossed lovers in French history. For nearly nine hundred years, the legendary romance has been studied through their eight surviving love letters. Héloise was the daughter born of an illicit affair between her mother, likely a nun, and her lover. She grew to be a beautiful, gifted young woman under the tutelage of her uncle Fulbert, a high placed church canon (i.e., board of directors). Her uncle raised Héloise, and he educated her well in the classics, languages, and the arts. She was already known academically for her insightful writings from the feminine viewpoint when she arrived in Paris and met Pierre Abélard who would become her tutor. Abélard was born into minor nobility and from a young age showed genius at scholarly learning. He eschewed the traditional military career and knighthood of his father and chose philosophy and the life of a theologian The beloved chanteuse Edith Piaf is in the same burial plot as her only child who tragically died at age two. Fresh mementos are placed on her grave. The crematorium was built in 1890s after French law authorized cremations, but it remained uncommon until the Catholic church overturned the cremation ban in 1963. Today, cremation represents 45% of burials in Paris. A French soldier’s gravestone: Memory of Regret, “our 17-year-old assassinated by the Nazis.” at the cathedral school of Notre Dame of Paris. His rose in popularity, drawing thousands of students. His attraction to Héloise, he later wrote in a letter, caused his teaching career to go awry. Despite his dedication to theology and vow of celibacy, Abélard struck an arrangement with Fulbert to tutor Héloise in exchange for boarding at Fulbert’s house and pursued the affair. Abélard may have boasted of the affair and his conquest. Fulbert was angered and separated the pair, but they continued to meet secretly. When Héloise became pregnant, Abélard sent her to his family’s home in Brittany to be cared for, and she bore a son. Fulbert pressed them to marry, but Abélard resisted, concerned that his career path could be in jeopardy, unless the marriage was kept secret. She opposed the idea of a secret marriage or any marriage, but gave in, and they did marry. Abélard whisked her away to Argenteuil convent to keep her safe from her uncle’s anger. Fulbert, convinced that Abélard was casting Héloise aside, and enraged about the downfall of his own reputation, sent a band of men into Abélard’s room in the dead of night and castrated Abélard. Humiliated and shamed, Abélard fled Paris and teaching to join a monastery. Héloise eventually rose to abbess at the Oratory of the Paraclete, a Benedictine monastery founded by Peter Abélard. The lovers continue to be a popular topic of inquiry today. Although the reburial of their remains at Père Lachaise contributed to the extraordinary success of the cemetery, their remains’ precise location is in dispute. See Americans in Paris on page 25

Demand for a plot is brisk, and there’s a waiting list. Except for the fortunate few buying a plot in perpetuity, a plot is a lease arrangement with the standard 30 years. Within budget, one may choose a longer lease of 50 years; or a shorter lease, for ten. Availability of burial sites is slim, and the populous foothill is overly crowded with memorials. Only a person who lived or died in Paris is eligible to be buried here. If there’s a lapse in the plot’s lease, the site could be emptied; declared legally abandoned and sold to the next buyer. Abandoned bones are “boxed and tagged” and placed in the ossuary. Possibly a million human souls are buried underground; and the remains of up two million more are interred in urns and ossuary at Père Lachaise. articles.text: Another strong summer showing of 39 walkers and five K-9 best friends was on hand for the Walking on Wednesdays group last week, August 2. Each year the group tries to walk every safe walking street in Piedmont. When they visit streets that border Oakland, there is an opportunity to see some great Oakland streets, too. A Piedmont street very few people ever go to is Florada Avenue on the southern border of Piedmont. At the end of Florada, just beyond the Oakland/Piedmont city line, is an impressive cactus garden in the front yard of an Oakland home. The walkers went on Highland Avenue to Wildwood Avenue and then to Wildwood Gardens. They recalled that this was the entrance to Frank C. Havens’ “Wildwood” estate in the early 1900s. They appreciated the redwood tree just beyond the old pillars that once marked the entrance to Wildwood. The tree seems to have been fed for decades by underground water that has led to its huge size. In Wildwood Gardens the walkers noted a home built on stilts above the ravine below, another home with a long swing in its front yard, and a sizable tree house in the backyard of a home. When the group came to the end of Wildwood Gardens they passed by the seldom visited Wistaria Way, and emerged on Woodland Way. At its end the walkers were at a street that to the left is Lafayette Avenue and to the right is La Salle Avenue. There is no clear explanation why. It’s one of the street naming mysteries in Piedmont and Oakland. The group came to the little traveled Florada Avenue and went directly to Dick and Mary Carter’s home. Dick didn’t have refreshments ready for the walkers so they pressed on down the street to the Oakland boarder, where for yet another unknown reason the street becomes Portal Avenue. On Portal they came to a beautiful cactus garden in a front yard. Some walkers remembered talking with the homeowner on a past walk a few years before. The garden is now full, complete, and lovely. The walkers took a group photo in front of it. Farther down the street was a large, colorful, pink bougainvillea, however tree stumps along the hillside indicated some past tree falling issues. The walkers came to Ashmount Avenue which required an uphill climb. They were impressed by the lovely, large homes, many of which were built during the 1920s when Piedmont also experienced a building boom. Some walkers remembered that in the past the group had been able to visit and shop a farmer’s market that operated by a young entrepreneur out of the garage of his parents’ home on Ashmount. But he has moved and there was no produce for the walkers to take home. However, the walkers noticed a distinguished house designed by Bernard Maybeck, a UC Berkeley architecture professor and Julia Morgan’s teacher in the late nineteenth century. Maybeck also designed the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco. With all the walking, sightseeing, and talking, the morning was getting on and it was time to return by way of Mandana Avenue, which also changes its name to Crocker Avenue upon entering Piedmont from Oakland. The group took a direct route back to the Community Hall parking lot. It had been about a three mile walk with interesting homes, stories, and street name mysteries. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Thirty-nine walkers and five K-9 friends participated in last Wednesday’s walk. Walkers patrol the city’s Southern border By Dick Carter Another strong summer showing of 39 walkers and five K-9 best friends was on hand for the Walking on Wednesdays group last week, August 2. Each year the group tries to walk every safe walking street in Piedmont. When they visit streets that border Oakland, there is an opportunity to see some great Oakland streets, too. A Piedmont street very few people ever go to is Florada Avenue on the southern border of Piedmont. At the end of Florada, just beyond the Oakland/Piedmont city line, is an impressive cactus garden in the front yard of an Oakland home. The walkers went on Highland Avenue to Wildwood Avenue and then to Wildwood Gardens. They recalled that this was the entrance to Frank C. Havens’ “Wildwood” estate in the early 1900s. They appreciated the redwood tree just beyond the old pillars that once marked the entrance to Wildwood. The tree seems to have been fed for decades by underground water that has led to its huge size. In Wildwood Gardens the walkers noted a home built on stilts above the ravine below, another home with a long swing in its front yard, and a sizable tree house in the backyard of a home. When the group came to the end of Wildwood Gardens they passed by the seldom visited Wistaria Way, and emerged on Woodland Way. At its end the walkers were at a street that to the left is Lafayette Avenue and to the right is La Salle Avenue. There is no clear explanation why. It’s one of the street naming mysteries in Piedmont and Oakland. The group came to the little traveled Florada Avenue and went directly to Dick and Mary Carter’s home. Dick didn’t have refreshments ready for the walkers so they pressed on down the street to the Oakland boarder, where for yet another unknown reason the street becomes Portal Avenue. On Portal they came to a beautiful cactus garden in a front yard. Some walkers remembered talking with the homeowner on a past walk a few years before. The garden is now full, complete, and lovely. The walkers took a group photo in front of it. Farther down the street was a large, colorful, pink bougainvillea, however tree stumps along the hillside indicated some past tree falling issues. The walkers came to Ashmount Avenue which required an uphill climb. They were impressed by the lovely, large homes, many of which were built during the 1920s when Piedmont also experienced a building boom. Some walkers remembered that in the past the group had been able to visit and shop a farmer’s market that operated by a young entrepreneur out of the garage of his parents’ home on Ashmount. But he has moved and there was no produce for the walkers to take home. However, the walkers noticed a distinguished house designed by Bernard Maybeck, a UC Berkeley architecture professor and Julia Morgan’s teacher in the late nineteenth century. Maybeck also designed the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco. With all the walking, sightseeing, and talking, the morning was getting on and it was time to return by way of Mandana Avenue, which also changes its name to Crocker Avenue upon entering Piedmont from Oakland. The group took a direct route back to the Community Hall parking lot. It had been about a three mile walk with interesting homes, stories, and street name mysteries. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. But there’s one important action that’s sometimes overlooked by retirees: sharing their financial situation with their grown children. And this knowledge can benefit everyone in your family. You might be surprised by the concern your children have for your financial well-being. Consider these findings from a 2023 study by Age Wave and Edward Jones: • 66% of millennials (generally defined as ranging from 27 to 42) worry that their parents or in-laws may not have enough money to live comfortably in retirement. • 83% of millennials would rather know their parents are financially secure in their retirement, even if it means their parents pass on less money to them. If you have children in this age range or older, or who soon will be, how can you address their concerns and potentially improve your financial outlook? Communication is the key. By openly communicating with your family about your financial status, you can reduce anxieties and misperceptions. If you’re in good financial shape, your adult children may be reassured that you won’t be needing their assistance. And if you are feeling some financial pressures, you can inform your children of the steps you are taking to improve your situation. One such step may be to reduce your cost of living — the less you spend day to day, the better your ability to preserve your investment and retirement accounts. You may be able to reduce costs in many small ways, such as ending streaming services you no longer use, but you could make an even bigger impact by downsizing your living arrangements. In fact, 72% of today’s retirees have downsized or are willing to downsize to reduce their housing costs, according to the Age Wave/Edward Jones survey. Downsizing isn’t for everyone, but if it’s a possibility for you, it may be worth considering because the savings could be significant. You may also be able to reduce or consolidate your debts. Start by understanding how much and what kinds of debt you have. Then, consider ways to lower your payments, such as refinancing. For example, if you’re carrying a balance on multiple credit cards, you might be able to transfer the amounts you owe onto a single card with a more favorable interest rate. Here’s another move to consider: Adjust your investment mix to possibly provide you with more income in retirement. During your working years, you may have invested primarily for growth — after all, you could be retired for two or more decades, so you’ll need to draw on as many financial assets as possible. But once you’re retired, your investment focus may need to shift somewhat toward income-producing opportunities. Keep in mind, though, that you’ll still need some growth potential to help keep ahead of inflation. One final suggestion: Let your children know if you already have a strategy in place to meet the potentially high costs of longterm care, such as a nursing home stay. This burden is certainly something you won’t want your children to take on. By informing your children about your financial picture, and how you’re trying to improve it, you can ease everyone’s minds — so keep the lines of communication open. articles.text: Consideration of Amendments to Piedmont City Code and to Piedmont Design Guidelines To Implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards and Accessory Dwelling Unit Incentives Notice is hereby given that the Planning Commission of the City of Piedmont will conduct a public hearing at a regular meeting at 5:30 pm on Monday, August 14, 2023 in Council Chambers, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA, to consider the following actions: (1) a recommendation to City Council to adopt an ordinance amending the Piedmont City Code to add a Pre-approved Plans incentive for Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), implement Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS), add ministerial review procedures, and make other conforming changes; and (2) a recommendation to City Council to adopt proposed amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code include amendments to Division 17.38, Accessory Dwelling Units, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use, including new incentives for rent-restricted ADUs for applicants using new City-approved plans for ADUs. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code also include amendments to create a new Division 17.67, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use to establish procedures and standards for ministerial review of multifamily and mixed-use building types in Zone C and Zone D. Proposed amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines include: (1) new objective standards for architectural elements to be used by City staff to review development applications for multifamily and mixed-use building types; (2) pre-approved plans for accessory dwelling units (ADUs); and (3) other conforming changes. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are exempt under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The amendments to address pre-approved architectural plans for ADUs are statutorily exempt from CEQA pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21080.17 and CEQA Guidelines section 15282(h) which exempts adoption of ordinances to implement Government Code section 65852.2 regarding accessory dwelling units. These amendments are also exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303.The amendments related to Multifamily Objective Design Standards are exempt because it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the adoption of Multifamily Objective Design Standards may have a significant effect on the environment. (Public Resources Code section 21065; CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Sections 15061(b)(3), 15378.) Further, these amendments are exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are available for public review on the City’s webpage at https://piedmont.ca.gov as well as https://piedmontishome.org. They are also available at City Hall located at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. INTERESTED PERSONS MAY be heard at the public hearing, and written comments may be submitted prior to the public hearing(s). Written comments will be made a part of the public record. If you challenge this matter in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you or someone else raised at the public hearing, described in this noticed, or in written correspondence, delivered to the City of Piedmont at or prior to the public hearing. You may choose to write your opinion and address the response to the Piedmont Planning Commission via email at Piedmontishome@piedmont.ca.gov or via U.S. Mail at Piedmont Planning Commission, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. All Planning Commission meetings are televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government access TV station and will be available through streaming video on the City’s website https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/meeting_videos The City of Piedmont will publish the meeting agenda not less than 72 hours prior to the meeting. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code include amendments to Division 17.38, Accessory Dwelling Units, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use, including new incentives for rent-restricted ADUs for applicants using new City-approved plans for ADUs. The proposed amendments to the Piedmont City Code also include amendments to create a new Division 17.67, of Chapter 17, Planning and Land Use to establish procedures and standards for ministerial review of multifamily and mixed-use building types in Zone C and Zone D. Proposed amendments to the City of Piedmont Design Guidelines include: (1) new objective standards for architectural elements to be used by City staff to review development applications for multifamily and mixed-use building types; (2) pre-approved plans for accessory dwelling units (ADUs); and (3) other conforming changes. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are exempt under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The amendments to address pre-approved architectural plans for ADUs are statutorily exempt from CEQA pursuant to Public Resources Code section 21080.17 and CEQA Guidelines section 15282(h) which exempts adoption of ordinances to implement Government Code section 65852.2 regarding accessory dwelling units. These amendments are also exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303.The amendments related to Multifamily Objective Design Standards are exempt because it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the adoption of Multifamily Objective Design Standards may have a significant effect on the environment. (Public Resources Code section 21065; CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Sections 15061(b)(3), 15378.) Further, these amendments are exempt under CEQA Guidelines, 14 Cal. Code of Regs. Section 15301 and 15303. The proposed amendments to the City Code and Design Guidelines are available for public review on the City’s webpage at https://piedmont.ca.gov as well as https://piedmontishome.org. They are also available at City Hall located at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. articles.text: your chest on some steep sections. Marching in humidity around 80 percent caused this Bay Area born-and-raised hiker to look like he jumped out of a pool when reaching Doi Suthep. But the path to Doi Suthep is extraordinary and cuts you away from the bounds of foot traffic on the Monk’s Trail to Wat Pha Lat. After hiking up the remainder of the Monk’s Trail, you’ll intersect with Sriwichai Alley (route 1004), walking left to take the Pilgrim’s Path on the opposite side of the road. The Pilgrim’s Path goes for 0.8 of a mile until greeting the road, once again, where you will follow the road up for the remaining half-mile up to Doi Suthep, where you will pass shops, restaurants, and taxi drivers at the bottom of the temple. Created in 1383, Wat Phra That Doi Suthep is named after the mountain which it is located and considered to be the most sacred temple in all of Thailand. There’s another magnificent Naga Staircase leading to the temple, this one much larger and colorful than the previous at Wat Pha Lat. Peer closely at the scales of the two serpents leading you towards Doi Suthep. Entrance to the monastery costs ฿100, which is just $2.85— it is also recommended to dress appropriately. You’ll find sweeping views of Chiang Mai from multiple overlooks on the grounds and several large statues of Buddha. You’ll also be required to take your shoes off when entering the primary section of the temple, where there’s a spectacular large golden Chedi, which towers 79 feet in height. Should hikers call it a day, you’ll end your hike at around 2.5 miles with over 2,000 feet in elevation gain. Taxis will be ready at the base of Doi Suthep to take your group back into town. Heading back down the road and onto the trails makes it a 4.5 mile day of hiking. Keep in mind some steep sections coupled with usual wet conditions in Thailand could make things difficult for a descent. Hikers should wear proper footgear for tackling the Monk’s Trail and Pilgrim’s Trail, along with packing mosquito repellent to keep away the pesky critters. One of the golden Buddha statues at Doi Suthep. The view of Chiang Mai from Wat Phra That Doi Suthep.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, August 9, 2023 Gran Torino Continued from page 20 principled and courageous. When a family of Hmongs – people from the hills of Thailand, Laos and Vietnam – move in nextdoor, Kowalski regards them as “slopes” and “zipper heads.” His prejudice is undisguised and blunt. He survived Korea, won the Silver Star, and has little desire to get to know these people he views as unwelcome and unfamiliar. At least until events make it impossible for him to remain apart and then he involves himself in a world that surprises him. Slowly, he becomes a neighbor. Gran Torino is eminently entertaining, if for no other reason to observe the changes Kowalski goes through as he takes a Hmong boy, Thao (Bee Vang) under his old man’s wing and becomes his protector. It’s impossible, with this film especially, to watch Eastwood on screen and separate him from the character Kowalski, in the same way that Cruise, no matter the role, is always Cruise. For an actor, it’s a strength and it’s a weakness. While these actors can inhabit a part, they can never completely submerge themselves to the point that the audience forgets who they are. We’re watching Eastwood doing Harry, doing Kowalski. In one scene, Kowalski points a vintage M-16 rifle at a gang member and snarls, through clenched teeth, “Get off of my lawn.” Ah, yes. You feeling lucky, punk? Are you? Is Gran Torino worth an afternoon and the price of a ticket? Definitely. It’s a familiar but involving story, and all the performances are excellent. There are moments of high tension and other moments that are downright comical and will make you laugh. Gran Torino. Starring Clint Eastwood, Christopher Carley, Bee Vang and Ashley Her. articles.text: Piedmont aims for carbon-neutrality by 2045 At their July 17 meeting, the City Council voted to update the city’s Climate Action Plan 2.0 goals to align them with new state, national and global goals. When the CAP 2.0 was adopted in March 2018, its goal was to reduce 2005 levels of greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030 and 80% by 2050, in line with state goals. In September 2018, however, state goals grew bolder, including 100% carbon-free electricity and carbon neutrality by 2045, and net negative emissions afterward. Nationally, the Biden Administration also aims to halve 2005 levels of U.S. greenhouse emissions by 2030. Globally, the United Nations panel on climate change aims to halve global emissions by 2030. In line with these, Piedmont is adopting updated emissions goals including halving 2005 emission levels by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2045. In a state of “carbon neutrality,” negative greenhouse gas emissions – in which carbon is reduced from the atmosphere – equal positive emissions, in which carbon is added to the atmosphere from the combustion of fossil fuels. The previous CAP 2.0 goals, which are now being overhauled for more ambitious ones, include the reduction of 2005 greenhouse emission levels 40% by 2030, and 80% by 2050. articles.text: As work on a new retaining wall continues, another fuel tank estimated to be 100 years old has been found on the Piedmont Community Pool site. Since the week of July 14, the general contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, has been building a 385-foot retaining wall for the new pool. Concurrently, grading and leveling the site is expected to take three weeks. Contractors began by digging holes for utility lines including gas, water, and Comcast for future facilities at the pool site. This utility work is expected to be completed by August 11, said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Meanwhile, the workers have been applying a waterproof ing substance to the retaining walls, a process which will finish by today, August 2. Contractors will then reinforce the retaining wall, installing steel rebar by Friday, August 11. Afterward, Gonzales said that they will spray the frame of the wall with “shotcrete,” a type of concrete which is applied to surfaces by being projected from a pump through a high-velocity hose.

articles.text: Shortly after midnight on Tuesday, June 5, a fire started in the clubhouse of Lake Chabot Golf Course. The golf course, which has served in prior years as the home course for Piedmont High School’s golf teams, has remained open, but the non-profit Lake Chabot Junior Golf Academy lost nearly all of its equipment in the blaze. Just days before the fire, the pro-shop suffered a major loss of golf clubs in a sophisticated middle-of-the-night burglary. The pro shop itself was the only part of the building left intact and operational after the fire, however items not stolen or burned were rendered valueless due to smoke and water damage. articles.text: Editor: My husband and I have had multiple near misses from cars speeding up to the stoplight, it is red on their approach. Generally these folks are going upwards of 30mph and they attempt to “slow down” as they have every intent of cruising around the corner without the semblance of a full stop,. When the light is Red in their direction there is a high chance the crosswalk for me, my dogs and the 26 children who live on the cemetery side of Moraga is Green, This morning at about 10:30, a little boy on his brightly colored bike and fluorescent green helmet was waiting with me to cross the street. It turned green and he started into the intersection. A woman driving a white Tesla either didn’t look or couldn’t see past the car to the left of her so she started into the intersection causing said child to swerve as to not hit her car. I have rallied the City of Piedmont and the police department for a No Turn on Red sign for years, but to no avail. We have had so many near misses and we are much more visible than my elementary aged neighbors. Our French grandma used to rap her cane on the hood of cars when drivers encroached into her walking space in Paris. I might start carrying a cane at this rate. I’d encourage all neighbors here to reach out to the City Hall and ask for the No Turn On Red sign. –Sydney Proctor For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has announced the August schedule of its “Cop on the Block” program, foot patrols in neighborhoods which began in June. It is the department’s firstever scheduled walking patrol. The following foot patrols are scheduled for August: • Friday, August 4, 12 p.m. – Muir Avenue between Lafayette and La Salle – Office Tyler Petit • Tuesday, August 8, 4 p.m. – Maxwelton Avenue and Nellie Ave. – Officer Jorge Faucher • Saturday, August 19, 9 a.m. – Rose Avenue between Greenbank and Linda – Sgt. George Tucker Described as a way to bring officers out of cars and into neighborhoods, neighbors are invited to bring their questions, comments and concerns to officers as they patrol the city’s blocks on foot at selected locations and times, announced by PPD monthly. Police Captain Chris Monahan, who oversees the program, said, “We rolled out Cop on the Block as a way to encourage more non-enforcement contact with the community. It’s very casual. We plan that each week a member of the department will walk up and down the block for a minimum of half an hour and for as long as people want to chat — about baseball, tree-trimming, parking, crime, anything.” “We plan to keep going with the program until we cover the whole city. Piedmont has about 145 streets and once we cover them all, a block at time,” he added, “we’ll start over again. We currently plan to keep it at one officer a week. So far, the program’s been very well-received; I’ve even had people call me and ask to schedule a time and date for us to visit their block.” Monahan encourages residents interested in bringing Cop on the Block to their street to contact him by phone at 520-3012 or by email at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov. More information on Cop on the Block events, including an interactive map of the blocks may be found on the Police Department’s website, bit.ly/42yYRTu. Piedmont Police Captain Chris Monahan greets the Walking on Wednesdays group at the Exedra on July 19 to describe the Police Department’s Cop on the Block foot patrol.

articles.text: As summer continues, Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping with special summer events or administrative tasks, helping at any of the 66 distribution sites throughout Alameda County. Visit mercybrownbag.org/volunteer to learn more. Piedmont Community Service Crew The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a coed youth-led organization that inspires teens to actively uplift the broader community through service activities. It is the largest of the Venturing Crews of Piedmont Scout Council, with approximately 150 members, It actively seeks high school and older middle school students, and parent volunteers for several ongoing programs. PCSC events and programs include meal preparation for low-income, elderly, and homeless members of the community; home renovation projects, and community engagement work such as youth tutoring. For more information on how to get involved, visit pcservicecrew.org. Alameda County Community Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank needs volunteers to prepare food in the ACCFB Oakland warehouse, and to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites throughout the county. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, email volunteer@accfd.org, or visit accfb. org/get-involved/volunteer. A calendar of all volunteer opportunities for adults and youth 10 years old and up is available at accfb.org/get-involved/volunteer-calendar. Donations are also welcome. East Bay SPCA The East Bay’s oldest animal welfare organization is always in need of volunteers. Volunteering is a wonderful way to improve the lives of animals in the shelter, and a variety of opportunities are available for all ages. East Bay SPCA’s Humane Education programs are particularly tailored for youth volunteers. Summer service projects can include making dog treats, assisting with shelter laundry, socializing with animals in the SPCA’s care, and more. Participants will learn about responsible pet care, the medical needs of animals, and pet behavior. Other Oakland volunteer opportunities for adults and youth include feline or canine animal care, customer service, shelter care, pet food pantry distribution, event assistance, and animal training class assistance. Visit eastbayspca.org/get-involved/volunteer/become-a-volunteer and learn more. “We don’t have a drawing board anymore, Dude. What do we go back to?”

articles.text: Application deadline is August 10 Piedmont Recreation Department is currently offering volunteer positions for teenagers 15 and older for its Sidekicks program. articles.text: District hires Trevor Meseroll from Berklee College of Music PHS Band Director Andria Mullan has resigned. Andria Mullan, the Director for both the middle and high school instrumental bands, resigned on July 8 prior to relocating to the East Coast. Taking her position in the district’s music program will be Trevor Meseroll, a recent graduate of Berkelee College of Music in Boston. Mullan has taught music in Piedmont since 2005. Her role in the district utilized her extensive set of skills and changed as Piedmont School District changed its music programs. Originally hired as the high school band teacher, she eventually taught 6th, 7th and 8th grade band classes, as well as Symphonic Band and Jazz Band at the high school. She also coordinated a schedule for the PHS Pep Band. Instrumental band directors must have the ability to play many instruments. Directing both middle and high school students required Mullan to guide students with skill levels ranging from beginner to adept. Mullan resigned to be closer to family. The impact comes at a time when the school district grapples with the need to find a replacement for legendary vocal music teacher Joe Piazza, who retired in 2019 after 31 years as anchor of the district’s music department. “It is a big loss; Andria left large shoes to fill,” said Piedmont High School Principal Sukanya Goswami. Goswami explained how difficult it is to find a replacement for Mullan. On July 10, the school district posted a job notice on Edjoin to replace Mullan. After receiving applications, a panel of administrators from the district and both high school and middle school conducted interviews. The district has hired Trevor Meseroll who graduated from the Berklee College of Music in 2022 with a degree in music education. Meseroll is a pianist and educator and will teach the AP Music Theory class left vacant since Piazza’s retirement. He will be in charge of both the high school and middle school band programs. Goswami confirmed that Meseroll will need some support in his first year as he takes on a wide range of responsibilities but expressed confidence in his capacities. Mullan’s departure comes at a time when the school district is already grappling with difficulites in replacing Piazza. His successor, Sid Quinsaat, stopped coming to work in January 2020 and officially resigned in February prior to the COVID pandemic. Erin Igoe, Assistant Principal at Piedmont High School recently confirmed that there will be no a cappella vocal music at the high school this year. Trevor Meseroll will be the new Band Director at PHS and PMS.
articles.title: Andria Mullan resigns as PUSD band director

articles.text: Summer vacation evokes blissful thoughts of time in the sun, bodies of water, games and sports. Conventional theory may hold that summer and math are antigens that do not cross, mix or have any relation, but that does not have to be the case. It need not be a foregone conclusion that summer will be a slow sapping-away of academic knowledge. Even small efforts to keep school skills sharp at the end of summer will pay dividends when class returns shortly. Math doesn’t have to be treated like a four-letter word; parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles and older siblings would be well served to know that fun aspects of math are plentiful during the summer. Math is everywhere, sometimes it just needs to be discovered. Baseball is America’s pastime and a summertime staple, learning about baseball statistics can be a great way to implement an incognito math lesson into summer. In all sports, statistics are a way a player’s success can be measured and stats help us better undertand the game. While watching a baseball game, have your student jot down a players statistical numbers from inning to inning, from at-bat to at-bat. Seeing the change in a player’s batting average can be a very tangible lesson to learn about fractions, and percentages. A pitcher’s earned run average (ERA) changes even more frequently, with every run or Contemplating which of these baseball records is “unbreakable” requires abstract thinking about the game and changes in rules and societal norms. out. Have your student watching a game try to calculate the ERA with every event of the game before they are updated in stadium or on the screen. For more advanced students, baseball is full of obscure statistics like WHIFF, dERA and VORP. Learning how certain statistics are calculated can help understand the game as well. For example the pitcher to start a game can only get credit with the W stat (win) if they pitch at least five innings and leave the game with the lead. Sometimes trying to earn this stat effects the game play, a pitcher’s desire for a personal statistic may negatively affect the entire team. Challenge your student to understand the changes in slugging percentage; which requires calculating the total amount of bases a hitter gets per at bat. Ask follow up questions like who might have a high slugging percentage, but not be a good player? So much of the world around us, even summer fun, has a numerical undertone. The universe can be understood more fully by checking the statistics. This tutor’s advice is to utilize whatever your student is already passionate about and challenge them to deepen their knowledge and understanding with data, number and statistics. A summer infusion of math doesn’t have to come from baseball or from sports. Pedometers can track how far a kid has run in a day, kids bouncing off the walls can be challenged to calculate how many calories they burn or need to eat to keep growing. Tracking height and weight versus time is a fun way to learn to graph and record data. In summer the classroom will look different. Whether on the baseball diamond, in front of the white board or on the black top, math is there and a deeper understand lies waiting for discovery.
articles.title: Summer math help on the diamond

articles.text: The popular Piedmont Junior Running Club is back for another school year and is calling all 4th and 5th graders who like to run and have fun doing it, to sign up. Registration opened yesterday, August 1st, through the Piedmont Recreation Department. This after-school sports program is for both boys and girls of all ability levels and provides an introduction to running. During the most recent school year, the program achieved several new milestones, including having a Winter season for the first time. It also had a mini track meet in the Spring for program participants. This Fall, the program is being expanded by two weeks, from September 11 to November 15. Each elementary school will host a Junior program with experienced adult coaches leading the practice sessions. Runners meet on Mondays from 3:15 to 4:30 p.m. and Wednesdays from 2:00 to 3:15 p.m. New runners will receive a t-shirt and be offered a healthy snack after every practice. To register, click on: https://register. capturepoint.com/reg/cat_program_class_detail.cfm?s=&t=&- season_id=24069&program_ id=1495830&family_mbr_str=. For more information., contact Len Goldman at lgoldman@pacbell.net. Parent volunteers are needed to help the program and provide supplemental staffing. Havens fifth grader Willa Brozowski-Schrader leads the way in a race with members of the Piedmont Junior Running Club.
articles.title: Signups now open for Junior Running Club

articles.text: Quite frankly, I still can’t believe I’m here. So far, this year’s Scout National Jamboree at the Summit Bechtel Reserve in West Virginia has been filled with amazing experiences and meetings. From trading glow-inthe-dark patches while talking about favorite constellations, to falling off a skateboard just to get back on, everything has been filled with wonder and excitement. On our very first day I had one goal in mind – to earn a NOVA patch a multi-part STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) patch earned by completing multiple activities in each area. This NOVA patch is only available at the Summit, as only 500 have ever been made. Because we got to the summit rather early in the morning, we had the whole day to explore the summit before everyone showed up. So, I corralled a group, asked for directions and hiked up to the Summit Center. Once we arrived, I dragged some of my friends over to the booth and started walking around, crossing off requirements. One of the exhibits talked about shaping stones into arrowheads, another put multiple items in liquid nitrogen. When we finally finished the patch, I was incredibly grateful for this group of people – one of whom I had met only 24 hours ago – to stay with me so I could finally earn this patch. Making new friends is a key part of the Jamboree. As we talked to people we met along the way, we began to feel a sense of community, sharing only one thing: our combined love of Scouting. The Summit has one of the largest skate parks in America. Before you even start the sheer amount of safety gear and warnings made me feel anxious. To be completely honest, I hadn’t wanted to come to the skate park. Some of my friends were heading there and I had decided to tag along. Sure, I’ve always wanted to try skateboarding, but it wasn’t something I was extremely enthusiastic about. A large “Jambo 23” sign in a meadow announces the Scout National Jamboree in West Virginia. Diego Branneria (left), Samantha Pell and Amelia Lee (Marin) proudly hold up their NOVA patches. As we walked out into the park, the skateboard felt heavy in my hand, like I wasn’t capable of carrying it. Once out on the large flat of concrete I managed to fall over before even stepping on the board. Fun. After basic instruction we were left with our boards and an enormous skate park. A couple of falls later I was comfortably gliding across the flat… until I fell again. All of these things, as well as everything else I’ve experienced at the summit, share one thing in common. They are all first time, life changing experiences. But they also opened up barriers to new friendships. Halfway through the NOVA patch we talked to a girl from my camp who was interested in earning it. At skateboarding I connected with a girl who kept returning my runaway board. With every new experience, booth visit, or even just chat on the road, we connected. Even if I barely knew most of these people, we shared a combined love and devotion to Scouts. Moving together – and as this year’s Jamboree motto says ­ – forward. Samantha Pell is an eighth grader at Piedmont Middle School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 1. A large climbing wall forms a backdrop to a cluster of tents at the National Scout Jamboree in West Virginia. Diego Branneria at the archery range The Piedmont-Marin Scout contingent prepares to make flood buckets for communities hit by recent flooding. Travers Kemp (left) and Dylan Wallway wait for a leadership program to start.
articles.title: Piedmont Scouts experience once in a lifetime Jamboree in West Virginia

articles.text: Forward. What exactly do we mean when we say forward? Do we mean trying new, death-defying things? Do we mean attempting a merit badge? Do we mean stepping up to a fellow Scout and complementing their class B? At Jamboree, a gathering of Scouts from throughout the U.S. every four years at the Summit Bechtel Reserve in West Virginia, there are countless ways to follow through with this year’s motto – Forward. One of the coolest things about the Summit are the impressive bronze sculptures scattered throughout and created by sculptor, artist, and songwriter Jamie Lester. Truth be told, I didn’t have high expectations for the new female “ascending eagle” sculpture. Surprisingly, Lester went above and beyond my expectations, creating a gorgeous bronze girl, hoisting a set of wings on her shoulders, torch raised, ready to take flight. While wandering around the tents I stumbled upon Lester, with whom I shared my opinions on his sculptures. Intrigued, I decided to return the next day to attend his sculpture merit badge. The day was hot and still, and I had been rather drowsy all day. But when he started talking, and shaping the clay, I was captivated. Unlike the other speeches and lessons I had attended that day, I kept awake and alert, desperately wanting to see what he would create next. There was something magical about his energy, the way he talked and interacted with the audience. There were about 25 of us crammed in the tent, some on chairs “borrowed” from other exhibits. I’m willing to bet that he touched each and every one of us in ways he didn’t realize. Maybe the Scouts attending his talk and demonstration didn’t even realize it at the time. Something he mentioned multiple times was the importance of connecting with people through art. With his Scouting bronzes, we were able to see ourselves through them, and relate to the energy conveyed through them. It was the same energy I’d been pushing mere days before at the 3D archery targets. It was that same energy that propelled me to try shooting with a shotgun, something I’d never done before. The feeling of shock after the first shot made me want to shoot a hundred more. Shooting has been one of those things that I’ve always wanted to do, something on my bucket list. However, it’s also something I’m morbidly afraid of. My safety instructor, a fun but also firm man, knew of Piedmont. After pointing it out on my shirt, we talked with him for a few minutes about the Bay Area. There was also the man who helped me load my gun when my fingers were fumbling around. All the experiences and memories made during Jamboree will be forever remembered, but it’s the people who will stick with me. The people who made the experiences and adventures memorable were people who helped create and push that energy. That energy that – created by us – will push us forward. articles.text: I am an ADHD Focus Coach located in Piedmont. I work with students and people with ADHD to help them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week I am writing about identifying and utilizing your personal strengths to make life easier and get more done. Strength spotting is the idea that people all have different skills and natural abilities and identifying individual strengths empowers people to utilize what they’re good at to get through difficult times and accomplish big tasks. This is true whether or not an individual has been diagnosed with ADHD. People with ADHD may have unique strengths, such as the ability to see the big picture. I use strengths spotting with my clients to help them understand what tools they already have in their toolbox. One way to identify strengths is to ask people who are closest to you what they think your best qualities are and why. This can provide you with a nice list of things that people around you see and that you might not even see in yourself. Another way to identify your strengths is to keep a journal about times that you succeeded; write down the things that you did well during those times. Then sit down with a coach or a friend to discuss what qualities about you are highlighted in the experiences you jotted down. The third and most popular way is taking a strengths spotting test online such as the Via Character Strengths Survey. They provide a list of common strengths and give you the tools to uncover and understand your results. A few examples of strengths listed are Creativity, Spirituality, Appreciation of Beauty and Excellence, and Love of Learning. Once you have a better sense of your strengths, you can utilize that information to help you get more done in a way that makes sense for you. I work with clients on both understanding what their strengths are and how to use them to overcome challenges. Reach out to me if you are interested in learning more about your strengths and how you can use them to make life easier and get more done. Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. She can be reached at 415- 680-6990 or mindsglowing@ gmail.com.

articles.text: Troop 4 Scouts started setting up for our annual Independence Day hot dog fundraiser the day before the Fourth of July. Around four o’clock we got the tents prepared, the windows on, and we brought out the grill. Then, on July 4th, starting at 6:00 a.m. we started the final preparations for customers, including picking up ice and the thoughtful donation of Piedmont Grocery of 700 hot dogs. We also practiced with the grill and at 10:30 a.m. we opened up shop. We were getting small amounts of customers until around lunchtime when it started getting busy. A hot dog starts its journey at the grill where there are three people grilling. It is grilled to perfection and handed over to Scouts in the tent who put the hot dogs in buns and foil wrappers. They are given to the cashiers who make sure that the customers also get their drinks. This happened over and over until 1:30 p.m., about an hour after the parade ended, when the giant amount of hot dogs finally ran out. We got the chance to take a break, and then returned to take down the hot dog stand and leave with memories to remember. Chase Mellers is an 8th grader and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 4. articles.text: Staff Photo Tanya Kononova is stepping into her senior year at Piedmont High after arriving to California as a refugee from Ukraine. Tanya Kononova made a big name for herself as a tennis player at Piedmont High School last year. She won the Western Alameda County Conference’s Player of the Year award after winning the league’s individual tournament’s singles bracket. But her path from Europe to the Highlanders’ tennis team wasn’t a typical journey for foreign students coming to Piedmont. Tanya and her family never envisioned moving to California as a refugee prior to February 24, 2022, the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived to Piedmont on July 22 that year from Odesa, a city in the south of Ukraine. Kononova arrived to help coach Jim Landes’ tennis clinic a week later, and she instantly impressed him. “It was the week I had the high school girls warm up clinic, one week before tryouts for the team. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. I knew she was a very good player the first time she hit. It was a good way for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russian invasion. Her father remains in Ukraine as men under the age of 60 are required to remain and help Ukraine’s war effort. Tanya stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months and waited at the border for 13 hours before passing into the neighboring country. She described the experience of leaving Ukraine. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine, because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova when speaking through a translator. Tanya and her family initially decided to relocate to Bulgaria after a town administration building in Moldova was targeted by Russian artillery. They were there from May through July 2022 and had no connection to anyone in the country. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived with my mother, my grandfather and my grandmother,” said Kononova. “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically took what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week to gather more belongings. She was visiting with a friend near the city center when a rocket struck a nearby building. Speaking through a translator, Kononova detailed the emotions she experienced: “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s when it really hit me. I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. Then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions. It was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family members are still in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncle’s home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends. One of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” Kononova said last year. When entering the U.S. last year, it marked the first time Kononova had an opportunity to play tennis since leaving Ukraine
articles.title: Tanya Kononova details her journey as a Ukrainian refugee to the Piedmont tennis courts

articles.text: Year-round swim team holding tryouts August 15-17 300 swimmers from seven Bay Area teams competed recently in the three-day Redwood Empire Swim League Championship meet Friday through Sunday, July 21-23, at the Mills College campus in Oakland. The Piedmont Swim Team, a year-round competitive team, won the overall meet by a large margin with 5,045 points over four other teams, defeating Hills Hurricane Swimming in second place with 3,845. Three Piedmont swimmers took home trophies for being the high point winners for their age group: Connor Carnazzo (boys 11-12), Magnolia Stoll (girls 13-14), and Paige Arnold (girls 15 & over). Asher Takazawa qualified for his first sectionals. It was the final swim meet for Recent PHS graduate Simon Lins (left) with PST head coach Stefan Bill and swimmer Paige Arnold. Arnold and Simon Lins before they enter college this fall. Piedmont Swim Team will begin tryouts on August 14 and welcomes all interested youth up to age 18. The year-round team focuses on individual excellence in a team environment. “Our goal is to create a safe and joyful environment for all, one that allows each athlete to excel,” said head coach Stefan Bill. Everyone from ages 6-18 who enjoys being in the water and is interested in learning new and different skills is invited to try out for the team. Swimmers should be able to do freestyle comfortably, with breathing to the side, backstroke comfortably, and have some basic breaststroke knowledge. Older swimmers should have more technical skill. “All of our swimmers are super friendly, and our parents are helpful and accommodating,” said Bill. “We are hopeful that swimmers joining us can find the passion for a sport they can ultimately do for the rest of their lives,” said Coach Stefan Tryouts will take place on August 15 to 17, Tuesday through Thursday, from 4:00 to 6:30 p.m. at Montclair Swim Club, 1901 Woodhaven Way, Oakland. Those interested are invited to e-mail joinpst@piedmontswimteam.org.
articles.title: Piedmont Swim Team wins RESL Championships

She described the experience of leaving Ukraine. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine, because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova when speaking through a translator. Tanya and her family initially decided to relocate to Bulgaria after a town administration building in Moldova was targeted by Russian artillery. They were there from May through July 2022 and had no connection to anyone in the country. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived with my mother, my grandfather and my grandmother,” said Kononova. “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically took what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week to gather more belongings. She was visiting with a friend near the city center when a rocket struck a nearby building. Speaking through a translator, Kononova detailed the emotions she experienced: “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s when it really hit me. I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were notified to go to a shelter because they detected a missile. Then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions. It was one of the days they bombed one of the many residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night, and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe and some family members are still in Moldova. Tanya and her mother moved into her uncle’s home in Piedmont and have since taken up residence at a separate home in town. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids… I’m still in touch with all of my friends. One of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” Kononova said last year. When entering the U.S. last year, it marked the first time Kononova had an opportunity to play tennis since leaving Ukraine See Tanya Kononova on page 30

articles.text: Sawasdee (hello) from Thailand, Piedmonters! With our time away from writing articles, this writer partook in his tradition of following his favourite football (soccer) team, Tottenham Hotspur of North London This time it was see a match during preseason tour in Bangkok’s Rajamangala Stadium. Parents and coaches at Piedmont High have observed me wearing a Tottenham hat or jersey of Heung-min Son and Lucas Moura. With PHS’ British coaching staff of girls’ head coach Dan Chubbock and boys’ head coach Todd Sullivan, it’s often a topic of conversation, especially with Sullivan being a devout Manchester United supporter. But how does an American become enamored with English football? Like many in my age group, EA Sports’ video game franchise, FIFA, played a large role – along with the World Cup being an obvious draw. My journey into world football started with finding Tottenham sometime around 2013 on FIFA, thinking, “Hah, that team has a funny name.” I discovering the Welsh Wizard Gareth Bale and then building teams around Harry Kane and Heung-min Son Son in the years to follow. Staff Photo The dark clouds over Rajamangala Stadium in Bangkok led to monsoon rain, resulting in the Tottenham match being called off. Staff Photo A photo of the monsoon rain pouring down at Rajamangala Stadium in Bangkok. Photo courtesy of ESPN Lucas Moura’s hat trick to send Tottenham to the 2019 Champions League Finals gave birth to a new Hotspur supporter in California. But I still wasn’t a devout fan. I was still unsure how to track start times of games and where to watch them. Now in 2023, applications on my phone do all that for me, thanks to Google. What drew me closer to Tottenham Hotspur was its run in the 2019 Champions League. The Champions League is considered the most prestigious club tournament in European football. The top teams in leagues like the Premier League, Spain’s La Liga, Italy’s Serie A, Germany’s Budesliga, and France’s Ligue 1 are represented, while the top teams from smaller leagues also make noise, like Portugal’s Premeira Liga, Scotland’s Scottish Premiership, the Dutch’s Eredivisie, and even country’s like Turkey, Ukraine, Russia, and more. It is considered the Crème-dela-crème of the world’s game. In 2019, Tottenham lost 2-0 in the finals to Liverpool, but stole hearts with its magical comeback victory against Ajax of the Netherlands. In that game Hotspur won with a second-half hat trick by Moura to beat Ajax on the away-goals rule in a 3-3 result. The Champions League knockout stages, other than the finals, are played in two legs. Tottenham lost the first leg 0-1 at its home stadium, but beat Ajax 3-2 on a magic night in Amsterdam—enabling the away-goal rule for outscoring an opponent in its home stadium. Moura, who came in as a second-half substitute when Tottenham trailed 0-2 scored goals in the 55th minute, 59th minute and then at the veryvery end at 90+6’ in the literal final seconds of the match. It would be comparable to a successful Hail Mary in American Football from your team’s own

articles.text: The 2023 Women’s World Cup’s group stages are nearing completion with the United States awaiting the winner of Group G, likely Sweden on August 5. It wasn’t easy for the back-to-back champs. In their final game of the Group stage Portugal appeared the better in a 0-0 draw. The U.S. went undefeated at 1-2-0, but couldn’t get the job done versus the Netherlands or Portugal in 1-1 and 0-0 ties. Three of the eight groups have yet to wrap up. Here’s how things are going, starting with the U.S.’ Group E. GROUP E: Photo courtesy of Sporting News Megan Rapinoe (left), Alex Morgan, and the United States narrowly escaped Group E, but the results appeared closer than the score-lines read. Netherlands (7 points, clinched) United States (5 points, clinched) Portugal (4 points) Vietnam (0 points) The fact the United States finished second in the group is a testament to the growth of the women’s game in Europe. Despite being second-best to the Dutch, the stats show the United States deserved some better results. In their 1-1 draw against the Netherlands on July 27, the United States recorded 18 shot attempts to the Dutch’s five. However, the Stars and Stripes lacked a finish; just four of those shot attempts were on target. The Netherlands, meanwhile, scored with their only shot on target in the 17th minute. Tuesday morning’s 0-0 draw against Portugal also left more to be desired. Portugal missed scoring in second-half stoppage time when their shot rang off of the post, inches away from a goal. The US took 17 shots with six on target to Portugal’s six and zero. Sometimes that’s just how the game goes in soccer. The United States will likely Sweden as the winner of Group G. The Swedes have looked good and have a strong side. GROUP A: Photo courtesy of fourfourtwo.com The United States will likely face Sweden in the round of 16. helped push Norway across the line by capturing its first win in World Cup history, a 1-0 victory over the Kiwis. On a personal note, s a son of a Filipina immigrant from Manila, it brought pride seeing how far the Philippines have come. GROUP B: Costa Rica 2-0, and then completely blanked group runners up Spain 4-0. Japan will face Norway while Spain squares off with Switzerland; both games are on August 5. GROUP D: Australia (6 points, clinched) Nigeria (5 points, clinched) Canada (4 points) Ireland (1 points) The other host nation, Australia, won Group B by beating Ireland 1-0, losing to Nigeria 3-2, but rallying to beat Canada 4-0. However, Nigeria’s win over Australia was its only win in the group stage with a pair of 0-0 draws to Canada and Ireland. Australia, FIFA rank No. 10, is set to face No. 13 Denmark on August 7. Nigeria, FIFA No. 40, will play Group D winner and title contenders, England, which is No. 4 in the world. GROUP C: England (9 points, clinched) Denmark (6 points, clinched) China (3 points) Haiti (0 points) No surprises out of this group. England came in ranked No. 4 while Denmark was No. 13. The Three Lions will face Nigeria on August 7 with the Danes playing Australia on the same day. GROUP F Switzerland (5 points, clinched) Norway (4 points, clinched) New Zealand (4 points) Philippines (3 points) Switzerland came in with the No. 20 world ranking, eight spots lower than Norway at No. 12. The Swiss won the group by defeating the Philippines 2-0 and followed up with 0-0 draws to Norway and New Zealand. The Norwegians actually lost 1-0 to New Zealand to open the tournament, but eclipsed the host-nation by goal differential after defeating the Philippines 6-0. The Philippines, meanwhile, Japan (9 points, clinched) Spain (6 points, clinched) Zambia (3 points) Costa Rica (0 points) No. 11 Japan is never a team to take lightly. Just ask the 2011 United States National Team. So far this tournament, the Japanese have yet to allow a goal. They dominated Zambia 5-0, shut out France (4 points) Jamaica (4 points) Brazil (3 points) Panama (0 points) This is a fun one. Group F will be determined today, August 2, with France playing Panama and Brazil up against Jamaica. France undoubtedly has the easier route, Taking at least a point (a draw( will get them into the next stage. Brazil, on the other hand, could be on the verge of a knockout as the No. 6 ranked team in the world. Jamaica is playing the role of David against a Goliath as the world’s No. 43 ranked team. GROUP G: Photo courtesy of The Japan Times Japan looked superb in its recent 4-0 defeat of Portugal, its third consecutive shutout in the Group stage. It has yet to allow a goal in this year’s Women’s World Cup. Sweden (6 points, clinched) Italy (3 points) South Africa (1 point) Argentina (1 point) Sweden entered the group atop the ladder at No. 3. They are set to face Argentina today, which would be at least an assured point. Italy, No. 16, plays South Africa and just needs to avoid a letdown. Group H: Colombia (6 points), Germany (3 points), Morocco (3 points), South Korea (0 points). Colombia leads the group and should at least get into the Round of 16, barring an enormous meltdown. Germany plays winless South Korea, playing on August 3—a win and a Colombia loss gets the German’s to the top of the group, For Colombia to drop out, Morocco would have to beat them by five goals given they currently have a -5 goal differential.
