articles.text: Photos courtesy of Cyprus Mail Danish rider Jonas Vingegaard won his second consecutive Tour de France. He was greeted at home with a massive celebration in Copenhagen. Its official: Jonas Vingegaard of Denmark has won back-toback Tour de France Yellow Jerseys. He led the general classification standings, finishing ahead of Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar, winner of Le Tour in 2020 and 202. The Dane wore the Yellow Jersey from Stage 6 all the way to Stage 21, the final stage, and finished with a 7 minutes, 29 second advantage. Vingegaard only held a nine second lead on Pogačar through Stage 13, but the Danish rider began tacking on seconds in the stages to follow. He gained one second in the Stage 14 mountains and the stalemate continued though Stage 15’s mountain. But it wasn’t the long courses that made the difference for Vingegaard; the Stage 16 time trial was a catalyst for him. On the brief 22.4 kilometer ride from Passy to Combloux, Vingegaard won the event, adding 1 minute, 38 seconds to his lead over r the Slovenian. Vingegaard car ried the momentum in Stage 17’s mountain ride from Saint-Gervais-lesBains to Courchevel, piling on an insurmountable 5 minutes and 45 seconds on Pogačar. From there, all Vingegaard needed to do was stay consistent. Pogačar found some solace by winning Stage 20, a mountain ride, but there was no change in the general classification. Pogačar wound up winning the Best Young Rider award for the fourth year in a row. Upon Vingegaard’s return to Denmark he was greeted to a massive crowd in Copenhagen celebrating his victory.
articles.title: Vingegaard wins second consecutive Tour de France

articles.text: to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. Photo courtesy of St. Lawrence Athletics Max Cole, PHS Class of 2022, is entering his sophomore year as a member of the St. Lawrence University rowing team MAX COLE Rowing My current fitness goal is to improve my VO2 max and prepare for fall season. I hope to make the 8 [boat] that goes to Head of the Charles in October. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my progress with erg splits (the time it takes to complete 500m). Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m working on my own; however, I have been given suggested workouts and goal paces. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished was racing and winning my first international race in England this past week. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? articles.text: Singer-songwriter Patti Smith Singer-songwriter Patti Smith will perform the penultimate concert of the Stern Grove Festival on Sunday, August 13. Smith gained popularity with her first studio recording, Horses in 1975, which was inducted into the National Recording Registry at the Library of Congress in 2010 by the National Recording Preservation Board. Her following albums include Radio Ethiopia, Easter, Wave, and Dream of Life, which included “People Have the Power” co-written with her late husband Fred Sonic Smith. Smith is a four-time Grammy nominee and Golden Globe nominee and has skyrocketed on the Billboard charts in the UK and United States for her widely popular song “Because of the Night,” co-written with Bruce Springsteen. She is often referred to as the “punk poet laureate.” The concert will be opened with a performance by Bob Mould, one of the founding members of Minneapolis-based punk band Hüsker Dü. The outdoor amphitheater at Stern Grove is located on the corner of 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. It is recommended to bring blankets or chairs. Stern Grove Festival concerts are free but registration is required. Registration is first come, first served. Visit https:// www.sterngrove.org/86th-concert-season/patti-smith-bobmould to register. Gates open at 12 p.m. and the concert begins at 2 p.m.
articles.title: Patti Smith performs at Stern Grove August 13

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet will perform Starry Nights at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheatre this week on Thursday and Friday, August 3 and 4. The performances are part of the Stanford Live! Summer Festival. The program includes Violin Concerto, Tchaikovsky Pas de Deux, Blake Works I Pas de Deux, Cinderella Act II Pas de Deux, Swan Lake Act III Pas de Deux and MADCAP; all selections from the company’s 2023 repertoire. The ballet company’s resident choreographer Yuri Possokhov reinvents Igor Stravinsky’s 1931 Violin Concerto in D, originally commissioned and created for San Francisco Ballet’s next@90 festival shown earlier this year. Choreographer William Forsythe’s Blake Works I Pas de Deux features a more modern twist, set to music by young English musician and songwriter James Blake. The production ends with Danielle Rowe’s MADCAP, another hit from the Ballet’s 2023 next@90 festival. The “carnival-inspired” score by Swedish rock artist Par Hägström is paired with Emma Kingsbury’s costumes, and gives the audience a sense of an after-dark carnival. Performances on both nights begin at 7:30 p.m. Gates open at 6:30 p.m. Visit https://live.stanford.edu/calendar/august-2023/ starry-nights to purchase tickets. A performance by San Francisco Ballet at the Stanford Live! Festival Photo courtesy of Stanford University
articles.title: SF Ballet’s Starry Nights at Stanford tomorrow & Friday

articles.text: SF JAZZ will host two iconic New Orleans brass band collectives at Miner Auditorium August 17 through 20. The Preservation Hall Jazz Band is a Crescent City favorite founded by tuba player Allan Jaffe in the early 1960s. The band takes its name from the French Quarter art gallery and has been a fixture there for decades, even performing and touring in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina although their studio was destroyed in the storm. They are regular performing guests at New Orleans’ JazzFest, the largest jazz festival in the country. The big brass band is now headed by Jaffe’s son, tuba player Ben Jaffe, and includes singer-instrumentalist Clint Maedgen, trumpeter Brandon Lewis, pianist Kyle Roussel, drummer Walter Harris, and trombonist Ronell Johnson. The August concerts will include a special rare appearance from longtime Preservation Hall Jazz Band member, 91-year-old saxophonist Charlie Gabriel. Tarriona “Tank” Ball, frontwoman of the two-time GRAMMY-nominated group Tank and The Bangas, is also a New Orleans native. She leads the R&B and funk group with guitarist Danny Abel, bassist Jonathan Johnson, saxophonist Etienne Stoufflet, and background vocalist Anjelika “Jelly” Joseph. All concerts begin at 7 p.m. The Thursday, August 18 show will be streamed live. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/summer23/ preservation-hall-jazz-band/ to purchase tickets. articles.text: Visit the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) this Friday, August 4, as the museum kicks off the 50th anniversary of HipHop curated by native Bay Area artist DJ Jahi. The free event “The Roots of Hip-Hop Culture” begins at 5 p.m. and marks the first time OMCA will have a practitioner of Hip Hop culture curating its “Friday Nights” lineup. Every Friday beginning at 5 p.m., the museum offers food truck options, music, and art activities inspired by the museum’s current exhibitions. This Friday, Hip Hop artist and Oakland native DJ Jahi will spin classic Hip Hop, breakbeats, Reggae, and African Rhythms. Also featured are producers and musicians Andrew Bearford, Ovrkast, OG Jarin, and Demahjiae. Free film screenings from KQED’s If Cities Could Dance series showcases Bay Area dancers and dance-makers. Oakland native Diamano Coura will host a drum circle in the museum garden. For a full lineup, visit https:// museumca.org/event/fridaynights-at-omca-the-roots-of-culture/. The event is free and open to the public. Photo by Katherine Levin Sheehan Hip-Hop artist and Oakland native DJ Jahi. articles.text: Visit Filoli House and Garden in Woodside any day this summer to view its many species of roses, the most bountiful blooms of this season. More than 500 rose bushes, representing 150 different varieties, are now in bloom. Horticulturist Rob Joice said that tending to the rose gardens is one of his favorite aspects of working at Filoli. “I really enjoy the many colors, the multitude of smells, and the challenge of working with each rose’s individual needs and making them as healthy as possible,” he said. Filoli has a variety of Hybrid Tea Roses, Floribunda and Grandiflora. Tea Roses have large blooms at the end of long stems and are commonly sold in florist shops. Floribunda are a modern group of garden roses with a wide color range from lavender to apricot. Grandiflora roses grow larger than their counterparts, sometimes reaching as tall as six feet. Also in bloom are sunflowers, zinnias, and dahlias. Visit https://filoli.org to learn more about what’s in bloom and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Filoli rose gardens in full bloom this summer

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now exhibiting Hell: Arts of Asian Underworlds through September. The new exhibition displays how different Asian cultures view the afterlife of the condemned. Hell exhibits over 40 paintings, sculptures, maps, puppets, and religious objects from India, Tibet, China, Korea, Japan, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, and the Philippines. “There is a presumption that all representations of Hell across Asian cultures are the same or continuous,” said Jeff Durham, Curator of Himalayan Art at the Asian Art Museum. “But in fact, whether they appear in ancient traditions or the work of contemporary artists, depictions of Hell have been extraordinarily diverse: some are terrifying and gruesome, but many are humorCourtesy of Asian Art Museum Detail of Utagawa Yoshifuji, Newly Published Comic Picture of Cats (Shinpan neko no giga), Japan, 1883 ous and playful.” The majority of artworks on view are on loan from other institutions and collections. Pieces owned by the museum are newly acquired and are being shown here for the first time. “This exhibition is like a rollercoaster taking the visitor from excitement to relief; in the end, it shows that Hell is only as bad as we imagine it to be,” Durham said. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/hell-arts-ofasian-underworlds/ to learn more and purchase museum passes.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum now exhibiting Hell: Arts of Asian Underworlds

articles.text: Come enjoy the events and activities at the Center for the Arts this Summer. Sunday, August 13, 5:30 p.m. In the Tradition Piano Trio In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, piano; Rich Trevor, upright bass; and Anthony Pegram, drums – will perform a concert in tribute to Richard Rodgers, the premier composer of the American musical. This concert will be loaded with jazz and pops favorites dating from the ‘20s through the ‘50s, including eleven songs composed by Richard Rodgers. Tickets are available in advance at https://www.bpt.me/5691334, and for $23 at the door. Cash or check only please. Friday, August 18, 7:00 p.m. Junko Kasahara Piano Recital International concert pianist Junko Kasahara from Osaka, Japan, will perform a piano recital of the French Impression music of Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel. Having studied piano in Osaka, St. Petersburg, Paris, and Saarbrücken, she has since performed recitals and in Japan, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, Israel, Russia, Finland, U,S, and Latin America. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, August 2, 2023 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The real music man By Joseph Gold “The bigger they are, the nicer they are.“ This was the philosophy of Rocky Marciano – undefeated heavyweight, boxing champion. His centennial is rapidly approaching on September 1, 2023. I think if Rocky had played music, he would have been great… He had a fabulous work ethic. Let’s explore the Marciano philosophy. In fact, his success rate was almost perfect. I knew him fairly well many years ago. Meredith was a pleasure to work with. He knew every aspect of the music biz. I enjoyed his stories about playing flute and piccolo in the Souza band, and how Souza actually conducted it. After Meredith left the Souza Band, he played first flute in the New York Philharmonic under the famous conductor Arturo Toscanini. And that is just the tip of the iceberg. There is a sad side to this story. People remember, Meredith mainly as a composer of musicals, but he was much more than that. Listen to his symphonic works. He really was one of America’s greatest composers. Another great American composer finally getting his due in concert halls is William Grant Still (1895-1978). I knew him also, but not on a first name basis. The Redwood Symphony under Director Eric K played his Panama Dances. Both composers Pianist Rachel Breen Songwriter Meredith Willson were truly great musicians. As human beings they were delightful to be with. One of the things I remember about William Grant Still was that kids would follow him everywhere he went. I never saw anything like it. Redwood Symphony concert A concert by Redwood Symphony on Saturday evening in Canada College was a mixed bag. Eric K (formerly Eric Kujowsky) is the founder of the orchestra. He is a master conductor with a clear beat and intelligent musicianship. To be honest, the first half of the concert was underwhelming. The second half was devoted entirely to Beethoven’s Fourth Symphony. This was a huge improvement. The direction from the podium was crystal clear, and the orchestra responded dynamically and energetically. I kept wondering what Eric K could do if he had a truly fine professional orchestra. Rachel Breen concert Some friends invited me to hear Rachel Breen’s concert on Sunday afternoon at Piedmont Piano Company. What an artist! She walked onto the stage with a simple demeanor, and then explained what she was about to play. Breen’s entire concert was devoted to the Goldberg Variations by Johan Sebastian Bach. Ordinarily, I want to muzzle the speeches before a concert. But her explanation was about as good as her playing. She said things that were absolutely necessary. And then she began to play. As a pianist, Rachel Breen endeavors to plumb the human condition that lies below the surface of the notes. All of her superb technique is put to the service of the music…and this allows her imagination to run wild. Her demeanor is simplicity itself. Her music making is the highest artistic caliber. articles.text: Well before the start of the bio pic “Oppenheimer” delineating the birth of the atom bomb, the historic mesa was the home of the Los Alamos Ranch School and little else. At 7,350 ft. altitude, the mesa was healthy enough, miles away from traffic, towns, congestion, drugs and booze, a good hour’s drive uphill from Santa Fe. In the words of Richard Colgate of the Long Island toothpaste family, one of the teenaged students boarding there, “It was where East Coast parents sent their unmanageable sons when they couldn’t control them. Horseback riding, stable cleanup, all that.” This was the Wild West escapade that shaped up youths like the Colgate brothers and propelled them, at times reluctantly, toward higher education. One day in the early 1940s, he recalled, a group of well-dressed men in dark overcoats came to check out the spartan campus, their group leaders being introduced as Mr. Smith and Mr. Jones, rather anonymously. “Wait a minute,” Richard thought. He scurried back to his room with its pile of science magazines and leafed through them, quickly unmasking them as J. Robert Oppenheimer, noted nuclear physicist, and “Mr. Jones,” and his buddies were in on the mystery, far ahead of the officials, reporters, and enemy agents. Soon after, the U.S. government took over the site, shut down the school, and left one rustic building, the Fuller Lodge, still standing today as testament to the early history prior to the super-secret research facility’s launching. Richard long reveled in the memory of his Wild West days, even after becoming an East Coast entrepreneur and founding a couple of companies. Bro Stirling became president of the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology and also went to work at the Los Alamos National Laboratories. There he lived in the employees’ housing till his death in 2013, 70 years after the Ranch School, in perhaps the longest tenure ever recorded there, striving to produce an ever more efficient commercial diesel engine. And today the Ranch School is all but forgotten, a footnote to one of the colossal weapons developments of the 20th century that ended and won World War Two abruptly in 1945. articles.text: Family Sanity is sponsoring a solo show by Brian Copeland at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Founded by former Piedmont resident Lisa Scimens, Family Sanity provides resources in mental health for parents of older teens and young adults. To celebrate its 10th anniversary, it is presenting a special performance of Copeland’s show, The Waiting Period at 7 p.m. on Friday, September 8, at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. As a fundraiser for the organization, adult tickets are $50, with older teens admitted at $20. Due to mature content, the show is not appropriate for children and younger teens. For advance tickets, please go to https://bit.ly/3rBLcy3. For more information on Family Sanity, please visit https:// www.familysanity.org. Copeland is an actor, comedian, playwright and author, and a former radio talk show host on KGO in San Francisco. The Waiting Period (Laughter in the Darkness) was winner of the 2015 Theater Bay Area Award for Outstanding Production of a Solo Play. This show is an unrelenting look at a 10-day period in Copeland’s life – the mandatory 10-day waiting period before he could lay his hands on the newly purchased gun with which he planned to take his own life. Even in the midst of severe turmoil. Copeland’s wonderful sense of the comedy of life does Actor and comedian Brian Copeland not desert him (how much should he spend on the gun?). Copeland hopes this very personal, and ultimately redemptive, story will reach people who struggle with depression, as well as their families and loved ones. Interspersed with interviews with others suffering from depression, the play offers an insider’s view. As critic Sam Hurwitt put it in The Idiolect: “It’s a play I’d strongly recommend to anyone who is now or has ever been depressed or who knows someone in that situation. But honestly, it’s such a strong piece that I’d recommend it just as heartily to anyone who’s ever been human.”
articles.title: Family Sanity brings Brian Copeland show to Piedmont

Yet he agrees to one more major job at Fenway Park. It turns out to be a riveting and protracted payroll robbery that demonstrates Affleck’s skills behind the camera. The action scenes are intense and tightly rendered. It’s all but impossible to watch The Town and not be reminded of the classic heist movie, Heat, an underrated film when released, starring Al Pacino and Robert De Niro. It summarizes, in so many ways, the power of the durable heist genre, spare and realistic with a gritty urban carapace that works from the first frame. The Town. Written and directed by Ben Affleck. I try to imagine what Sally Field thought when she first read the screenplay for Hello, My Name is Doris. I assume she was both moved and excited. She recognized in the role of Doris Miller a character that while eccentric, was also deeply human. And she must have immediately understood that while the story had its comedic moments, there was also a sad, lonely quality to Doris that transcended all of her peculiar idiosyncrasies. This is a film about isolation and regret and a life not fully lived. The movie opens with a funeral. Only a few friends and family members are in attendance. Doris sits alone, grieving; the deceased is her mother, whose profile is barely visible in the coffin. Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with brica-brac. Doris, now in her 60s, works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry, and despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves, To most of her young co-workers she remains essentially invisible – seen but not seen. That is until a new co-worker, John Fremont (Max Greenfield), thirty-something, arrives and for a few moments on a crowded elevator sees Doris… really sees her. He smiles and because she’s holding a lamp, reaches up and adjusts her rhinestone cat glasses. And that moment begins a transformation for Doris, one that takes her completely by surprise Sally Field and Max Greenfield in Hello, My Name Is Doris and touches her to the core. She is awakened, consumed by feelings that cause her to all but levitate, as if she had been this loose string on a violin that is now taut and vibrates as she begins to have these Walter Mitty moments where John is concerned. Reality and fantasy begin to merge. Doris has fallen in love. A woman just past middle age, so taken that she begins to cyberstalk John on his Facebook page, convinced that he imagines a Doris of almost 40 years ago and not the person she has become, a woman on the cusp of old age. Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field is such a consummate actress that she manages to create a person who while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues) is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood. She is in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. Adding to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of decades old unread magazines. But her pack rat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology. Like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train has, long ago, left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it. Now, suddenly, she has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Directed by Michael Showalter. Starring Sally Field, May Greenfield, Tyne Daly. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

Her brother, Todd (Stephen Root), and his wife Cindy (Wendi McLeadon-Covey) are across the aisle in another pew. Doris has spent her life living with and caring for her mother, sharing a rather funky Long Island house that is filled (or you might say stuffed) with brica-brac. Doris, now in her 60s, works for a New York company that has recently morphed into a hip millennial clothing outfit. She is a holdover, quietly tending to the business’ accounting and data entry, and despite her flea market retro outfits – wide skirts and sweaters and colorful scarves, To most of her young co-workers she remains essentially invisible – seen but not seen. That is until a new co-worker, John Fremont (Max Greenfield), thirty-something, arrives and for a few moments on a crowded elevator sees Doris… really sees her. He smiles and because she’s holding a lamp, reaches up and adjusts her rhinestone cat glasses. And that moment begins a transformation for Doris, one that takes her completely by surprise Sally Field and Max Greenfield in Hello, My Name Is Doris and touches her to the core. She is awakened, consumed by feelings that cause her to all but levitate, as if she had been this loose string on a violin that is now taut and vibrates as she begins to have these Walter Mitty moments where John is concerned. Reality and fantasy begin to merge. Doris has fallen in love. A woman just past middle age, so taken that she begins to cyberstalk John on his Facebook page, convinced that he imagines a Doris of almost 40 years ago and not the person she has become, a woman on the cusp of old age. Doris could easily have become a caricature; however, Field is such a consummate actress that she manages to create a person who while deeply flawed (of course Doris has issues) is not a comic crazy lady in the neighborhood. She is in possession of a wisdom which she reluctantly shares. Adding to Doris’ complexity is the fact that she is a hoarder. Her house is filled with items (old shampoo bottles, lids, one wooden ski, stacks of decades old unread magazines. But her pack rat instincts are not offered up as an insurmountable pathology. Like her mode of dress, she resists the idea that all those years have slipped by. Now she suddenly and painfully realizes that the train has, long ago, left the station and she failed to get on board. She explains as much to John as they sit in a small café and talk. John is clueless about what his presence means to Doris. She had a chance to make a life, to grasp the ring, and she missed it. Now, suddenly, she has convinced herself that she has another chance. Hello, My Name is Doris is a charming and brave character study, carried almost entirely by Field. She is convincing and wonderful as she inhabits completely the persona of Doris. Watching her is a troubling wonder. Hello, My Name is Doris. Directed by Michael Showalter. Starring Sally Field, May Greenfield, Tyne Daly. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated R. articles.text: Part 66 Just as Architecture and Landscape architecture are made up of separate pieces that thoughtfully combined together make up a comprehensive whole, so too does my favorite field of Urban Design. We have defined Urban Design before in this column as, simply stated, the siting or arrangement of buildings and the design of the spaces between them – the “interstitial spaces” around and between buildings. This discipline involves a combination of Planning, Architecture, and Landscape Architecture and includes streets, courtyards, plazas, parks with all their related details. The field of Urban Design I would say most often deals with these public spaces. A common and important component of Urban Design is the associated outdoor (or indoor/outdoor) food service venues. Seen in all shapes and sizes all over the world, these eating areas often are found at and form an integral part of the heart of a place. There is something very valuable about these spaces--they usually provide a vitality and energy while acting as a useful, functional part of a neighborhood. Not only do we eat at these public venues, but lingering while sitting, eating, drinking, relaxing, and people watching facilitates interaction with our current neighbors and meeting new ones. articles.text: Alkali Rye and Mikami Vineyards Alkali Rye is located at 3256 Grand Avenue in Oakland. Phone (510) 488-3637 (sipalkalirye.com). This month’s profile features two Asian owned businesses, Alkali Rye and Mikami Vineyards. Alkali Rye is a beverage shop at 3256 Grand Avenue in Oakland that highlights underrepresented makers. Kori Chen is one of the owners. Q: What inspired you to open Alkali Rye? KC: I opened this with my business partner, Jessica Moncada-Konte. She and I have worked in the food and beverage industry for many years now. And we thought about a retail business that highlights a lot of the drinks that we love and also the rhythm of how we kind of drink throughout the day. So we call it a beverage shop. We like to start our day with coffee. We also like to drink a lot of tea during the day, have some wine or a cocktail at night. Q: How do you decide which beverage makers and producers to support? KC: We taste a lot. It’s a tough job. It has to be delicious. But we also have a mission of trying to be intentional about working with underrepresented producers or people that are being very intentional and values driven, with how they approach their practice and their businesses. Alkali Rye is also a champion for sustainable agriculture, and carries Mikami Wines, founded by Jason Mikami of Oakland and whose grandfather immigrated to Lodi in 1896. He spent his time farming grapes until 1942 when Jason’s grandfather and father were forced into a Japanese internment camp in Arkansas and had to give up their property. Jason’s mother was in Hiroshima, Japan and is an atomic bomb survivor but suffered burn injuries. When his dad and father eventually returned to Lodi in 1945 they went back to growing grapes, the only work they knew. However, they didn’t own the farm anymore and had to rent it. Finally, they saved enough to purchase the farm in the 1950’s and in 1963 they expanded as a result of their hard work to 15 acres of land in Lodi. Q: How did Mikami vineyards start? JM: It goes back almost 120 years now. It started with my grandfather, who immigrated from Japan to California in 1896, and eventually that led to a life in grape growing. The grape growing tradition has gone, until carried on by my father before me. And then when my father passed away in 2004, it was my turn to figure out what to do with our family vineyard and that led to a decision to start making wine in 2005. We released our first vintage in 2008. Q: What is it like being a third generation grower? JM: It’s something that I’m really proud of in the sense that if you look at the Japanese-American community and growing up in Lodi, we were one of very few The Mikami family circa 1925-1930

articles.text: In the heart of the Yamhill-Carlton region the WillaKenzie Estate is named for two of the Willamette Valley’s major rivers: the Willamette and McKenzie. The estate began in 1991 when Burgundian Bernard Lacroute and his wife Ronni purchased a cattle farm near the town of Yamhill and began to plant grapes. In 1997 they opened their tasting room and started their wine club becoming one of Willamette Valley’s first direct-to-consumer wine programs. Over the years the wines gained notoriety including being served at several White House state dinners. In 2016 the Lacroutes retired, and the estate was sold to Jackson Family Wines who lovingly shepherd this lovely property. Favorite Wine 2019 WillaKenzie Pinot Noir Terre Basses This is one of the most powerfully concentrated Pinot Noir I have tasted. It could pass for a Cote Rotie from France. Bursting with aromas of raspberries and sweet red fruits mingled with rose petals, orange, exotic spices and a subtle hint of espresso, its’s full-bodied, layered and enveloping with incredible depth at the core, beautifully refined tannins and a long expansive finish.
articles.title: WillaKenzie Estate

articles.text: Our first stop was Domaine Willamette which has several facilities including a huge new tasting room with restaurant. Founded in 1983 by Jim Bernau, who has become one of the leading forces in Oregon wine. Jim hosted us to a gourmet lunch highlighted with both his sparkling and still wines. The sparkling Brut Rose was light and crisp with hints of strawberries. The many Pinot Noirs were finely formed, complex and layered and showed great aging potential. I didn’t expect to be served a Syrah on this trip, but Jim purchased some vineyards in Walla Walla Washington and created the Maison Blue label. The Syrah was deep, rich, full-bodied, and voluptuous reminding me of the Syrahs from Rhone Valley’s Hermitage region. articles.text: The weather was great and there was another large turnout of 47 walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra last Wednesday, July 26, for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk. An unusual yucca in Piedmont that is visible right now is in front of a home on Hampton Road at Crest Road. It will be in bloom for a short time, so the Wednesday walkers chose it as their destination. The group could then continue on to some of the streets they don’t see very often. The walkers headed off going up Highland Avenue. They decided to have a little variation from their usual route to Wildwood Avenue by continuing down Highland to the little walked, lovely Caperton Avenue and going to Sheridan Avenue. They wanted to check on the new garage that has been under construction at a previously garageless 1906 Albert Farr designed home on Crocker. The group has been monitoring its progress for months and noticed a new, spiral staircase at the back. After their inspection, the walkers went on Hampton Road past Crocker Park (also known to locals as Bear Park due to the Benjamin Bufano sculpture of a mother bear and her two cubs), where they noticed a magnolia tree starting to bloom. After a short walk they came to Crest Road. The walkers were immediately impressed by this unusual blooming tree. Jim Kellogg advised the walkers that it was a chaparral yucca, also known as our Lord’s candle, Spanish bayonet, Quixote yucca, and foothill yucca. A Wikipedia search further revealed that this is a flowering plant native to southwest parts of North America. It has a stemless cluster of long, rigid leaves which end in sharp points of gray-green color. The leaf edges are finely saw-toothed. These trees grow extremely fast, and reach three to ten feet tall, bearing hundreds of bell-shaped white to purplish flowers about an inch in diameter. The fruit is a dry winged capsule, which splits open at maturity to release seeds. The plant usually takes over five years to reach maturity. The group thought the tree was wonderful with its plume of flowers and lizard skinlike bark, which they chose as a backdrop for a group photo. Those who didn’t feel like climbing further returned to the center of town, and the rest of the group continued to Hampton to Inverleith Terrace and Estates Drive, and then down Estates to Selborne Drive. Along the way they enjoyed the view of Oakland, but San Francisco was hidden in haze. At Selborne they went onto Sandringham Road and then a quick side trip on the lovely Marlborough Court culde-sac. In the front of one home there was a forest of beach ball sized and shaped box hedges almost blanketing the yard. Back on Sandringham, the walkers made their way down to Hampton to La Salle Avenue and St. James Drive to see some different streets on the way back to the Community Hall. In all, it was a 3-½ mile walk with some good climbing and lots of interesting vegetation on a beautiful, Piedmont summer morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. The Walking on Wednesdays group took a photo by a yucca plant in bloom at the corner of Crest and Hampton. articles.text: Patricia Lyons White of Piedmont, California, passed away surrounded by family on Wednesday, July 19, 2023, at age 68, following eight months with pancreatic cancer. Born on April 25, 1955, in Dearborn, Michigan, Patty was the youngest of seven children of Raymond McKenzie Lyons and Dorothy Jean Walsh. Patty demonstrated her sense of independence and adventure early on when in first grade she was told to sit by herself in the hallway for disruptive behavior. Seeing no point in that, she decided to walk home instead. In high school, she earned top grades, served one year as class president, and graduated a semester early. Early graduation allowed her to spend eight months in the Virgin Islands with her mother, who was there recovering from a health condition. Patty went on to attend Michigan State University, again earning top grades, completing her graduation requirements early, and serving (while also having a lot of fun) on the University Events and Entertainment Committee. She spent part of one summer hitchhiking with a couple of friends through the Northern Rockies and did another trip traveling on her own on the Alaska Ferry to visit a friend in Fairbanks. Not long after graduation from college at age 21 she decided one day, ‘I think I’ll move to California’, just to ‘see what the big deal was.’ She packed her bags the next day with no real plan and a check from her Dad to cover one way airfare back to Michigan for when her ‘California dream inevitably fails.’ Patty settled in sunny Santa Barbara right on the beach. Her dad was surprised when he received his check in the mail a few weeks later. For the next 47 years, California was her home. Proving her dad wrong was just icing on the cake. After enjoying her time in Santa Barbara, Patty enrolled at UC Hastings College of Law in San Francisco, working as a bouncer at a local bar to help pay her way. Following graduation, she was hired as an assistant district attorney with the city of San Francisco, where she developed a reputation for her effective court room ferocity. Patty then met the love of her life on a blind date after skeptically agreeing to have dinner with Dan White. Her skepticism was due to her involvement at the time with the prosecution of the infamous SF criminal Dan White. Thinking her friends must be having a laugh, she was pleasantly surprised when she arrived for her date to find not only Dan White was real but he was a perfect match for her. The couple got married in 1982 and were hard to separate for the next 40 years. Dan and Patty moved to Piedmont, California in 1986 where they raised three kids and many Patty White on the first day of school at Beach School with children Mike, Katie, and Brian Former Piedmont Mayor Patty White in her cheerful pink dress at a city function. dogs. Despite her talents as an attorney, Patty left her job so she could focus on her true calling, being a mom. In Piedmont, Patty quickly became a pillar of the community, taking on numerous public service roles. She served as the hearing officer for the Piedmont Minor Offender program, as well as numerous school committees. She was appointed to the Piedmont Planning Commission in 1988, serving as chair for six years. She was then elected to the Piedmont City Council in 1994, serving for eight years, including as Mayor from 1998 to 2000. She also served on the Alameda County Waste Management and Recycling Board for six years as chair. Her friends and family will always remember her wit, charm, and limitless hospitality. Strongwilled and self-assured, Patty often did things her own way with a focus on making the lives of those she touched better. Her rare blend of intelligence, determination, humor, and generosity will be missed. Patty passed away at 6am on Wednesday July 19, 2023, from pancreatic cancer. Dan, Brian, Mike, and Katie took turns staying with her all night, and were able to be with her in the moments before she passed. Our last days together as a family were filled with music, singing, and countless expressions of love. We will miss her and are forever grateful for the time we had with her. Patty is survived by her husband Dan, children Brian and wife Cristina, Mike and Katie, and grandchildren Anthony and Francis White. She is also survived by her sister Holly Connell and brothers Paul and Kelly Lyons. A funeral mass will be held at 11 a.m. on Thursday, August 10, at Corpus Christi Church, 322 St. James Drive at Park Boulevard in Piedmont, followed by a reception at Lake Chalet. The White family: Katie (left), Brian, Patty, Mike, and Dan

articles.text: A stolen BMW without plates entered Piedmont on Oakland Avenue shortly after 2 a.m. on Tuesday July 18. Officers initially could not located the 2020 gray BMW 330, but two hours later the vehicle, being driven by a 16-year-old crashed in Piedmont Park. At approximately 4:00 a.m. a Piedmont officer in the area of Highland & Oakland avenues noticed the stolen BMW speeding on Highland not far from Piedmont Park. As the officer made a U-turn in pursuit, the speeding vehicle crashed in Piedmont Park instead of negotiating the turn in the road by the Exedra. The BMW damaged the grass, a stone retaining wall, and came to rest in a collision with a drinking fountain and park bench. The suspect immediately fled on foot, but another police officer heard the sound of the crash and saw the suspect, a 16-year old, hiding under a bench, where he was detained. He was not injured and was arrested without incident. Police recovered stolen Amazon packages, license plates, burglary tools and knives from the stolen vehicle. Piedmont Fire Department transported the juvenile suspect to Children’s Hospital, where he was medically cleared and later booked into Juvenile Hall. The scene of the crash near the bridge in Piedmont Park. The stolen gray 2020 BMW 330 was found to have stolen Amazon packages in the trunk, burglary tools, stolen license plates, and knives.

articles.text: “According to the investigators who watched video from the premises: it appeared to be an accidental fire,” said Michael Hunt, Chief of Staff for the Oakland Fire Department. “There was a slow smoldering fire in the kitchen area.” The original clubhouse was built as WPA project in 1939. The kitchen, bar, restrooms, and restaurant of the clubhouse were destroyed. Chabot GC has reopened a concession stand, called the Hill House, near holes 3 and 12, for on-course food and drinks. Oakland Fire Department’s Station 28 was the first to respond, but the blaze was large enough to trigger a two-alarm fire requiring 40 firefighters to respond. The Fire Department was able to prevent the flames from spreading to the nearby areas which include heavily wooded residential areas near the Oakland Zoo. Phone lines are still disabled at the golf course. Golfers wanting to schedule a tee time on the 18-hole public course need to go online to: Lakechabotgolf.com. The 9-hole golf course and frisbee golf course are also open for walk-on play. articles.text: On Saturday afternoon July 29 shortly before 2 p.m., a Piedmont resident near Park Way and Monte Avenue was walking from his driveway to the front door when he saw two young men running towards him from across the street. One person pointed a black firearm at the victim’s face and demanded he give them his keys and wallet, fearing for his safety the victim handed over the items without a struggle. The two suspects then drove off in the resident’s dark gray 2021 BMW X3. The resident observed a second vehicle, a Lexus IS 300, following behind the BMW. Both vehicles fled up Moraga and towards Highway 13. A short time later, a Piedmont officer located the BMW and the Lexus. Piedmont officers were already looking for the Lexus after receiving multiple calls regarding a suspicious vehicle in the area of Lexford Avenue and Huntleigh Road. After a brief pursuit, the Lexus was involved in a single vehicle collision. The suspect driving the Lexus ran from the crashed vehicle and was picked up by the occupants of the stolen BMW. The suspects all fled south in the BMW on Highway 13. The Lexus was recovered by Piedmont Police. It was wanted by San Jose Highway Patrol for a carjacking incident one week prior on July 22. The BMW was eventually tracked to a location in unincorporated Hayward and was located by Alameda County deputies. The vehicle was towed for evidence in an effort to identify the suspects. The suspects are described as three Black males. The suspect armed with the black handgun is described as in his teens or early 20s, 6’ tall, thin build, with a brown and black hoodie, and a full-face mask. The second suspect is described as thin, 5’8”, wearing a black hoodie. There is no description of the third subject who was driving the Lexus. Anyone with information or video of these vehicles or incidents is asked to contact Piedmont Police Department at 510- 420-3000.
articles.title: Carjacking in Piedmont on July 29

Because the tank still contains gasoline, it is considered a toxic substance, and the city is required to submit an inspection and work plan to the county for its removal. Gonzales said that Public Works staff is currently preparing a plan to submit to the Alameda County Department of Environmental Health. As of Monday, July 31, it has not yet been submitted. It typically takes two to three weeks for the county to return a review and authorize the removal of the toxic substance. When the previous tank was found, this process took the County two days about three weeks later: one to pump out the fuel in it, and another to physically remove it. Once the new tank is removed, the subcontractor GEOCON will sample the soil where the tank was found to test it for contamination. Polluted soil found on the pool site is hauled off a waste management landfill in Livermore. The cleaner soil “is being hauled off for ‘beneficial reuse’ for future construction projects elsewhere,” Gonzales said. The pool project is still on track to finish on-schedule, in summer 2024. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. Climate Goals Continued from page 1 August 2022, said that Piedmont is joining nine other cities in Alameda County that have committed to net zero emissions by 2045, joining this state, national and global trend. Policies and recommendations which achieve these climate goals in Piedmont, said Roberts, “must be centered on decarbonization efforts in combination with lifestyle changes.” Some examples of the city’s decarbonization efforts, she said, are an all-electric aquatic facility at the future Piedmont Community Pool, a rebate program for Piedmonters interested in electrifying their homes, public electric vehicle charging stations, bike lane and pedestrian crosswalk improvements, and an upcoming initiative for easier solar energy permits. Examples of the city’s efforts addressing lifestyle changes include free compost giveaway, three-series recycling and waste bins in parks and public areas, public drinking water stations, and a free curbside organic materials collection service. City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore said that within about 90 days, city staff will present the Council with specific policies and recommendations to meet the updated climate goals. CRIME REPORT Carjacking in Piedmont on July 29 By Jay Russell On Saturday afternoon July 29 shortly before 2 p.m., a Piedmont resident near Park Way and Monte Avenue was walking from his driveway to the front door when he saw two young men running towards him from across the street. One person pointed a black firearm at the victim’s face and demanded he give them his keys and wallet, fearing for his safety the victim handed over the items without a struggle. The two suspects then drove off in the resident’s dark gray 2021 BMW X3. The resident observed a second vehicle, a Lexus IS 300, following behind the BMW. Both vehicles fled up Moraga and towards Highway 13. A short time later, a Piedmont officer located the BMW and the Lexus. Piedmont officers were already looking for the Lexus after receiving multiple calls regarding a suspicious vehicle in the area of Lexford Avenue and Huntleigh Road. After a brief pursuit, the Lexus was involved in a single vehicle collision. The suspect driving the Lexus ran from the crashed vehicle and was picked up by the occupants of the stolen BMW. The suspects all fled south in the BMW on Highway 13. The Lexus was recovered by Piedmont Police. It was wanted by San Jose Highway Patrol for a carjacking incident one week prior on July 22. The BMW was eventually tracked to a location in unincorporated Hayward and was located by Alameda County deputies. The vehicle was towed for evidence in an effort to identify the suspects. The suspects are described as three Black males. The suspect armed with the black handgun is described as in his teens or early 20s, 6’ tall, thin build, with a brown and black hoodie, and a full-face mask. The second suspect is described as thin, 5’8”, wearing a black hoodie. There is no description of the third subject who was driving the Lexus. Anyone with information or video of these vehicles or incidents is asked to contact Piedmont Police Department at 510- 420-3000. Lake Chabot Golf Continued from page 1 “According to the investigators who watched video from the premises: it appeared to be an accidental fire,” said Michael Hunt, Chief of Staff for the Oakland Fire Department. “There was a slow smoldering fire in the kitchen area.” The original clubhouse was built as WPA project in 1939. The kitchen, bar, restrooms, and restaurant of the clubhouse were destroyed. Chabot GC has reopened a concession stand, called the Hill House, near holes 3 and 12, for on-course food and drinks. Oakland Fire Department’s Station 28 was the first to respond, but the blaze was large enough to trigger a two-alarm fire requiring 40 firefighters to respond. The Fire Department was able to prevent the flames from spreading to the nearby areas which include heavily wooded residential areas near the Oakland Zoo. Phone lines are still disabled at the golf course. Golfers wanting to schedule a tee time on the 18-hole public course need to go online to: Lakechabotgolf.com. The 9-hole golf course and frisbee golf course are also open for walk-on play. Junior Golf Academy looks for donations The Lake Chabot Junior Golf Academy, a non-profit, all volunteer, totally free junior golf instruction program, was founded in 1993 by former Oakland Raider Raymond Chester, then the General Manager of Lake Chabot. Tommy Scales, the longtime golf coach at Piedmont High, was instrumental in helpThe fire originated in the kitchen of the Clubhouse according to fire inspectors. ing the Academy grow. As a result of the fire in June and the loss of all its equipment, Lake Chabot Junior Golf Academy is seeking donations of golf clubs and golf equipment for its young aspiring golfers. The Academy was created with the original goal of helping youth living in urban areas and underserved communities to have free access to the sport. “One of the things that is unique [about the Academy] is that we teach the parents how to play golf, too. The kids in the inner city only know their own little environment; we expand that,” explained David Killingsworth, Vice President of the Academy. “The code of conduct for the kids is based upon life lessons. We sort of subtly teach these kids how they are supposed to conduct themselves in life, like being on time and how to talk to people. They are rules to live by,” he added. The academy loans out sets of clubs to kids and provides instruction year round totally free. Not only was all of its golf equipment and instructional material destroyed, but the computer containing all its records was lost to the fire. Memorabilia, including signed footballs and golf balls were also destroyed. “[The academy] also serves as a melting pot. It’s not just giving towards disadvantaged kids of color, we have all kids here,” said President of the Academy Clarence Traywick. Piedmont resident Ted Lehye created a video to raise money and create awareness about the Lake Chabot Golf Junior Academy. Firefighters kept the fire from spreading to the nearby woods in the Oakland hills. articles.text: 40-yard line as the time expired. Watching Moura’s final shot in the waning seconds trickle across the line past Ajax’s Andre Onana’s dive gave birth to a new a fan thousands of miles away in California, I was jumping and screaming in my apartment like I had been a lifelong follower. In the time since then, discovering the organization’s 140 years of tradition gained my interest. Like college football in America, the majority of European clubs have been around a long, long time and are steeped in traditions. For Tottenham, they were a haven for England’s Jewish population in the 1930s. They became the target of racist chants of other English fan bases, which called Tottenham fans “Yids” or “Yiddos”. In the 1980’s, Hotspur supporters reclaimed the slurs and have used them as a term of endearment ever since. This year, Tottenham took its preseason tour to Bangkok, perfectly lining up with my vacation at the Piedmont . The match was Hotspur squaring off with Leicester City, which recently got relegated from the Premier League to the division below it. The tour marked possibly the final time for Hotspur supporters to watch England’s captain, Harry Kane, in person amidst trade rumors bubbling with German superpower Bayern Munich. However, Tottenham scheduled the match during Thailand’s monsoon season. On Sunday, July 23, rain began to build an hour before kickoff, resulting in a water-logged pitch that prevented balls from bouncing off of the ground – literally sticking like an arrow shot into the grass. The match resulted in a cancelation, but it was a joy to sit with fellow Tottenham supporters and practice all the chants I’ve spent time learning over the years. And for a Hotspur supporter, any time is a good time to talk trash about Arsenal, our North London arch nemesis. Even with the match called off, hundreds of devout Thai fans stayed in the stands to chant the songs they’ve been rehearsing in their homes. Though the match wasn’t played, it was an unforgettable experience to be huddled in a hallway with people from Thailand, South Korea, and England—often answering questions about what made me a Spurs fan willing to come all the way from California. It’s not the pursuit of glory that makes a fan, but the seeking of passion and tradition. And with July 23 being a totally inglorious day, the passion in each Thai Hotspur supporter was unmistakable. Lilia Afrasiabi shows off the outline of a flower she plans to paint. painting techniques, children attending the camp brainstorm stories with a sketchbook, and explore how to tell them through different media, such as paper models of a setting, drawings and ceramic sculptures of characters, and designing and coloring real objects, like a backpack which one of their characters might use. Goldstein, who has taught for over 15 years in Piedmont, Berkeley, and San Francisco is a Fulbright Scholar and a Yale University National Teacher Fellow. Her love for art first began through a cartooning class she took at the age of eight with Al Baruch, who created the character of Captain Hook in the Disney film Peter Pan. “Cartoons and comics are often central to the questions when I ask kids to consider what art means,” she said. “For example, how does the idea of other people who may look at your art someday change or shape the possibilities of the work? How may it inspire the audience to create their own work? When the kids go traveling in the summer, I ask them to consider the places, people and things that they’re most inspired to bring back with them, and to consider what’s most fun about using them to create their own story.” A question she asks kids at Creativity Camp is: “What about a story – one you read, one you make – makes you interested in it? Much of what makes main characters interesting owes to the differences between them, so we start there. On the visual level this means drawing a variety of different eyes, noses, and mouths. On the conceptual level this means thinking about differences in where these characters could live, how they could think, what they may be doing with their lives. The great thing about creating a story is that it always leads to another.” Audrey Wong displays a drawing of a room in her dream home. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir (PEBCC), led by Artistic Director Eric Tuan, hosted 10 visiting choirs last week to put on the 12th Golden Gate Choral Festival. Three hundred and fifty youth singers from some of the most celebrated international choirs, including six from outside the U.S., participated in the event which builds global ambassadorship and puts on a world class choral competition. The festival, which began in 1991, takes place every three years but has not happened since 2018 due to COVID. This year’s festivities brought talented choral groups with singers ranging in age from nine to 20 from near and far. Celebrated choirs from across the globe traveled from the Philippines, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, and Australia. They joined the four ensembles from PEBCC and other acclaimed U.S. choral groups. The festival spanned six days from July 9 to July 15, with an opening concert at the Spreckels Band Shell in Golden Gate Park in San Francisco and a closing concert at Kohman Auditorium on the Alameda High School campus. articles.text: Inside the construction project at Witter Field In a recent visit with Piedmont School District Facilities Director Pete Palmer, he explained that 111,000 square feet of Witter Field have been removed, and 10-15 inches of the material below has been hauled out by nearly 200 truckloads as of July 17. Palmer currently is overseeing construction of the $4,150,000 turf and irrigation replacement project at Witter Field, a job expected to last until December. FieldTurf, the synthetic turf which covers the field, had not been replaced in over 16 years, causing drainage issues, rendering Witter into a shallow lake during heavy rains. The new field will utilize a 9-inch deep section of permeable rock below the synthetic turf field and no sand. All the sand from the previous substrate has been removed and will be replaced with larger particles. “The sand acted like a piece of plastic under there; moisture would just sit on top of it,” explained Palmer. articles.text: After 17 years of service in Piedmont, City Clerk John Tulloch will end his tenure on Friday, August 4. The City Council declared at its meeting on July 17 that August 4 will be declared John Oliver Tulloch Day. “John’s support has been invaluable as I embark on this journey with the City of Piedmont,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, who was hired in early April. “His devotion to public service and to this community was apparent from our very first meeting,” Moore continued. “Though we’ve worked together only a short time, I will miss his counsel, companionship, and insight. I’m sorry to see him go and wish him the best in future endeavors.” In a discussion with the Post on July 10, Tulloch described his long association with the city in which he grew up. “One of the reasons that I went into government in the first place is because of my experience working with the city as a kid,” said Tulloch, a third-generation Piedmonter. “After being in Schoolmates during my time at Havens and Wildwood, I volunteered in basically every department in Piedmont, particularly working with the Recreation Department in several different jobs,” he said. “When I was five,” he continued, “I would even hang around the fire station to stare at the engines until the firefighters gave me a set of their old gear; I still have it. Under the former Recreation Director Mark Delventhal I worked my first high school job as tennis monitor, where I would supervise the tennis courts on weekends. This community has been a part of me since the very beginning.” Tulloch graduated from Piedmont High School in 1996 and studied at the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Washington, earning an undergraduate degree in politics and government in John Tulloch, who has worked in City Hall for 17 years, is leaving his position as City Clerk on Friday, August 4.
articles.title: City Clerk John Tulloch leaving on August 4

articles.text: At their Monday, July 17, meeting, the City Council awarded planning firm JZMK Partners a contract for $588,000 to prepare the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, which provides guidelines for potential implementation of housing in Moraga Canyon. At the meeting, Councilmember Tom Ramsey provided some clarity. The city “is not producing a design … to build something that we’re going to pay for. That’s not what this is. It’s a plan to study the economic and on-site impacts of potential housing in Moraga Canyon,” he said. “This is part of our Housing Element and it’s a requirement of state law. To not do this, we would not be in compliance with state law.” Moraga Canyon Specific Plan JZMK, a Costa Mesa-based firm, will study facets of the Moraga Canyon site including existing land use, utility locations, and topography. The firm will then use this information to create hypothetical housing plans, which will be evaluated for their economic feasibility and effect in Piedmont. After a period of community engagement to determine a preferred plan, JZMK will then create a more detailed site plan, including development standards which will be met for any future housing in Moraga Canyon. One of the key parts of the city’s Housing Element, the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is intended to plan for potential housing and infrastructure additions on city-owned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. The main parts of the plan, which allows two years for implementation, are 132 units of new housing, 60 of which would be lower-income; improved city facilities and recreational open space; improved bicycle, pedestrian, and traffic safety; and wildfire safety measures. Piedmont’s Housing Element, currently in its 6th cycle, outlines proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031, a number assigned by the state. This cycle is repeated every eight years. Per state law, “If we chose not to go down this path, we would need to find alternative sites for the units of new housing” than Moraga Canyon, said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. Funding The City Council agenda report for the consultant contract states, “An estimated two- thirds of the [Moraga Canyon Specific Plan] work is anticipated [to be completed] in FY 2023-2024 which amounts to $400,000 in the Approved Budget” from the General Fund for that year. Another $200,000 for the Moraga Canyon will be set aside for the budget in 2024-2025. pages.text: Wednesday, July 19, 2023 3 Witter Field Continued from page 1 Moisture from the area surrounding Witter Field, including Piedmont Park, runs downhill until congregating on the southern end zone side, towards Wildwood Avenue. The new field will slightly slope towards the existing manhole located near the southern end zone. The manhole is connected to the existing city box culvert. The field project directly affects the residents of over 75 homes in the area which have to adjust to new no-parking restrictions in front of their homes. Residents near the Winsor Gate are also concerned about flooding and the impact of the new drainage system which feeds into the end point of Bushy Dell Creek. Residents have been less than satisfied by City and school district hydrology reports to handle large rains like the ones that came last winter. But Palmer is confident the drainage being installed will do the job. “There won’t be any water on this field. If this field doesn’t drain water, I’ll be working somewhere else,” said Palmer, who is a PHS alumni, and has been the Facilities Director since 2015. Along the sides of the field a new perforated subdrain trench is capturing water that feeds through the base rock and drain rock. Piping up to 15 inches wide will sit below drainmat and organic fieldturf, the same kind of turf as at Memorial Stadium at UC Berkeley. This week, the project has currently moved to the fine grading and leveling process. In August, the construction The dark circle in the bottom right is a manhole which leads to the Bushy Dell Creek pipe to a sewer. project is bringing in Class 2 drain rock which will lead to nine days of trucking in August and 10 days of trucking in September. Residents affected by parking changes have commented that parking has remained 100% in a no-parking state, whether trucking happens or not. “People have asked if the no-parking signs can be removed when there are no trucks going, but its unpredictable when deliveries can be made,” said Palmer. When the school year starts on August 9, Palmer expects there to be a bigger demand placed on the Wildwood Avenue dropoff area for the elementary school. He is working with Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalez to get the loading zone at the school extended by up to four car lengths. Palmer hopes to be able to open up the main concourse walkway above the Witter Field bleachers for pedestrians when school opens. The Wildwood lower playground is fenced off now except on weekends. During the school year, teachers will have access to bring Wildwood students to the lower playground. “The main thing we will be focusing on in the fall is safety, that is the number one priority,” said Palmer. articles.text: For one week in July, the Piedmont Community Church gym becomes the site of battle for determined young students at a fencing camp operated by Piedmont Fencing Team coach David Sinkkonen has been conducting the summer camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department for 10 years now. The camp held the week of July 10-14, was attended by 18 boys and girls from 3rd through 9th grade, Of the three weapons and associated styles used in fencing – the epee, sabre, and foil – students in the beginning and intermediate-level camps learned to use the most popular, the foil. The students were taught footwork and bladework tactics, en garde drills, and one-on-one matches. Their matches, Sinkkonen explained, were often punctuated with a game somewhere between Lord of the Flies and Capture the Flag, where students with foils are broken into two teams, with one from each team appointed its king or queen. The others, according to their position as guard or knight, are tasked with using their foils to defend or attain territory, marked by orange plastic cones, which surround the other team’s leader. As Sinkkonen plays his preferred soundtrack, “Back in Black” by AC/DC, the gym floods with suited-up youth learning the fine art of fencing – in a whirlwind of controlled chaos. “It’s fantastic seeing the students put the techniques they’ve learned through the drills to the test in engaging, free-for-all games like these,” he said. “It’s a Eighteen students from grades three to nine were enrolled in this year’s summer fencing camp. Staff photos David Sinkkonen has taught fencing in Piedmont and coached the Piedmont Fencing Team for 10 years. fun, win-win dynamic when you combine kids and swords, but it’s always disciplined. We’ve never had any safety problems, as I am super vigilant at all times. “Furthermore,” he continued, “fencing is a very safe sport. For all the years that I’ve been teaching, I’ve never had an accident with anyone being really hurt. For those starting out, I put a lot of emphasis on correct use of the protective masks and jackets before we get into the active play.” A fencer for nearly 50 years, he said that some students from the summer camp go on to join the year-round Piedmont Fencing Team which he coaches. The team has grown from just six members 10 years ago to more than 70 fencers at all skill levels today – an impressive feat for the coach of such an uncommon sport in a small town of 11,000 residents. “For those introduced to fencing through these camps, it takes about three to four years to really gain traction with the sport. The competitive season runs nearly 12 months, from the end of August into July the following year,” he explained. “We’re lucky if we get three weeks off from touring the country” to participate in events like the USA Fencing National Championship, which is held every summer in Phoenix. “This summer camp is a mix between kids interested more in non-competitive activity, primarily learning something new, and those who may be interested in continuing to pursue the sport after the camp is over,” said Sinkkonen. “It’s been difficult building the program for such a non-mainstream sport from scratch in Piedmont, especially given how long it takes to learn the basics. The most rewarding part is seeing how students take to it while they progress here right before you.” Two young fencers in a match on Thursday, July 13

articles.text: Schoolmates registration for the coming 2023-2024 school year opens at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, July 19. Starting this fall, Piedmont Recreation Department’s popular playbased after school care program will have an increased capacity with new, flexible schedule options. This year’s programs offer two choices. “Block Booking” provides a full year of traditional, full afternoon care. A new “Flexi-Care” option offers families the opportunity to register in hourly increments and pay only for the care they need, with a chance to adjust schedules each month, pending available space. A new program, “Camp Kaleidoscope,” offers expanded care options to accommodate early dismissal for grades K-3 during the first few weeks of school. Registration will take place online via Community Pass, at bit. ly/3K43zlM. Detailed information on program options, dates, registration, scheduling, tuition, withdrawals, adjustments, and waitlists is available at piedmont.ca.gov/schoolmates. For questions about Schoolmates, contact Eva Phelan at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov. Block Booking The Schoolmates “Block Booking” option offers predetermined time slots for families needing consistent weekly care throughout the year: • Register once for the full school year (program runs September 5 to May 24) • Sign up by day of the week for full afternoon care (3-6 p.m. most weekdays, 1:45-6 p.m. on Wednesdays) • Waitlist available Tuition for Schoolmates Block Booking is $11.20/hour, billed monthly. Flexi-Care The new Schoolmates “FlexiCare” program offers registration in hourly increments, allowing families to select only the days and times they need: • Separate enrollment periods for fall (September 5 to December 21) and spring (January 8 to May 24) • Option to adjust schedule monthly, pending availability • No waitlist Tuition for Schoolmates FlexiCare is $13.40/hour, billed monthly. Camp Kaleidoscope Another new offering this year, Camp Kaleidoscope, provides expanded care during the first few weeks of school, when demand is the highest. Camp Kaleidoscope offers weekly flexibility and a rotation of fun enrichment activities ranging from sports and scavenger hunts to cooking and arts & crafts. Camp Kaleidoscope runs from 2 to 6 p.m., August 14 to September 1. Spots are available at the Beach School and Havens School locations. Minimates The Minimates program offers Piedmont students in transitional kindergarten opportunities to learn, grow, and have fun with age-appropriate games, crafts, and sports. • Register once for the full school year (program runs August 14 to May 24) • Sign up by day of the week for full morning (8:30 a.m. class start) or full afternoon (class release at 3 p.m.) • Waitlist available Tuition for Minimates is $11.20/ hour, billed monthly. Schoolmates registration for the upcoming 2023-2024 school year opens on Wednesday, July 19.
articles.title: Registration for Schoolmates opens July 19

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School’s Annie Holland retired at the end of the school year after teaching for 24 years in the district. Holland started in 1999 as a 7th grade core teacher and became the history teacher at the middle school. Her career was honored at the May 24 school board meeting by colleagues and community members. Holland expressed her gratitude for the Piedmont community as well. “It’s been 24 years that went by in a blink of an eye, even longer since our first son started kindergarten 37 years ago. It’s going to be the first fall without some buttress of the district holding us up,” Holland said. Each board member took time to thank Holland, as did teachers’ union president Elise Marks. “A student once told me ‘we will always be kind to Ms. Holland because she is always kind to us.’” said PMS Principal Karyn Shipp. Holland thanked her husband Bill whom she met in the third grade. “I could never have taught distance learning without Bill honestly. I did not know enough about computers. I was weeping, saying ‘what am I going to do,’ Piedmont Middle School history teacher Annie Holland retired in June this year. but he was right there and fixed everything,” said Holland. “Both of our kids remember you so fondly,” said board member Hilary Cooper. “You are the kind of teacher that a parent hopes their kids will have.” Holland looks forward to being kept busy in retirement by spending time with her seven grandchildren. “My mother was also a teacher and her advice that I always have in my mind is ‘treat your students the way you would want a teacher to treat your own children or grandchildren.’ That has been a guiding principle,” said Holland.
articles.title: Annie Holland retires after 24 years at middle school

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center will present its annual BubbleFest event this Saturday and Sunday, July 22-23 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Now a two-day event, BubbleFest explores the wonders of the remarkable spheres we know as bubbles. BubbleFest will bring together learners of all ages to learn about bubble physics and how bubbles can teach us about star formation and all its applications in space science. BubbleFest is geared towards a family audience but welcomes all visitors to celebrate the joy of bubbles with hands on bubble fun, music, and the experience of being inside a giant bubble. Returning this year are bubble artists Tom Noddy and Sterling Johnson. Johnson will create beautiful, large bubbles with found objects. Kids can experience the wonder of Tom Noddy’s Bubble Magic as well. Participants are encouraged to join the whirlwind of fun, playing in our outdoor bubble play area and making bubbles out of everyday objects. pages.text: Wednesday, July 19, 2023 7 Registration for Schoolmates opens July 19 Schoolmates registration for the coming 2023-2024 school year opens at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, July 19. Starting this fall, Piedmont Recreation Department’s popular playbased after school care program will have an increased capacity with new, flexible schedule options. This year’s programs offer two choices. “Block Booking” provides a full year of traditional, full afternoon care. A new “Flexi-Care” option offers families the opportunity to register in hourly increments and pay only for the care they need, with a chance to adjust schedules each month, pending available space. A new program, “Camp Kaleidoscope,” offers expanded care options to accommodate early dismissal for grades K-3 during the first few weeks of school. Registration will take place online via Community Pass, at bit. ly/3K43zlM. Detailed information on program options, dates, registration, scheduling, tuition, withdrawals, adjustments, and waitlists is available at piedmont.ca.gov/schoolmates. For questions about Schoolmates, contact Eva Phelan at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov. Annie Holland retires after 24 years at middle school By Jay Russell Piedmont Middle School’s Annie Holland retired at the end of the school year after teaching for 24 years in the district. Holland started in 1999 as a 7th grade core teacher and became the history teacher at the middle school. Her career was honored at the May 24 school board meeting by colleagues and community members. Holland expressed her gratitude for the Piedmont community as well. “It’s been 24 years that went by in a blink of an eye, even longer since our first son started kindergarten 37 years ago. It’s going to be the first fall without some buttress of the district holding us up,” Holland said. Each board member took time to thank Holland, as did teachers’ union president Elise Marks. “A student once told me ‘we will always be kind to Ms. Holland because she is always kind to us.’” said PMS Principal Karyn Shipp. Holland thanked her husband Bill whom she met in the third grade. “I could never have taught distance learning without Bill honestly. I did not know enough about computers. I was weeping, saying ‘what am I going to do,’ Piedmont Middle School history teacher Annie Holland retired in June this year. but he was right there and fixed everything,” said Holland. “Both of our kids remember you so fondly,” said board member Hilary Cooper. “You are the kind of teacher that a parent hopes their kids will have.” Holland looks forward to being kept busy in retirement by spending time with her seven grandchildren. “My mother was also a teacher and her advice that I always have in my mind is ‘treat your students the way you would want a teacher to treat your own children or grandchildren.’ That has been a guiding principle,” said Holland. articles.text: George Stein (left), Oliver Amen, Everett Villiger, and Will Sprague, members of Piedmont Scouts Troop 11, attained the rank of Eagle Scout on June 11. Four Scouts in Piedmont Troop 11 achieved the rank of Eagle on June 11. The Scouts are: Will Sprague, a sophomore at the University of Michigan, Oliver Amen and George Stein, seniors at Piedmont High School, and Everett Villiger, a senior at HeadRoyce School. Each completed the Leadership, Service and Merit Badge requirements. The final requirement to earn the rank of Eagle is finding, planning and executing a service project. Each Scout’s project is detailed below: Will Sprague worked with Friends of Joaquin Miller to install split rail fencing in the park to mark off an area closed to mountain bikers. The area had been stripped of its native plants because of the constant pressure of mountain bikers. Will posted signage along the fence informing bikers the area was closed. The goal of the fence is to bring back the soil that allowed native plants to thrive. Oliver Amen worked with Friends of Sausal Creek to build an 85-foot split rail fence along the Fern Ravine Trail in Joaquin Miller Park to protect the endangered redwood understory from being destroyed by mountain bikers who enter trails meant for hikers and walkers only. Oliver’s project was connected to fences built by other Eagle Scouts for the common goal of allowing the fragile vegetation to take hold once again and thrive. George Stein also worked with Friends of Sausal Creek. He led the construction and installation of seven wooden map boxes. The boxes were designed to keep maps dry and protected from the elements. The trailside boxes were installed in East Bay Regional Parks to help visitors navigate the parks by holding maps. Everett Villiger designed and built a large outdoor storage cabinet to organize & secure toys for Piedmont Playschool located at Hampton Park. The cabinet was constructed of manufactured wood, weatherproofed with paint and was secured to the wall. The cabinet is a much-needed addition, providing a central location for storing small toys.
