articles.text: As part of a new Free Children’s Book Day program, kids aged 12 and under can take home a free children’s book of their choice on the second Sunday of every month at The Bookmark Bookstore in Old Oakland. Laura Guzman, who co-manages The Bookmark with Sven Geddes, said that the program began on June 11, and recently held its second Free Book Day on July 9. The event is run by the nonprofit Friends of the Oakland Public Library (FOPL), which manages the bookstore. “Each time so far, we’ve had about 20 families with children coming in,” said Guzman. “As there were a few repeats at the second event, we’re hoping to build a crowd month by month. Because all of our books are donated, the selection is very eclectic. Most books in the store have been published within the last 10 years, although children’s books tend to have a longer life due to the generally perennial subjects they deal with.” “We had talked about the free book program with the library about two to three months before it began, so they could start getting the word out in the community,” said Geddes. “That first time in June the kids were so excited to come in that we had three families waiting outside the store 15 minutes before we opened. That’s been the best part – seeing that the program is so kid-driven. They’re the ones who want to come in and who are overjoyed to be getting a book,” said Geddes. “The library is an invaluable resource, but it’s also crucial for any kid to grow up with books available in their own home to grab and read.” The Bookmark recently received a staggering donation from Bibliomania, a bookstore in Oakland which closed their brickand-mortar location on Telegraph Avenue to operate online. They donated nearly 3,000 children’s picture books, mostly published in the 1970s and ‘80s and all in excellent shape. “For children’s books, our inventory is completely updated every month. Books sit on our shelves for about four months maximum, and if they don’t sell by then, we give them a new life and send them out to another Friends public library system or to a nonprofit, like the Prisoners Literature Project in Berkeley,” said Guzman. “Nothing’s stale - it’s fun to come back to the store. What you’ll find is different every time.” “Not only are children’s books free every second Sunday,” added Geddes, “but we’re still the cheapest used bookstore around. We’re proud that the proceeds all go back to the community.” Other than Guzman and Geddes, the children’s book program and the bookstore itself are run entirely by a pool of approximately 50 volunteers, working three to four people at a time across three shifts a day to help sort, shelve, process, and sell donated books on- and off-site. More information about Friends of Oakland Public Library is available at fopl.org. The next Free Children’s Book Day event will take place at The Bookmark on Sunday, August 13. The Bookmark Bookstore, located at 721 Washington Street in Old Oakland, is open on Saturdays and Sundays from 10:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Wednesdays through Fridays from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Kids aged 12 and under can take home a free children’s book on the second Sunday of every month at The Bookmark Bookstore. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. A new session, a new group of campers, but the same fun activities and evening programs. With the heat rising this weekend, campers are using the lake more and more. Misters and sprinklers decorate the woodchips at all times of the day, and water bottles are everyone’s best friend. Level bracelets are cut on the daily for those completing difficult tasks in clinics. Although it is in the middle of the summer officially, that does not mean that the fun has stopped. We have a lot more planned for Session 4 including trips to the Yuba River, more horseback riding clinics, and Crow’s Nest (the tallest climbing activity on site). articles.text: If you are in the North Lake Tahoe area, take a worthy side trip to Washeshu Peak for a million-dollar view while hiking at an elevation of 8,000 feet. articles.text: The Piedmont Fencing Team just wrapped up its season at the prestigious National Championships in Phoenix from June 30 – July 9, where 5,300 athletes from 43 states came to compete. Piedmont Fencing Team sent seven athletes to this year’s event, including five current Piedmont residents. Representing the program were Piedmont High juniors Teresa McKay and Oliver Greenebaum, sophomores Jonah Kim and Niko Kalamas, and Piedmont Middle School 8th grader Dario Banuelos. Tamalpais senior Lorenz Finney also competed, and Sophie Choi, who moved from Piedmont to Danville, also competed at the Y-12 level. It’s a remarkable achievement considering the program had under 10 members when coach David Sinkkonen took over a decade ago to now 70 while training at the Piedmont Community Church. “The National Championships are hard and everyone had a great time. It’s an achievement to even make it to National Championships and all of it is coming out of the community church [where the team practices]. When I think of it that way, it’s pretty incredible,” said coach David Sinkkonen. At National Championships, Kim competed in five events. He was 46th of 203 in the Division 3 men’s foil category, 92nd of 302 in the Y-14 men’s foil, finished 151st of 220 in the Division 2 men’s foil, was 216th of 344 in the junior men’s foil, and 254th of 269 in the cadet U-16 men’s foil. Jonah Kim competed in five events at the National Championships. The Piedmont Fencing Team sent seven members to the National Championships in Phoenix from June 30 to July 9. Pictured are PHS junior Oliver Greenebaum (left), PHS sophomore Jonah Kim, PHS junior Teresa McKay, Tamalpais senior Lorenz Finney, and coach David Sinkkonen. “Jonah fenced in five events; he was there the whole time. He made it out of the preliminary rounds in each event, but couldn’t get traction after that… I feel really good about his development. He’s definitely going places,” said Sinkkonen. Greenebaum was also busy, competing in three events. He placed 108th in the D3 men’s foil category, 162nd in the cadet men’s foil, and 336th in the junior men’s foil. Niko Kalamas, meanwhile, was 300th in the junior men’s foil. McKay was in the cadet U-16 women’s foil category, finishing 126th of 212. In the Y-12 category was Banuelos finishing 220nd. “For Teresa and Niko, it was their first National Championships. Teresa made it out of the preliminary round. She did well and just missed making it into the top-64. That was great for her. Oliver made it out of the preliminary round in three events,” said Sinkkonen. Choi is an exciting prospect, who moved to Danville after attending Piedmont Middle School. She is a nationally ranked athlete at No. 87 in the Y-12 category and No. 15 in her region. At National Championships, Sophie was 85th of 202 in the Y-12 women’s foil. “She’s great, she’s awesome. She’s going to be going to be really, really good,” said Sinkkonen. To qualify for the National Championships, each athlete had to achieve a necessary amount of points by competing throughout the year in their region, which stretches from the Pacific Coast to New Mexico and Colorado. Piedmont Fencing Team’s season starts in August with the National Championships in early July. “They all travel to compete regionally. It’s a pretty large region that includes Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, and Colorado,” said Sinkkonen. The team will take a training excursion to London from August 29 through September 1 ahead of the start of their next season, where they will learn from maestro Ziemek Wojciechowski, who coaches England’s Olympic team and is a former Olympian. Their next goal will be to build points towards qualifying for the Junior Olympics in February. Sophie Choi (left) is a nationally ranked prospect with Piedmont Fencing Team. She’s pictured here with coach David Sinkkonen and Jonah Kim.
articles.title: Piedmont Fencing Team sends 7 to National Championships in Phoenix

articles.text: The third annual Badminton Tournament with the theme of “Peace-embracing; Stand Against Violence” was successfully held in the Bay Area on July 1. The charity tournament was organized by Jessica Liu and Jeremy Tuan, two seniors at Piedmont High School, with help of Jerry Liu, a sophomore at UC Berkeley. The charity event was co-sponsored by the American Entrepreneur Association (AEA) and the San Francisco Youth Peace Association (SFYPA). Funds raised from the event will be dedicated to support UC Berkeley students in their efforts in peace-promoting activities. Jessica Liu went addressed an important topic: hate crimes against the AAPI community. “These acts of hate go against our values of equality, inclusivity, and peace”, she said, calling for everyone’s action to work towards raising awareness, promoting tolerance and inclusivity, and advocating for the rights and safety of AAPI communities. She hopes that sports can not only cultivate physical well-being but also foster teamwork, discipline, and perseverance, which can result in positive change in our society. “This tournament can serve as one of the many platforms that can inspire changes and foster an inclusive environment,” she said. Ben He, president of the AEA, a non-profit organization representing businessmen from different industries, expressed his gratitude to the organizers as well as the participants in the tournament. “Through their dedication and commitment, these youth inspire us all to embrace an active, vibrant and healthy lifestyle”. Tournament group picture, in the sports club of Eastbay Badminton Association
articles.title: Promoting peace and anti-violence – a charity badminton tournament in support of AAPI Community

articles.text: Staff Photo Ben Breber is entering his third year on the varsity tennis team. He’ll be a key singles starter next spring. With the new school year approaching, the Class of 2024 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. BEN BREBER Tennis Ben Breber is already a leader on the tennis team and will enter his senior year as a three-year varsity starter. He received an All-League selection as a singles starter after reaching the semifinals of the Western Alameda County Conference individual tournament. In the WACC tournament, Breber received the No. 5 seed and a first-round bye. He defeated Dencedy Guevarra of Mt. Eden 6-0, 6-0, following up with a 6-2, 6-4 win over O’Dowd’s Neo Chai in the quarterfinals. The following day, Breber battled in a narrow two sets against eventual WACC champion Elijah Cho of San Leandro in the semifinals, losing 7-5, 7-5. In the match for third place, Breber lost to Leighton Sproul of Berkeley in three sets, 4-6, 6-1, 10-8. He’ll return to the team in 2024 alongside key starters Lucas Smolko, Monte Imburg, Graham Alban, Arun Brahma, Derek Chan, Will Tenney, and Nate Welch. Photo by Todd Marshburn Elle Ruegg received All-League honors as a defender on the North Coast Section champion soccer team. Biehn, and defenders Charlotte Davies and Amy Derr. JOHN CHAMPION Volleyball ELLE RUEGG Soccer John Champion will enter his senior year on the volleyball team as a three-year starter, and will be the Highlanders’ leading outside hitter in 2024. In 2023, he helped Piedmont finish with a 14-7 overall record and reach the North Coast Section quarterfinals for the second consecutive year. He earned an honorable mention for All-League honors. In the NCS postseason. PHS, the No. 6 seed, defeated No. 11 Encinal 3-0 on May 2 and eventually fell to No. 3 Acalanes on May 4. Champion’s season required a lot perseverance after suffering an ankle injury in the offseason which carried over into the spring. After missing a stretch of matches, he returned to the starting lineup to make a big impact in the team’s final month. Elle Ruegg didn’t make a lot of headlines as a center back on Piedmont’s North Coast Section champion team, but as a central defender played a vital part in the team’s success. She earned an honorable mention for AllLeague honors. The strength of Piedmont’s back line shined throughout last winter, helping the team go 13-1-6 (W-T-L) including 10 shutout victories. During Piedmont’s run to an NCS title, the Highlanders limited their opponents to two goals in four matches and a an 11-2 goal differential. With 10 seniiors having graduated, Ruegg will be a key leader of the returning cast alongside striker Miranda Liu, midfielders Arden Sorensen-Wald, and Lola Staff Photo John Champion will be Piedmont’s leading outside hitter on the volleyball team next spring.

articles.text: Men’s varsity eight rowers and cox receiving medals after placing second at Nationals. The Oakland Strokes junior crew, consisting of over 200 youth rowers, competed in the Southwest Youth Championships on Lake Natoma, in Sacramento the first weekend in May. The top boats qualified for the Youth Nationals held in Sarasota, Florida from June 8-11. Years of training and countless hours spent at the boathouse all came down to one weekend in Sacramento for Oakland Strokes rowers trying to advance to Nationals. A total of 31 Oakland Strokes boats raced at the regional championship, and eight qualified for the Youth Nationals. “It was a lot of fun to race against the best rowers across the country,” said PHS senior Zachary Feldstein. The Strokes had impressive results for both the men’s and women’s boats. The Oakland Stroke’s top boat, the Men’s Varsity Eight, placed second at nationals, the Men’s Junior Varsity Eight placed fourth, and the Women’s Straight Four placed Oakland Strokes Women’s four receiving first place medals at nationals, with senior Ali Gallagher econd from left. first. Additionally, the Women’s U-17 Eight finished in sixth place. A total of seven Piedmont rowers competed at the regional championships: Taran Griffis, Ryan Ehteshami, McKeane McBrearty, Jackson Violich, Gray Young, Zachary Feldstein, Ali Gallagher, and Cleo Tahawi. Six Piedmont athletes – McBrearty, Violich, Young, Feldstein, Gallagher, and Tahawi – qualified for nationals and raced in Florida. Members of the Oakland Strokes Men’s JV eight rowing up to the start, with Gray Young on the left.
articles.title: Oakland Strokes’ season sent 6 Piedmont rowers to Nationals

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform at Stern Grove Festival on July 23. The Symphony is a recurring guest of the festival every year. Stern Grove Festival is a series of ten summer concerts, held on Sundays from June 18 through August 20 at a natural amphitheater in San Francisco surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees. articles.text: Cal Performances’ 21st annual Berkeley/Oakland AileyCamp will perform at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall on Thursday, July 27 at 7 p.m. Performances are by students from Berkeley, Oakland, Richmond, and Albany as part of Cal Performances’ nearly 60-year relationship with the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, the iconic modern dance company based in New York City. AileyCamps students participate in a six-week program with a concluding performance in summer. The performance on July 27, entitled “Points of View,” features professional staging, lights, costumes, and live music. It is free and open to the public. “AileyCamp gives young people an opportunity to have a quality arts experience, make friends, express themselves, and recognize that they matter,” said Nasha Thomas, AileyCamp National Director. “Every year, it is a joy to witness the campers’ transformation from the first day to the final performance. It’s incredibly special to watch our former campers step into leadership roles that pay it forward to the next generation. It’s a testament to Alvin Ailey’s mission of enriching the lives of youth through dance.” For more information and tickets, visit Cal Performances’ website at www.calperformances.org/ aileycamp.
articles.title: AileyCamp kids to perform at Zellerbach Hall July 27

articles.text: Blues musician Henry St. Claire Fredericks Jr., better known by his stage name Taj Mahal, will perform at Miner Auditorium at SF Jazz in San Francisco August 3 through 6. Blues legend Taj Mahal plays a plethora of instruments including the guitar, piano, banjo, and harmonica. His 50-year career spans several genres that blend sounds from the Caribbean, Africa, India, Hawaii and the South Pacific. Originally from Harlem in New York City, Fredericks began his music career after moving to Los Angeles in 1964 where he formed the band Rising Sons with fellow blues rock musicians. He has performed at venues throughout the Bay Area, including at Stern Grove Festival last year. The blues icon returns to Miner Auditorium with a tribute to the legendary Harlem swing music of the 1930’s and 40’s. The performances, hosted by SF JAZZ, will feature folk singer Blues musician Taj Mahal Maria Muldaur and will include an orchestra. All shows August 3 through 6 begin at 7 p.m. Miner Auditorium is located at 201 Franklin Street in San Francisco. Call the box office at 415-788-7353 or visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/summer23/taj-mahal/ to purchase tickets. ®
articles.title: Taj Mahal to perform at SF Jazz August 3 - 6

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse presents the musical A Chorus Line now through September 16. Directed by the Playhouse’s Bill English and based on the book by James Kirkwood Jr. and Nicholas Dante, A Chorus Line follows 17 Broadway dancers who are auditioning for eight spots on a chorus line. The play explores the inner lives, desires and ambitions of the performers, while capturing the spirit, tension and hope of an audition. A Chorus Line has the distinction of Broadway’s longest-running musical, and is the winner of the 1976 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, winner of nine Tony Awards, four Drama Desk awards, and three Obie Awards. The play was conceived and originally directed and choreographed by Michael Bennett with music by Marvin Hamlisch and lyrics by Edward Kleban. Music direction at SF Playhouse is by Dave Dobrusky with choreography by Nicole Helfer. The cast includes Dalton Bertolone, Samatha Cardenas, Danielle Cheiken, Gabi Chun, Tony Conaty, Maggie Connard, Chachi Delgado, Zeke Edmonds, Alison Ewing and Elihu Guerrero. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/2022-2023-season/achorus-line/ to purchase tickets and learn more. Cast of “A Chorus Line” at SF Playhouse
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents A Chorus Line through September 16

articles.text: Visit the Treasure Island Museum this Saturday, July 22, to view the museum’s newest exhibition “Treasure Island: Inspiring Artists Since 1939.” Treasure Island Museum is a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage. The program this Saturday focuses on the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition, where hundreds of artists were commissioned to create sculptures and murals for the island’s buildings and gardens. Almost all signs of the World Fair are gone, but since the museum’s creation in 1975 the City of San Francisco has made earnest efforts to preserve the island’s rich history. Color photography emerged during this time to capture and preserve the legacy of the Golden Gate International Exposition. The program will include how this history inspires contemporary and modern, local artists. Katy Boynton and Tom Loughlin are artists who use materials and ideas from the past to create new public art on and off Treasure Island. The exhibition program will be presented by museum board member and historian Anne Schnoebelen, and artists Boynton and Loughlin. The program begins at 10:30 a.m. Tickets are $10. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/treasure-island-inspiring-artists-since-1939-3. Treasure Island Museum General Dentistry & Advanced Prosthodontics
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum to host “Inspiring Artists Since 1939” exhibit this Saturday

BRAVO is presented in partnership with the Opera and the Museum of Performance and Design and is open to the public through October 22. The exhibition traces the history of Italian opera in San Francisco from the Gold Rush to the establishment of San Francisco Opera in 1923, as well as modern day. articles.text: Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander in The Danish Girl It’s 1926 in Copenhagen, Denmark. Two artists, Einar Wegener (Eddie Redmayne) and his wife, Gerda (Alicia Vikander), married some six years, live a contented, Bohemian life, both in search of galleries that will carry their work. Einar, a landscape painter, is finding more success than Gerda, who has thus far confined herself to portraits of wealthy burghers. Their connection, through touch and gaze, reflects a sustained intimacy, revealing in countless subtle ways a relationship that they both cherish as they stand before easels, working, or waking in the early morning, basking in the soft early morning light, the diaphanous curtains of the bedroom creating a luminescent glow. Looking out the woodframed windows of their starkly furnished flat is a harbor filled with working boats, their cinnabar and white sails raised, swaying ever so slightly in the wind. The Danish Girl is replete with achingly gorgeous moments, not only between Einar and Gerda, but horizons framed by pink sunsets and bucolic hills obscured by orange and red wildflowers, each image suffused with color and beauty. Together they share life’s continuum, a kaleidoscope of small and not so small changes. But the depth and breath of their marriage, a touching and visible bond, is seemingly inviolable. What they are unprepared for is the change that Einar will embark on, a journey that will take him into the distance where his once very masculine image begins to fade until it is barely visible, as if he were standing behind a scrim, his outline growing increasingly dim. What Gerda is unprepared for is what she set in motion, simply on a lark. She initially asks Einar to pose, covered by a formal gown, her intention only to finish a portrait; she needed the lower legs and feet completed. Einar’s reaction to the feel of the dress, the sheer hose covering his calves, catches him by surprise, stirring emotions that both surprise and disturb. Gerda is oblivious, her focus on the painting. And so begins for them both a long and unsettling goodbye, defined by anguish and love and an unflinching commitment. Einar is headed into the unknown, to a point on the far end of the spectrum of change. To look at Gerda, her face lovely to behold, even when broken by a wrenching agony, is to find Einar’s choice seemingly inexplicable. And yet to be human, fully human, is to engage in what can be a lifelong quest for self – to be fully oneself. If that is a truism, then it gradually becomes clear that Einar feels incarcerated, often against his will in a body he does not feel is his own. Gerda, however, cannot initially, begin to comprehend what is made manifest. The Danish Girl is breathtaking. It is wondrous in so many ways, not the least of which are the portrayals of Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander. They completely inhabit their characters. And it is not just Redmayne who must make an astonishing transformation to Lili Elbe. Vikander must summon a depth of understanding and loyalty that encases her in a steely resolve that is for her also a precipice. There are images of each of them in which their eyes convey a sense of torment and loss that they are both powerless to change. The heartbreaking arc of their lives has been set. Keep in mind that in 1926 what Einar was moving toward was the breaking of a taboo for which there was no name, other than schizophrenia. He could only look to Gerda, pleadingly, hopelessly, while she reassured him that he was not mentally deranged or confused. He simply was. She was remarkable. As is this deeply human and moving film. The Danish Girl. Directed by Tom Hooper. Starring Eddie Redmayne, Alicia Vikander and Ben Whishaw. 120 min., Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv

The Beach Boys have found the fabled fountain of youth. Whether they have discovered the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow is a moot point. I think they just revel in performing. That was obvious in the concert a week ago in Reno. Truth be told, I knew the Beach Boys as a name only. My high school friends knew all the songs. But what I experienced a week ago at the Beach Boys’ concert was a revelation. Some of the original Beach Boys are no longer with us. A small band provided excellent accompaniment throughout the program. They should have added a few violins to the usual combination of electric guitars and keyboard. In this critic’s opinion, Carole King’s music lends itself more to the orchestral than the artificially amplified. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet 3rd dateline: Tatzin Auditorium, Lafayette. Some artists are overlooked, despite an abundance of legitimate talent. Gregory Taboloff might be included in the short list. His concert on Saturday evening proved this. As a pianist, he has a tone somewhat like the immortal Arthur Rubinstein. It is rich and resonant, fortified by clean articulation and intelligent musicianship… all put to the service of the music. The format of Taboloff’s concert was something like a good music appreciation program. The spoken program notes increased the audience’s appreciation. That’s how music education should be. His program was well chosen and included music by Debussy, Schubert and Rachmaninoff. Taboloff finished the concert with the premiere of his own sonata inspired by Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet. It is a one-movement fantasy, comparing favorably to Tchaikovsky‘s overture on the same subject. 4th dateline: Piedmont Center for the Arts. The Diluvian String Quartet is establishing itself as an important presence in the East Bay. Their concerts contain an excellent balance of classics and modern works. Musically speaking, they evince a cultured approach to all that they do. In general, they prefer to be somewhat informal and by doing so they draw the audience in. This format works very well for them. One of the things I enjoy doing at concerts is asking people around me for their opinions. Since my own son is the violist in the Diluvian String Quartet, I thought I would print what members of the audience thought of the concert. One person enjoyed the precision of the ensemble. Others spoke of the beautiful sound, and their enthusiasm for making music. I enjoyed the ensemble’s ability to change musical styles in an instant. MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Danish Girl an acting tour de force Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander in The Danish Girl By Chris Honoré It’s 1926 in Copenhagen, Denmark. Two artists, Einar Wegener (Eddie Redmayne) and his wife, Gerda (Alicia Vikander), married some six years, live a contented, Bohemian life, both in search of galleries that will carry their work. Einar, a landscape painter, is finding more success than Gerda, who has thus far confined herself to portraits of wealthy burghers. Their connection, through touch and gaze, reflects a sustained intimacy, revealing in countless subtle ways a relationship that they both cherish as they stand before easels, working, or waking in the early morning, basking in the soft early morning light, the diaphanous curtains of the bedroom creating a luminescent glow. Looking out the woodframed windows of their starkly furnished flat is a harbor filled with working boats, their cinnabar and white sails raised, swaying ever so slightly in the wind. The Danish Girl is replete with achingly gorgeous moments, not only between Einar and Gerda, but horizons framed by pink sunsets and bucolic hills obscured by orange and red wildflowers, each image suffused with color and beauty. Together they share life’s continuum, a kaleidoscope of small and not so small changes. But the depth and breath of their marriage, a touching and visible bond, is seemingly inviolable. What they are unprepared for is the change that Einar will embark on, a journey that will take him into the distance where his once very masculine image begins to fade until it is barely visible, as if he were standing behind a scrim, his outline growing increasingly dim. What Gerda is unprepared for is what she set in motion, simply on a lark. She initially asks Einar to pose, covered by a formal gown, her intention only to finish a portrait; she needed the lower legs and feet completed. Einar’s reaction to the feel of the dress, the sheer hose covering his calves, catches him by surprise, stirring emotions that both surprise and disturb. Gerda is oblivious, her focus on the painting. And so begins for them both a long and unsettling goodbye, defined by anguish and love and an unflinching commitment. Einar is headed into the unknown, to a point on the far end of the spectrum of change. To look at Gerda, her face lovely to behold, even when broken by a wrenching agony, is to find Einar’s choice seemingly inexplicable. And yet to be human, fully human, is to engage in what can be a lifelong quest for self – to be fully oneself. If that is a truism, then it gradually becomes clear that Einar feels incarcerated, often against his will in a body he does not feel is his own. Gerda, however, cannot initially, begin to comprehend what is made manifest. The Danish Girl is breathtaking. It is wondrous in so many ways, not the least of which are the portrayals of Eddie Redmayne and Alicia Vikander. They completely inhabit their characters. And it is not just Redmayne who must make an astonishing transformation to Lili Elbe. Vikander must summon a depth of understanding and loyalty that encases her in a steely resolve that is for her also a precipice. There are images of each of them in which their eyes convey a sense of torment and loss that they are both powerless to change. The heartbreaking arc of their lives has been set. Keep in mind that in 1926 what Einar was moving toward was the breaking of a taboo for which there was no name, other than schizophrenia. He could only look to Gerda, pleadingly, hopelessly, while she reassured him that he was not mentally deranged or confused. He simply was. She was remarkable. As is this deeply human and moving film. The Danish Girl. Directed by Tom Hooper. Starring Eddie Redmayne, Alicia Vikander and Ben Whishaw. 120 min., Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv

articles.text: For the first time in 43 years the actors’ union, Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) joined the Writers Guild of America on the picket line, bringing the $134 billion American movie and television business to a halt. One of the unresolved issues is, of course, pay; however, keep in mind that there are a combined 170,000 members of The Writers Guild and SAG who want to make what they refer to as a living wage. What makes this strike unique is that both groups added to their contract negotiations/demands the inclusion of new guidelines that address the fast-changing technology now being utilized not only in moviemaking, such as A.I. (artificial intelligence), but also digitally altering actors’ images as well as scripts absent any residual payments (royalties). And there is also the impact on the industry of streaming. I would add to the analysis of the strike the effects on the overall industry of the recent and long-lasting COVID pandemic, which indisputably altered the movie-going experience resulting in countless empty theaters. Thus far we are finding that there is a slow and tenuous return of what was a once robust audience. The advent of streaming platforms such as Netflix, Prime, Paramount+, and Apple tv, combined with home entertainment screens offering unparalleled size and clarity. have been revolutionary. The drop in industry revenues and box office earnings have resulted in layoffs by the studios, to include the effects on adjunct businesses such as background actors, grips, techies, and even catering companies who will soon begin feeling the impact of lost business. The question now is how long will the strike last? The writers have already been out more than 70 days and neither the studios – Disney, Sony, Universal, Paramount – or the unions have shown a willingness to return to the bargaining table. At this point there is no red carpet that leads to a comprehensive solution.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The Longest Ride is the 10th film adaptation of a Nicholas Sparks novel. If you’ve read or seen The Notebook, this film will seem very familiar. But then Sparks is a master at recycling his plots by merely changing the context and rarely the content. He’s a master of the formulaic love story, and The Longest Ride is no exception. Two young people from different worlds meet cute at a rodeo., Luke Collins (Scott Eastwood) is a champion bull rider, and Sophia (Britt Robertsons) is a college senior at Wake Forest, majoring in art, preparing to accept an internship at a major New York gallery. They manage to arrange a first date, have an idyllic picnic by a lake, and on their way home spot a traffic accident. They rescue an old man, Ira Levinson (Alan Alda), from his burning car and take him to the hospital. Apparently he’s had a heart attack. His one wish, before being pulled from the car, is that Sophia grab a small wicker basket of old letters from the front seat. Naturally, waiting in the hospital, Sophia reads one of the letters and akin to The Notebook, a second story is introduced: Ira, a young man working in his father’s clothing store, meets Ruth (Oona Chaplin), a radiant young Austrian woman whose Jewish family has just fled Nazi Scott Eastwood and Britt Robertson star in The Longest Ride Germany. The two stories are seamlessly woven together, each running on parallel tracks, and each about the power of love. It’s about how such a commitment requires sacrifice, but is always filled with promise and brimming with life. Luke and Sophia and Ira and Ruth run into several speed bumps which must be carefully resolved if they are ever going to find “happily ever after”. Each man has sustained injuries that are life altering, Ira in World War II, and Luke a year prior when thrown from a rogue bull. The women must find a way to adapt and overcome the circumstances. All the people are so beautifully rendered (as are the towns and the homes) that it can feel like a fairytale. And that is exactly what Sparks is really good at – creating fairytales. He has mastered the myth of love. And he knows his audience, one that gravitates toward his fantasies like moths to a flame. Is it all overly sentimental and improbable? Indeed. But if it were any different, it would be breaking the pact Sparks has made with his fan base. Like all of his adaptations, this movie is a strawberry smoothie that goes down with a refreshing chill and delivers just what is expected. Fans will not be disappointed. The Longest Ride. Starring Scott Eastwood, Britt Robertson and Alan Alda. Directed by George Tillman. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2015. Now streaming on VUDUF/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: The Longest Ride – like a strawberry smoothie

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Your Name is a remarkable coming-of-age story, written and directed by the Japanese animator and storyteller Makoto Shinakai who is considered the next Hayao Miyazaki (Spirited Away), founder of Ghibli Sudios. In 2017, Your Name it was one of Japan’s highest grossing anime films and eventually was embraced by most of Asia. This beautifully rendered film (using hand-drawn and CGI animation), set in 2013, focuses on two teenagers, Taki Tachibana (Michael Sinternikiaas) and Mitsuha Miyaamzu (Stephanie Shen). Both are in high school. Taki lives in urban Tokyo and Mitsuha in a rural village, a place she finds missing even a hint of excitement. In other words, she is a restless, bored teen. And then the extraordinary happens. One morning the two wake up and discover that though they don’t know each other, they have swapped bodies and soon come to realize that each must now go through the other’s day at school while grappling with this unexpected, confusing occurrence. Your Name is a tale that centers on perspective, asking how their lives will change regarding their daily activities and old friendships. Mitsuha becomes more popular and gregarious. Taki seems more withdrawn. The teens soon figure out how to communicate, leaving notes and calls, (even messages on each other’s skin); however, they never actually meet. As you might guess, their connection gradually deepens and they begin to have a crush on each other. And so Your Name morphs into a teen romance. The story also unexpectedly becomes one touching on time travel, disasters, a ghost story, and a comedy of errors, and reveals itself to be a meditation on identity and connection. As an aside the artwork is stunning, and, of course, there are the signature eyes that are extraordinary while asking the question, to what degree are we defined by our appearance. Your Name. Directed by Makoto Shinakai. Starring Michael Sinternikiaas and Stephanie Shen. Metaphysical fantasy-Anime. Japanese subtitles/or dubbed in English. 1 hr., 46 min. Rated PG. Released in 2017. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. A scene from Makoto Shinakai’s Your Name

All visiting singers and many of the visiting adults were put up in homestays by current or former members of the PEBCC. “They give them somewhere to sleep. They provide them meals, including box lunches for all the days of the festival, and transport them to all the festival events. And they also tour a lot of sites. This marked Tuan’s first year as Director of PEBCC during the 2023 festival, which accords international status to all those involved. Piedmont’s Sue Malick, a member of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir board of directors, has been a supporter of the choir since the 80s when her children were involved. She said she was blown away by the high quality of musicianship. “I’ve been working with the choirs for a long, long time and I thought this was probably the best festival I’ve ever seen. It was really good,” Malick said. Willrich, who moved to Piedmont 20 years ago to raise a family of two boys, previously worked in accounting, venture capital, and software firms. In 2003 she said, ‘Why don’t you do it?’ I thought ‘No way.’ It was in my blood, but I never thought of it as a career. But two years later, I began,” she said. The move proved successful, as Willrich became the first former student of Dailey to bring her combination of ballet barre work, pilates stretching, core conditioning, and yoga exercises to the East Bay. The Piedmont Avenue studio now boasts 15 instructors, some of whom have been with Willrich throughout this 18-year arc, and none for less than eight years. “Even those instructors who have had to move away or take a break for a while have found a way to step back in,” she said. “There’s something so rewarding and gratifying about helping people in your own community. Our clientele has grown organically over the years. While it’s predominantly women, it’s not exclusive to them by any means. Many bring their spouses who end up getting hooked on the exercises. It’s useful, safe, and effective for everybody, across all ages and physical abilities,” she said. Why, then, the change from The Dailey Method to Honor Barre? “During the pandemic the Dailey Method corporate folks decided to refocus their energies on training instructors online. The choreography and formats offered became a bit limited, and I felt it was time to expand how we could serve our community in Piedmont,” Willrich explained. While she started broadcasting classes virtually on Zoom through an on-demand library for studio members, she also began holding in-person classes outside, in an adjacent parking lot. She couldn’t amplify music or instructors’ voices in the urban setting of Piedmont Avenue, so she had students wear individual headphones in the manner of a ‘silent disco.’ The outdoor classes proved so popular that they continue to this day, now on an outdoor pavilion built on the lot with sun shields and ballet barres. She also expanded her class focuses to range from gentle, repetitive, low-weight barre movements, to higher-intensity, higher-weight cardio, and often to a blend of the two. Attendance can range from four to 20 people depending on the day and time, and not including participants over Zoom classes, which often number about 10. “The common denominator for all of us is that we want to feel strong and connected to our community,” said Willrich. “Especially given that most who come to Honor Barre are very busy with careers and families, I’m proud that we’ve done well on our intention: to serve everyone effectively at the level of their own needs, in a format that best suits them.” Explaining the palm tree on Honor Barre’s new logo, Willrich said, “During the storms last winter, I went to work one day and looked outside. Among the trees and power lines downed all around, there were palms dancing in the breeze - calm, cool, Piedmont resident Susan Willrich, is owner of Honor Barre, formerly The Dailey Method, a fitness studio on Piedmont Avenue. collected - and I knew that was our new icon. I wanted to represent an oasis of welcoming and warmth, as well as a place of resilience and strength. I want everyone who exits our studio to feel a sense of balance and vitality. That’s a tall order, but we’ve been at it for a long time.” Details on classes at Honor Barre can be found at honorbarre. com. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s 2nd Thursdays Flix Fest had its July showing on July 13 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts and featured a classic. Some movie directors — very few — are as famous as the actors whose performances they shape: Orson Welles, Alfred Hitchcock and Steven Spielberg are among them, and Stanley Kubrick is in that company, for helming a series of iconic films: Spartacus, Lolita, Dr. Strangelove, 2001, A Clockwork Orange, and The Shining. All movie careers begin somewhere, and though Kubrick had directed a couple of previous films, his first notable work is 1956’s stark, taut The Killing, which Piedmonters had a chance to see at last week’s Thursday Film Fest in the Center for the Arts. Filmed nearby in San Mateo and at Bay Meadows Racetrack, the film was written by Kubrick and Jim Thompson and photographed in pungent black and white by cinematographer Lucien Ballard. It’s set in seedy hotel rooms but mostly at that racetrack, which in the story has two million in cash in its safe, just waiting to be boosted. Career criminal Johnny Clay (an edgy Sterling Hayden) is the chief booster, recruiting a sharpshooter, a crooked policeman, a bartender, and a betting teller to help him complete the heist. He’s got a soft spot, though – all he wants to do is retire with his innocent fiancée, Fay, played by a tremulous Colleen Gray. Needless to say, as in all noir films, Fate comes to call, and it’s not a Fate that looks kindly on Johnny Clay, who ends watching all that stolen cash fly away on the wind. The Piedmont screening was introduced by Mike Gallant who after the movie led a discussion with the attendees. Their reactions to the movie were very positive. They enjoyed this view back in time to the 1950s and the start of Kubrick’s career. The movie brought back memories of the classic Dragnet television series of that time. Just like it, The Killing was filmed in black & white, and it would not have been right to do it any other way. The music might be a little overly dramatic by today’s standards, but the viewers enjoyed Kubrick’s use of multiple story lines to tie the different characters’ actions together. It was noted that Kubrick was originally a photographer for Life magazine, which may have influenced the look of his film. Viewers were taken aback by the use of a disparaging racial slur by a bad guy, and wondered how it was received at the time. Those attuned to the subtleties of Kubrick’s fun style noted that one of the racehorses was named “Stanley K.” Everyone agreed this and The Killing were fun. Coming next in the movie series on August 10th is the Italian comedy, Pranzo di Farragusto (Lunch in August). Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Flix Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Guests are welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group had a strong turnout of 19 readers on July 10 for a discussion of How Beautiful We Were by Cameroonian-American novelist Imbolo Mbue. This novel was inspired by Mbue’s own experiences growing up in Cameroon. It is an environment-themed novel set in a fictional village of Kosawa in Africa, in the 1980s. The story follows a set of villagers who challenge their government and an American oil company. The people are angered by the firm, Pexton, which causes oil spills and fatal illnesses. A villager, Kanga, convinces the villagers to revolt. However, they are repressed by the corrupt president of their country. There is a revolution by the young adults led by a woman named Thula. She has grown up in the village and has experienced the harm Pexton’s pollution has caused her people. She is talented and wins scholarships and to a college in the United States. She develops a relationship with a young American and has the potential for a bright future, but she gives it all up to forge a militant organization to protest against Pexton and her government. Sadly it does not end well for the people. How Beautiful We Were received mixed, but on the whole, positive reviews from the readers. They benefited from the view into this world that the book provided. It was an “eye opener” for some readers regarding the destructive colonialism that exists in parts of the world today. The book provided an understanding of the harm that can be caused by bad governments and exploitive corporations from the victims’ perspectives. Children are dying because of the pollution and government soldiers kill the people too. These are gentle people who are dragged down by one hurtful thing after another. The readers hoped something good would happen to them, but it doesn’t. The book’s ending was liked best by some, but it was still a sad story. Readers could relate to the personal experience stories of abuse, corruption, and injustice. They recognized the same type of environmental exploitation is happening around the world and in parts of the United States too. Leaking, capped oil and gas wells in our South, with their harmful effects on the land and people, were considered. Readers felt we have a responsibility for what is happening abroad and at home, but there are no good answers for what to do about it. So, there was also a feeling of guilt by some readers. How Beautiful We Were is thought-provoking and it generated some conversations on: Should individuals contest powers that are not aligned with their values, and if so, how? Can working within a system that you don’t agree with result in greater good than fighting it? What should we teach our children and what can they teach us? The questions made How Beautiful We Were a worthwhile read. How Beautiful We Were by Imbolo Mbue was the July book for discussion. The readers had previously selected Four Fish: The Future of the Last Wild Food by Paul Greenberg for their August read. There were a number of good suggestions for future books. The group decided on A Visit from the Goon Squad by American author Jennifer Egan for September, The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid by Bill Bryson for October, The Trees by Percival Everett for November, and The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman for December. The group’s next discussion will be on August 7 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Tea House by the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group and there is no fee, Registration is required at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4. A large group of readers attended the July 10 gathering for a discussion of How Beautiful We Were. On hand were Albert Chen, Bella Almanzan, Lisa Euphrat, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Darby Gragg, Pat McMahon, Adriene Hamlin, Martin Levy, Gerry Gragg, Carol Warren, Hilary Honore, Carol Long, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus, Carol Long and Albert Chen WE PROVIDE: • Excellent in-home care • Quality caregiver training • Errands and transportation Start home care today. Those attuned to the subtleties of Kubrick’s fun style noted that one of the racehorses was named “Stanley K.” Everyone agreed this and The Killing were fun. Coming next in the movie series on August 10th is the Italian comedy, Pranzo di Farragusto (Lunch in August). Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Guests are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. articles.text: It is with heavy hearts that the Lambing family announces the passing of our mother, long time Piedmont resident Pat Lambing. In recent years she lived in Walnut Creek, and then moved to Reno, Nevada, to be closer to family. Pat attended Bishop O’Dowd High School, and then matriculated at Holy Names College where she attained a degree in Speech Pathology and Audiology. She met Dr. Robert Lambing on a blind date, and six months later, they were married – a marriage that lasted for 41 years. She put her degree and possible career aside to raise four children who all attended Piedmont schools. Susan Lambing of Puyallup, WA, Linda (Dee-Dee) Lambing, deceased in 1983, Dr Robert Lambing of Monterey, CA, and Patricia Lambing Nishkian of Reno, NV. Pat was always involved in the greater good, serving as the past president of the Alameda County Cancer League, Easter Pat Lambing Seals Society, Junior League of the East Bay, Mothers Against Drunk Driving, Piedmont Boy Scouts and countless other volunteer positions throughout her life. She had an amazing ability to nurture and love children, which she enjoyed immensely. She was a classy and graceful woman, with an epic sense of style. We all find solace knowing that she is reunited with her beloved husband Bob, and her adored daughter Dee-Dee in God’s Kingdom.
articles.title: Former longtime Piedmont resident Pat Lambing dies

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, July 19, 2023 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers head to Witter Field There was a large turnout of 53 walkers and three K-9 best friends at the Exedra on July 12 for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays weekly walk. One week earlier Pete Palmer, Piedmont School Director of Facilities, had given the walkers a tour of Ellen Driscoll Playhouse and its historic ceiling. Pete mentioned the work that he is supervising at Witter Field to replace the turf and irrigation system. This is a major, overdue project. It requires the removal of the 15-year-old artificial turf, excavation of the field and drainage trenches, installing a new drainage trench drain surrounding the entire field, and providing a new turf surface. Hundreds of trucks will go in and out of the Winsor Avenue gate at the field. The bulk of the project is about the drainage. It will require a large, probably 10-inch diameter storm drain that will redirect storm water directly into Bushy Dell Creek. Currently storm drainage from the high school and middle school runs down P.E. Hill, hits the Witter Field parking lot and goes directly under the field. During heavy rains this sometimes creates “Lake Witter.” In 2007 when the old turf was installed and still under warranty, it cost $219,000 and was installed in two weeks. The current project will cost over $4,150,000 and hopefully will be finished by December. Funding for this project is not expected to come from PUSD’s General Fund. Rather, State Modernization Funds, that are tied to the City’s H1 bond and paid for the new PHS theater and STEAM building, will come from the State Office of Public School Construction and Division of the State Architect. The construction will require PHS sports teams to use different facilities for their practices and games this fall. The football teams will practice at Laney College in Oakland and have all road games. It will also affect residential parking on El Cerrito, Winsor, and Park View Avenues, as well as Palm Drive. The construction work is underway, and there is no public access to Witter Field. However, the walkers could get a view of the construction from the bottom of El Cerrito Avenue. The group could also see how the work is affecting the neighborhood by walking the surrounding streets. The Walkers headed down Magnolia Avenue, past the construction work being done for the city’s new swimming pool. The earth moving is done and work on retaining walls has started. The walkers peeked through holes in the fence to see the progress. Then they group continued on to El Cerrito Avenue and looked at the field below. The turf has been removed and initial ground work has been completed. They took a short side trip to see the three homes on the Larmer Court cul-de-sac. Then it was on to Park View Avenue and Winsor Avenue. Karin Fetherston’ s home is near the Winsor gate. She said that when Witter’s turf removal was in full swing up to 22 trucks a day made trips to Alameda County’s contracted dump site in Tracy. The walkers retraced their steps back to Palm Drive where they saw No Parking signs all along the way. The group went past Wildwood School to the Piedmont Park entrance and had a lovely walk up its lower path to the top of the park. A path along its top took the group to steps that returned them for an on-time, noon arrival at the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers pose for a photo on El Cerrito Avenue above Witter Field. articles.text: As the seasons change, it’s important to be mindful of fire safety in and around your home. Each season brings its own unique set of hazards, and taking proactive steps to prevent fires can help protect your home and your family. Here are some summertime fire safety tips to help you remain cool-headed as temperatures begin to rise: 1. Check your smoke and carbon monoxide detectors to make sure they are working properly. 2. Replace batteries as needed. Clean out gutters and remove any debris from your roof. Dry leaves and twigs are literal tinder. 3. Inspect exterior lights and plugs to ensure they are working properly. 4. Keep your grill at least 10 feet away from your home and any other structures. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby in case of an emergency. 5. Never leave your grill unattended while in use, and make sure it has cooled completely before storing. 6. Check that windows and doors potentially used in case of evacuation remain unobstructed and functional. 7. Make sure everyone is familiar with your home’s fire escape plan. articles.text: Sharon Ho started her career as an RN at Children’s Hospital in 1980. The Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) was in its nascent stage and she had the incredible opportunity to witness firsthand the wonderful work done by the dedicated nursing and medical staff in the NICU. She found the work gratifying and challenging at the same time as she witnessed the immense dedication of the staff. For parents of the NICU, it can be one of the most stressful and terrifying times of their lives. To this end, the nursing staff was ever present to lend support and their expertise to these families in need. One of Sharon’s real estate colleagues, Mavis Delacroix holds a special place in her heart for Children’s Hospital as well. Her eldest son was in a near fatal car accident when he was brought to Oakland’s Children’s Hospital by ambulance. After more than five hours in surgery and several weeks in the hospital, the entire family celebrated when he was able to return home. Mavis and her family were impressed with the expert level of care and compassion her son received from the surgeon to the house keeping staff. Their shared personal connections to the hospital is what brought this idea together. It has been a privilege to witness the compassion, dedication of the hospital team, who work tirelessly to improve the lives of children and their families. They wanted to express gratitude and show support for the foundation’s invaluable efforts. Together they made the decision to organize a fundraiser at a newly renovated home in Piedmont where handcrafted cocktails and light bites were served. With the help of Davide of Belotti Ristorante e Bottega of College Avenue, a successful event was enjoyed by all! Local realtors Mavis Delacroix (left) and Sharon Ho raised $12,500 to support the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit.
articles.title: Realtors help support Children’s Hospital

articles.text: As one of the old-timers in a college reunion parade, I forwent the golf cart and was walking along when a South Asian alum in the crowd about one third my age called out, “What’s your secret for survival?” Amid the din of cheers and revelry, I yelled back something akin to, “Regular exercise! Physical activity!” I saw that dictum underscored among my male classmates back for the reunion, all of them nonagenarians now. About 15% were remarkably alert physically and mentally, well beyond the peers. Quizzed, little by little these catalytic super-survivors gave away their secrets: #1 is an animated mixer at age 90, heavily into nonprofit work, including parks projects and classmate contacts. #2 is an avid rare-book collector, constantly battling various receptor libraries and institutions in admirable feistiness. #3 has had three heart operations but still made it to 91, thanks to swimming three miles a week in a pool. And happily married. #4 does daily hikes (never strolls) in the hills with the dog, on orders from his cardio doc in 2011. Back then he had died in the ER and, through electric shocks, was brought back with singed chest hairs. He visits his partner/ girlfriend daily. An avid writer, Paul Hertelendy and Samba at the 5K Turkey Trot in Piedmont in 2022. he has lived six more years than any male antecedent. #5 uses a treadmill daily, writes a monthly column for an alumni magazine, and has a girlfriend a good 20 years younger. #6, I don’t know how much he exercises, but he remains a committed chamber musician as a violinist. Ever since undergrad days he has sought out new colleagues ever raveling. An A-1 organizer and catalytic presence. #7 says he used to walk five miles a day. He assured good health “by staying active, minimizing my intake of medicine, cigarettes, and unsolicited advice.” If I had to summarize them, I’d say the Great Secret resides in regular vigorous exercise, companionship, and stimuli of the senses, including the brain. I’m no MD, and none of these guarantee a life as long as Methuselah’s, but if the advice helps others, all the better. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include every-

articles.text: – Joseph Campbell As seniors get older, they may face many challenges in life. Loss of health or loved ones can affect them deeply. While life is filled with ups and downs for all of us and we will not be happy at every moment, it is important to try and help seniors when they are experiencing sadness. Caregivers can play a crucial role in spreading joy to those in their care. Here are four ideas to assist you in bringing happiness to a senior. take to help fill their time with enjoyable activities. Here is a list of a few that they can try: Activities for Seniors • Yoga. There are many yoga classes designed specifically for seniors. Yoga can help calm the mind and body, especially yoga exercises that are slow and gentle. Seniors with limited mobility can try doing chair yoga which will allow them to increase strength, flexibility and breath awareness, all from a seated position. • Painting. Art is an excellent form of self-expression and a great outlet for seniors to share their experiences with the world. Studies have shown that art therapy has many benefits, both physical and mental, for seniors. Picking up a paintbrush can help seniors keep their motor skills sharp and improve hand-eye coordination. The bright, vibrant colors can boost their mood and help reduce depression or anxiety. Painting can also assist seniors with concentration skills and memory, all while improving confidence and giving them a sense of control. • Cooking. There are many cooking classes geared towards seniors which may offer advice regarding specific diets, such as making nutritious meals or meals with low salt content. These classes can be taken in-person which allows seniors to make social connections and establish friendships. Or, for the senior who has a hard time getting out or who prefers to take classes from the comfort of home, there are online options as well. Treat them with compassion. When interacting with parents, grandparents and other loved ones, it’s important to remember to speak with compassion. Seniors want to know that their voice matters and that they will be treated with dignity. We should strive to always speak to seniors with care, patience, and respect, being mindful of any physical or mental challenges they are experiencing. If you can do this, you will see that your efforts go a long way in bringing joy to seniors and making them feel appreciated. Homewatch CareGivers is located at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmonters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. Encourage the use of assistive devices to maximize independence. As people age, they may become less mobile and experience difficulty performing daily tasks. They might not know how to ask for help but there are many products they can use to make their life simpler and more comfortable. Reach out to your healthcare provider for a PT/OT consultation to ensure that you are using the correct devices for your particular needs. If your senior loved one is having a hard time walking, they can use a scooter or walker to help them get around. It may also be helpful to have a shower seat or grab-bars installed in their bathroom, to assist them in safely moving around the room. Seniors experiencing dexterity issues can also utilize products to make their life easier, such as an electric toothbrush. Ask for their stories. Just like all of us, older adults want to know that their life has meaning. Ask them to tell you about one of their favorite memories – for example, “What did you enjoy doing most as a kid?” “Did you have a favorite pet when you were growing up?” “What has brought you the most joy in life?” It’s important to listen closely and ask relevant questions as they share details from their life. Many seniors feel like no one remembers them or that they are a burden to their loved ones. You can counteract these feelings by asking to know more about them and their past. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, July 19, 2023 Seniors The secret of longevity (from someone with a few ideas) By Paul Hertelendy As one of the old-timers in a college reunion parade, I forwent the golf cart and was walking along when a South Asian alum in the crowd about one third my age called out, “What’s your secret for survival?” Amid the din of cheers and revelry, I yelled back something akin to, “Regular exercise! Physical activity!” I saw that dictum underscored among my male classmates back for the reunion, all of them nonagenarians now. About 15% were remarkably alert physically and mentally, well beyond the peers. Quizzed, little by little these catalytic super-survivors gave away their secrets: #1 is an animated mixer at age 90, heavily into nonprofit work, including parks projects and classmate contacts. #2 is an avid rare-book collector, constantly battling various receptor libraries and institutions in admirable feistiness. #3 has had three heart operations but still made it to 91, thanks to swimming three miles a week in a pool. And happily married. #4 does daily hikes (never strolls) in the hills with the dog, on orders from his cardio doc in 2011. Back then he had died in the ER and, through electric shocks, was brought back with singed chest hairs. He visits his partner/ girlfriend daily. An avid writer, “We cannot cure the world of sorrows, but we can choose to live in joy.” – Joseph Campbell Paul Hertelendy and Samba at the 5K Turkey Trot in Piedmont in 2022. he has lived six more years than any male antecedent. #5 uses a treadmill daily, writes a monthly column for an alumni magazine, and has a girlfriend a good 20 years younger. #6, I don’t know how much he exercises, but he remains a committed chamber musician as a violinist. Ever since undergrad days he has sought out new colleagues ever raveling. An A-1 organizer and catalytic presence. #7 says he used to walk five miles a day. He assured good health “by staying active, minimizing my intake of medicine, cigarettes, and unsolicited advice.” If I had to summarize them, I’d say the Great Secret resides in regular vigorous exercise, companionship, and stimuli of the senses, including the brain. I’m no MD, and none of these guarantee a life as long as Methuselah’s, but if the advice helps others, all the better. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? -Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. Loss of health or loved ones can affect them deeply. While life is filled with ups and downs for all of us and we will not be happy at every moment, it is important to try and help seniors when they are experiencing sadness. Caregivers can play a crucial role in spreading joy to those in their care. Here are four ideas to assist you in bringing happiness to a senior. take to help fill their time with enjoyable activities. Here is a list of a few that they can try: Activities for Seniors • Yoga. There are many yoga classes designed specifically for seniors. Yoga can help calm the mind and body, especially yoga exercises that are slow and gentle. Seniors with limited mobility can try doing chair yoga which will allow them to increase strength, flexibility and breath awareness, all from a seated position. • Painting. Art is an excellent form of self-expression and a great outlet for seniors to share their experiences with the world. Studies have shown that art therapy has many benefits, both physical and mental, for seniors. Picking up a paintbrush can help seniors keep their motor skills sharp and improve hand-eye coordination. The bright, vibrant colors can boost their mood and help reduce depression or anxiety. Painting can also assist seniors with concentration skills and memory, all while improving confidence and giving them a sense of control. • Cooking. There are many cooking classes geared towards seniors which may offer advice regarding specific diets, such as making nutritious meals or meals with low salt content. These classes can be taken in-person which allows seniors to make social connections and establish friendships. Or, for the senior who has a hard time getting out or who prefers to take classes from the comfort of home, there are online options as well. Treat them with compassion. When interacting with parents, grandparents and other loved ones, it’s important to remember to speak with compassion. Seniors want to know that their voice matters and that they will be treated with dignity. We should strive to always speak to seniors with care, patience, and respect, being mindful of any physical or mental challenges they are experiencing. If you can do this, you will see that your efforts go a long way in bringing joy to seniors and making them feel appreciated. They might not know how to ask for help but there are many products they can use to make their life simpler and more comfortable. Reach out to your healthcare provider for a PT/OT consultation to ensure that you are using the correct devices for your particular needs. If your senior loved one is having a hard time walking, they can use a scooter or walker to help them get around. It may also be helpful to have a shower seat or grab-bars installed in their bathroom, to assist them in safely moving around the room. Seniors experiencing dexterity issues can also utilize products to make their life easier, such as an electric toothbrush. Ask for their stories. We had some schedule conflicts, with some kids arriving late and some having to leave early due to other summer plans.. But at the trip’s peak, we had three boys and five girls.” Students who attended the trip included Mina Dao Hoang, Darcy McKee, Stephanie Lee, Sara Adams, Zenn Donatiello, Nico French, Alyssa Tang, Aliana Tang, and Bryson Cheney. The boys on the team stayed with Nilson and his wife at their Medford ranch, and the girls stayed with David’s sister, Julie, on her farm. Each property was about 15 minutes from the build site. Although the team had a few takeout dinners, including barbecue and pizza, they prided themselves on mostly cooking their own meals. “Dinners were usually a group prep effort, with the menu picked by one person. On the first night we went on a major grocery shopping spree at the local Food4Less store. Five carts later we had a massive $500 check-out. On the days after that we ate our meals outside on the property where the boys and girls were staying,” said Li. A culinary highlight was vegetable lasagna and garlic bread. Two memorable activities on the team’s two days off were hiking and whitewater rafting on the Rogue River, which goes underground through a lava tube nearby. The trip was a departure from the usual range of PCSC projects, which are generally student-planned. Previous PCSC trips have included working at a special needs school in Bangalore, India in 2016, and a service trip to renovate houses damaged by Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans in 2019. “We had two service trips in mind, one to Puerto Rico and one to the Appalachian Mountains, which we had to cancel during the pandemic,” explained Li. “This Oregon trip was a great return to the heart of what we do,” continued Li, “which is community service and youth leadership development simultaneously. We’re excited to keep on with more trips as the year progresses. Currently, we’re brainstorming a trip to Uganda, and one to Italy. We start with a location and a host. The city also plans to secure approval by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors by the end of 2024 to use up to $2,100,000 of funding for affordable housing through Measure A1, a housing development bond adopted by the County in November 2017. Community engagement At the meeting, Claire Parisa — a UC Berkeley lecturer in city and regional planning — implored the Council to focus its community outreach for changes to Moraga Canyon “not just on its [negative] impact to neighbors,” e.g. traffic congestion, but on what benefits the neighbors want to see,” e.g. dog areas, enhancement of Spring Path, or bike lanes. “We should not just be bringing initial design ideas to them, but welcoming them at the very beginning in the design process to make sure we capture everything that they’re looking for,” she added. Public engagement regarding preferred housing additions and infrastructure updates in Moraga Canyon will begin this fall in the form of surveys, community meetings, and City Council and Commission workshops. No dates or specific programs have yet been set. Community members may stay updated about progress and outreach by subscribing to the city’s Moraga Canyon Specific Plan email newsletter at bit. ly/3O0ymkm. articles.text: Shortly after 4 a.m. on Sunday morning, July 9, suspects in three vehicles drove to the side door of Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue, disabled the alarm and made entry into the store. After two sessions of ransacking the store, the suspects stole an estimated $100,000 in merchandise and money. Based upon surveillance photos, after one ten-minute session ransacking the business for valuable merchandise, the suspects left, and briefly parked at Safeway. When no alarm or alert was heard, they returned to enter the building again to the back of the building and spent 25 minutes stealing items. According to Ace Hardware Manager Shaun Braga it was the second stint of burglary that resulted in the biggest loses. Power tools and cash were taken, and items were strewn all around the store and parking lot. A door on the side of the building was pried open and bolt cutters were used to cut a padlock. Piedmont police found the bolt cutter left behind. Surveillance video showed one of the three suspect vehicles leaving the city two hours later, at 6:17 a.m. Police Dispatch was notified of the loss at 8:40 a.m. Grand Ace Hardware, which has been in business for 50 years, has hired a security guard since the robbery.
