pages.text: 30 Wednesday, July 19, 2023 John Tulloch Continued from page 1 2000. He then worked for Washington State Senator Paull Shin as his only full-time, year-round staff member until 2006. That year, Tulloch received a call from his City Clerk predecessor Ann Swift. “Ann said that the City Council authorized a new position as Administrative Services Technician in next year’s budget and asked me to consider applying for it,” he said. He applied, and in August 2006 he joined the city, primarily focusing on IT and records management. He was among four candidates interviewed for the job. Four years later, in 2010, Tulloch was appointed to the position of Interim City Clerk following the retirement of Swift and was fully appointed City Clerk in 2011. In 2018, he again took on new responsibilities when thenCity Administrator Paul Benoit named Tulloch the Assistant City Administrator. “The position of City Clerk in Piedmont is fairly unique,’ explained Tulloch. “In many other bigger cities the Clerk is focused on statutory duties like elections and agenda preparation. But here we’re 100 people, and half of our staff are police and fire, so everybody gets to do a little bit of everything. This variety in different tasks that I’ve been responsible for during my time with the city has always kept me fascinated, alongside my love of the community I get to work with.” “My time in City Hall has shown me that where Piedmont works best is where the community comes together — take Hampton Field, or the pool project,” he continued. “When I came into City Hall, even as a kid, I was always taken seriously. I walked in with a question, an idea and I got an answer, a response. And I’ve really been proud of continuing that for community members of any age who come in with a question,” he continued. “John has been an indispensable member of our small City team,” said Vice-Mayor Betsy Andersen. “Throughout City Hall he’s admired for his unparalleled knowledge of Piedmont history, unmatched expertise in all things elections, and unwavering commitment to delivering high-quality, good government core services. But for me, what has always stood out the most about John is his dedication to putting the community first. In this, he sets a remarkable benchmark for us all to aspire to. He will truly be missed.” Why, then, depart from City Hall now, Tulloch was asked. “It’s something I’ve been thinking about for a while,” Tulloch said. “I think that the City Council made a fantastic decision in hiring Rosanna Bayon Moore as City Administrator; she comes with a wealth of knowledge and experience. When Sara Lillevand, the former City Administrator, announced that she was going to leave, I wanted to remain here long enough to get Rosanna on her feet before I decided to go on. It’ll be four months since she started, when I leave.” He will not immediately be looking for another job and will use the time to decompress from the 23 years he has been working since graduating from college. Tulloch said that he is looking forward to spending more time with his wife, Karen, and two children – Colin, a sophomore at Piedmont High, and Molly, a seventh grader at Piedmont Middle School. “The past few years took a lot out of all of us, and I’m lucky to be able to take a break,” Tulloch said. “I’m certainly not leaving the community, and this is definitely not a retirement. I love this city, and I want to continue to help it grow. The possibility that I’ll return to City Hall is absolutely there, but I don’t know right now what form that would take. I will always be proud of the work I’ve done here.” The City has engaged Bob Murray & Associates, an executive recruiting firm, to conduct a nationwide search for a new permanent City Clerk. On the firm’s website, the filing deadline is shown to be August 20, 2023. Until a permanent replacement is hired, the City Council has appointed Sheri Hartz to serve as interim City Clerk in Piedmont, effective after Tulloch’s departure on August 4. Hartz served as the City Clerk of Novato from 2010 to 2016, and as City Clerk of Emeryville from 2016 to 2022, when she retired. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, July 19, 2023 Hiking with Jon Continued from page 12 right as opposed to the steep jaunt toward the ski lift on the left where park attendants are working. Moreover, the trail on the right provided an unforgettable walk with bushels of wildflowers lining the path and butterflies fluttering around unbothered around you. Off to your right will be the magnificent Granite Chief Mountain and the Desolation Wilderness. From Washeshu Peak, hikers get a clear view of Lake Tahoe and get a glimpse of Five Lakes while panning to the right—which is a The view of Granite Chief from the peak near the Watson Monument. The Watson Emigrant Pass Marker is an original trail marker for the Placer County Emigrant Road. trail we covered in September of last year. Pack a lunch to eat with the view. There are also mounds of shale enclosures to protect from the wind if needed. Returning to High Camp from Washeshu Peak will round out your day at four miles. However, those interested can hang a left at the Gold Coast Express ski lift to take the route up to the Watson Monument Emigrant Pass Marker. Walking to the marker adds .4 miles to your day and another 300 feet in elevation gain, while the nearby peak to the left of the marker (when facing the plaque) gives an even closer look of Granite Chief. Trails which led to the Granite Chief Wilderness were closed for maintenance. The Watson Monument marks the former Placer County Emigrant Road. It reads an inscription: “The Placer County Emigrant Road, known today as the Western States Trail, extended from Yankee Jim’s on the Foresthill divide to the Washoe Valley in Nevada. Built in 1852, the road served emigrants before providing a link to the Comstock boom towns such as Gold Hill, Silver City and Virginia City in Nevada. In September 1931, pioneer horseman Robert Montgomery Watson, along with the Native Sons of the Golden West, completed marking the portion of the trail from Lake Tahoe to Auburn. The granite monument before you is the original trail marker constructed by Robert Montgomery Watson during the summer of 1931.” Finish your six mile day with a bite to eat at High Camp before traveling back down. Those interested can take the Shirley Canyon Trail if they’d rather descend by foot. The aerial tram ride to-andfrom is $30. Foot traffic was seldom on a Monday at noon with just 18 people on the trail. However, you can expect a crammed tram-ride reminiscent of a Monday-morning on BART. For more information at things to do at Palisades Tahoe and High Camp, visit www.PalisadesTahoe. com. This article updates information in a column published in the Post in August 2021. articles.text: Camp 1973, Piedmont’s popular day camp created is based upon the idea of no screens and good old fashioned fun. On Friday, July 7, the Post caught up with David Hopkins and the campers at Hampton Field. The idea of naming a camp after the year 1973 came from former Recreation Supervisor Erin Rivera, and has been embodied for decades by Hopkins and former retired Rec. Dept. Supervisor Michael Murphy. The year brings to mind tie-die and flower power. Campers initially shy of photos, quickly loosened up as Hopkins and a band of Recreation staff members and teens as summer camp counselors started up a giant bubble rope. Kids in the camp, free from the constraints of grammar and arithmetic, filled their day with face painting, and tromping through the bounce house. David Hopkins will retire at the end of the summer after 34 years with the Recreation Department.

articles.text: As the trucks complete the 10 weeks of removing soil at the Piedmont Community Pool site, contractors are beginning to build a retaining wall for the new pool. The soil work, which began on May 8 and was initially expected to last through June, is now expected to finish by July 14, two weeks behind schedule due to delays on the part of PG&E to disconnect gas and electric lines in the former pool buildings. The contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, is beginning to construct a 385-foot retaining wall, a process that will involve three weeks of grading the site. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that contractors will be digging holes in the wall for utility lines including gas, water, and Comcast for future facilities. Next week the workers will apply a waterproofing substance to the retaining walls, a process which will take one to two weeks. Contractors will then reinforce the retaining wall with rebar and will spray the wall with “shotcrete,” concrete which is applied to the wall through a high-velocity hose. The pool project is still on track to finish by summer next year. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/newpool. Those with questions about the project may contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. articles.text: The decision about pickleball vs. tennis at Linda Park will inevitably disappoint some; so, how can an ethical decision be made? Utilitarianism suggests that an ethical choice is the one that leads to the greatest good for the greatest number, while avoiding extreme negative impact. When it isn’t possible to make everybody equally happy, it is right to emphasize making most people as happy as possible, while displeasing as few people as little as possible. Dedicated pickleball at Linda would eliminate current part-time availability of 2 non-regulation-sized tennis courts, currently marked inconveniently for dual-sport use. This reduction would be offset by converting the two Hampton courts to tennis-only use. Typical tennis use of the Linda courts involves one set of two players. Pickleball use of the courts often involves 16 simultaneous players, with many more waiting their turn; using this down time spent speaking with friends and neighbors, providing daily civic engagement and connectivity. Four full-size, regulation tennis courts are available 3/4 miles away at the Community Tennis Courts. Nearby Hampton Field offers two regulation-sized courts; re-striping these for tennis would significantly enhance serious tennis play. Tennis often requires advance planning and arrangement with similarly skilled, similarly inclined players; open pickleball play welcomes the young and old, agile and wonky-kneed, skillful and inept, players who arrive with friends, and solitary newcomers hoping to connect. Barking from the dog park across the street is almost continuous from morning till dusk. Linda Avenue itself, which is a relatively busy traffic street for Piedmont, has buses traversing this route all day. To single out noise from pickleball as “excessive” seems like an exaggeration given all the activities on that stretch of the street. Nevertheless, in the spirit of compromise, we [pickleball players] have begun using softer, quieter, balls in an attempt to mitigate any noise from play. If pickleball noise is excessive and needs to be curtailed, why not mandate the same for the athletic field, playground, dog park, and schoolyard? That’s not terribly practical. Neither are the requests to limit or exclude pickleball from these seldom used courts. The sport of pickleball is growing exponentially and is loved by all who play. –Neal S. articles.text: Although the trial of full-time pickleball play at the Linda Beach courts was not a topic on the last Recreation Commission agenda, Piedmonters voiced both their support and concerns for nearly an hour during the public comment period at a two-hour meeting on Wednesday, June 21. Among the approximately 20 speakers, most were pickleball players who supported the trial. However, many neighbors countered that city staff and supporters were not adequately addressing the noise created by the play, which impacted their lives daily. Lisa Neville, who lives near the dog park, said, “I am very much affected by the noise of pickleball. It’s being played 12 to 13 hours a day, seven days a week. This involves not only the game itself but all the noise that goes along with it – the yelling, the shouting, the cheering particularly later at night … I’m all for having a good time playing a sport you love, but when it impacts the entire neighborhood it needs to be reimagined.” Neighbor Elane Rehr said that her “major concern among many concerns is that the constant loud noises from pickleball may be having ill effects on the children’s bodies and on their behavior. I taught psychology for 40 years, and stress has major effects on health. Constant loud noises throughout the day can create stress. Stress can create lifelong negative health consequences.” Former Recreation Commission member Christine Free said that although she had never had a noise complaint for the 38 years she’d been living near the courts, the impact of pickleball play was different. “This issue should not be viewed as a popularity contest between pickleball players and neighbors with each side marshaling supporters to show up and be heard. The numbers are overwhelmingly on the players’ side. It’s an issue of fairness and the Commission doing the right thing for the members of the Piedmont community who have a valid position supported by a wide range of scientific acoustical studies and, more importantly, the testimony of its citizens,” Free added. Constance Whitting, whose backyard is 50 feet from the courts, said that although a program for part-time pickleball play may have been acceptable, “seven days a week is way too much. For those of you who are playing, you’ve made a very good presentation as to why pickleball is great, but you only listen to the ‘pock, pock, pock’ while you play. You don’t listen to it nonstop, in your yard, on your deck, in your home, in the kitchen. It even goes to the living room and bedroom, so I need some relief.” Jamie Patterson said, “There’s not quite enough openness around the noise study. We requested the opportunity to have some say or review of what the structure of the [Recreation Commission’s] noise study was going to be prior to it occurring. That request was not granted.” Although the public comments lasted more than 40 minutes, no action was taken by the Recreation Commission because per state law, items not on the agenda for the public meeting of a board or commission may not be acted upon or discussed. The Commission will address the trial of full-time pickleball play at its next meeting, on Wednesday, July 19, when it is expected to make a recommendation regarding future use of the Linda Beach courts, which will then be brought to the City Council. Community members can send questions and comments about the trial to BeachPickleballTrial@piedmont.ca.gov. “The equation shows that you suits are entirely justified in your feelings of moral uncertainty.”
articles.title: Pickleball neighbors voice concerns at June 21 Rec. Commission meeting

articles.text: Next Wednesday, July 19, the Recreation Commission is expected to make a recommendation regarding the future use of the Linda Beach courts. The sport of pickleball is in a trial period of full-time play at the courts which will conclude at the end of July. Currently the courts are available for organized drop-in pickleball play Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. First-come, firstserved informal drop-in play is available during remaining weekday hours: 9 a.m. to 10 a.m., and 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. (or dusk, whichever comes first). Community members can share their feedback in-person at the meeting, which will be held in the City Council chambers at City Hall (120 Vista Avenue) at 7:30 p.m. on July 19. After a positive response from most responders to a noise survey sent to neighbors of the courts at Hampton Park and Beach four weeks into the trial, the trial period continued for six more months. In January 2020, the city council approved permanent pickleball play during limited hours at Hampton and Beach. On February 15, 2023, the Recreation Commission approved an exclusive pickleball trial at the Beach Field Tennis Courts for five months, from February 27 through July 31. Since the trial began, city staff and the Recreation Commission have received public feedback with nearly 100 in-person comments at public meetings, over 300 emails, and over 800 responses to a recent online community survey on the trial. Many of these comments regard impacts of safety and noise. In response, the city engaged an acoustical consulting firm, Salter, to study noise levels at the Beach courts during and outside of pickleball play hours. Salter’s report, published on July 6 and available at bit.ly/3NK1UTs, concludes that “pickleball noise [does not] exceed standards set forth by the City General Plan or Municipal Code.” Pickleball players at the Linda Beach courts.

articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Planning Commission discussed two programs for increased housing in Piedmont at their meeting on July 10. Included were design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings and ADU incentives. Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) Senior Planner Pierce MacDonald told the Commission, “In 2020, the city received a [state] planning grant in the amount of $160,000 and the City Council approved an agreement with Lisa Wise Consulting to begin work on objective design standards for multifamily and mixed use buildings using this grant funding.” Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The plans don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. “generally urban infill areas and less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont,” said MacDonald. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking - they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, MacDonald said that the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs - which are three Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont - can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (though construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). She added that the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing for homeowners to submit ADUs larger than the city’s standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Both the permit-ready ADU styles, and information on building larger ADUs, is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Commission to make decision on pickleball courts By Selen Ozturk Next Wednesday, July 19, the Recreation Commission is expected to make a recommendation regarding the future use of the Linda Beach courts. The sport of pickleball is in a trial period of full-time play at the courts which will conclude at the end of July. Currently the courts are available for organized drop-in pickleball play Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. First-come, firstserved informal drop-in play is available during remaining weekday hours: 9 a.m. to 10 a.m., and 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. (or dusk, whichever comes first). Community members can share their feedback in-person at the meeting, which will be held in the City Council chambers at City Hall (120 Vista Avenue) at 7:30 p.m. on July 19. After a positive response from most responders to a noise survey sent to neighbors of the courts at Hampton Park and Beach four weeks into the trial, the trial period continued for six more months. In January 2020, the city council approved permanent pickleball play during limited hours at Hampton and Beach. On February 15, 2023, the Recreation Commission approved an exclusive pickleball trial at the Beach Field Tennis Courts for five months, from February 27 through July 31. Since the trial began, city staff and the Recreation Commission have received public feedback with nearly 100 in-person comments at public meetings, over 300 emails, and over 800 responses to a recent online community survey on the trial. Many of these comments regard impacts of safety and noise. In response, the city engaged an acoustical consulting firm, Salter, to study noise levels at the Beach courts during and outside of pickleball play hours. Salter’s report, published on July 6 and available at bit.ly/3NK1UTs, concludes that “pickleball noise [does not] exceed standards set forth by the City General Plan or Municipal Code.” Pickleball players at the Linda Beach courts. Planning Commission to discuss programs for more housing in Piedmont By Selen Ozturk Members of the Piedmont Planning Commission discussed two programs for increased housing in Piedmont at their meeting on July 10. Included were design standards for multifamily and mixed-use buildings and ADU incentives. Multifamily Objective Design Standards (MODS) Senior Planner Pierce MacDonald told the Commission, “In 2020, the city received a [state] planning grant in the amount of $160,000 and the City Council approved an agreement with Lisa Wise Consulting to begin work on objective design standards for multifamily and mixed use buildings using this grant funding.” Under this proposal, applications for development of multi-family and mixed-use commercial and residential buildings that conform to a set of measurable architectural standards would be approved directly by city staff, without a public hearing. These standards include elements like building placements, facade designs, window and balcony configurations, and location of parking areas. The plans don’t add any new zoning where these buildings could be developed. They apply only to the existing mixed commercial and residential districts in western Piedmont including parts of Grand, Linda, and Highland Avenues, i.e. “generally urban infill areas and less than 1% of the total land area of Piedmont,” said MacDonald. The standards also don’t change existing zoning rules for building density, height, or parking - they just simplify the process for reviewing applications. Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) To make it easier for Piedmont property owners to build new ADUs, MacDonald said that the City developed permit-ready ADU designs. Any of these designs - which are three Tudor, Craftsman, and Mediterranean styles common to homes throughout Piedmont - can be submitted as-is to receive a planning permit from the city, giving applicants a head start on the development process (though construction reports for the site’s slope and soil conditions still need to be created before a building permit is issued). She added that the city also instituted a program at the beginning of 2023 allowing for homeowners to submit ADUs larger than the city’s standard size “in exchange for a deed restriction mandating that if the ADU is rented out, the rent must be affordable to tenants who meet ‘very low income’ affordability thresholds set by the Association of Bay Area Governments.” Both the permit-ready ADU styles, and information on building larger ADUs, is available at bit.ly/43hbjHD. Commission meeting By Selen Ozturk Although the trial of full-time pickleball play at the Linda Beach courts was not a topic on the last Recreation Commission agenda, Piedmonters voiced both their support and concerns for nearly an hour during the public comment period at a two-hour meeting on Wednesday, June 21. Among the approximately 20 speakers, most were pickleball players who supported the trial. However, many neighbors countered that city staff and supporters were not adequately addressing the noise created by the play, which impacted their lives daily. Lisa Neville, who lives near the dog park, said, “I am very much affected by the noise of pickleball. It’s being played 12 to 13 hours a day, seven days a week. This involves not only the game itself but all the noise that goes along with it – the yelling, the shouting, the cheering particularly later at night … I’m all for having a good time playing a sport you love, but when it impacts the entire neighborhood it needs to be reimagined.” Neighbor Elane Rehr said that her “major concern among many concerns is that the constant loud noises from pickleball may be having ill effects on the children’s bodies and on their behavior. I taught psychology for 40 years, and stress has major effects on health. Constant loud noises throughout the day can create stress. Stress can create lifelong negative health consequences.” Former Recreation Commission member Christine Free said that although she had never had a noise complaint for the 38 years she’d been living near the courts, the impact of pickleball play was different. “This issue should not be viewed as a popularity contest between pickleball players and neighbors with each side marshaling supporters to show up and be heard. The numbers are overwhelmingly on the players’ side. It’s an issue of fairness and the Commission doing the right thing for the members of the Piedmont community who have a valid position supported by a wide range of scientific acoustical studies and, more importantly, the testimony of its citizens,” Free added. Constance Whitting, whose backyard is 50 feet from the courts, said that although a program for part-time pickleball play may have been acceptable, “seven days a week is way too much. For those of you who are playing, you’ve made a very good presentation as to why pickleball is great, but you only listen to the ‘pock, pock, pock’ while you play. You don’t listen to it nonstop, in your yard, on your deck, in your home, in the kitchen. It even goes to the living room and bedroom, so I need some relief.” Jamie Patterson said, “There’s not quite enough openness around the noise study. We requested the opportunity to have some say or review of what the structure of the [Recreation Commission’s] noise study was going to be prior to it occurring. That request was not granted.” Although the public comments lasted more than 40 minutes, no action was taken by the Recreation Commission because per state law, items not on the agenda for the public meeting of a board or commission may not be acted upon or discussed. The Commission will address the trial of full-time pickleball play at its next meeting, on Wednesday, July 19, when it is expected to make a recommendation regarding future use of the Linda Beach courts, which will then be brought to the City Council. Community members can send questions and comments about the trial to BeachPickleballTrial@piedmont.ca.gov. “The equation shows that you suits are entirely justified in your feelings of moral uncertainty.”

articles.text: T he Cit y of Pied mont encourages residents to complete a short online survey that will help identify improvements needed to better serve people with disabilities. The seven-question survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ADASurvey and will remain open through Friday, August 25. The survey asks: • If you’re aware of specific concerns, complaints, or problems regarding access to city facilities, services, or programs for people with disabilities • Whether you’ve requested an accommodation in the past, and if so, how it was handled • What should be the city’s highest priority for accessibility improvements For questions about the survey or an update on an ADA transition plan, contact Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont. ca.gov.

articles.text: As part of Piedmont’s annual Sidewalk Repair Program, 901 locations on sidewalks throughout the city were repaired by shaving in early July. The work was done to eliminate tripping hazards where the concrete has been lifted due to street tree roots. According to Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales the process of concrete shaving “looks a lot like grinding it down, except it’s a cleaner, faster way to eliminate tripping hazards presented by offset sidewalks. It’s more of a repair than a sidewalk replacement.” The project was done quickly and completed by July 7. The City Council awarded Precision Concrete Cutting a $102,140.63 contract for this project and was funded by the city’s Facilities Maintenance Fund. A full list of all sidewalk areas throughout the city that were affected by this project, including location, size, and cost, is available in the city’s contract report at bit.ly/43BpIiP. pages.text: Wednesday, July 12, 2023 5 Troop One brings 100 years of history By Samantha R. Pell No one knows the history of Piedmont’s Troop One better than former longtime Troop One Scoutmasters John Stewart and Rich Harms, so I turned to them for a story as rich and juicy as the famed Troop One burgers. Scouting in Piedmont dates back to 1910 under the leadership of Rev. Sturchell, minister of Piedmont Community Church. It was six years before the national organization, Boy Scouts of America, was chartered by Congress. The Piedmont Council was chartered in 1921, and Troop One was its first troop. Troop One prides itself on training leaders and having a strong structure, all while enforcing one of Scouting’s core values of empowering and enabling Scouts, ready for real life situations. Roughly 20 years ago Rich Harms, the Scoutmaster, decided to start a Scout-run fundraiser. At the time the hamburger stand was not so elaborate. Parents brought their own barbecue charcoal, and lighter fluid. It was operated out of a few pop-up tents and was by no means a grand affair. The Troop recognized the need Samantha Pell (left), Brigid Gaffikin, Susannah Cantrill, Eleanor Hawthorn, Dave Larson, Cade Ogles, Ciaren Gallagher, Nicholas Markopolous, and Liam Leahy at Troop One’s annual hamburger stand on the Fourth of July for new equipment, and in true Scouting fashion, came up with an innovative idea – sell hamburgers on the 4th of July at the parade. It soon became the main source of funding. Ready for the lunch rush after the 4th of July Parade, watermelon pieces await hungry parade goers. Earlybird hamburger customers prior to the 4th of July Parade However, other interests were at hand. “We wanted to open an opportunity to have Scouts learn about retail,” explained Stewart, whose e-mail address remains at scoutmaster.stewar t@gmail.com. During his years as Scoutmaster, the stand was expanded with the purchase of four commercial, natural gas grills. Troop One always emphasizes preparing Scouts for their future life, having Scouts portray a positive image of Scouting with the burger stand. Some of the early challenges were getting Scouts to sign up to help. “From the beginning, I made it very clear that the Scouts would have to step up to help,” Stewart said. As previously mentioned, Troop One values leadership and having Scouts step up, take initiative, and lead. One of the many things that makes Troop One unique is that it requires all of its youth leaders to attend the National Youth Leadership Training. It’s an intense, oneweek camp of sorts that “provides a solid training foundation which will assist in training young leaders”. A reminder from Stewart is: “Good leaders are not born, they are trained.” After operating for more than 100 years, raising future leaders is part of Troop One’s DNA. Part of the goal of training leaders ties into the burger stand. Scouts are involved in every step in the preparation, execution, and follow up for the stand. Promoting the stand is one of the largest responsibilities that the Scouts have. In addition to being Piedmont’s first Scout Troop (and possibly first in the country), Troop One can also claim many other firsts. Its hamburger stand was the first Scout-run fundraiser for a troop. In addition, it was the first to start going to Kirby Cove (in Marin near the Golden Gate Bridge) each March to prepare for the busy upcoming camping season. Furthermore, only a few years ago Troop One had no girls whatsoever. After joining as the Troop’s first girl two years ago, two more followed suit. And last spring we had six more girls join. All this goes to show that they can grow, adapt and change rapidly – another core value of Scouting... and life in general. Troop One has been pioneering Scouting for the past 100 years but has never failed to lose sight of what’s important: community. Always ready to step up, it stands out by always volunteering, and giving back. Our burger stand is both a service to the community and a fundraiser, but it’s far more than a fundraiser. It’s an event that celebrates and brings together the Scouts and community. Troop One offers its huge thanks to its burger stand committee of Bernice and Mike Gallagher, Kristen and Tim Ogles, and Siow Fang Tan and James Pell. In addition, it extends thanks to its generous sponsors, Dave Larson of Piedmont Grocery, Teresa Baum of Compass Real Estate, Trader Joe’s of Rockridge, and many parent volunteers. Former Troop 1 Scoutmaster John Stewart congratulates Alex Cantrill (left) and Hayden Jahn on the look of this year’s hamburger stand. Eleanor Hawthorn and Susannah Cantrill attach the American Flag on the Troop 1 hamburger stand.

articles.text: Two days before the start of new school contracts, the Piedmont School Board announced on June 28 the appointment of Joseph Marik as a new Assistant Principal at Piedmont High School. For the last seven years, Marik held the Assistant Principal and Principal positions at Aspire Lionel Wilson Prep in Oakland. Marik will take the position at PHS vacated by Irma Muñez, who was named principal of Millennium High School. Marik joins Principal Sukanya Goswami and Erin Igoe, also an Assistant Principal. “As an educator, I believe nothing is more important than building meaningful connections and relationships with students and colleagues. I am also passionate about post-secondary readiness and enjoy building programs and systems that support students to develop and pursue a meaningful plan for college and career,” said Marik. Marik has held a variety of roles during his 17 years in education, including positions in Memphis, Denver, Atlanta, and Los Angeles. Prior to being an administrator, he taught high school economics and middle school math. “In addition to his experience, he struck me as having the focus, skills, and energy to move PHS to the next level,” said the school district Finance Director Ruth Alahydoian. Marik graduated from Boston College with degrees in History and Economics. He also received a Masters in Teaching from the University of Memphis and earned his CA Administrative Services credential at UC Berkeley. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, July 12, 2023 SchOOLs By Jay Russell Romi Bhatia, an incoming senior at Piedmont High School, orchestrated a book drive at the three Piedmont elementary schools this spring which totaled 1,600 books, all to be donated to East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP), The East Bay Children’s Romi Bhatia book drive generates 1,600 books Book Project, whose mission to improve the literacy of local youth, was founded in 2005. Since then, it has placed more than 2,000,000 books in the hands of children with limited or no access to reading material. Bhatia asked each Piedmont elementary school if he could run a small announcement about the book drive in each school’s weekly newsletter. The shool obliged and Bhatia put donation boxes at each school. “I did not expect 1600. I thought it would be maybe half that. It was an overwhelming amount of books, especially in the first couple of weeks; I was so surprised by it,” said Bhatia. With the help of his father Rajeev’s car, Romi packed up hundreds of pounds of books, mostly for K-5 readers, and delivered the books to EBCBP on Harrison Street in Oakland. There to receive the donation coincidentally was Bhatia’s former librarian at Havens School, Ellen Reed. “I really enjoyed reading a lot as an elementary schooler, and I still do. I thought it would be great if I could help foster the love of reading in kids who didn’t have access to books,” Bhatia said. Last year Bhatia volunteered six hours a week with the Reading Intervention program at Havens. Havens Reading Intervention faculty members Michelle Song and Giena Vogel found that Bhatia’s group of five kids were able to quickly get up to their grade level reading proficiency by April. “Because I taught my students so quickly, I was then given five more students, who I again taught individually for an hour a week until the end of the year,” Bhatia explained. To learn more about the East Bay Children’s Book Project visit Eastbaychildrensbookproject.org. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s College and Career Center will have to find a new Director next year. Gwenly Carrel, its Director for the last four years, has retired. Although she only had a short stint at PUSD, she sat down with the Post to discuss the past, present and future of her career, and college admissions in general. Carrel spent 2002-2014 as the College & Career Advisor at Campolindo High School in Moraga, where she worked with Carol Kitchens, the wife of former Piedmont High principal Rich Kitchens. That connection brought her to Piedmont in 2019, a time of great transformation in college admissions. The biggest event of the year for the College and Career Center is Mock College Admission Night. Just as Carrel was getting ready for the event which helps juniors and underclassmen understand what makes a strong college application, the Covid pandemic hit. It was March 13, 2020. Her first class of seniors, already finished with their college applications, faced the dilemma of deciding which college admission to accept. “[The class of 2020] couldn’t even go on trips to look at the campuses where they were accepted to make their decisions.” Carrell explained. “I would tell them you can at least go there and drive around the campus. The poor class of 2021 was just starting, and they couldn’t go look at things. They couldn’t put their lives together,” she added. Then the University of California got rid of standardized testing. “Why did that happen? Could you go to a SAT or ACT testing center? Parents were sending the landscape of college admissions, however. “There were so Gwenly Carrel in Piedmont High Counseling office. their kids out of state just to take the test. That was really crazy,” said Carrel. Carrel believes the SAT and ACT “test optional” format is here to stay, and pointed out that a 2021 lawsuit now makes schools in the UC system unable to consider those test scores for admission. “UC was always was going to come up with their own sort of test, but that remains to be seen if that will ever happen,” she said. Carrel has experience working on both sides of admission, with students and as an Articulation Analyst for Admission in the University of California’s office of the President, Janet Napolitano. Carrel’s interview with the Post coincided with the announcement that Affirmative Action was struck down. “When that came out this morning as breaking news, I said to my husband, ‘all they have to do is to look to what California had to do almost 20 years ago,’” Carrel explained. articles.text: “I’m not one of those creative types.” “Sure, I made something that I posted online just for fun, but I’m really not that good at art.” “I used to do a lot of creative writing, before I had kids, but it was just a hobby, it wasn’t like actual writing.” “Well, I guess I have to be creative at work with problem solving – I work in HR – but that’s different from REAL creativity.” Do any of these statements look familiar to you? When I work with folks on accessing their creative selves, oftentimes, the first thing they tell me is that they aren’t creative or that they used to be but aren’t creative anymore. I see two issues in these statements: One, we have limited the definition of “creative” to only encapsulate a level of excellence that is recognized on a huge scale. Two, we are all “doing” too much and not taking time for “being.” Let’s tackle the definition of creative living. There is no requirement that all of us become the next Monet or Lizzo. In fact, that would likely be statistically impossible. But it is possible that we can exist in a way that allows our personal creative spirit to thrive. This could mean picking up a paint brush, but it can also mean adding in more play to life, Take the time to relax and get your creative juices flowing. taking time to really notice the world around you, taking more strategic risks at work, coming up with a new way to get your kids to bed. All of these are creative actions that support creative living. So, let’s give up the myth that creativity means “famous” artist or inventor and instead embrace our everyday creative self. Have you ever noticed how whenever you ask a friend or another parent in the camp pick up line, “How are you doing?” the answer almost always comes back, “You know, we are Busy!” And that’s true for most of us. We have filled our time with activities and engagements and functions and events. And while all of these things can be fun or important for a variety of reasons, it doesn’t leave much space for doing nothing. And it is in the “nothing” that we often find and access our creative voice–the voice that exists in all of us and wants to come out and express but can be easily shoved down amidst the hustle and bustle of daily busy-ness. To let the creative voice out to play, it needs moments of quiet. Times when there is not a planned activity and the mind can just wander and find the spark that inspires a creative act of some kind. So, if you are searching for your creative voice or want creativity in your daily life, let’s put aside stories of greatness and look for quiet moments of reflection where creativity can thrive in small acts. pages.text: Wednesday, July 12, 2023 9 Summer Thoughts Letting out the Creative Voice through Creative Living By Nina Meehan “I’m not one of those creative types.” “Sure, I made something that I posted online just for fun, but I’m really not that good at art.” “I used to do a lot of creative writing, before I had kids, but it was just a hobby, it wasn’t like actual writing.” “Well, I guess I have to be creative at work with problem solving – I work in HR – but that’s different from REAL creativity.” Do any of these statements look familiar to you? When I work with folks on accessing their creative selves, oftentimes, the first thing they tell me is that they aren’t creative or that they used to be but aren’t creative anymore. I see two issues in these statements: One, we have limited the definition of “creative” to only encapsulate a level of excellence that is recognized on a huge scale. Two, we are all “doing” too much and not taking time for “being.” Let’s tackle the definition of creative living. There is no requirement that all of us become the next Monet or Lizzo. In fact, that would likely be statistically impossible. But it is possible that we can exist in a way that allows our personal creative spirit to thrive. This could mean picking up a paint brush, but it can also mean adding in more play to life, Take the time to relax and get your creative juices flowing. taking time to really notice the world around you, taking more strategic risks at work, coming up with a new way to get your kids to bed. All of these are creative actions that support creative living. So, let’s give up the myth that creativity means “famous” artist or inventor and instead embrace our everyday creative self. Have you ever noticed how whenever you ask a friend or another parent in the camp pick up line, “How are you doing?” the answer almost always comes back, “You know, we are Busy!” And that’s true for most of us. We have filled our time with activities and engagements and functions and events. And while all of these things can be fun or important for a variety of reasons, it doesn’t leave much space for doing nothing. And it is in the “nothing” that we often find and access our creative voice–the voice that exists in all of us and wants to come out and express but can be easily shoved down amidst the hustle and bustle of daily busy-ness. To let the creative voice out to play, it needs moments of quiet. Times when there is not a planned activity and the mind can just wander and find the spark that inspires a creative act of some kind. So, if you are searching for your creative voice or want creativity in your daily life, let’s put aside stories of greatness and look for quiet moments of reflection where creativity can thrive in small acts. articles.text: The United States nearly saw their Gold Cup run come to an end on Sunday, July 9, before edging past Canada on penalty kicks in the quarterfinals. After ending regulation in a 1-1 draw and in overtime at 2-2, the U.S. defeated the Canadians 3-2 in a penalty shootout. They are now set to face Panama in the semifinals today, July 12, at Snapdragon Stadium in San Diego. In spite of the score, the U.S. dominated possession and continuously tested Canada’s defense Can Jamaica pull off the upset of Mexico? with 21 shots, eight of which were on target. Canada, was held to five shots on goal, only two on target. Despite the Stars and Stripes putting up a lot of shots, Brandon Vasquez broke the 0-0 deadlock in the 88th minute after receiving a perfect cross into the area by DeJuan Jones. But in second-half stoppage time, Canada was awarded a penalty kick after the ball came into contact with Miles Robinson’s hand. Canada nearly stole the match when Jacob Shaffelburg scored in the 109th minute, but with six minutes left in overtime, the U.S. scored on an own goal by Canada’s Scott Kennedy. Goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair’s attempted clearance bounced off Kennedy and into the net. It with the game now tied at 2-2, the game went to penalty kicks to provide a winner. U.S. keeper Matt Turner stopped Canada’s first two penalty shots, and San Jose Earthquakes’ Cade Cowell put the U.S. ahead, 3-2. The United States won when Canada’s shot by Charles-Andreas Brym hit the crossbar. Turner is blossoming into the country’s next standout goalkeeper. Not counting penalty shootouts, Turner has been successful in 11 of 25 penalty kicks against him. Penalties are typically converted at an 80 percent success rate, making Turner one of the most successful PK defenders in world football. Looking ahead to the semifinals, the United States squares off with Panama, which is coming off a mighty 4-nil win over Qatar. Despite Panama being a tough group, I’m taking the Americans, but it’s a little closer than wanted. The Posts Prediction: U.S. wins 2-1 In the other semifinal, Mexico, always a tournament favorite, is set to face the Reggae Boyz today, July 12, at 7:00 Photo courtesy of CONCACAF.com The United States pulled off a dramatic win over Canada in penalty kicks to reach the semifinals today with Panama. p.m. at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas. This is a tough one to predict because Mexico is playing well after beating Costa Rica 2-0 and are the Vegas favorites to reach the finals. Josh Bernstein, PHS Class of 1975, just finished a swim across the English Channel with a team of open water swimmers from the South End rowing Club in San Francisco. JOSH BERNSTEIN Distance Swimmer Piedmont High Class of 1975 University of California Class of 1979 Josh Bernstein, PHS Class of 1975, is a lifelong swimmer who, at the age of 66, just finished one of the most prestigious open-water swims in the world, On June 29 he crossed the 21-mile English Channel with a group of six swimmers, finishing the crossing in 13 hours, 58 minutes. He’s done countless endurance swims, including swimming the width of Lake Tahoe, from Alcatraz to San Francisco numerous times, and recently the aquatic Bay to Breakers, from the Bay Bridge past the Golden Gate Bridge to Ocean Beach on June 10. across the English Channel in the June 6 edition of the Piedmont Post. Below, he highlights his training schedule and his approach to swimming and athletics. What is your workout program this summer? I get up at 4:00 am and drive to San Francisco so I’m at the South End Rowing Club by 5:15 or so. I do a gym workout that includes a lot of stretching, joint support, and strengthening. Then, our Swiss Pod gets in the Bay promptly at 6:16 a.m. – yes, precisely 6:16! We typically swim for about an hour. Where we go is entirely dependent on the tides and other conditions. On weekends we get in at 7:27 and go longer. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Now that my big swims are behind me, I’m focusing on strengthening, nutrition, and trimming down a bit, along with constantly working on my swimstroke. How are you measuring your development? I’ve long since abandoned that sort of thing. I spent decades watching the clock and counting mileage. Now, I swim for fun. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? One of my podmates, Rick Mulvihill, spent his career coaching. He keeps an eye on my technique and he pushes me to improve. When I’m training for a big event, I check in with some of my previous coaches I’m still in touch with. I’m also friends with some pretty amazing open water swimmers like Lynne Cox and Suzanne Heim-Bowen, who generously offer helpful suggestions. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Starting last November, I completed a 5-mile swim in pretty cold water from Kirby Cove to Aquatic Park. Then in May I swam another cold 5-miler, the “5 Coves of Death.” In early June, I swam the 10-mile “Bay to Breakers” from the Bay Bridge out the Golden Gate then south to Ocean Beach. Finally, I just got back from England where I swam an English Channel relay with five teammates. In the fall, there are two fundraising swims dear to me. Swim Across America raises money for UCSF Children’s Hospital for cancer research and treatment by swimming from St. Francis Yacht Club to Aquatic Park. And I personally sponsor a Golden Gate swim to support the UCSF Cardiology Council. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Find sports you really enjoy and have a great time doing them every day with like-minded friends. Winning medals, breaking records, and accomplishing goals is nice, but the real race is longevity and quality of life spent with family and friends. Terrill competed in the 2023 Pac-12 Championship in the Pole Vault, where he cleared f 16 feet, 3.5 inches. He was named Co-Athlete of the Year by the Post in 2022, sharing the honor with distance runner Jack Stein. What is your workout program this summer? Aside from playing sports all day with the campers, our Cal coach has us on a summer workout plan that includes daily sessions to maintain our fitness and strength. It also includes balance and stability exercises and general conditioning. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goal is to just stay in shape. So far, so good. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development by improvement overall; jumping higher, faster times, and lifting more weight. At the start of the season, I was benching 185 pounds and was up to 215 by the end of the season. I was squatting, 315 pounds at the beginning of the season and 405 pounds at the end. In competition, I started the season pole vaulting 16 feet and finished with 16 feet, 6 inches at the Big Meet, Cal vs. Stanford, in April. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Mostly on my own with workout plans sent to me by my coach. I’ve been playing a lot of pick-up basketball games also. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I qualified for the Pac12 Championships at Mt. Sac in Los Angeles where I came in 9th out of 19 vaulters with a height of 16 feet, 3 inches. I also PR’d this season at 16 feet, 6 inches. I’m working really hard to get to 17 feet next season for the regional qualifiers. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes?

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Wimbledon.com Mackie McDonald, a former Piedmont High tennis star, competed at Wimbledon on July 3. Mackie McDonald’s entry at Wimbledon was more brief than desired. He lost in the first round to No. 23 seeded Alexander Bublik on July 3, Scores of the fourset match were close all the way, 6-7 (7-3), 6-4, 6-4, 6-4. It was an rough result for Mackie after winning the first set and leading the third at 3-0, but Bublik found his rhythm and carried the momentum throughout the remaining sets. The result brings McDonald’s world-ranking to No. 53. He was ranked No. 48 in August last year. Bublik is currently No. 30 on the ATP World Tour. Although he took the final three sets, it was a battle all the way until the finish. McDonald and Bublik traded games in the second set as the server until Bublik pulled ahead by winning the fifth game as the returner. McDonald led 4-1 in the third set, but Bublik won five straight games to pull ahead. In the final set, Bublik jumped out to a 3-1 lead and although Mackie made things closer at a 5-4 deficit, Bublik took match point as the server. Bublik largely took over the match with his effectiveness in serves, recording 24 aces on the afternoon. McDonald, meanwhile, only recorded six. He also had a loss in the first round at the French Open on May 28 to No. 24 seeded Sebastian Korda in three sets, 6-4, 7-5, 6-4. Korda, a 22-year-old American, entered as the world’s No. 30 ranked player and is now No. 25. McDonald led the first set 3-2, but conceded three straight games to fall behind 5-3. He won the next game as the server to make it closer 5-4, but Korda won setpoint after going up 40-15. In the second set, McDonald led 4-3 but Korda tied 4-4 as the server and went ahead 5-4 as the returner. McDonald tied it 5-5 by taking a break point of his own, but Korda won as the returner, once again, 6-5. With set-point, McDonald initially led 30-15, but Korda wound up winning the next two points to win 40-30. In the third set, Mackie the two traded games until McDonald led 4-3, but Korda tied 4-4, then won his fifth game as the returner before closing out in service winning in deuce for match point. McDonald had an opportunity to win while holding Advantage as the returner, but Korda effectively responded. The Wimbledon is the grass court portion of the Grand Slam tournament schedule. McDonald now looks ahead to his strongest season, the hard court season that stretches from July to November. Mackie will next compete in the U.S. Open in New York City from August 28–September 4. Mackie McDonald lost in four sets at Wimbledon to No. 23 seed Alexander Bublik. Mackie McDonald’s next Grand Slam tournament will be the U.S. Open at the end of August.

articles.text: Nearing the 2-week mark of the 2023 Tour de France. with defending champion Jonah Vingegaard of Denmark claimed the Yellow Jersey after jumping to the front in Stage 6. But it is a highly competitive race, with Slovenian rider Tadej Pogačar in second place just 17 seconds behind. Vingegaard established a 25-second lead on Pogačar following Stage 6 and continued the advantage through Stage 9’s mountain course to Puy de Dôme, where the Slovenian trimmed eight seconds from the Dane’s lead. This year’s race has been a terrific tour for American rider Nielson Powless, who currently has a good lead in the mountain climber classification with 46 points, ahead of Felix Gall of Austria with 28 points. Fellow American, Sepp Kuss, is in 10th place, but he’s playing a support role to leader Vingegaard as a member of the Jumbo-Visma team. Le Tour progresses through a flat Stage 11 today, July 12, and a medium mountain run for Stage 12 on Thursday, July 13. That’s when the tour begins three straight mountain stages before a rest day on July 17, followed by a Stage 16 time trial and another mountain course for Stage 17. The Stage 13 mountain ride occurs on Bastille Day, France’s Independence Day, traveling 86 miles from Châtillon sur Chalaronne to Grand Colombier. It features two steep ascents, including a summit finish on Grand Colombier via a 17.4 kilometer climb at a 7.1 percent grade. Stage 14 is a 94-mile ride from Annemasse to Morzine with six Photo courtesy of Eurosport Jonas Vingegaard, the defending 2022 Tour de France champion, returned to the lead in General Classification following Stage 6. Photo courtesy of Nielson Powless official Twitter American rider Nielson Powless currently leads the mountain rider classification. different climbing sections and varying ascents and descents along the way. The ride opens with a 4.2- kilometer climb at a 4.6 percent grade up Col de Saxel, followed by a seven-kilometer ride up Col de Cou at a grade of 7.4. From there, they will climb 5.8 kilometers up Col de Feu at a steep 7.8 percent. After a brief 1,029 meter climb up Col de Jambaz, the tour then has two long climbs. They will go 13.9 kilometers up Col de la Ramaz at 7.1 percent and then have one more 11.6 kilometer ride up Col de Joux Plane at a killer 8.5 percent grade. It equates for a total elevation gain of over 14,000 feet. Stage 15 is another 14,000- plus foot day of elevation gain and a grueling 111 miles. The stage’s three marquee climbs go 7.2 kilometers up Col de la Forclaz at a 7.3 percent grade. From there, the tour turns 11.3 kilometers up Col de la Croix Fry, another 7 percent grade. It finishes with a summit finish on Saint Gervais MountBlanc for seven kilometers at a 7.7 percent grade. Photo courtesy of CyclingWeekly

By Jonathan Comeaux Mackie McDonald’s entry at Wimbledon was more brief than desired. He lost in the first round to No. 23 seeded Alexander Bublik on July 3, Scores of the fourset match were close all the way, 6-7 (7-3), 6-4, 6-4, 6-4. It was an rough result for Mackie after winning the first set and leading the third at 3-0, but Bublik found his rhythm and carried the momentum throughout the remaining sets. The result brings McDonald’s world-ranking to No. 53. He was ranked No. 48 in August last year. Bublik is currently No. 30 on the ATP World Tour. Although he took the final three sets, it was a battle all the way until the finish. McDonald and Bublik traded games in the second set as the server until Bublik pulled ahead by winning the fifth game as the returner. McDonald led 4-1 in the third set, but Bublik won five straight games to pull ahead. In the final set, Bublik jumped out to a 3-1 lead and although Mackie made things closer at a 5-4 deficit, Bublik took match point as the server. Bublik largely took over the match with his effectiveness in serves, recording 24 aces on the afternoon. McDonald, meanwhile, only recorded six. He also had a loss in the first round at the French Open on May 28 to No. 24 seeded Sebastian Korda in three sets, 6-4, 7-5, 6-4. Korda, a 22-year-old American, entered as the world’s No. 30 ranked player and is now No. 25. McDonald led the first set 3-2, but conceded three straight games to fall behind 5-3. He won the next game as the server to make it closer 5-4, but Korda won setpoint after going up 40-15. In the second set, McDonald led 4-3 but Korda tied 4-4 as the server and went ahead 5-4 as the returner. McDonald tied it 5-5 by taking a break point of his own, but Korda won as the returner, once again, 6-5. With set-point, McDonald initially led 30-15, but Korda wound up winning the next two points to win 40-30. In the third set, Mackie the two traded games until McDonald led 4-3, but Korda tied 4-4, then won his fifth game as the returner before closing out in service winning in deuce for match point. McDonald had an opportunity to win while holding Advantage as the returner, but Korda effectively responded. The Wimbledon is the grass court portion of the Grand Slam tournament schedule. McDonald now looks ahead to his strongest season, the hard court season that stretches from July to November. Mackie will next compete in the U.S. Open in New York City from August 28–September 4. Mackie McDonald lost in four sets at Wimbledon to No. 23 seed Alexander Bublik. Mackie McDonald’s next Grand Slam tournament will be the U.S. Open at the end of August. Defending champ Jonas Vingegaard leads through Stage 10 By Jonathan Comeaux Nearing the 2-week mark of the 2023 Tour de France. with defending champion Jonah Vingegaard of Denmark claimed the Yellow Jersey after jumping to the front in Stage 6. But it is a highly competitive race, with Slovenian rider Tadej Pogačar in second place just 17 seconds behind. Vingegaard established a 25-second lead on Pogačar following Stage 6 and continued the advantage through Stage 9’s mountain course to Puy de Dôme, where the Slovenian trimmed eight seconds from the Dane’s lead. This year’s race has been a terrific tour for American rider Nielson Powless, who currently has a good lead in the mountain climber classification with 46 points, ahead of Felix Gall of Austria with 28 points. Fellow American, Sepp Kuss, is in 10th place, but he’s playing a support role to leader Vingegaard as a member of the Jumbo-Visma team. Le Tour progresses through a flat Stage 11 today, July 12, and a medium mountain run for Stage 12 on Thursday, July 13. That’s when the tour begins three straight mountain stages before a rest day on July 17, followed by a Stage 16 time trial and another mountain course for Stage 17. The Stage 13 mountain ride occurs on Bastille Day, France’s Independence Day, traveling 86 miles from Châtillon sur Chalaronne to Grand Colombier. It features two steep ascents, including a summit finish on Grand Colombier via a 17.4 kilometer climb at a 7.1 percent grade. articles.text: Reservations still available, space is limited The San Francisco Symphony will perform a summer concert outdoors at the Stern Grove Festival on July 23. The Symphony is a recurring guest of the festival every year. Stern Grove Festival is a series of ten summer concerts, held on Sundays from June 18 through August 20 at a natural amphitheater in San Francisco surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees. The Grove’s natural acoustics have been preserved as a park in which the public could enjoy admission-free music, dance, and theatre performances. Stern Grove Festival has brought 80 years of a diverse range of performing arts to the City. The Symphony will be joined by special musical guest Lettuce, a Boston-based funk band that formed in 1992. Its members are San Francisco Symphony cellists with Peter Wyrick. The symphony will perform a concert at Stern Grove on July 23. guitarist Adam Smirnoff, Nigel Hall (keyboards, Hammond B-3 organ, piano, vocals), Adam Deitch(drums/percussion), Erick “Jesus” Coomes (bass), Ryan Zoidis (saxophone) and Eric “Benny” Bloom (trumpet). The band has gained a cult following in major cities and released its newest album Unify last year. The event is free but reservations are required, Space is limited. Visit https://www.sterngrove.org to reserve your spot.
articles.title: SF Symphony plays at Stern Grove July 23

articles.text: In Our Time, a retrospective of over 100 photographs of Ansel Adams at the deYoung Museum in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park, has been extended to August 6 due to popular demand. Adams (1902 - 1984) was a revered American photographer and environmentalist known for his black and white images of the American West. The photo shown, Monolith, was his first photograph that gathered the attention of the public and the art world. The exhibition is displayed in seven sections that trace Adams’s artistic development, and features some of his most-loved photographs with images of Yosemite, San Francisco, and the American Southwest. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ ansel-adams-in-our-time. Ansel Adams’ Monolith, The Face Of Half Dome, Yosemite Valley, captured in 1927, is considered his most well-known image.
articles.title: Ansel Adams exhibit at deYoung extended to August 6

articles.text: SF JAZZ celebrates its 10-year anniversary with a photo exhibit displayed on the windows of the venue at 201 Franklin Street. The exhibition displays a selection of photos featuring memorable live concerts and artists from the Center’s first decade in San Francisco. “Opening night at the SFJAZZ Center was a landmark event,” said Richard Scheinin, in-house staff writer at SF JAZZ. “The house was packed. You could feel the audience’s anticipation; a buzzing vibration ran through the hall. And then there was the astonishing array of musicians, legends, who gathered on stage to perform a kind of benediction for the venue.” The exhibition photo gallery includes pictures of trumpeter Wynton Marsalis, drummer Brian Blade, saxophonist Marshall Allen, singer and songwriter Rosanne Cash, gospel icon Mavis Staples, Cuban pianist Chucho Valdés, and many more. For more information about the exhibition and the Center’s ten year anniversary, visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/exhibit/. SF JAZZ’s anniversary photo exhibition
articles.title: SF JAZZ celebrates 10 years with photo exhibit

articles.text: Visit the Oakland Museum of California’s local artists marketplace this Sunday, July 16, from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. It is free and an opportunity to browse or purchase crafts made by vendors featured in the museum’s galleries. The festive marketplace features artwork produced by artists from the three collaborating studios of Into the Brightness: Artists from Creativity Explored, Creative Growth and NIAD, all represented in the galleries now. Included are prints, ceramics, magazines, textiles, buttons, trinkets, and jewelry. All are the work of Donald Gruneisen, Donzell Lewis, Jean McElvane, Larry Randolph, Lulu Sotelo, and Gerald Wiggins. The event is the launch of the museum’s new Spotlight Sundays series. Every third Sunday, the museum invites guests to explore a deep dive into topics, experiences, and practices generated by California culture makers and artists. Spotlight Sundays will include performances, provocative discussions, films, workshops, and crafts marketplaces. Visit https://museumca.org/ event/summer-of-joy-marketplace/ to learn more. A crafts marketplace is the launch of Oakland Museum’s new Spotlight Sundays series.
articles.title: Crafts Marketplace opens July 16 at Oakland Museum

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s production Out of Character is playing onstage now through July 30. Tony Award-winner Ari’el Stachel, director for Out of Character, is an Israeli American of Yemeni Jewish descent living in Berkeley. This new single-character show follows Stachel’s attempts to hide his Middle Eastern background post 9/11 as a young adult. Covering his identity and culture led the artist to experience years of anxiety, prompting him to eventually explore it as a play theme. Stachel joins former Berkeley Rep artistic director Tony Taccone to tell his story in his new solo show. Out of Character looks at the intersections of race, mental health and survival. Post show discussions led by Berkeley Rep’s staff take place on July 13 and 18. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/out-of-character/ to learn more and purchase tickets. Director Ari’el Stachel ®
articles.title: Berkeley Rep’s Out of Character through July 30

articles.text: Student showcase is free and open to the public Cal Performances’ 21st annual Berkeley/Oakland AileyCamp will perform at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall on Thursday, July 27 at 7 p.m. Performances are by students from Berkeley, Oakland, Richmond, and Albany as part of Cal Performances’ nearly 60-year relationship with the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, the iconic modern dance company based in New York City. AileyCamps students participate in a six-week program with a concluding performance in summer. The performance on July 27, entitled “Points of View,” features professional staging, lights, costumes, and live music. It is free and open to the public. “AileyCamp gives young people an opportunity to have a quality arts experience, make friends, express themselves, and recognize that they matter,” said Nasha Thomas, AileyCamp National Director. “Every year, it is a joy to witness the campers’ transformation from the first day to the final performance, and it’s incredibly special to watch our former campers step into leadership roles that pay it forward to the next generation.” For more information, visit Cal Performances’ website at www.calperformances.org/aileycamp.
articles.title: AileyCamp performance at Zellerbach Hall July 27

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet will perform Starry Nights at Stanford University’s Frost Amphitheatre on Thursday, August 3, and Friday, August 4. The event is part of the Stanford Live! Summer Festival. The performance program includes Violin Concerto, Tchaikovsky Pas de Deux, Blake Works I Pas de Deux, Cinderella Act II Pas de Deux, Swan Lake Act III Pas de Deux and MADCAP; all selections from the company’s 2023 repertoire. The ballet company’s resident choreographer Yuri Possokhov reinvents Igor Stravinsky’s 1931 Violin Concerto in D, originally commissioned and created for San Francisco Ballet’s next@90 festival shown earlier this year. Choreographer William Forsythe’s Blake Works I Pas de Deux features a more modern twist, set to music by young English musician and songwriter James Blake. The performance ends with Danielle Rowe’s MADCAP, another hit from the Ballet’s 2023 next@90 festival. The “carnival-inspired” score by Swedish independent rock artist Par Hägström is paired with Emma Kingsbury’s costumes and gives the audience a sense of an afterdark carnival. Performances on both nights begin at 7:30 p.m. Gates open at 6:30 p.m. Visit https://live.stanford.edu/calendar/august-2023/ starry-nights to purchase tickets and for directions to Frost Amphitheater. The performance is part of the Stanford Live! Festival. 12-MONTH FINANCING *some restrictions apply CL#788850

articles.text: John Krasinski directed, co-wrote and starred in A Quite Place A Quiet Place is almost totally without dialogue, but still conveys a sense of dread more loudly than the familiar horror trope so common with this genre. It is a film of faces, close-ups, capturing a spectrum of deep familial affection to unequivocal terror. It is brilliant in its premise – simple and elegant. The opening scene tells us it is DAY 89. Immediately it is evident that something terrible has taken place, an apocalypse of a kind. The what, and how is unclear. The place is a small, bucolic town in upstate New York. A family (three children and their mother and father) is scavenging the pillaged shelves of a grocery/drug store searching for supplies and medicine. They walk slowly, carefully, each is barefooted, no one speaks or makes a sound. They speak to one another not in hushed whispers but in sign language. Within minutes the tension that will haunt the film throughout is palpable. What is the source of their fear? When they leave the store they walk, inexplicably, on a ribbon of sand that cushions their footsteps. The parents, Lee and Evelyn Abbott (John Krasinski and Emily Blunt), are hyper-vigilant, pausing to listen. Whatever is out there represents an existential threat in the extreme; only the audience is not given even a hint of what it might be. Not until there is a moment that is completely unexpected, involving only a flash of movement, resulting in the couple’s youngest being taken. Lee’s face is twisted in anguish as he runs toward his son, realizing he is too late to save him. What was a blindingly quick reveal is followed by the screen informing us that more than 400 days have passed and we see a Victorian farmhouse that has been turned into a survivalist island. It is inviting, cozy even, surrounded by crops, powered by a generator, a necklace of lights at night are strung form the house to the outbuildings. A wide path of sand leads to the front porch. Thus far, by what we see, we’re told that this family has endured. Actually, they have thrived, for we also notice that Evelyn is pregnant. In the basement, in Lee’s gear-laden workshop, are electronics and multiple screens monitoring the exterior. On one wall are newspapers with headlines warning people to avoid all sound. There’s a shortwave radio on a work bench. The house is filled with light, for apparently whatever “they” are, they cannot see, only hear, even the faintest crunch of a dried leaf beneath a carelessly placed foot. A frequent gesture, universal in its understanding, is an index finger placed in front of the lips, conveying most often to the children that above all, in that moment, silence is their only defense. Remain still, hushed, wait, listen, their very lives depend on it. Even when the family spends an evening playing Monopoly, the pips are covered with material. I’m hesitant to continue to reveal anything more than what is evident in the first act. This is a film that must be seen fresh. To know any more would diminish what are emotions of trepidation and uncertainty, wrapped in a plot that grows and unravels silently, step-by-step, so-to-speak. All of this film is completely authentic and believable – though a certain suspension of disbelief is required. The family is impossible not to care about. We wish above all that no harm will come to them; it’s an investment in the characters that is impossible not to make. A Quiet Place is a title that seems benign. It isn’t. As a film, it is a harrowing allegory. What is out there is vague and predatory and beyond comprehension. In other words, Krasinski, along with his co-writers, Bryan Woods and Scott Beck, handle all aspects of this very excellent film with artistry and finesse, implicitly understanding that less can be more when dealing with imagination. A Quiet Place. Directed by John Krasinski. Starring John Krasinski, Emily Blunt, Millicent Simmonds. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/Ptime/Paramont+.
articles.title: A Quiet Place – surviving an apocalypse

articles.text: The power of fine filmmaking can be extraordinary: take the issue of illegal immigration, generally regarded in the abstract – our borders are porous, hence there are 11 million undocumented workers in America. It is a problem that is distant, political, a conundrum and one from which we are often insulated. But create an irresistible story about a gardener, Carlos Galindo (Demian Bichir), living in East Los Angeles, without documents, a single parent raising a 16-yearold boy, Luis (Jose Julian), and suddenly the problem becomes real, even personal. At the center of this splendid film is a principled man, cutting and trimming the grounds of the wealthy, while struggling to keep himself and Luis above water. His goal, his dream, is to have his own truck, his own tools and mower, and to create a life that has at its center, family and stability. A Better Life is a moving portrait of Carlos, who leaves his one-bedroom bungalow each morning at dawn and returns long after dark, falling exhausted onto the hard-used sofa in the living room. He is unaware that his son is drifting away, who finds the faux family security of gangs more inviting than the home offered by his father. Luis, who was born in America, stands with one foot in the culture of his parents and one foot in the culture he finds at school and on the street. His connection to Mexico is tentative, the language and customs seeming ever more strange. Each day Carlos copes with anxiety because of his illegal status, ever fearful that he will be stopped by “la migra” and asked for some form of identification. When the gardener he works for announces that he is returning to Mexico and offers to sell him his truck and include his client list. Carlos, who has no license and no I.D., decides to take the risk. He views the truck as the path to what he calls the American dream. Filled with pride, he drives through Los Angeles, looking out the window of the truck. He sees parts of the city that are hidden from the usual traveler. Sadly, many of the inhabitants, though they contribute to America, are part of a shadow population that is seen but not seen, residing in a place apart, living in immigration ghettos with drapes tightly closed. pages.text: 18 Wednesday, July 12, 2023 MOVIES FOR ADULTS A Quiet Place – surviving an apocalypse Demián Bichir and José Julián in A Better Life A Better Life a well-made film of quest for the American dream By Chris Honoré The power of fine filmmaking can be extraordinary: take the issue of illegal immigration, generally regarded in the abstract – our borders are porous, hence there are 11 million undocumented workers in America. It is a problem that is distant, political, a conundrum and one from which we are often insulated. But create an irresistible story about a gardener, Carlos Galindo (Demian Bichir), living in East Los Angeles, without documents, a single parent raising a 16-yearold boy, Luis (Jose Julian), and suddenly the problem becomes real, even personal. At the center of this splendid film is a principled man, cutting and trimming the grounds of the wealthy, while struggling to keep himself and Luis above water. His goal, his dream, is to have his own truck, his own tools and mower, and to create a life that has at its center, family and stability. A Better Life is a moving portrait of Carlos, who leaves his one-bedroom bungalow each morning at dawn and returns long after dark, falling exhausted onto the hard-used sofa in the living room. He is unaware that his son is drifting away, who finds the faux family security of gangs more inviting than the home offered by his father. Luis, who was born in America, stands with one foot in the culture of his parents and one foot in the culture he finds at school and on the street. His connection to Mexico is tentative, the language and customs seeming ever more strange. Each day Carlos copes with anxiety because of his illegal status, ever fearful that he will be stopped by “la migra” and asked for some form of identification. When the gardener he works for announces that he is returning to Mexico and offers to sell him his truck and include his client list. Carlos, who has no license and no I.D., decides to take the risk. He views the truck as the path to what he calls the American dream. Filled with pride, he drives through Los Angeles, looking out the window of the truck. He sees parts of the city that are hidden from the usual traveler. Sadly, many of the inhabitants, though they contribute to America, are part of a shadow population that is seen but not seen, residing in a place apart, living in immigration ghettos with drapes tightly closed. But just as Carlos senses that life is about to turn around, events occur that put him and his son in jeopardy. Know that A Better Life is not a political tract nor a polemic about immigration. It is a deeply human story, both touching and compelling, about a father and his son who learn about one another as they set about recovering something they have lost. Their journey is transformative. A Better Life. Directed by Chris Weitz. Starring Demian Bichir, Jose Julian, and Dolores Heredia. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.
