Courteous, Reliable Service Eric (510) 841-2891 (510) 982-9757 cell John Krasinski directed, co-wrote and starred in A Quite Place By Chris Honoré A Quiet Place is almost totally without dialogue, but still conveys a sense of dread more loudly than the familiar horror trope so common with this genre. It is a film of faces, close-ups, capturing a spectrum of deep familial affection to unequivocal terror. It is brilliant in its premise – simple and elegant. The opening scene tells us it is DAY 89. Immediately it is evident that something terrible has taken place, an apocalypse of a kind. The what, and how is unclear. The place is a small, bucolic town in upstate New York. A family (three children and their mother and father) is scavenging the pillaged shelves of a grocery/drug store searching for supplies and medicine. They walk slowly, carefully, each is barefooted, no one speaks or makes a sound. They speak to one another not in hushed whispers but in sign language. Within minutes the tension that will haunt the film throughout is palpable. What is the source of their fear? When they leave the store they walk, inexplicably, on a ribbon of sand that cushions their footsteps. The parents, Lee and Evelyn Abbott (John Krasinski and Emily Blunt), are hyper-vigilant, pausing to listen. Whatever is out there represents an existential threat in the extreme; only the audience is not given even a hint of what it might be. Not until there is a moment that is completely unexpected, involving only a flash of movement, resulting in the couple’s youngest being taken. Lee’s face is twisted in anguish as he runs toward his son, realizing he is too late to save him. What was a blindingly quick reveal is followed by the screen informing us that more than 400 days have passed and we see a Victorian farmhouse that has been turned into a survivalist island. It is inviting, cozy even, surrounded by crops, powered by a generator, a necklace of lights at night are strung form the house to the outbuildings. A wide path of sand leads to the front porch. Thus far, by what we see, we’re told that this family has endured. Actually, they have thrived, for we also notice that Evelyn is pregnant. In the basement, in Lee’s gear-laden workshop, are electronics and multiple screens monitoring the exterior. On one wall are newspapers with headlines warning people to avoid all sound. There’s a shortwave radio on a work bench. The house is filled with light, for apparently whatever “they” are, they cannot see, only hear, even the faintest crunch of a dried leaf beneath a carelessly placed foot. A frequent gesture, universal in its understanding, is an index finger placed in front of the lips, conveying most often to the children that above all, in that moment, silence is their only defense. Remain still, hushed, wait, listen, their very lives depend on it. Even when the family spends an evening playing Monopoly, the pips are covered with material. I’m hesitant to continue to reveal anything more than what is evident in the first act. This is a film that must be seen fresh. To know any more would diminish what are emotions of trepidation and uncertainty, wrapped in a plot that grows and unravels silently, step-by-step, so-to-speak. All of this film is completely authentic and believable – though a certain suspension of disbelief is required. The family is impossible not to care about. We wish above all that no harm will come to them; it’s an investment in the characters that is impossible not to make. A Quiet Place is a title that seems benign. It isn’t. As a film, it is a harrowing allegory. What is out there is vague and predatory and beyond comprehension. In other words, Krasinski, along with his co-writers, Bryan Woods and Scott Beck, handle all aspects of this very excellent film with artistry and finesse, implicitly understanding that less can be more when dealing with imagination. A Quiet Place. Directed by John Krasinski. Starring John Krasinski, Emily Blunt, Millicent Simmonds. 1 hr., 30 min. Rated PG-13. Now streaming on VUDU/Ptime/Paramont+.

articles.text: Richard Madden and Lily James in Disney’s live-action remake of Cinderella If you see the title of the recently released Cinderella and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative. Know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. And once again done by Disney. This is a contemporary version of an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented Kenneth Branagh. The story, in essence, is simple and direct, and unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), relies very little on special effects or CGI. There is, out of necessity, the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. In the main, and to its credit, this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, and mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. It is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the den fireplace because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether she is a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the tale soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disney idea of “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity into the story. Ella is, indeed, courageous and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be. Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. Starring Lily James, Cate Blanchett and Richard Madden. Disney-Live action. 1 hr., 45 min, Rated PG. Released 2015, Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: Wow. Kids are going to love How to Train Your Dragon. Let’s start with an inspired, breathtaking scene: a young Viking named Hiccup, seated securely on the back of Toothless, an ebony dragon, soars through the clouds in a prolonged flight. The colors are lush and gorgeous, the sky a startlingly blue in contrast to the enormous cumulus clouds. Hiccup, eyes wide, is both exhilarated and terrified. This scene, like so many in this film, is testimony to the depth and breadth of the imagination of the filmmakers, and illustrates how state-of-the-art animation, combined with the technology of 3-D, has made quantum strides in the last several years. Of course, neither technology nor 3-D can save a film if the story lacks serious mojo. How to Train Your Dragon has all the right stuff: a sweet if recognizable story that will resonate with kids ages nine and above. And the characters are, to a person, perfect. Briefly, there’s young Hiccup (Jay Baruchel), the son of Stoick the Vast (Gerard Butler), who lives on a small island, Berk, off the coast of Scotland. For 300 years dragons have been attacking their village, making off with their livestock. The Vikings have fought back and along the way developed an abiding hatred for and fear of dragons. Hiccup, a newbie adolescent, rebelling against his chieftain father and his community, resists learning to fight dragons. Stoick is both frustrated and angry with his son. Clearly Hiccup, lean in stature (the Vikings are all more than hefty), and not inclined to fight back when the dragons attack, is not cut out to be a dragon slayer. This becomes all too clear when, wandering in the forest, he comes across a fallen dragon, Toothless. Instead of killing the dragon he befriends him. And that budding friendship sets the story in motion. Hiccup not only helps Toothless regain his ability to fly (he designs and makes him a prosthetic tail) with the assistance of Astrid (America Ferrera), a wonderful tween-teen-tomboy (first it’s boy meets dragon, then it’s boy meets girl). They begin to work out a plan that will change the attitudes of the village toward dragons. Hiccup soon discovers that he and Astrid are not alone. With the help of his friends – Tuffnut, Fishlegs, Snotlout – they transform the future of Beck. What is also so much fun is that the dragons are marvelous – Hideous Zippleback, Monstrous Nightmare and the uberdragon, Night Fog. As well, all the kids speak in hip teen vernacular (“Vikings have stubbornness issues”), absent the brogue of his father and Gobber the Belch, and they dress like they buy their clothes from the Gap’s Viking annex, to include Ugg boots. Very cool. Astrid has a nifty hairstyle, leggings, short skirt and tons of ‘tude. They’re a goofy but delightful group and youngsters will identify with them and their situation. So, if the gremlins are hanging out this weekend complaining there is nothing to do, suggest How to Train Your Dragon. They might not remember to thank you, but they will enjoy themselves. And so will you. How to Train Your Dragon. Animated. Directed by Christopher Sanchez. Starring Jay Barnchel, Gerard Butler, America Ferrera. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG. Released 2010. Streaming on Prime/VUDU/Net Flix/Apple tv.

After his boxing career he retired in Southern California where he became a successful real estate developer. On the 5th of July (known as Boxing Day in the UK but with no relevance to the sport of the same name), my wife and I boarded the Amtrak train to Reno. Our trip was both relaxing and beautiful. We met a number of German visitors and had the opportunity to brush up on our own German. Reno is a strange town. Casinos are small cities in themselves. Each casino has restaurants and stores galore. The din is disconcerting. Loud music is piped in everywhere and amplified in such a way that you hear no music at all. It is just noise. They don’t call it noise these days; they call it “ambience.” Reno has an absolutely fabulous antique car museum. It also has two orchestras. The Reno Philharmonic is celebrating its 55th birthday. An artistic difference caused a rift and another orchestra, the Reno Chamber Orchestra was formed. I hope to report on these in the near future. While there we attended a concert of the music of the Beach Boys. Can you believe it? My next article will be devoted to this concert, so be prepared. Guitarist Bruce Conte in the Philippines. In 2012 Conte announced in Los Angeles that he had leukemia. A fund for his medical treatment was established via the Jeremy Wilson Foundation. Bruce died of leukemia nine years later, on August 8, 2021. articles.text: Bruce Conte was an R&B and funk and jazz guitarist known for his performances with Tower of Power from 1972 to 1979. Born in 1950 in Sanger, California, he grew up in Fresno. He and his cousin Victor Conte began playing in a family R&B band in high school in the early 1960s. At first, Bruce played bass, then switched to guitar. Through high school they performed in the rhythm sections of local bands, including Common Ground, playing the local club scene from 1967 to 1969. Conte’s musical influences included Maceo Parker, Dyke and the Blazers, Jimmy Nolan (guitarist with James Brown), Albert King, George Benson and Grant Green. In 1969, Conte moved to the Bay Area and joined the Loading Zone, with vocalist Linda Tillery and organist Tom Coster (from Santana’s band). At Conte’s Loading Zone audition, bassist Doug of the Santana band said, “This guy totally locks in with the drums, he’s obviously the cat.” Bruce Conte was one of the greatest soul/funk rhythm guitar players ever and was an expressive and unique soloist. You’ll recognize him in just a few notes. Around that time, Bruce would sit in at the basement jam sessions at La Val’s Pizza in Berkeley with blues/soul musicians Charlie Musselwhite (harmonica, vocals), Clay Cotton (piano), Terry Hanck (sax, vocals) and others. The Loading Zone gig led to Bruce’s joining Tower of Power. The Loading Zone shared rehearsal space with them and regularly opened for them. In 1972 Castillo changed the TOP lineup and hired Conte, saxophonist Lenny Pickett and vocalist Lenny Williams, all from the Loading Zone. Bruce became close to Tower of Power’s founder and songwriter, Emilio Castillo and the other primary TOP songwriter Stephen Kupka. Conte began co-writing songs with them, occasionally sitting in with the band. With Conte, drummer David Garibaldi, bassist Rocco Prestia, and organist Chester Thompson, Tower of Power formed a ground-breaking rhythm section that influenced countless musicians world-wide. Conte remained with Tower of Power until 1979, performing on the group’s seven albums from Tower of Power to Live And In Living Color. With TOP, Bruce mainly played his 1957 Gibson Les Paul Goldtop with a pickup on the neck and his 1967 Super Reverb amp in the studio and a Quad Reverb or Twin Reverb for live gigs. In 2006 Conte rejoined TOP, touring with the band for 14 months, before moving to Cebu

Perhaps some of you know that I am a boxing historian. The Fourth of July was famous for heavyweight championship fights. One of the most famous took place on the Fourth of July in 1910 in Reno, Nevada. It was billed as the Fight of the Century. But there is more to this fight and its aftermath than most people know. The champion, Jack Johnson, a black man, defeated former champion Jim Jefferies, a white man. What I want my readers to know is that Jack Johnson grew up as a very poor black child in Galveston, Texas. He wrote an excellent autobiography and without the help of a ghost writer, by the way. The book is worth reading. It reveals that Jack Johnson was also an outstanding musician, who played the string bass and was a successful jazz band conductor. Each casino has restaurants and stores galore. The din is disconcerting. Loud music is piped in everywhere and amplified in such a way that you hear no music at all. It is just noise. They don’t call it noise these days; they call it “ambience.” Reno has an absolutely fabulous antique car museum. It also has two orchestras. The Reno Philharmonic is celebrating its 55th birthday. An artistic difference caused a rift and another orchestra, the Reno Chamber Orchestra was formed. I hope to report on these in the near future. While there we attended a concert of the music of the Beach Boys. Can you believe it? My next article will be devoted to this concert, so be prepared. Bruce Conte, R&B and jazz guitarist By Jim Gleason Bruce Conte was an R&B and funk and jazz guitarist known for his performances with Tower of Power from 1972 to 1979. Born in 1950 in Sanger, California, he grew up in Fresno. He and his cousin Victor Conte began playing in a family R&B band in high school in the early 1960s. At first, Bruce played bass, then switched to guitar. Through high school they performed in the rhythm sections of local bands, including Common Ground, playing the local club scene from 1967 to 1969. Conte’s musical influences included Maceo Parker, Dyke and the Blazers, Jimmy Nolan (guitarist with James Brown), Albert King, George Benson and Grant Green. In 1969, Conte moved to the Bay Area and joined the Loading Zone, with vocalist Linda Tillery and organist Tom Coster (from Santana’s band). At Conte’s Loading Zone audition, bassist Doug of the Santana band said, “This guy totally locks in with the drums, he’s obviously the cat.” Bruce Conte was one of the greatest soul/funk rhythm guitar players ever and was an expressive and unique soloist. You’ll recognize him in just a few notes. Around that time, Bruce would sit in at the basement jam sessions at La Val’s Pizza in Berkeley with blues/soul musicians Charlie Musselwhite (harmonica, vocals), Clay Cotton (piano), Terry Hanck (sax, vocals) and others. The Loading Zone gig led to Bruce’s joining Tower of Power. The Loading Zone shared rehearsal space with them and regularly opened for them. In 1972 Castillo changed the TOP lineup and hired Conte, saxophonist Lenny Pickett and vocalist Lenny Williams, all from the Loading Zone. Bruce became close to Tower of Power’s founder and songwriter, Emilio Castillo and the other primary TOP songwriter Stephen Kupka. Conte began co-writing songs with them, occasionally sitting in with the band. With Conte, drummer David Garibaldi, bassist Rocco Prestia, and organist Chester Thompson, Tower of Power formed a ground-breaking rhythm section that influenced countless musicians world-wide. Conte remained with Tower of Power until 1979, performing on the group’s seven albums from Tower of Power to Live And In Living Color. With TOP, Bruce mainly played his 1957 Gibson Les Paul Goldtop with a pickup on the neck and his 1967 Super Reverb amp in the studio and a Quad Reverb or Twin Reverb for live gigs. In 2006 Conte rejoined TOP, touring with the band for 14 months, before moving to Cebu Guitarist Bruce Conte in the Philippines. In 2012 Conte announced in Los Angeles that he had leukemia. A fund for his medical treatment was established via the Jeremy Wilson Foundation. Bruce died of leukemia nine years later, on August 8, 2021. Listen to and see my transcriptions of three Bruce Conte solos for this column and music for my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: A photo of Piedmont High School from the 1925 Clan-O-Log. Piedmont Junior High School was built in 1924, just west of the high school. behind. Arched arcades on each side led to the home economics and music classrooms on the left. The science, chemistry and biology labs were to the right, and the cafeteria was on the lower level. The main entrance to the school opened to an oak paneled foyer with a fireplace and the principal’s office beyond. Traditions Once the school was built, the student body set many of Piedmont High School’s traditions that first year. The student body chose purple and white as the school colors and “Achieve the Honorable” as the school motto. Jack Cook designed the school shield, still on the school’s website. Students chose a Scottish theme. Piedmont is a highland, just like Scotland. The Scottish have never been conquered by an invading force; hence we derive the Piedmont spirit that never gives up. The Scottish theme also extended to the athletic teams (the Highlanders and Scots), the yearbook (the Clan-O-Log), the school newspaper (the Highlander) and the annual carnival (the Highland Fling.) Since so many students came from different schools that first year, the student body felt it was important to create an inclusive A 1921 sketch shows the future Piedmont athletic field. nature throughout the school. The yearbook was named the Clan-OLog, a log of the clans or all who came to Piedmont. The yearbook was to be a record of all students. Expansion Piedmont Junior High School was built in 1924 to ease the crowding in the high school. The building had 13 classrooms, a gymnasium, print shop and auto shop. Seventh, eighth and ninth graders attended class in the junior high, relieving the crowding in the high school. Landscape architect Howard Gilkey designed the new athletic field. It was built on the site of the former hedge Maze in Piedmont Park. Gilkey’s plans included a football field, quarter mile track and a baseball field. It was completed in 1924. Piedmont’s teams finally had a home field. Piedmont’s football team on the athletic field in 1922 before Gilkey’s improvements. Note the dirt field.

articles.text: Piedmont Park, created by Frank C. Havens, was to be sold in 1916. Havens was deeply in debt, and his creditors planned to sell the park at a foreclosure auction in 1917. With news of the eminent sale of the park, the Piedmont School District approved a bond measure to purchase 13 acres for a new high school and athletic field. (The city also passed a measure to reimburse Wallace Alexander for the purchase of the remaining park land. The School District immediately began plans to build a new high school. Officials conferred with architect William H. Weeks and ultimately approved his plans in November, 1920. Although construction did not begin until 1921, school officials started the new school curriculum in August, 1920. For the first year, only a junior high school curriculum was offered. Forty students who completed the 8th grade at Havens and Lake (now Beach) schools formed the new 9th grade. The 7th and 8th graders from the elementary schools joined this first junior high school population. Their classes were held in the old Piedmont Park buildings, in classrooms in the remodeled Piedmont Springs Clubhouse, the Art Gallery and in temporary shacks for two years. Wildwood School was not built until 1923. High School dedicated in 1922 Piedmont High School was dedicated on June 1, 1922. Originally constructed as a junior-senior high school, the school offered classes for 7th through 12th grades. When the school opened in September 1922, school officials expected 260 students, but 325 students enrolled. Many of these students formerly attended high school in Oakland, and paid a fee. Enrollment grew to 400 students by the end of the first semester and to 600 by the end of the year. Architect William H. Weeks planned to make the Piedmont High School design his masterpiece. It was considered the finest high school in the state, with two floors of classrooms, an auditorium, study halls, science laboratories, a cafeteria and a radio room. It was among the first schools to have a public address system in all the classrooms. Weeks designed an elegant Mediterranean style school with a symmetrical façade. The central auditorium had five tall, arched windows trimmed with glazed terra cotta. Two stories of classrooms overlooked the ravine The oak paneled foyer in Piedmont High School had a fireplace with the school’s shield. Double doors led to the Principal’s office to the left of the fireplace. ❏ New Membership

articles.text: Part 65 in a biweekly series Good landscape design is very much like the good architectural design we spoke of last time. Before anything else, there needs to exist an overall strong concept that is pervasive throughout and is supported by all the components. This basic requirement is fundamental and logical to my way of thinking, but it is often neglected. What we often see as a result is a collection of pieces, or components, that don’t “work together” aesthetically or functionally rather than a comprehensive whole. Each landscape design in our built environment contains any number of design components: paving, grading, fences, gates, retaining walls, outdoor furniture, lighting, signage and of course planting. How these pieces are treated by the landscape architect and then assembled together determines not only the landscaping style and character, but also its overall quality. These components can be derived from many sources including historical models, or from common usage, or simply by fashion (which is quite common). And like all of landscape architecture, there is a melding of use and appearance. There is a function for most all components to accommodate as well as an aesthetic to express. Landscape architectural design evaluation ultimately requires a review of the totality of the components together – the coordination of and synergy between all of the parts – the complete project. But just as the entire detailed landscape project can’t be envisioned and designed all at once, it is helpful in the design process and in judging quality to evaluate the separate design components themselves – to work with the more manageable separate parts, as we often do in this column. It is sometimes difficult to articulate why we like or dislike certain design components and why they are considered good or bad. This is certainly in part because our tastes are all somewhat different, formed by our experiences, education, and personal philosophy. And too probably because we prioritize our Architectural and landscape architectural improvements often become contagious in neighborhoods, such as these fine examples adjacent to the project above, all on Carmel Avenue in Piedmont. What is most aesthetically impressive to me is the value of various planting and paving upgrades as they soften the somewhat high retaining walls and even turn them into features and accents.

articles.text: If you read last week’s column you can skip the first two paragraphs. Recently the Sonoma County Vintners Association put on a huge tasting at Kendall-Jackson Winery in Santa Rosa. The “Taste of Sonoma” event was one of the largest and most interesting wine events I have ever participated in. Over 100 wineries from all over the county were pouring their wines often 5 or 6 different wines per provider. The quality was astonishingly high as I had come to expect from Sonoma County. After many years of living in the shadow of its big brother Napa County I feel Sonoma has really come into its own. Certainly, in terms of the experience of wine touring. When friends come to visit, I never take them to Napa to taste. It has become wildly expensive and terribly crowded. Better to ramble around the scenic roads of Sonoma County looking for gems. One thing that was evident from this tasting is that Pinot has hit it big. The grape was everywhere with most regions of the county producing it extensively. Pinot was closely followed by Chardonnay by far the most popular white grape. Throw in some fine Zinfandels, Cabernets and Syrahs and the result was an exceptional and varied day of tasting. The following wines and the ones I reviewed in Part One represent the best of the tasting and even more, represent the best of Sonoma County. • 2021 Arista Pinot Noir Russian River Valley This is a very natural wine bottled unfiltered and unfined. It has a pale to medium ruby color and spicy notes of baking spices, earth, and leather over a core of red and black berry fruit. The medium bodied palate is elegant and nuanced with spicy character and a grainy, fresh frame, continuing to blossom on a long, detailed finish. These wines are made to age and should improve for a decade in the cellar. • 2021 Sangiacomo Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast Sourced from five different vineyards, the Sangiacomo Pinot Noir has singular, alluring scents of violets, rose petals, cranberries and red cherries- this is incredibly layered, deep and detailed. The medium-bodied palate is packed with plum fruit, spices, earth and amaro layers, supported by a fine grain and seamless freshness, finishing long and layered. A great effort. • 2021 Bricoleur Pinot Noir Founder’s Block This is the second release from Bricoleur vineyards. It has a medium ruby color and scents of cranberries, forest floor and spice. It’s light bodied, smoothly textured but firm, with great freshness to lift the savory finish. Perfect accompaniment to beef bourguignon. • 2020 Pride Claret Reserve The Pride vineyard straddles the county line and this wine is 81% Sonoma and 19% Napa fruit. The cepage is 72% Merlot and 28% Cabernet Sauvignon. The Pride Claret has aromas of cassis, blueberry, tobacco, earth with floral notes. Medium-bodied, seamless and fleshy bursting with black fruit, it’s a layered, concentrated wine with rich tannins and a long, savory finish. This is only going to get better in the cellar. 2021 Arista Pinot Noir Russian River Valley Owners of Thirty-Seven Wines pouring their wines.

This is only going to get better in the cellar. 2021 Arista Pinot Noir Russian River Valley 2019 Flambeaux Cabernet Sauvignon Alexander Valley • 2019 Flambeaux Cabernet Sauvignon Alexander Valley Flambeaux are the dancing torchbearers of New Orleans Carnaval and the wine is named to honor the owner’s New Orleans roots. The wine combines notes of tobacco, earth, plum and dark chocolate on the nose. It’s full-bodied, velvety, and open knit, drinking beautifully now but with the requisite stuffing and balance to go another decade or longer. Guests relax at the Sonoma County Vintners Association Wine Tasting. • 2020 Merry Edwards Pinot Noir Sonoma Coast The lovely nose has notes of currants, blueberries, cured meats and pepper. Medium-bodied, silky and intense, it blossoms in the mouth with tons of spices, flowers, fruits and earth flavors, expertly framed by tannins and seamless acidity, finishing long and flavorful. • 2019 Notre Vue GSM Blend A blend of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre from the Chalk Hill AVA the wine shows notes of blackberries, blueberry jam and currants with touches of herbs and black pepper. Full-bodied and powerful in the mouth, everything is big yet in balance on the palate, with velvety tannins and just enough freshness to support, finishing long and spicy. • 2018 Thirty-Seven Petite Verdot I’m glad to see Petite Verdot, a minor blending grape from Bordeaux, showcased in its own bottling as it makes interesting wine. It offers up elements of cassis, chocolate, and coffee bean in the glass. Full-bodied, firm and expressive the palate displays a slightly tight edge that will loosen in time and be fantastic when paired with grilled meats and chops. Just give it a little more time in the cellar and enjoy it past its 10th birthday. • 2018 Gary Farrell Pinot Noir McDonald Mountain Vineyard This wine hails from the Sebastopol Hills area of the Russian River Valley a cool-climate growing area. It shows aromas of eucalyptus, tobacco, cherries, cedar and dried flowers. The stunning palate boasts a concentrated core of wild, savory fruit framed by firm tannins and acidity that begs you to take another sip on the long finish. This complex, well-made wine will live long in the cellar. • 2019 Rams Gate Pinot Noir Silver Eagle Vineyard This Russian River Pinot Noir has alluring, botanical-toned aromas of cassis, amaro and fir with a core of pomegranate, cranberry and blueberry. The medium-bodied palate is ultra-silky and energetic, loaded with perfumed red fruit, and it has a long, nuanced finish. • 2019 Cartograph Pinot Noir Estate This lovely wine was new to me. The Russian River fruit has a deep nose and shows cherry fruit with a nice precision, notes of forest floor and a touch of vanilla oak, this is a broad, charmingly fruity and elegant Pinot with a silky texture, very fine tannins and a clean, smooth finish. It is drinking beautifully now but should improve in the cellars for some years to come. • 2020 Sonoma-Cutrer Chardonnay Founders Reserve Sonoma-Cutrer is an iconic Chardonnay producer celebrating their 40th anniversary. The Founders Cuvee is their selection of the best barrels and their most outstanding wine. It is powerful yet elegant with a direct delivery of creamy fruit aromas. There is lemon, pastry, oak and spice but the wine remains sharply focused throughout. You get a full-bodied white with a laser focus and bright acidity to close. • 2019 Balletto Pinot Noir Sexton Hill Vineyard Pale ruby-purple, the Balletto Pinot Noir is gorgeous, with deep tones of cranberry, and plums plus accents of lavender, honey and black tea. The medium-bodied palate explodes with concentrated, layered flavors supported by grainy tannins and seamless freshness, it finishes very long, detailed and flavorful. Try with grilled salmon fillets. • 2021 Kanzler Pinot Noir Russian River Valley The Kanzler Pinot Noir has a lovely nose of mushroom, potpourri, licorice and earth with loads of floral nuances and a core of black and red berries. Medium-bodied and silky, it’s big and round in the mouth with a long, lingering juicy finish. Perfect partner to roast chicken. Advertise Here! With the... articles.text: Bread pudding is a dessert I make on short notice without needing to make a trip to the store. Bread, milk, heavy cream, and/or half and half, eggs, sugar, and vanilla are the basis. Brioche creates a light-textured pudding. Absolutely go with what’s available to you: challah, sweet bâtard or white bread are fine. Other summer fruits can be substituted for the strawberries. Advance notes: • Added sugar is minimal as brioche is already sweet. Other breads may be less sweet, so add sugar to your taste, up to another 1/4 cup. • Baking in a bain marie (hot • water bath) is optional. Direct baking (no water bath) works, but the bread pudding’s bottom and sides will brown and form a crust. Bread pudding is traditionally served with a crème anglaise. A super-premium ice cream has the same ingredients, so a shortcut is melting some ice cream. Strawberry Brioche Bread Pudding Makes 6–8 servings INGREDIENTS • 3 tablespoons unsalted butter, divided 1 tablespoon for the pan and 2 tablespoons to dot onto the bread pudding • 8 ounces brioche bread, about five 1+ inch thick slices
articles.title: Celebrate July with Strawberry Brioche Bread Pudding

articles.text: It was the 5th of July, the weather was cloudy and cool, and there was a large turnout of 46 walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays. Karin Fetherston was interested in the historic ceiling panels in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, and arranged for Pete Palmer, the school district’s Director of Facilities to meet the walkers at the and provide some history. Pete told the walkers about the ceiling, as well as needed repairs that were done to the building. Piedmont’s first public elementary school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 19 . It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. The school was expanded under the New Deal in the 1930s. After the school board gained funding from the Public Works Administration (PWA) in 1933, work on a new five-classroom wing and an auditorium on the eastern edge of the school began in 1936. The classrooms were built in 1937-38 and the auditorium was added in 1940-42. It was named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, the school’s first principal, who taught at the school for 20 years. The ceiling panels were painted by students in the fifth and sixth grade in a paint-by-number fashion before they were applied to the ceiling. The theme at the Playhouse is California history. Pete explained that some panels’ cultural representations are not considered appropriate today. Those panels have been turn around and their blank backs are now seen. The walkers continued down Highland Avenue to Park Way, then turned around and walked to Hazel Lane. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, July 12, 2023 Celebrate July with Strawberry Brioche Bread Pudding By Deborah Quok Bread pudding is a dessert I make on short notice without needing to make a trip to the store. Bread, milk, heavy cream, and/or half and half, eggs, sugar, and vanilla are the basis. Brioche creates a light-textured pudding. Absolutely go with what’s available to you: challah, sweet bâtard or white bread are fine. Other summer fruits can be substituted for the strawberries. Advance notes: • Added sugar is minimal as brioche is already sweet. Other breads may be less sweet, so add sugar to your taste, up to another 1/4 cup. • Baking in a bain marie (hot • water bath) is optional. Direct baking (no water bath) works, but the bread pudding’s bottom and sides will brown and form a crust. Bread pudding is traditionally served with a crème anglaise. A super-premium ice cream has the same ingredients, so a shortcut is melting some ice cream. Strawberry Brioche Bread Pudding Makes 6–8 servings INGREDIENTS • 3 tablespoons unsalted butter, divided 1 tablespoon for the pan and 2 tablespoons to dot onto the bread pudding • 8 ounces brioche bread, about five 1+ inch thick slices • • • • • • • 3 extra large eggs 3 cups half and half, substitute 2 cups whole milk and 1 cup heavy cream (Avoid low fat milk in this recipe. It needs the richness for a creamy custard texture.) 1/4 cup granulated sugar 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 1/8 teaspoon sea salt 10 medium strawberries, halved. About 1-1/4 cups. Use very ripe fruit. Crème anglaise, or melted ice cream (see notes) INSTRUCTIONS Preheat oven to 300°F. Cut the brioche into 1-1/2 inch cubes. Spread in one layer on a 9” x 13” baking sheet and bake for about 5 minutes. Turn the cubes and bake for 3-ish minutes until they are dry, but still pale. Remove from the oven. This is all the baking for now. Butter a 2-quart, shallow baking dish (no taller than about 2-inches), with 1 tablespoon of butter. Transfer the bread cubes to the baking dish. Whisk the eggs, vanilla, sugar, and salt in a large bowl until the sugar is dissolved. Mix in the half and half. Pour over the bread cubes. Nestle the strawberries throughStrawberry Brioche Bread Pudding out. Press down gently for even absorption. Cover in plastic wrap and let soak in the refrigerator at least an hour or up to overnight. When ready to bake, bring the bread pudding to room temperature (or close). Once at room temperature, position an oven rack in the center position and preheat the oven to 350°F. Discard the plastic wrap then dot with bits of the remaining two tablespoons of butter. Cover tightly with aluminum foil. Cut a few slits in the top to vent. Place the bread pudding-filled casserole dish into a larger pan and fill the larger pan with hot water to halfway up the sides of Photo by Deborah Quok the casserole dish, creating a bain marie. Transfer both to the preheated oven. Avoid water splashing into the bread pudding. Bake covered for 40 minutes, then remove the foil and bake for 25–35 minutes until golden brown, fully puffy to the center. Test for doneness by inserting a clean, dry knife into the center of the pudding. It should come out clean (no eggy coating). Serve warm. Deborah Quok is the Piedmont Post’s longtime Food Editor. Earlier columns are available at: https://www.piedmontpantry. com/ Walking on Wednesday Extra large group on July 5 Wednesday Walk By Dick Carter It was the 5th of July, the weather was cloudy and cool, and there was a large turnout of 46 walkers and two K-9 best friends at the Exedra for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays. Karin Fetherston was interested in the historic ceiling panels in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, and arranged for Pete Palmer, the school district’s Director of Facilities to meet the walkers at the and provide some history. Pete told the walkers about the ceiling, as well as needed repairs that were done to the building. Piedmont’s first public elementary school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 19 . It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. The school was expanded under the New Deal in the 1930s. After the school board gained funding from the Public Works Administration (PWA) in 1933, work on a new five-classroom wing and an auditorium on the eastern edge of the school began in 1936. The classrooms were built in 1937-38 and the auditorium was added in 1940-42. It was named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, the school’s first principal, who taught at the school for 20 years. The ceiling panels were painted by students in the fifth and sixth grade in a paint-by-number fashion before they were applied to the ceiling. The theme at the Playhouse is California history. Pete explained that some panels’ cultural representations are not considered appropriate today. Those panels have been turn around and their blank backs are now seen. The walkers continued down Highland Avenue to Park Way, then turned around and walked to Hazel Lane. At the turn of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have a good education, and she got Isaac Requa to build a oneroom schoolhouse on his property. Long hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children. This was the very first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Amy leased a house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane, and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and early California families and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classrooms and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913 for students from first grade through high school. In 1924 the school had 186 students and by 1928 it had 21 teachers and 42 graduating seniors. However, the Stock Market crash in 1929 and the following Depression created financial difficulties for many parents sending their daughters to the school. Piedmont High was less expensive and Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and the school closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The group walked around the Hazel Lane loop to the school’s former site at 141 Hazel Lane. As they admired the home, the owner, Jody Cornelius, came out and talked with the walkers. The walkers completed the loop and took the hidden pathway on Hazel to Guildford Avenue and the town center to complete their fun 5th of July parade walk. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: On June 13, Piedmont Scout Troop 11 sent eight scouts, six boys, and two girls, with three adults, to a high adventure backpacking trek. The Scouts, ages 13 to 15, hiked Philmont Scout Ranch in Cimarron, New Mexico for 11 days, traversing over 80 miles with altitudes reaching nearly 12,000 ft. A ranger guided the crew for the first two days of the hike, coaching and reviewing skills needed to complete the trek, such as setting up camp in a “Bermuda Triangle” formation to avoid attracting bears. Then the Scouts were on their own to navigate the steep trails and high altitudes through the rugged New Mexico wilderness. Although the crew had planned for a 60-mile hike, they ultimately covered 80 miles due to additional day hikes. Provisions, including food and water, were carried by the Scouts, and stream water was filtered along the way for drinking. Most of the hike was mountainous but the terrain included dirt trails, large boulders, streams, and river crossings. They faced altitude challenges as they climbed, including reaching Mount Phillips, a 12,000-foot peak. They could see the devastation of the Ute Park fire in 2018 that burned more than 30,000 acres. To help with the restoration they participated in the Philmont conservation effort to rebuild trails. The Scouts also engaged in horseback riding, rock climbing, and fly fishing. articles.text: Part of the Piedmont 4th of July parade made the Pick of the Week in this weeks’ police blotter, PPD Blue. A man wearing a mask, driving a vehicle without a license plate stole a 7-foot long inflatable corgi dog decoration from the Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital float that one day before was named Best Float in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade. At 6:45 a.m. on Wednesday, July 5, a man can be seen taking the inflatable off the float which was parked on Manor Drive. Surveillance photos further show him trying, but failing, to stuff the oversized corgi into his vehicle without deflating it. When the blow-up decoration wouldn’t fit, he decided to drive away with it, with a passenger holding it on the windshield. Though the owner of the float filed a police report, she admitted the incident had a humorous aspect. The owner intended to post a notice online offering the inflatable free for anyone who would take it away. Surveillance photos at 6:45 a.m. show a suspect eyeing an inflatable decoration of a corgi on a parade float. Far from incognito, the perpetrator flees the scene with the large blow-up dog held onto the window by a passenger. check on the parking issue. Some have claimed that the parking on Linda Avenue has been monopolized by pickelball players. There have been unsubstantiated claims that pickleball players perform illegal and unsafe moves to grab parking close to the four courts. Starting in February and ending the last day of school, parking spaces were counted at different pickup times, 1:30-3:30 pm. With the exception of 2:55 – 3:05 pm on a few days, there were always available spaces. Pickleball players were asked to park below the crosswalk, closer to the bridge overpass. And we did. Many players walked blocks or rode bikes to commute to the courts. I never observed parking in the red zone or U- turns performed by pickleball players. We do try to be good citizens. It is impossible to quantify the significant impact on parking by the numerous caregivers at the playground and the many sports parents and coaches and adult soccer players that use Beach Playfield. An independent professional firm has examined the noise issue and pickleball is within limits legally defined in the General Plan. Safety has never been an issue that could be documented. The final element, utilization of the space, is obvious. Even the most casual observer can see that the formerly under-utilized Linda Beach courts are now a thriving community asset and PRD has the supporting data. I urge the Piedmont Recreation Commissioners to approve permanent pickleball courts at Linda Beach. –Lisa Tuck

articles.text: On Sunday morning, July 2, the city introduced 200 goats to the hillside behind the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. Tasked with reducing fire hazard by eating dry vegetation on city property, the goats arrived in town after completing a shrub-eating job at the former Oak Knoll Naval Base near the Oakland Zoo. After the four-legged grazers complete their work on the slope behind the Corporation Yard, they will be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park. Owned by Ecosystem Concepts, their vegetation-eating is crucial in advance of fire season. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan has said that a good rule of thumb to prevent ladder fuel — a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the landscape upward to tree or shrub canopies — is to leave three times the amount of space above the potential culprit. Thus, for one foot of grass, the goats are expected to eat enough to leave at least three feet of space between it and any tree or shrub canopies above. articles.text: In preparation for African American History Month this year, I am reading Against The Hounds of Hell: A Life of Howard Thurman by Peter Eisenstadt. I highly recommend the book. It is a definitive biography of one of the great spiritual leaders of our time. (Thurman’s most wellknown book, Jesus and the Disinherited, was, along with the Bible and United States Constitution, one of the three books that Martin Luther King Jr. carried with him when he traveled.) As the story of Thurman’s life unfolds, Eisenstadt describes the then 44-year-old pastor and scholar arriving in San Francisco in July 1944 after a five-day cross country train ride from Washington D.C. where he had been Dean of the Chapel at Howard University. After settling into a home that needed much care (think rodent infestation), Thurman began his work as the Senior Minister of the recently founded Church for the Fellowship of All People. Thurman told the church leaders that he wanted the church’s highest commitment to be to a peace rooted “in the quality of life that emanates from the place rather than from pronouncements of one kind or another.” His words describe my hope for this year’s celebration of AAHM. While it is important, especially in the face of efforts like those being made by Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida to deny the significance of African American history, that we make pronouncements about the significance of this celebration, the lessons we carry with us from the study of African American history are of greater significance than the statements we make about it. That being said, Jemar Tisby, President of the Black Christian Collective, provides five helpful pronouncements about the celebration of Black History Month. • Celebrating honors the historic leaders of the Black Community • Celebrating helps us to be better stewards of the privileges we’ve gained • Celebrating provides an opportunity to highlight the best black history and culture
articles.title: Remembrances of Howard Thurman

And so of course they’re not used as much... I kind of love that the courts aren’t regulation size because I can drop in and I can’t do that other places.” Oddly on April 19 the same speaker asked why PRD has “no open play for tennis” when previously they stated “drop in” was always available at Linda Beach. Piedmont Pickleball has transformed the previously underused 2/3rds sized Linda courts into a wonderful and community asset. We are 100% open play so everyone enjoys themselves. 10 yearsolds play with 80 year-olds and families play together with other families. We enhance the fabric of our community. The City has nothing to do with monthly pickleball tournaments. These and many other activities are originated by resident volunteers. We actively undertake teaching pickleball to children at Schoolmates, Beach PE, Play Like a Girl and the upcoming Try (It) Out Tuesdays. We organize monthly potlucks and Brew Pub gatherings. We support injured players away from the courts. Behind the scenes there are many ongoing tasks that pickleball volunteers take on. One person suggested that setting up portable soccer nets and portable pickleball nets are the same. Setting up and tearing down pickleball nets takes at least several minutes if the net was stored away properly. The nets are stored in locked boxes and volunteers have [can[ open and close boxes and gates. We have a robust community of volunteers that keeps the wheels turning. Opponents suggest that pickleball should have reservations, but neither volunteers nor PRD can be expected to set up temporary pickleball nets for reserving players. Dedicating Linda Beach to pickleball will be a lasting legacy for the Recreation Commission and will greatly enhance recreation opportunities for all ages, maximize use of a previously underused space and make a positive difference for all of Piedmont. –Rick Schiller READ IT IN THE POST Remembrances of Howard Thurman By Pastor Jim Hopkins In preparation for African American History Month this year, I am reading Against The Hounds of Hell: A Life of Howard Thurman by Peter Eisenstadt. I highly recommend the book. It is a definitive biography of one of the great spiritual leaders of our time. (Thurman’s most wellknown book, Jesus and the Disinherited, was, along with the Bible and United States Constitution, one of the three books that Martin Luther King Jr. carried with him when he traveled.) As the story of Thurman’s life unfolds, Eisenstadt describes the then 44-year-old pastor and scholar arriving in San Francisco in July 1944 after a five-day cross country train ride from Washington D.C. where he had been Dean of the Chapel at Howard University. After settling into a home that needed much care (think rodent infestation), Thurman began his work as the Senior Minister of the recently founded Church for the Fellowship of All People. Thurman told the church leaders that he wanted the church’s highest commitment to be to a peace rooted “in the quality of life that emanates from the place rather than from pronouncements of one kind or another.” His words describe my hope for this year’s celebration of AAHM. While it is important, especially in the face of efforts like those being made by Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida to deny the significance of African American history, that we make pronouncements about the significance of this celebration, the lessons we carry with us from the study of African American history are of greater significance than the statements we make about it. That being said, Jemar Tisby, President of the Black Christian Collective, provides five helpful pronouncements about the celebration of Black History Month. • Celebrating honors the historic leaders of the Black Community • Celebrating helps us to be better stewards of the privileges we’ve gained • Celebrating provides an opportunity to highlight the best black history and culture • Celebrating creates an awareness for all people • Celebrating reminds us all the Black History is our history Yet, as important as these pronouncements are, repeating or re-posting them is no substitute for learning from a book like Against the Hounds of Hell, which reminds us in memorable ways of heroes like Howard Thurman. Heroes who faced constant danger, disrespect and disparagement simply because of the color of their skin. Heroes who were still able to teach “Wherever [Jesus’] spirit appears, the oppressed gather fresh courage; for he announced the good news that fear, hypocrisy and hatred, the three hounds of hell that track the trail of the disinherited, need have no dominion over them.” Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue at Mandana Blvd., Oakland. jim@labcoakland.org Previosly printed in the Piemdont Post on February 28, 2023. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Selen Ozturk Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Sohrab “Seb” Ford (intern) Micah Temple (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Mended Hearts, a nonprofit offering support to heart disease patients, their families, and their caregivers, is holding its annual summer barbecue picnic on Saturday, July 15, at Middle Harbor Shoreline Park in Oakland. Attendance is free and does not require membership in Mended Hearts. Those interested in attending may call Carter Dunlap at 415-298-1956 for more information and event details. The mission of Mended Hearts is to inspire hope and improve the quality of life of heart patients and their families through peerto-peer support, advocacy, and education of patients on all aspects of cardiac healthcare. Through the organization, caregivers of heart patients can get informed about their loved one’s condition and treatment options that are available. Knowing what to ask and how to ask it are important tools for everyone. If you are a heart patient or a caregiver and interested in learning more about Mended Hearts, the picnic is a great way to meet members of the chapter. The local Oakland chapter of Mended Hearts also hosts monthly meetings that feature medical professionals who inform members on relevant, up to date information about heart health care and lifestyle management. Additional information about these meetings is available on its website: mendedhearts.org.
articles.title: Mended Hearts annual picnic on July 15

articles.text: The Scout National Jamboree will take place this summer from July 19 to 28 at the Summit Bechtel Reserve, an area of 10,600 acres in West Virginia. Piedmont Scouts will be part of a group from Marin and will include Troop Leader Joe Anastasi (Troop 4), Travers Kemp, Samantha Pell, and Dylan Wallway of Troop 1; Nico Jerez and Joey Anastasi of Troop 4 and Diego Branneria, Ganden Deming, and Simon March-Cunningham of Troop 15. Jim Pell and his wife Siow Fang Tan will be part of the National Jamboree Service Team (staff). Piedmont Scouts will be joined by four adult leaders, and 12 Scouts from Marin. The last Jamboree took place in 2017 and was scheduled to be followed by one in 2021 but delayed due to COVID. Jamboree is a 10-day, exciting and eye-opening experience where Scouts from all over the nation can connect with each other. Starting in 1937, the first Jamboree was meant to commemorate Scouting’s 25th anniversary two years earlier. However, it was delayed two years due to a polio outbreak. Hmm… doesn’t that sound familiar? While details on the exact events of the first National Jamboree remain fuzzy, this year’s events have me squealing in excitement. While eagerly looking through the Jamboree website a few activities really stood out to me. From what I have seen, it looks like my favorite will be “The Ropes.” Thirty feet off the ground and a complex maze of floating objects and railthin bridges, it looked absolutely exhilarating. Another air suspended activity that caught my eye is “The Canopy”. It’s like the Ropes but consists almost entirely of a variety of zip lines. To be completely honest, I am absolutely in love with the idea of a zip line. To me it feels like the pinnacle of adventure. Confession: I’m also partially terrified of them. As I watched a video on mountain biking, I felt mortally terror-stricken. Here was yet another thing whose idea I love but am afraid of doing in real life. Am I really scared of the activity or is it the thought that I might mess up, or not be able to master the course within the first five seconds? But what is Jamboree? What is Scouting really all about? It’s about taking new risks, exploring, and growing as a person. I took a deep breath, pushed aside my doubts and added both “zip lining” and “mountain biking” to my ever-growing mental list of things I intend to do this July. Due to the delay of Jambo, as it’s affectionately called, many Scouts are eager to enjoy this once-in-a-lifetime experience. However, with the enormous amount of preparation, the Piedmont contingent and many others across America are practically bursting with anticipation and responsibility. According to the official National Jamboree website contingent members are expected to work together and be able to understand each other over the course of an outing or camping trip The Piedmont contingent has been meeting since last year and, even after suffering a minor setback due to a lack of female chaperones, we bounced back by collaborating with the Marin Scout Council. What exactly have we been doing to prepare for this epic adventure? We have been having meetings since last school year, and more recently, Zoom meetings with the Marin Scouts. Additionally, we have been arranging a potential day outing and camping trip. I have been putting together packing lists and charts on the activities I want to do. I have set aside clothes and raised money. A huge thank you to everyone who donated and bought my cookies. I could not have dreamed of doing this without them. I’m getting ready for one of the best summers of my life, so keep your eyes on The Post to follow our adventure. Samantha Pell is a member of Piedmont Scout Troop 1, and an intern with the Piedmont Post. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

She sent the following letter to all school parents, teachers, and staff: Dear Students, Parents, Friends and Colleagues: Today, it is with great pleasure that I officially join the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) team as your new Superintendent. I recognize the profound importance of this role and the trust you have placed in me, and I am fully committed to ensuring the highest quality educational experience where every student feels a sense of belonging in order to achieve and thrive to the fullest potential. And, I confess, I am simply thrilled to get started after my appointment at the March 8th Board meeting. It is wonderful to finally be here. I am excited to share an update on our new leadership team, which began under Dr. Donald Evans and finalized at our most recent Board meeting. We are so fortunate to have Melissa Daymond as our new Principal at Wildwood, Ariel Dolowich as our new Assistant Superintendent of Educational Services, and Joseph Marik as our new Assisopen communication is valued, and all voices are heard. To this end, I look forward to working with our Board, students, staff, parents and community members. We are better together, and it is, indeed, joyful work. articles.text: Have you ever felt frustrated during meal times? Have you spent 20 minutes attempting to convince a three-year-old master negotiator to eat “just a tiny little bite” of cauliflower? Have you drowned green beans in cheese? Have you hid miniscule shreds of butternut squash in macaroni in cheese, praying that your child won’t notice your trickery? If so, you are not alone. From birth, babies are expected to do two things: eat and breathe. The majority of time that most parents spend with their newborns and young children revolve around food. With the time it takes to prepare food, feed kids, and clean up, it is a miracle that parents of young children have time for anything else. The CDC recommends feeding toddlers and young children at least six (YES…SIX) times per day. This means that when feeding becomes a challenge, parents can feel like they are “failing” six times per day. While a majority of toddlers and young children experience a certain degree of “picky eating” as a part of their typical development, there is a line where strict food restrictions and aversions can become dangerous and indicative of an underlying condition, such as Pediatric Feeding Disorder. Here are six signs that your child’s limited diet may be more than just “picky eating” and may be signs of “problem feeding”: 1. Sudden or significant weight loss or failure to gain or maintain weight: If your child is losing weight, or having trouble gaining the expected amount of weight for their age, it is recommended that you consult with your pediatrician to ensure that there is not a serious underlying cause. 2. Limited diet of less than 30 foods: Problem feeders present with a significantly restricted range and variety of tolerated foods, typically less than 30 foods. 3. Eating the same food over and over, then suddenly stopping eating that food: A “food jag” is a typical developmental pattern that occurs when a child eats the same foods prepared in the same way, every day or at every meal. Eventually they are likely to get burned out on these foods and they are usually lost from the child’s diet permanently. Picky Eaters will normally accept and eat that food after taking a two week break without eating it but Problem Feeders will rarely ever accept that food again, even after taking a break. 4. Crying, yelling, running away from the table when new/nonpreferred foods are presented: Picky eaters will typically tolerate novel or nonpreferred foods in their vicinity. On the other hand, problem feeders may cry, protest, or “fall apart” when presented with new or nonpreferred foods. 5. Refusing entire food groups or only eating foods of similar textures/shapes/colors: Picky Eaters will eat at least one food from most food texture/ nutrition groups (i.e., starch, protein/dairy, fruit/vegetable). However, Problem Feeders will refuse to eat entire categories of food textures or nutrition groups. 6. Consistent picky eating: Problem Feeders are persistently reported by a parent as a “picky eater” across multiple well-child check-ups, typically for more than two years. If your child presents with one or more of these signs, your child may be a Problem Feeder. Please consult with your pediatrician for a referral to a feeding specialist. Paige is a pediatric speech language pathologist and feed therapist. She is owner of Speech at 650-451-5381, or by e-mail at Paigebaileyslp@gmail.com.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Josh Bernstein, a lifelong swimmer, has turned a hobby into an activity that motivates him every day, typically starting at daybreak. He is perhaps Piedmont’s most celebrated open water swimmer, routinely swimming under the Golden Gate Bridge and from Alcatraz to the city. At age 66 he is just getting started. To prove the point, he recently was part of a six-person relay team from South End Rowing Club in San Francisco that swam the storied English Channel, an open water swim of approximately 21 miles from Dover, England to Calais, France. To prepare, he swam the aquatic version of the Bay to Breakers race – from the Bay Bridge to the Golden Gate Bridge. – Josh Bernstein Bernstein’s group crossed the channel in 13 hours, 58 minutes amidst less than ideal conditions. After 12 days of delays due to weather and high waves, his group was given the go-ahead to enter the water on June 29. “We had a window from June 17 to July 2 and we were hoping to swim earlier in the window just to put it behind us, described Bernstein. “We didn’t get to swim due to the conditions until June 29 and there were a couple of false alarms, too. We were called four days prior and were set to start at 2:00 a.m., but we got a call at midnight saying conditions wouldn’t allow.’ ‘I learned very quickly when we were out there that conditions Josh Bernstein recently completed the challenging swim across the English Channel between England and France. can get gnarly,” he added. Bernstein, Bill Wygant, Susan Blew, Conny Bleul, Carol Merryfield, and Jen Karlin began their swim at 6:10 p.m., four hours before darkness set in, rotating swimmers on one-hour intervals. A boat from the Channel Swimming Association carried each of them and whistled when it was time for them to switch. “It was rough right off of the bat for the first swimmer, but then it mellowed out for a few hours. As the evening wore on, conditions really got rough with big whitecap swells and it was dark, cold, and windy. Plus we’re sleepy because we were staying up all night. But we had a great team with a lot of experience,” said Bernstein. “Shortly after we arrived in Dover, a swimmer who was going solo died. He just disappeared under the waves and they couldn’t find him, he was near France at the time. It was really tragic, and a harsh reminder that what we were about to undertake was no small thing. It wasn’t going for a little swim. We all knew it was a big deal,” said Bernstein. “I had to really keep in mind to keep an eye on the boat and try not to worry about the jellyfish. There were tons and tons of jellyfish and they sting. I’m fortunate to not react heavily to jellyfish other than it stings for a moment, I didn’t get a lasting rash but several people on our team did. There’s also a condition called Salt Tongue and it can cause your tongue to swell up so much that you can’t eat or drink. Several of our swimmers got mild cases of it, I luckily didn’t get either,” said Bernstein. Bernstein’s team followed a current along the channel, following its bending path arcing from north to south. “We’re all seasoned open-water swimmers and we know what our long distance pace is, so we just kept that for an hour. We followed the current and our path was one of the flattest curves I’ve seen for a channel crossing. It’s usually a huge dip north, a huge dip south, then another dip to the north. [The organizers] picked a good time for us to swim because the current was a little bit mellow,” said Bernstein. In his younger years, Bernstein swam with the Piedmont Josh Bernstein swam the English Channel as part of a six-person relay team with members of San Francisco’s South End Rowing Club. Pictured are: Bill Wygant (left), Susan Blew, Conny Bleul, Bernstein, Carol Merryfield, and Jen Karlin.
articles.title: Josh Bernstein completes English Channel swim

articles.text: Staff Photos Sadie Town was Piedmont’s leading outside hitter as a junior and will be tasked with the same role as a senior. With the new school year approaching, the Class of 2024 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. She’ll be a big part of next season alongside other potential returners like Izzy Grimmer, Maddy Mullin, Elena Stevens, sisters Bauer and Beck Peterson, Molly Wagener, and Klara Zietlow. DIMITRI PAPAHADJOPOULOS Baseball SADIE TOWN Volleyball Sadie Town will step into a leading role on Mariah Cardenas’ volleyball team as Piedmont’s leading outside hitter. She helped lead the team to a 10-14 overall record last season, which was a considerable improvement from its 3-12 finish in the fall of 2021. Town closed the season with seven kills in a 3-0 win over San Leandro. She also recorded nine kills a 3-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd, nine kills in a 3-1 loss to Alameda, and 11 kills in a 3-0 win over Encinal. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos capped off a strong season on the baseball team last spring, becoming one of the most productive hitters over the final stretch of the year. The Highlanders went 14-11 and battled their way to the North Coast Section semifinals, where PHS narrowly lost 11-10 to No. 5 Justin Siena. He was instrumental in helping the No. 8 Highlanders reaching the semifinals, recording three RBIs in Piedmont’s 4-3 extra-innings win over No. 9 Branson in the first round, where Dimitri Papahadjopoulos led Piedmont’s baseball team in RBIs as a junior. Jamie Schwarz is a four-year starter on both the cross-country and track teams.
articles.title: A look ahead at the Class of 2024

What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t overthink anything. Find what you love to do and work hard at it every single day, even if it is outside of sports. Surround yourself with people who support you and have similar interests that will push you to be a better athlete and person. Piedmont High Class of 2022 Chico State Class of 2026 JoJo Murphy, PHS Class of 2022, finished his freshman year at Chico State as California Collegiate Athletic Association’s 2023 Freshman of the Year honors and was selected as the conference’s Freshman of the Year. He finished last season as Chico State’s leading scorer with a 15.7 points per game, converting 55 three-pointers and scored at least 30 points a game five times. In 2022-23, Murphy led Chico State in several categories, including 456 points, 55 three-pointers, 173 field goals, and 960 minutes. He was also second on the team with 80 assists, second in steals with 37, and was sixth on the team in rebounds with 105. Chico State finished with a 13-16 overall record. During his time at Piedmont High, Murphy earned League co-Player of the Year honors as a senior in 2022 and finished his high school career with 1,488 points. He was a sophomore starter on Piedmont’s Division 4 NCS title in 2020 and was named The Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020. What is your workout program this summer? Primarily, I have been working out with Bryan Gardere every day focusing on skill development in the mornings and lifting weights prior to each session three times per week. During evenings and afternoons, I spend my time going against other collegiate players at Saint Mary’s College and professionals (NBA or overseas) at the San Francisco Pro-Am. I also travel to gyms around the Bay Area to get the most exposure possible and to compete at the highest level. What are your fitness goals for the summer? Stack days. Every day is an opportunity to get 1 percent better than yesterday, whether that’s on the court, weight room, track, or pool. There are always ways to improve and new ways to push yourself harder. I’m also working on a few other things. Diet and Nutrition – Maintain a healthy balanced diet, while gaining muscle, and be open to all food groups that elevate condition. Recovery – Ice, stretch, foam roll, therapy gun, and NormaTechs. Daily use helps limit inflammation, pains, and injuries, and helps preserve longevity. Mentality – Log days and establish mini-milestones inside of bigger goals within a certain time frame. Be a student of the game, and watch film on yourself and others. Practice meditation and be able to attain a level of focus where nothing can distract you. How are you measuring your development? I’m setting mini-milestones within bigger goals in mind. For example, in our workouts, we finish with 50 threes and in order to be able to finish, a mini goal I set was that I must make 35/50 to be done, every day that number will increase by one or more to keep building. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? My father and I go to the gym or a park every day and go through the same routine that we have done every summer, with some variations to make it more difficult. Individually, I will focus on my ball handling and footwork, while my dad will help rebound, sharpen my shot, and touch around the rim. I have been working with several coaches around the Bay, but primarily with Bryan Gardere, Teohn Conner, and other former AAU coaches and mentors. It is important to accumulate as much as I can when working with these specialists and incorporating what I have learned into my game. CHIARA LUNDIN Softball Chiara Lundin, PHS Class of 2022, finished her freshman year as a starter at Wellesley. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Sports are great and definitely good for the college experience, but you have to remember that sports aren’t everything. Before college and while in college, academics and other extracurricular activities are just as important to build connections and a good quality college experience. Piedmont High Class of 2022 Wellesley Class of 2026 Chiara Lundin, PHS Class of 2022, was a four-year starter on Piedmont’s softball team. She recently completed her freshman season at Wellesley College in Massachusetts, where she stepped into a starting role, appearing in 29 games in her debut year. In 2023, she recorded 20 hits, 14 RBIs, scored 10 runs, drew five walks, and finished with a .238 batting average. Her best performance was a 3-for-4 performance in a 7-6 win over Dean, including a double, two RBIs, and a run scored. As a senior at Piedmont, she helped lead the school to a Shoreline Division title with a sterling average of .581 batting average, 43 hits, nine doubles, three triples, and two home runs. What is your workout program this summer? I am working out three times a week, as I have been directed by our weight trainer for the team. For the summer, when not everyone has access to a full gym, there is a lot of use of dumbbells, but there is still some heavy weightlifting involved. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I hope to reduce my running time from home to first-base and to increase my running speed in general. How are you measuring your development? In order to track my stamina, I have been running on a treadmill and trying to increase the pace I go at each week. Are you working on your own or with a coach or trainer? For weight lifting, I work on my own and track my progress with a phone application. I am also working with a batting coach to fine-tune my hitting. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? This season, I led my team in RBIs and hit a walk-off double to win our first game against Dean College. CHRISTIAN TAYLOR Cross Country & Track Piedmont High Class of 2023 UC Davis Class of 2027 Christian Taylor, PHS Class of 2023, just finished his time at Piedmont as a three-year varsity starter on both the cross country and track teams. He earned AllLeague honors in both sports as a senior. Last spring, Taylor wound up winning the North Coast Section Bayshore Championship’s 800 meter run, which was his secondary event, with a time of 1:56.27 in a field of 23 runners. He also finished fourth of 24 runners in the 1600 with a time of 4:20.77.

Australia’s Jai Hindley took the lead of the General Classification standings after winning the Stage 5 mountain course. articles.text: Following the Coastal Trail with a pit stop at Pelican Inn Tennessee Valley Beach and Muir Beach are among the most popular destinations in Marin County, so why not connect them for your own beach-hopping excursion? Walking the Coastal Fire Road trail gives some tough leg-work with ascending and descending elevation, but provides a beautiful jaunt along the Pacific Ocean. The Post’s Hiking with Jon series starts at the Tennessee Valley Beach trailhead, taking the main path until intersecting with the Coastal Trail after a mile, walking roughly 3.1 miles to Muir Beach with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. According to historians, Muir Beach itself was once known as Bello Beach when Portuguese settler Antonio Nunez Bello bought the entire hillside for a $10 gold piece in 1910. About 2.4 miles from the Tennessee Valley Trailhead, you’ll pass Pirates Cove, a small boulder laden beach surrounded by steep hills. It requires about 350 feet of descent from the main trail and will provide a leg-burner of a walk back up. The remaining 1.8 miles to Muir Beach, hikers will pass bushels of stunning red-flowering currant and possibly spot a rabbit or two hopping across the trail. Large turkey vultures are a common sight throughout the Marin Headlands, while you may see a red-tailed hawk scouring for food. After the grueling walk, take a rest at Muir Beach or cool off with your feet in the cold ocean Follow the signs to Muir Beach. Tennessee Valley Beach is on the left as seen from the Coastal Fire Road trail. The walk along the coast is picturesque, and depending on the weather, you can see the marine layer of clouds burning off over the hills. Take time for lunch and a pint at the historic Pelican Inn for prior to heading back.

The Post’s Hiking with Jon series starts at the Tennessee Valley Beach trailhead, taking the main path until intersecting with the Coastal Trail after a mile, walking roughly 3.1 miles to Muir Beach with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain.
