The remaining 1.8 miles to Muir Beach, hikers will pass bushels of stunning red-flowering currant and possibly spot a rabbit or two hopping across the trail. Large turkey vultures are a common sight throughout the Marin Headlands, while you may see a red-tailed hawk scouring for food. After the grueling walk, take a rest at Muir Beach or cool off with your feet in the cold ocean Muir Beach is a prime destination in Marin County for hikers, bikers, families, and beach goers. Staff Photos Follow the signs to Muir Beach. Tennessee Valley Beach is on the left as seen from the Coastal Fire Road trail. The walk along the coast is picturesque, and depending on the weather, you can see the marine layer of clouds burning off over the hills. water. Should those interested skip out on packing a lunch, a worthy and delicious pit stop at the historic Pelican Inn is just half a mile away. Pack on the protein for the travel back with some delectable Miyagi oysters on the half shell or reward yourself with a pint. The Pelican Inn is named after Sir Francis Drake’s galleon that visited the area in the 1570s. The white building looks something out of fairy tale; surrounded by a lush green lawn and giant 10 foot wall of bushes to keep the wind out. Inside the inn feels like you just stepped a classic 1800s era British pub. Everything from the floor boards to the roof are shipped in from England, Scotland, or Ireland to give the place its authentic English persona. “All the wood, all the tables, all the cushions, all the drapes — everything in here was shipped from England, Scotland or Ireland,” hotel manager Amaya Cotton told SFGate. For the hike back to the Tennessee Valley Trailhead, the Fox Trail provides the fastest route with 2.4 miles and 500 feet in elevation gain—the last 1.5 miles descends. This trail goes along Coyote Ridge and overlooks the Marin Headlands toward Larkspur on your left with the Pacific Ocean to your right. You’ll likely be walking with your head right below the clouds as the marine layer rolls over the hills. As far as foot traffic goes, expect heavy traffic—but conscious hikers will always have ample space for passersby with trails that range over 6 feet wide for the entire duration. articles.text: New school Superintendent Jennifer Hawn, just four days into her tenure, rode in Shelly Symonds’ 1961 Thunderbird, with her husband Andrew, then took a seat on the reviewing stand with the parade judges. Other judges included Hopkins, School Board President Veronica Anderson Thipgen, Vice Mayor Betsy Andersen, and Mayor Jen Cavenaugh. Perpetual parade favorite the Pleasanton-based Balloon Platoon pleased the crowd with their 21-Mop Salutes and their costumes of innertube-laden sailor suit. New entries wowed the crowd and even took home awards, including Best Youth Entry to the Piedmont High Mountain Bike Club and Most Artistic Entry for a giant U-S-A walking letters by the Olcott, Kelleher, and Pillsbury families. As is tradition The California Repercussions, a 50-piece marching band finished the parade in grand fashion as its last entry. As they passed the reviewing stand the band merged with the crowd and entered Piedmont Park. While continuing to play, the musicians shimmied onto the grass to the front of the bandstand. Notably missing from the parade was Bruce Wolfe, the parade’s longtime Uncle Sam, who died in December last year. The parade extended to Guilford Road this year. Much of the crowd followed the last entry of the parade into Piedmont Park.
articles.title: Piedmont Parade

Sculpture in the Garden, held this year from June 17 to August 13, is an annual art show and sale that combines sculptural art with the natural sculptural beauty of the Garden. All sculptures in the Garden are for sale. Admission to the event is free with regular garden admission. Sculpture “sip and strolls” are held July 7 and August 4, where attendees may stroll the Garden after hours, wine or cocktail in hand. “Sip and strolls” take place in the garden between 5:30 p.m. and 6:30 p.m. To learn more, and to see this year’s featured artists, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/sculpture-in-the-garden/.
articles.title: Sip and Stroll this Friday at Bancroft’s “Sculpture in the Garden”

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibition is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The museum advises visitors that some artwork contains sensitive and difficult imagery, as well as depictions of nudity. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa), fetishised by Dutch colonizers and slave traders. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. A museum patron views artwork in the Black Venus exhibition, on view now through August at the Museum of African Diaspora in San Francisco.
articles.title: Black Venus exhibition on view at MOAD to August 20

articles.text: Diego Rivera’s famous fresco piece, “Pan American Unity,” will remain on view to the public at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art until March 2024. On June 17, 2021, Diego Rivera’s colossal fresco “Pan American Unity” was carefully moved from San Francisco City College to SFMOMA. The priceless 4,000-pound series of panels, created in 1940, is arguably one of San Francisco’s greatest art pieces of the 20th century. Rivera’s mural was the centerpiece of the Art in Action exhibit, which featured different artists engaged in creating art pieces while the public watched. The fresco on plaster measures 670 by 2,260 centimeters and was created on 10 robust steel-framed panels bolted together and weighing about 21 tons. It was designed to be portable, and was moved to the college campus from Treasure Island after the end of the World’s Fair. It is the largest of the artist’s works, and completely spanned the narrow lobby of the college’s Diego Rivera Theater. A four-year, multimillion dollar undertaking resulted in its careful removal and transport across the city to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, where it officially went on display. In partnership with City College, SFMOMA presents Rivera’s “Pan American Unity” in the museum free to the public until March 2024, when it will then return to City College to be installed in a new performing arts center. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pan-american-unity/ to learn more. Diego Rivera’s famous fresco piece “Pan American Unity”
articles.title: Diego Rivera’s historic “Pan American Unity” at SF MOMA

articles.text: Outdoor performances by musicians every Thursday Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden any Thursday night through the end of September for its summer activities. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli and serve as a time to gather with family and friends and enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. The Bluebird Bar is serving cocktails and wine nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove every Thursday night for “Summer Nights.” Ticket holders will be invited to attend a free garden talk focused on what’s in bloom with Filoli staff. Horticulturists will set up “pop-up learning spots” in the gardens. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance style garden to the south. Summer performances On select days throughout the summer, a range of performances and artists will be hosted by Filoli. Coming up on Saturday, July 9, local Redtone recording artists Effie Zilch and Miko Marks will perform from 6 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. For a full list of upcoming performances this summer, visit https://filoli.org/summer-stage. The Estate Trail Closes at 7 p.m., and the Café is open from 10 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. every day. All admission, including for Summer Nights, must be reserved in advance. Weekend tickets are likely to sell out. Visit https://filoli.org/summer-nights/ for more information. Filoli’s reflecting pool in summer
articles.title: Filoli “Summer Nights” continue through September

articles.text: Performances of Hurricane Diane at Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre will continue through July 16. The play by Madeleine George follows protagonist Carol, a seemingly ordinary if not materialistic woman who resides on a New Jersey cul-de-sac. One day, she is visited by the Greek god Dionysus, under the guise of a lesbian gardener named Diane. Diane is determined to reverse climate change and restore earthly order by seducing a band of mortal followers, and sets out to woo Carol from her picture-perfect suburban life. George, a Pulitzer Prize finalist, calls it a “hilarious evisceration of the blind eye we all turn to climate change and the bacchanalian catharsis that awaits us, even in our own backyards.” Hurricane Diane is directed by Jennifer King. A post-show discussion will be held on Thursday, July 13. Purchase tickets at www. auroratheatre.org, at by calling the box office at (510) 843-4822. Hurricane Diane playwright Madeleine George
articles.title: Aurora Theatre’s Hurricane Diane plays until July 16

articles.text: To become an accomplished physician requires dedication, long hours, and a strong love for the art of medicine. This is also true of becoming an accomplished musician. To be both is remarkable. Meet Joel Richmon, MD. Born into an extended family of many physicians, he followed suit and graduated from medical school at the University of Rochester in 1965. He completed his internship and residency at Johns Hopkins and his training in neurology at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Beth Israel Hospital in Boston. Having finished his training in 1971, Richmon moved to Piedmont and joined the Internal Medicine Department at Kaiser Oakland. A few years later, he was appointed as the hospital’s first chief of the Department of Neurology at Kaiser Oakland. In 1995 he established the first Headache Clinic at Kaiser. He retired from Kaiser in 2001, after 30 years of medical practice. Richmon’s musical career has its roots in his extended family. As a young boy, he lived in Waukegan, Illinois with his maternal grandmother and his aunt Janet Eisenberg, who loved to play classical piano. He recounts the story that his crib was often placed under his aunt’s piano, which she played every day. Her playing never failed to soothe him and germinated his love for classical piano. At the age of nine, Richmon started formal lessons in Chicago and studied with the distinguished Russian teacher Vitaly Schnee. At age 19, he continued his studies with Dr. Rudolph Ganz, president of the Chicago Musical College. He continued playing and practicing through medical school and residency, even arranging for his piano to be moved to Johns Hopkins. Before leaving to begin his career in Oakland, Joel played two pieces for Dr. Ganz, who told him, “My boy, you have two careers.” Richmon continued his studies in California with famed piano scholar Adolph Baller in Palo Alto. He has previously performed with members of the Oakland Symphony Orchestra and the San Francisco Symphony, as well as the faculty of the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. In 1977 Richmon had his most memorable experience as a musician, He admired Gitta Gradova, a world-famous concert pianist who abruptly retired from performing in 1941. She dropped out of the public eye and married Dr. Maurice Cottle, a renowned otolaryngologist and an accomplished amateur violinist. Coincidentally, a friend of Richmon’s was also a friend of the Cottles, and he arranged for Richmon to visit them in Chicago so he could “fulfill his dream of playing the piano” for her. Richmon wrote at the time: “In the Cottles’ drawing room sat two Steinway concert grand pianos positioned back-to-back across the room from each other. My hostess briefly remarked that one of the pianos was the favorite of Horowitz; the other, the favorite of Ashkenazy. Humbly and in awe, I seated myself at one of the storied pianos and played Rachmaninoff’s Second Piano Sonata, after which Mrs. Cottle graciously offered me her expert critique. Then, with an unbelievably sumptuous tonal quality, she played for me an excerpt from the beautiful, slow movement of Schumann’s Piano Quartet in E-flat Major. Mrs. Cottle gave Richmon one more gift, and that was the suggestion to play chamber music. This led him to a collaboration with other accomplished musicians and opened a new area of classical music for him. A year later, Joel held his first recital at the Berkeley Piano Club, where he played two pieces of chamber music with other musicians and two solo works. This was the first of 10 recitals, most of them held at Holy Names University in Oakland, performed for family and friends, including Kaiser colleagues. His latest and final recital was held on March 26, 2023, at Hertz Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. An estimated 400 to 500 people heard him perform Bach’s Piano Concerto No. 5 in F minor and his Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor with the members of the Oakland Symphony conducted by Bryan Nies. He also performed Franck’s Prelude, Fugue and Variation in B minor, Op. 18, Liszt’s Funerailles, and Chopin’s Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op.52. Each piece was saluted by the applause of an enthusiastic audience. Richmon entertained audiences with stories about his Aunt Janet, to whom he dedicated the recital in March. He listed Elvis, Janis Joplin, Van Cliburn with the Chicago Grant Park Symphony, and trumpeter Chet Baker in Paris as his favorite concerts. Richmon will continue to play and entertain friends. After all, it’s what he loves. Piedmont resident Joel Richmon, a retired physician, plays his last recital with the Oakland Symphony at Hertz Hall on the UC Berkeley campus on March 26.
articles.title: Retired MD plays final recital with Oakland Symphony

articles.text: Weeklong event hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir The Golden Gate International Choral Festival, held every three years, will welcome hundreds of singers from around the globe to Sing the World and connect. The 12th Golden Gate International Choral Festival organized and hosted by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, will take place from July 9 through July 15. The choirs will fill the Music Concourse and Golden Gate Park Bandshell with voices on opening day, July 10, with a free opening concert at 5:30 p.m. Since its founding in 1991, the Golden Gate Festival has attracted high performing children’s and youth choirs from all over the world to perform and compete. Choirs will display the breadth of their ability in four competing categories. All competition performances, community spotlight concerts, and the Opening Day events are free to the public. The Closing Concert is a ticketed event on Saturday, July 15. For more information, visit www.goldengatefestival.org, or call the choir office at (510) 547- 4441 (www.goldengatefestival. org; e-mail: info@goldengatefestival.org).
articles.title: Golden Gate Intl. Choral Festival opens July 9

Mrs. Cottle gave Richmon one more gift, and that was the suggestion to play chamber music. This led him to a collaboration with other accomplished musicians and opened a new area of classical music for him. A year later, Joel held his first recital at the Berkeley Piano Club, where he played two pieces of chamber music with other musicians and two solo works. This was the first of 10 recitals, most of them held at Holy Names University in Oakland, performed for family and friends, including Kaiser colleagues. His latest and final recital was held on March 26, 2023, at Hertz Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. An estimated 400 to 500 people heard him perform Bach’s Piano Concerto No. 5 in F minor and his Piano Concerto No. 1 in D minor with the members of the Oakland Symphony conducted by Bryan Nies. He also performed Franck’s Prelude, Fugue and Variation in B minor, Op. 18, Liszt’s Funerailles, and Chopin’s Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op.52. Each piece was saluted by the applause of an enthusiastic audience. Richmon entertained audiences with stories about his Aunt Janet, to whom he dedicated the recital in March. He listed Elvis, Janis Joplin, Van Cliburn with the Chicago Grant Park Symphony, and trumpeter Chet Baker in Paris as his favorite concerts. Richmon will continue to play and entertain friends. After all, it’s what he loves. articles.text: Robert Capron, Zachary Gordon, and Chloë Grace Moretz in Diary of a Wimpy Kid You’re 12-years-old, on the cusp of that long, tortuous road known as adolescence, and it’s the first day of middle school. Middle school is like Triple A ball before you get called up to the big show, also known as high school. Meanwhile, there’s a lot to learn because, well, look around, everyone’s changing. No one’s a kid any longer. But then, no one’s a serious teenager either. Middle school is purgatory. Weird and awkward, it can be brutal. Which is the point of Diary of a Wimpy Kid, based on the popular illustrated books by Jeff Kinney. The movie should have been rich with material about kids trying to figure out not only who they are but how things work. This is not elementary school. There are no white lines on the tarmac, no recess, no tetherball or games of four-square or tag. Adios to those comfy classrooms with Nancy the hamster in that cage filled with sawdust and shredded newspapers and the walls covered with colored paper, the alphabet strung in an arc above the large-face clock and a few friendly admonitions on the bulletin board next to exemplary homework assignments. So Diary of a Wimpy Kid easily could have been comedic, insightful and, well, fun. It isn’t. For reasons that are difficult to understand. Perhaps it’s not possible to take Kinney’s book to the screen. But how to understand that the central character, Greg Heffley (Zach Gordon), is neither wimpy nor sympathetic; rather, he’s a self-absorbed, dishonest kid whose mission is to become instantly popular and is willing to do whatever it takes. His older brother, an older version of Greg, tries to explain the middle school rules: Don’t get noticed. Don’t go to the bathroom. Try and be cool. And speaking of cool, Greg is constantly on the verge of ditching his best friend, Rowley (Robert Capron), who is so endearingly dorky that he’s impossible not to like. But since Greg is in the hunt for cool, he cringes at how un-cool Rowley is. As example when the two are leaving school, Rowley yells from the top of the steps, with older kids everywhere, “Hey Greg, wanna come over and play?” Greg wants to hide because he knows that in middle school no one plays. Cool kids hang out. Later, when Greg is confronted with a moment of truth, he sells Rowley out and never looks back. He’s not a good friend. a conclusion, Greg is a well-established creep. And even with a final 10 minutes for an epiphany, with redemption for Greg at the edge of the school grounds, it all seems a bit contrived and too late. He’s not a kid you want to hang out with. All of these kids have an interior life, one filled with questions and confusion and insecurities; however, nothing in depth is ever really explored. Diary of a Wimpy Kid shoulda, coulda been a serious/funny/ touching movie, helped perhaps by a nice voice over. And not to forget honest. It’s not; it’s another missed opportunity. Diary of a Wimpy Kid (2010). Directed by Thor Freudenthal, Starring Zach Gordon, Robert Capron, Rachel Harris, Steve Zahn, Devon Bostick and Chloe Grace Morentz. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG. But first, back to the egg. “This is your brain.” And then, “This is your brain on NZT.” No frying pan, just one small, clear tab, placed on the tongue. Within minutes everything glows, bathed in an intense light. All things become possible. If you were cruising through life in first or second gear, using some 20 percent of your brain cells (which we’re told is par), with NZT you are suddenly in fourth gear and revving the engine to full capacity. Which is what happens to We first see Eddie – scruffy, depressed, suffering from serious writer’s block – walking down a busy New York City avenue, wondering where he will find the juice to even write the first sentence of a book for which he has received a generous advance. His long-suffering girlfriend, Lindy (Abbie Cornish), has just broken up with him and he is significantly bummed. That’s when he bumps into his ex-brother-in-law, Vern (Johnny Whitworth), a longtime street hustler and dealer. Vern slips Eddie a small, plastic baggy with a gel-like pill inside and tells him it is FDA approved, no worries. Eddie, at first skeptical, takes it on his way back to his grungy apartment. And that’s when things profoundly change. This pill is not experiential. In other words, it’s not a self-induced hallucination buttressed by a lava lamp. This is extreme, fuel injected, pedal to the metal, hyper-cognitive stuff. Eddie writes most of his book in one sitting and looks around and realizes that there are other dragons to slay, like the stock market. It’s at this juncture that things get very tense. Hooked, Eddie returns to Vern’s apartment and tells him that whatever that was, the NZT, well, he’ll need a steady supply. Vern agrees and suggests that first Eddie might go and pick up some breakfast and his dry cleaning. When Eddie returns, things go dark and dicey and Eddie’s path to a brave new world is suddenly replete with predators. Meanwhile, jacked up on NZT, he is transformed: designer clothes, new haircut, and an arbitrage office with computers and graphs, showcasing his newest talents. He’s a rock star of high finance. Limitless is hot. A ride. Flawed to be sure – the ending is a bit weak – but who cares, really? It is simply a good B-movie entertainment. Limitless. Directed by Neil Burger. Starring Bradley Cooper, Robert DeNiro, Abbie Cornish and Johnny Whitworth. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Recently the Sonoma County Vintners Association put on a huge tasting at Kendall-Jackson Winery in Santa Rosa. The “Taste of Sonoma” event was one of the largest and most interesting wine events I have ever participated in. Over 100 wineries from all over the county were pouring their wines often 5 or 6 different wines per provider. The quality was astonishingly high as I have come to expect from Sonoma County. After many years of living in the shadow of its big brother Napa County, I feel Sonoma has really come into its own, and certainly in terms of the experience of wine tours. When friends come to visit, I never take them to Napa to taste. It has become wildly expensive and terribly crowded. Better to ramble around the scenic roads of Sonoma County looking for gems. One thing that was evident from this tasting is that Pinot Noir has hit it big. The grape was everywhere, and most regions of the county produce it extensively. Pinot was closely followed by Chardonnay, by far the most popular white grape. Throw in some fine Zinfandels, Cabernets and Syrahs and the result was an exceptional and varied day of tasting. The following wines and the ones I will be reviewing in Part Two represent the best of Sonoma County. Medium-bodied, the palate is packed with perfumed red berry flavors with a solid frame of tannins and seamless freshness, finishing on a spicy note. • 2021 Ernest Pinot Noir Freestone Valley The Freestone Valley is a cold weather section of the Sonoma Coast appellation, and the wine is Burgundian. It has a lovely floral nose of violets and roses over a core of cherries and pomegranate with hints of cinnamon and toast. Limerick Lane Winery made a strong impression. • 2021 Limerick Lane Rocks and Fog Limerick Lane has long been one of my favorite producers of high quality Zinfandel and Rhone blends and the 2021 Rocks and Fog is no exception. Round and elegant on the palate, is a medium-bodied, finessed straight forward stimulating Pinot with finely grained tannins and a delicate acidity with a long spicy finish. • 2019 Monroy Cabernet Sauvignon Hailing from the Chalk Hill AVA this wine offers up deep, sweet-smelling notes of blueberries, plums and earth accented by a hint of vanilla. It should last for a couple of decades in the cellar. • 2021 Rockpile Zinfandel Rockpile Ridge Vineyard Produced by Mauritson Winery in Healdsburg the Rockpile Zinfandel is dark and intensely flavored with blackberry and black cherry notes, its full-bodied and smooth-textured, almost creamy without being overly heavy or rich- then finishes easy and silky. • 2019 Enkidu Pinot Noir Tina Marie This Russian River Pinot is harmonious, expressive, and ultra-perfumed. articles.text: Studio 415 Interiors – helping Piedmonters feel right at home Since creating their interior design firm Studio 415 three years ago, Piedmonter Beatriz Martinez and Hailey Johnson have been making their clients’ dream spaces a reality. Originally from Cuernavaca, south of Mexico City, Martinez earned her bachelor’s degree in architecture from Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City in 1995, and a master’s degree in interior design from Pratt Institute in New York in 1997. Having then worked for two years at New York City design firm Skidmore Owings & Merrill, she moved to San Francisco and joined the hospitality design firm BraytonHughes in 1999, working there on and off until founding Studio 415 in 2020. “When we started during the pandemic,” said Martinez, “everyone was locked down and looking for home offices, and we found a design niche we didn’t know existed. I decided to start a company. Hailey, who I used to work with at BraytonHughes in San Francisco, joined me.” Johnson, who grew up in Pleasanton, earned a bachelor’s degree in Interior Design from San Francisco State University. “I know not many kids can say this, but from a very young age I loved floor plans,” she said. “I was always moving friends’ furniture around and knew I wanted to go for the interior design route.” Though she joined BraytonHughes and met Martinez in 2016, she moved to New York to do hospitality design work for InterContinental Hotels. “With Studio 415, Bea gave me an opportunity to return to San Francisco that I couldn’t pass up,” said Johnson. “Though I loved New York, my heart and life is in the Bay, and I came back in spring 2020. “At our studio we provide a full range of interior design services from design drawings, permit packages, design selections, to turn-key installations,” she added. The entire process for a large project, from the permit phase to the end of design, often takes two years or more. Though the pair are working on 10 projects at any given time, they’ve moved from their hospitality background to a strong focus on residential design. “My favorite part of the residential work is that much of it depends on knowing your clients really well on a personal, individual level — what colors and patterns make them feel the best, and how they live in their own spaces overall,” said Martinez. Some of their current projects include a commercial motorcycle shop in San Francisco, a private residence in Temescal, two in the Oakland Hills, and an upcoming kitchen, bathroom, and dining room remodel in Piedmont. While every city planning department has its own culture, said Martinez, “We’d previously heard that the one in Piedmont was very difficult. However, they’ve been extremely responsive, effective, and approachable in our experience. While their guidelines are strict, they’re clear.” For example, said Johnson, to replace the windows in a Piedmont house, another is required of the exact same size and look as the existing type. “Alongside a window replacement schedule, the department would require an existing floor plan with exterior elevations of the entire home. I think that the city really protects the look of the houses here and prides itself on keeping everything cohesive, which is very admirable,” she added. Martinez, who moved from San Francisco to Piedmont in 2014 due to the quality of the schools once her two children came of age, said, “While we’re satisfied with where we are with Studio 415, we aim to grow the company and bring in more consultants. However, the uniqueness of the community here in Piedmont is a model for us in that our priority is to keep that personal, individualized involvement with every project and client we have.” More information about Studio 415, including samples of past projects, can be found at their website, studio415interiors.com. articles.text: Nancy DeRoche offered to take the group on a tour of her neighborhood above Oakland Avenue, which includes historic Blair and Scenic Avenues. Nancy told the group she became interested in the history of her neighborhood, and has used the research of Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi. The area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of a Bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters, including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Some of them built their own homes. Nancy led the group to the home of George Sterling, who was Frank C. Havens’ nephew. Sterling was a frustrated artist and poet and traveled in a circle of artists. He met Jack London and encouraged London to live in Piedmont. As the walkers were making their climb of Blair, Nancy pointed out the Sutro Mansion at the top of the street, hidden by other homes. The mansion was not the first house on this hilltop site. Initially, a much smaller, craftsman-style home was built there in 1876-77 by Joseph Worcester. This house has a special claim to fame. It was there that Jack London lived and wrote his classic novel, The Call of the Wild, in 1902-03. After London lived there, the house was moved two lots up the street in 1910 so that the Sutro mansion could be built and have expansive views of the Bay. The house. It has a lovely, cedar shake shingle exterior, and was enlarged after it was moved by adding a new first floor. London was a prominent part of the artists’ colony that occupied this part of Piedmont in the early 1900s. He was a free-spirited man who sailed to the Orient, drank freely, and had at least three important women in his life. The success of The Call of the Wild provided him with considerable wealth. He built a separate home for first wife, Bessie, and their two daughters on Scenic Avenue. The walkers continued up Scenic, went past Bessie’s home, and stopped at a turn in the bend of the street to enjoy the view of San Francisco and the Bay. As they were admiring the view, longtime resident Karen Eliassen welcomed the group to the view. The group made their way up to the Scenic loop and came to the rustic bungalow home of another famous member of the Piedmont Bohemian community, painter Xavier Martinez. This home/studio was inhabited by his daughter and artist, Kai Martinez, until her death in 1989. The group made their way down the narrow part of Scenic and decided to have an adventure on their way home, descending the hill via Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway and set of stairs, the 281-foot Blair and Scenic Path. All of the walkers safely got back to Blair, and then down to Pacific and Mountain Avenues to the Community Hall parking lot. The group gave Nancy a round of applause at the walk’s end for the wonderful tour of her historic neighborhood. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. And there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required.at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

He credits a big part of his love for swimming to his father. “My dad started Master swimming when I retired from agegroup swimming. I remember my dad always admired the guys who would swim the Golden Gate and always hinted that he wished he did that. My dad swam well into his 80s, but he saw me swim the Escape From Alcatraz triathlon in 1996.” “I think he really would’ve been excited to see me swim across Lake Tahoe, or Bay to Breakers, or the double Alcatraz, but I think he would’ve been just absolutely out of his mind to see us swim the English Channel,” said Bernstein. JAMIE SCHWARZ Cross Country & Track his Stage 5 result, Vingegaard’s climbing ability is already making an impact. Le Tour returns for another mountain course for Stage 6 for another 90 miles of riding. Friday’s Stage 7 will be a 110 mile flat stage before a 125 mile medium-mountain Stage 8 on Saturday. The course turns up, once again, for a 113.4 mile mountain Stage 9 this Sunday. Stage 6 also features three ascents, but they are considerably longer than the previous stage. The course includes a 12 kilometer climb up Col d’Aspin at a 6.5 percent grade, a 17.7 kilometer, 7.3 percent grade ride up Col du Tourmalet, and a final 16 kilometer summit finish at Cauterets-Cambasque, which has a 5.4 percent grade. The Stage 9 mountains only has one steep ascent to a summit finish, which will be a 13.3 kilometer climb up Puy de Dôme at a 7.7 percent grade. It marks the first time the Grand Tour returned to the mountain since 1988. It’s a famous location where a spectator punched cycling legend Eddy Merckx in 1975. Jamie Schwarz enters her fourth year as a starter on both cross country and track. Last spring, she ran to a fourthplace finish in the 800 meters in a field of 24 with a time of 2:23.05, which marked a personal record. She went on to qualify the NCS Meet of Champions, where she ran a 2:24.28 to place 18th of 24. Schwarz also helped the 4x400 relay team reach the NCS Meet of Champions with Ella Yasar, Emily Fitzgerald, and Skylar Best by finishing fourth of 13 teams at the Bayshore Championship with a time of 4:17.04. At the Meet of Champions, the same group finished 15th of 23 with a time of 4:17.32. On the cross country team, Schwarz finished 51st of 110 runners at the NCS Finals, coming in at 21:17.82. At the WACC Championship, she was 16th of 59 runners in 20:27.05. Summer Workout Continued from page 13 With a coach? A trainer? I have a training plan that my coach at Davis has given to me.
